This is a digital copy of a book that was preserved for generations on library shelves before it was carefully scanned by Google as part of a project to make the world’s books discoverable online.

It has survived long enough for the copyright to expire and the book to enter the <term>public domain</term> <note>A legal status where a work is no longer protected by copyright, allowing it to be used freely by the public.</note>. Whether a book is in the public domain may vary from country to country. Public domain books are our gateways to the past, representing a wealth of history, culture, and knowledge that is often difficult to discover.

Marks, notations, and other <term>marginalia</term> <note>Handwritten notes, comments, or marks made in the margins of a book by previous owners or readers.</note> present in the original volume will appear in this file—a reminder of this book’s long journey from the publisher to a library and finally to you.

## Usage guidelines

Google is proud to partner with libraries to digitize public domain materials and make them widely accessible. Public domain books belong to the public and we are merely their custodians. Nevertheless, this work is expensive, so in order to keep providing this resource, we have taken steps to prevent abuse by commercial parties. This includes placing technical restrictions on <term>automated querying</term> <note>The use of computer programs or "bots" to automatically search or download large amounts of data.</note>.

We also ask that you:

+ **Make non-commercial use of the files:** We designed Google Book Search for use by individuals, and we request that you use these files for personal, non-commercial purposes.
+ **Refrain from automated querying:** Do not send automated queries of any sort to Google’s system. If you are conducting research on machine translation, optical character recognition <note>OCR: the technology used to convert images of text into editable digital text.</note>, or other areas where access to a large amount of text is helpful, please contact us. We encourage the use of public domain materials for these purposes and may be able to help.
+ **Maintain attribution:** The Google “watermark” you see on each file is essential for informing people about this project and helping them find additional materials through Google Book Search. Please do not remove it.
+ **Keep it legal:** Whatever your use, remember that you are responsible for ensuring that what you are doing is legal. Do not assume that just because we believe a book is in the public domain for users in the United States, that the work is also in the public domain for users in other countries. Whether a book is still in copyright varies from country to country, and we cannot offer guidance on whether any specific use of any specific book is allowed. Please do not assume that a book’s appearance in Google Book Search means it can be used in any manner anywhere in the world. Copyright infringement liability can be quite severe.

Google’s mission is to organize the world’s information and to make it universally accessible and useful. Google Book Search helps readers discover the world’s books while helping authors and publishers reach new audiences. ## Some Opinions of the Press.

> "The book is written with all the mature knowledge of one who has lived and taught for years among the natives of Melanesia, and it offers a welcome contribution to the solution of an obscure problem of scientific philology <note>The branch of knowledge that deals with the structure, historical development, and relationships of a language or languages</note>."—*Academy.*

> "We can recommend it to all students and scholars who are interested in the questions and problems with which it deals."—*British Quarterly Review.*

> "It will be appropriately valued by philologists."—*Westminster Review.*

> "It is difficult for even the most demanding critic to find either omissions or unnecessary repetitions, while an excellent map at the beginning will show those whose ideas about Melanesia are not quite definite its precise position on the map of the world."—*Guardian.*

> "A most important contribution to linguistic science. . . . The patience, the care, the insight, and above all the good sense shown throughout the work cannot be too highly praised, and the value of the book will increase with time."—*New York Evening Post.*

# PREFACE.

---

I have tried in the following pages to gather the results of observations made during my many years of acquaintance with the Melanesian people. I once hoped to provide a more complete account of the beliefs and practices of the local people on those islands where I had the opportunity to collect information; however, my stay during my last return to the Melanesian Mission <note>The Melanesian Mission was an Anglican missionary agency operating in the South West Pacific, established in 1849.</note> was too brief for this. Consequently, I must now present what I know is a very incomplete work.

I conducted my observations and inquiries and kept notes between 1863, when I first visited the islands, and 1887, when I left the Mission. This work took place partly in the Melanesian Islands themselves, but mostly on Norfolk Island <note>Norfolk Island served as the headquarters and training center for the Melanesian Mission between 1867 and 1920.</note>, where residents from many different islands have been gathered for education over many years. Twice during this time, I worked with individuals from various islands to conduct a systematic study of Melanesian religious beliefs, practices, and the social rules and conditions prevailing among them. On the first occasion, I received invaluable help regarding the Banks Islands from a local man who had reached adulthood before his people were influenced by contact with Europeans or had heard any Christian teachings—the Reverend George Sarawia <note>George Sarawia (c. 1845–1901) was the first Melanesian to be ordained as a Christian priest.</note>, the first...

<summary>In this preface, the author explains that his research into Melanesian culture and religion was conducted over twenty-four years, primarily through interviews with islanders at the mission headquarters on Norfolk Island.</summary>
<keywords>Melanesian Mission, Norfolk Island, Banks Islands, George Sarawia, ethnographic methodology, 19th-century anthropology</keywords>

# PREFACE.

---

—and has now been the leader of the native clergy of that group for many years. The results of these first inquiries appeared briefly in the *Journal of the Anthropological Institute* in February 1881. I carefully reviewed these during my last stay on Norfolk Island in 1886 and 1887. At that time, I was fortunate enough to meet several old friends and pupils there who had returned for their health or other reasons after living as teachers among their own people. They had been living on their various islands in positions and at ages that made them familiar with the views and habits of their fellow islanders. They were able—and, I believe, entirely willing—to communicate what they knew freely.

Consequently, I was able to examine the subjects treated in this book with native instructors from the Solomon Islands, the Banks Islands, and the Northern New Hebrides. These included Marsden Manekalea from Ysabel <note>Santa Isabel Island in the Solomon Islands.</note>, Benjamin Bele from Florida <note>Nggela Islands.</note>, Joseph Wate from Saa, Walter Woser from Motlav, Arthur Arudulewari from Aurora <note>Maewo Island.</note>, Lewis Tariliu from Pentecost, and Martin Tangabe from Lepers' Island <note>Now known as Ambae Island in Vanuatu.</note>. In my opinion, every one of them was a competent and trustworthy witness, though they were not all equally intelligent.

My goal has been to present as much as possible what the native people say about themselves, rather than what Europeans say about them. For this reason, although I have included the results of my own personal observations, I have refrained from asking for or recording the information that my colleagues in the Mission would have willingly and abundantly shared—except in a few instances where I have given credit. No one is more aware than I am of the incompleteness and inadequacy of what I am venturing to publish. I know I must have made many mistakes and missed much that I could have learned. I have felt the truth of what Mr. Fison <note>Lorimer Fison (1832–1907), an Australian anthropologist and missionary.</note>, a former missionary in

# PREFACE.

---

A person from Fiji <note>Codrington is likely referring to the ethnologist Lorimer Fison, who worked extensively in Fiji and corresponded with him.</note>, to whom I am indebted for much instruction, has written: "When a European has been living for two or three years among indigenous people <note>original: "savages"</note> he is sure to be fully convinced that he knows all about them; when he has been ten years or so among them, if he is an observant man, he finds that he knows very little about them, and so begins to learn." My own time of learning has been all too short. I have endeavored as far as possible to give the people's <note>original: "natives'"</note> account of themselves by recording what I took down from their lips and translating what they wrote themselves. It is likely that under the circumstances of such inquiries, much of the darker side of native life may be out of sight, and the view given may seem generally more favorable than might be expected; if that is so, I shall not regret it.

I should have been glad if space had allowed me to treat the subject of the native Arts of Life <note>This refers to traditional crafts, technologies, and social skills.</note> at greater length, and to have included more of the folktales, which throw so much light upon native life and thought. The comparison of Melanesian languages, customs, beliefs, and arts with those of the islands of the Pacific and Indian Oceans will establish the ethnological place <note>The cultural and historical classification of a group of people.</note> of the Melanesian people while aiding the general study of mankind.

In conclusion, this book—though written by a missionary with his full share of the biases and preferences belonging to missionaries—is not meant to have what is generally understood to be a "missionary character." However, the writer is convinced that one of the first duties of a missionary is to try to understand the people among whom he works, and to this end, he hopes that he may have contributed something that may help.

->WADHURST:<-
->*March 12, 1891.*<-

# CONTENTS.

---

## CHAPTER I.

### INTRODUCTORY.

Groups of Melanesian Islands. Connection to the East and West. Discovery. Spanish, French, and English discoverers. Native and geographical names of the islands. Identification. Condition at the time of discovery. Native views of the discoverers. Geology. Volcanoes. Coral. Reef islands. Lakes. Waterfalls. Zoology . . . . . . . . . pp. 1–19

## CHAPTER II.

### SOCIAL REGULATIONS. DIVISIONS OF THE PEOPLE. KINSHIP AND MARRIAGE CONNECTION.

Ethnology and origins. Division of the people into exogamous classes <term>social groups where members must marry someone from outside their own group</term>, or kindreds, with matrilineal succession <note>original: "Succession through the Mother"</note>. Absence of tribes. Exceptions in the eastern Solomon Islands. Regulation and restriction of sexual intercourse. Incest. Guest-wives. Division into two kin groups. Banks Islands: families and adoption. New Hebrides <note>now known as Vanuatu</note>. The question of communal marriage. Evidence from language. Blood relations. Multiple divisions in Florida and Bugotu. Prohibited things or taboos <term>original: *buto*</term>. Totems. Customs at Ulawa. The shifting dominance of the Florida *kema* <term>clans or social divisions</term>. The relationship between a nephew (sister’s son) and his maternal uncle (mother’s brother). The Banks Islands system of relationship: within the kindred, the family, and by marriage. Pedigree of a Mota family. Step-fathers. Terms of relationship in Florida. Systems where descent follows the father. Social reserve. Avoidance customs <note>social taboos regarding how certain relatives must avoid one another</note> in the Banks Islands. The practice of avoiding names as common words. New Hebrides . . . . . . . . . . 20–45

## CHAPTER III.

### SOCIAL REGULATIONS. CHIEFS.

Chiefs recognized by visitors. Their power in the Solomon Islands, Banks Islands, and New Hebrides <note>now known as Vanuatu</note>. The absence of history and tradition. A remarkable exception at Saa. The origin of that settlement. Chiefs in that location and the hereditary element of leadership. Chiefs in Florida Island; in the Banks Islands. The alternation of dominance among kinship groups. Chiefs in the New Hebrides and Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae Island</note> . . . . . . . . . 46–58

## CHAPTER IV.

### PROPERTY AND INHERITANCE.

General consensus regarding property and succession. Divisions of land: forest, gardens, and villages. The sale of land. Ownership of fruit trees. The trend of inheritance passing from father to son. The Solomon Islands and Florida Island. Land and personal property. The Banks Islands: the reclaiming of a father's land, the sale of land, and wills. The New Hebrides: Pentecost Island and Lepers' Island . . . . . . . . . 59–68

## CHAPTER V.

### SECRET SOCIETIES AND MYSTERIES.

The widespread presence of secret societies in Melanesia. Differences from Australian mysteries; no "Making young men" <note>referring to specific puberty initiation rites found in Australia</note> ceremonies. Social significance. The exclusion of women. A prominent feature of indigenous life. The Banks Islands: *Tamate* <note>meaning "ghosts"</note>, masks, badges, and meeting houses. *Salagoro* <note>a sacred enclosure or society</note>; hats, mysterious sounds, admission, the isolation of new members, and social liberties. Smaller societies. *Qatu* <note>a secret society named after a legendary figure</note>; dances and initiation. The New Hebrides and Aurora Island <note>now Maewo</note>. The handiwork of "ghosts." Indigenous accounts of initiations and dances. Pentecost Island and the *Qeta* <note>a secret society</note>. The Solomon Islands and Florida Island: the *Matambala* <note>a powerful secret mystery</note>; its origin, indigenous accounts, and the end of the secret tradition . . . . . . . . . 69–100

## CHAPTER VI.

### SOCIETIES. CLUBS.

The prominent presence of these societies in the Torres Islands, Banks Islands, and New Hebrides. The *Gamal* <note>the communal clubhouse</note>; the club itself, known as the *Suqe*. Ranks and social significance. Mota in the Banks Islands: images and hats. Santa Maria and the Torres Islands. Admission and promotion in rank; methods and procedures. Feasts and dress. Women's clubs. *Kolekole* <note>a festival or ceremonial performance</note>; decorations, charms, and the feast of deliverance. The New Hebrides: Aurora Island and Lepers' Island. Ranks and titles. Pentecost Island . . . . . . . . . 101–115

## CHAPTER VII.

### RELIGION.

**The difficulty of the subject. The language used by native people and Europeans. *Mana* <note>a supernatural power or influence</note>; stones; charms. How spirits and ghosts are distinguished by the natives. The differences between the religions of Eastern and Western Melanesia. The misuse of terms like ‘god’ and ‘devil.’ The Banks Islands, spirits known as *vui*. The Solomon Islands, *tindalo* <note>ghosts of the deceased who are worshipped</note>. The example of Ganindo. Prayers and offerings.** . . . . . . . . . 117-127

## CHAPTER VIII.

### SACRIFICES.

**Offerings made to the dead during meals. Differences between sacrifices in Eastern and Western Melanesia. The Solomon Islands: sacrifices to ghosts; an example at San Cristoval <note>now Makira</note>. Florida Island sacrifices, both public and private: first-fruits, sacrifices for war, and for crops. Human sacrifices. Seven types of sacrifices at Saa. San Cristoval; the practice of substitution. Santa Cruz. The Banks Islands: offerings to spirits at sacred stones; offerings using money. Familiar spirits. The New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>: Aurora <note>Maewo</note>, Pentecost, Lepers’ Island <note>Ambae</note>, and Ambrym.** . . . . . . 128-144

## CHAPTER IX.

### PRAYERS.

**Prayers and invocations. To ghosts in the Solomon Islands, Florida, San Cristoval, and Saa. To spirits in the Banks Islands, Motlav, and Mota. Invocations spoken at sea. The New Hebrides.** . . . . . . . . 145-149

## CHAPTER X.

### SPIRITS.

**The minor role of belief in spirits in the Solomon Islands. Kahausibware. The Banks Islands: *vui*. Native understandings: the two orders of spirits. *Nopitu* <note>spirits that possess people or reside within them</note>. Qat <note>a hero-spirit or deity</note> and the Creation. The stories and adventures of Qat: Marawa and Qasavara. The story of the flood. Santa Cruz. The New Hebrides: Tagaro and Supwe; the Creation; winged women. Changeling spirits.** . . . . . 150-172

## CHAPTER XI.

### SACRED PLACES AND THINGS.

**Why images are not considered idols. Sacred stones. The Solomon Islands: sacred places of burial; shrines. Other sacred places, such as streams. Florida and Bugotu. Sacred animals: sharks, snakes, frigate birds, and crocodiles. The Banks Islands and New Hebrides: stones, heaps, streams, pools, trees, sharks, snakes, changeling snakes, and kingfishers.** . . . . . . . . . . 173-190

# CHAPTER XII.

## MAGIC.

*Mana* <note>a supernatural power or influence</note> and equivalent terms. Native belief in magic. (1) **Sickness**: causes. Solomon Islands. Treatment with charms; medicine. Ghosts fighting; Sea-ghosts. Santa Cruz. Banks Islands. New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>. (2) **Weather**: weather doctoring; Banks Islands, charms. (3) **Witchcraft**: fragments of food; bones; 'ghost-shooter' <note>a bamboo tube used to "shoot" a ghost's power at an enemy</note>; Metamorphosis <note>shape-shifting</note>. (4) **Dreams**: dreamers. (5) **Prophecy**: possession by ghosts; prophets. (6) **Divination**: methods in the Solomon Islands and Banks Islands. (7) **Ordeals**. (8) **Poison**. (9) ***Tapu*** <note>original: Tapu</note>, or taboo: Curses; Oaths . . . 191-217

# CHAPTER XIII.

## POSSESSION. INTERCOURSE WITH GHOSTS.

### *NOTE.*

The spelling systems <note>original: "orthography"</note> used in the various native languages are generally not used for native words in this book, but they do appear occasionally. In such cases, it is sufficient to note that **b** represents the sound **mb**, **d** represents **nd**, **n** represents **ng**, **g** represents **ngg**, and that **g** and **q** represent unique local sounds. An apology is necessary for the very awkward-looking **ngg**, which represents the **ng** sound in "finger." This sound is so distinct from the **ng** in "singer" that it is impossible to use the same symbol for both, as we do in English. It is necessary to note that **ng** in this text always represents the sound as heard in "singer."

# CHAPTER I.

->INTRODUCTORY.<-

Within the region of the Western Pacific known as Melanesia, four island groups form a curved belt that roughly follows the outline of the Australian coast, at a general distance of about fifteen hundred miles. This belt turns away from the important outlying archipelago of Fiji and includes the Solomon Islands, the Santa Cruz group, the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides <note>Now the sovereign nation of Vanuatu.</note>, and New Caledonia along with the Loyalty Islands. 

There is an undeniable connection in race, language, and customs among the people who inhabit these groups. This connection extends throughout the region called Melanesia, reaching westward to New Guinea and eastward to Fiji. The distinction between the Melanesian people of these groups and the Polynesians to the east of Fiji is clearly marked and recognized; the boundary line separating Melanesian from Polynesian culture falls between Fiji and Tonga. However, no such clear boundary can be drawn to the west until one reaches the continent of Asia itself. 

Two currents of cultural influence have flowed—and continue to flow—into Melanesia: one from the Polynesian islands of the eastern Pacific and the other from the Asian islands of the Malay Archipelago. The Polynesian influence is much more modern and direct, while the Asian influence is ancient and has followed a more fragmented path. These two currents are represented, respectively, by the kava root and the betel nut. The use of betel <note>The seed of the areca palm, chewed with lime and betel leaf as a stimulant; its use is a cultural marker of Asian influence.</note> is common from India and China through the Melanesian islands as far east as Tikopia. On the other hand, the Polynesian kava <note>A traditional drink made from the roots of the *Piper methysticum* plant, known for its sedative properties.</note> has established itself in the New Hebrides and is a novelty in some of the Banks Islands; it has not yet been carried across...

<summary>This introductory page defines the geographical boundaries of Melanesia and identifies the dual cultural influences—Asian and Polynesian—that shape the region's customs, specifically noted through the use of betel nut and kava.</summary>

<header>Introductory. [CH.</header>

...the boundary of the betel nut <note>original: "betel-nut"</note> was established by the Polynesian settlers in the Reef Islands of Santa Cruz. This book is not concerned with one of the four groups mentioned earlier—New Caledonia and the Loyalty Islands—nor with the larger southern islands of the New Hebrides group <note>Now the nation of Vanuatu.</note>. Instead, its scope is limited, except for occasional examples, to the Solomon Islands (specifically Ysabel, Florida, Savo, Guadalcanal <note>original: "Guadalcanar"</note>, Malaita <note>original: "Malanta"</note>, San Cristobal <note>original: "San Cristoval"; now also known as Makira</note>, and Ulawa), the Santa Cruz group, the Banks and Torres Islands, and three of the northern New Hebrides: Aurora <note>Now Maewo</note>, Pentecost, and Lepers' Islands <note>Now Ambae</note>. 

Within this region are certain islands inhabited by Polynesian colonists from the East who still speak Polynesian languages. These include Nupani, Pileni, Nukapu, and other reef islands in the Swallow group. In these places, the physical traits of the Polynesian people might be traced, but they are certainly not obvious, having been lost through intermarriage with neighboring Melanesians. On Rennell Island and Bellona Island, which are southern members of the Solomon group, the people are physically Polynesian. For instance, a young man from Bellona who was in New Zealand with Bishop Patteson was—in his name (Te Kiu), skin color, tattoos, and speech—very similar to a Maori. Similarly, men from the Polynesian settlements on Mae and Efate <note>original: "Fate"</note> in the New Hebrides found the language of Ontong Java to be much like their own.

The European discovery of these islands spanned three centuries and was carried out by Spanish, French, and English explorers. The Spaniards reached the Solomon Islands, Santa Cruz, the Banks Islands, and the northern New Hebrides. Much later, the French added significantly to the discoveries in these groups. The English, under Captain Cook, found the principal islands of the New Hebrides and New Caledonia and completed the mapping of the region. The Dutch discovered Fiji. The earliest and certainly most fascinating discoveries were those of the Spaniards: Alvaro de Mendaña during his two voyages in 1567 and 1595, and Pedro Fernandes de Queirós and Luís Vaz de Torres in 1606¹.

Through the kindness of Mr. Woodford, I have also read the narrative of *Cotoira* <note>Gómez Hernández de Catoira, the chief purser of the expedition.</note>. In both the...

# Discoveries.

<sig>B 2</sig>

**Mendaña**, dispatched by the Viceroy of Peru, reached the first Melanesian land seen by Europeans in 1567: the large island which he named Santa Isabel de la Estrella <note>original: "Santa Ysabel de la Estrella"</note>. From there, the voyagers under his command continued their discoveries and named the large islands of Malaita, Guadalcanal, and San Cristóbal <note>original: "San Cristoval"; now also known as Makira</note>, as well as the smaller islands: Sesarga (which is Savo), Florida with its surrounding islets, Ulawa, and the small islands near San Cristóbal. He gave these the name "Solomon Islands" to indicate his theory—or perhaps to encourage the belief—that he had discovered the source of King Solomon's legendary wealth. 

In his second voyage of 1595, undertaken to colonize the Solomon Islands, Mendaña discovered Santa Cruz and attempted to establish a settlement there. This attempt was abandoned after only two months due to his death and the illness of the surviving members of his crew. Quirós <note>original: "Quiros"</note> had been with Mendaña and was permitted in 1606 to carry out a project he had been tirelessly advocating: finding and colonizing the Solomon group. However, fortune led him instead to discover the New Hebrides <note>Now the nation of Vanuatu</note>, when he believed himself to have reached the great Southern Continent <note>original: "Austral Continent"; the mythical Terra Australis</note>, at the island which still bears the name he gave it: Espiritu Santo. The first Melanesian islands he actually saw, however, were those now known as the Banks Islands; one of these, Santa Maria, retains the name he gave it. Torres, after parting from Quirós, saw and named the Torres Islands. 

After an interval of more than a century and a half, the French explorer Bougainville added Pentecost, Lepers' Island <note>Now Ambae</note>, and Malekula <note>original: "Malikolo"</note> to Quirós’s discoveries in 1768. He named the group the Great Cyclades and found the large islands of Choiseul and Bougainville beyond those discovered during Mendaña's first voyage.

<note>
The Polynesian word *Te Ariki* (the Chief) appears in the form *Taurique* as the title for chiefs in Isabel <note>original: "Ysabel"</note>, where it is now completely out of place. This is difficult to explain, as the other native words recorded from that time appear to be the same ones still in use today. I should add that I have discussed the accounts of Mendaña's discoveries (as recorded in the collections of James Burney and Alexander Dalrymple) with natives from the Solomon and Santa Cruz Islands; unfortunately, my notes on this subject have been lost.
</note>

<page-num>4</page-num>

# Introductory

In the following year, Jean-François de Surville passed through the same group of islands. Later, the disastrous voyage of Jean-François de Galaup, Count of Lapérouse <note>A famous French explorer whose expedition vanished in the Pacific</note>, ended at Vanikoro in 1785. The southern islands of the group, which have since kept the name he gave them—the **New Hebrides** <note>Now the nation of Vanuatu</note>—were discovered by James Cook during his second great voyage in 1774. Following these, he discovered **New Caledonia** and the **Loyalty Islands**. William Bligh, during his remarkable voyage in an open boat after the mutiny on the *Bounty*, passed through and named the islands of the **Banks Islands** group.

The names given by the Spanish to the Solomon and Santa Cruz groups have remained in use. These include the islands of *Isabel* <note>original: "Ysabel"</note>, *Florida*, *Guadalcanal* <note>original: "Guadalcanar"</note>, *San Cristóbal* <note>original: "San Cristoval"</note>, *Santa Ana* <note>original: "Santa Anna"</note>, and *Santa Catalina*. The names *Espíritu Santo* <note>Spanish for "Holy Spirit"</note> in the *New Hebrides* and *Santa Maria* <note>Spanish for "Saint Mary"</note> in the Banks Islands have also survived. Some of the French names have disappeared, while others—such as *Aurora*, *Pentecost* or *Whitsuntide*, *Star Island*, and *Gulf Island* (for *Ugi*)—have taken on English forms. For some islands, no new names were given. Instead, native names (or what were thought to be native names) were provided by the locals, such as *Ambrym*, *Api*, and *Malakula* <note>original: "Mallicollo"</note>. In some cases, the native name—or what was mistaken for it, such as *Malaita*—became more common than the name given by the original European discoverer. 

For a visitor, determining the true native name and its correct spelling is a very difficult task. Large islands rarely have a single name for the entire landmass. When an inquirer points to an island as a whole, a resident might give the name of the specific district or village they are pointing at. Alternatively, the resident might provide the name of a small islet located between the visitor and the mainland, or the visitor might even mistake the name of a person for the name of a place. <note>1. The island of *San Cristóbal* has been called *Bauro* by Europeans, but not by the locals, who use that name only for one part of it. One village on that island is even marked on the Admiralty chart with the name of its chief. Similarly, the island of *Florida* and its language became known as *Anutha* or *Anudha* from a small islet between *Mboli* and *Ravu*. During a visit in 1862, Bishop Patteson was given the name *Anudha* by a native boy on board; the boy meant the islet *Anuha*, but the Bishop took it to be the name of the whole island. Melanesians who could not pronounce "th" called it *Anuta*. People from the Banks Islands, assuming the first syllable was the preposition "at" (commonly used with place names), called it *Nuta* or *Nut*. The large island of *Isabel* may be seen on some maps marked as *Mahaga*, which is actually the name of a single village in *Bugotu*, the language of which was documented by Bishop Patteson.</note> Of the islands discovered—

--- Page 34 ---
<meta>This page continues from the previous discussion regarding how European explorers often misnamed islands or applied regional native names to entire landmasses. ### Discoveries.

[...the native name—or what was mistaken for the native name, such as those given to the islands discovered] by Mendaña <note>Álvaro de Mendaña de Neira, a Spanish explorer who led expeditions to the Solomon Islands in 1567 and 1595</note> in his first voyage. The islands of **Santa Isabel** <note>original: "Ysabel"</note>, **Guadalcanal** <note>original: "Guadalcanar"</note>, and **San Cristóbal** <note>original: "San Cristoval"</note> actually have no native names for the islands as a whole, though names of specific parts are often used to designate the entire landmass. The second of these (Guadalcanal), as far as the locals know it, is called *Gera* by the natives of southeast **Malaita** <note>original: "Malanta"</note> and San Cristóbal. The latter has become known as *Bauro*, taking the name of its most prominent district. It is strange that the large island which has somehow acquired the name *Malaita* actually has a native name—at least all along the west side—which is *Mala* or *Mara*. 

The native name of **Florida Island** is *Nggela*, which is the same word as *Gera*; the island is known in *Mala Masiki* <note>Small Malaita</note> as "beyond Gela." **Savo** is undoubtedly the island called *Sesarga* by the Spanish, who likely heard the name *Sabo* and recorded it in the wrong location. The native name **Ulawa**—heard by the Spaniards as *Uraba*—has lost its Spanish name, *La Treguada* <note>Spanish for "The Truce"</note>, and retains the name *Contrariété* <note>French for "Opposition" or "Annoyance"</note> on sea charts, given to it by the explorer Surville. The native name of **Santa Cruz**, discovered during Mendaña's second voyage, is *Ndeni*, from which the name *Nitendi* found on charts was probably derived ¹.

The discovery of the **Banks Islands** and the **New Hebrides** <note>Now Vanuatu</note> by Quiros <note>Pedro Fernandes de Queirós, a Portuguese navigator serving the Spanish crown</note> was preceded by a visit to **Taumako**. There, he obtained information concerning some sixty islands known to the native voyagers. Nearly all of these are likely the small islands inhabited, like Taumako, by people of the Polynesian race.

***

¹ There can be little doubt that the *Florida* mentioned by Gallego <note>Hernán Gallego, the chief pilot of Mendaña's first expedition</note> is a part of the natives' *Nggela*, and probably *Buena Vista* is *Vatilau*. The names *San Dimas*, *San German*, and *Guadalupe* have been shown by Mr. Woodford <note>Charles Morris Woodford, a naturalist and the first Resident Commissioner of the British Solomon Islands</note> to be parts of Florida as they appear from the sea, rather than how the island is actually divided by hidden channels. 

The native names of the smaller islands near San Cristóbal are: *Ugi* for **Gulf Island** (the Spanish *San Juan*); *Olu Malau* <note>meaning "Three Malau"</note> for the **Three Sisters** (the Spanish *Las Tres Marias* <note>The Three Marys</note>); *Owa-raha* <note>"Great Owa"</note> for **Santa Ana**; and *Owa-rii* <note>"Little Owa"</note> for **Santa Catalina**. 

It is remarkable how much more accurate Gallego's *Aguare* is than the *Yoriki* found on charts or the *Orika* provided by Dr. Guppy <note>Henry Brougham Guppy, a naval surgeon and naturalist who wrote about the Solomon Islands</note>. Gallego's *Hapa* may represent *Owa*, though not as clearly as *Oo-ah* or *Oa*. *Uraba* is actually closer to the native *Ulawa* than *Uaua* is, because the native tongue—like Spanish—readily swaps the sounds for "l" and "r," and "w" and "b." It cannot be explained how Mr. Brenchley <note>Julius Brenchley, a 19th-century explorer</note> arrived at the name *Ulakua*, nor why the new form *Ulaua* was introduced. It should be noted that a correct native name is rarely obtained from a trader; early seafaring visitors usually establish the form that becomes the official name and pass it on. The only way to be certain is through the writing of a native who actually knows the language.

# Introductory. [CH. I]

...who are great voyagers at the present day and are easily distinguished by their Polynesian language, though where they live near larger islands with Melanesian populations, the Polynesian appearance has been lost¹. Many of these islands are easily identified and lie away from the New Hebrides <note>now the nation of Vanuatu</note>, but Quiros <note>Pedro Fernandes de Queirós, a Portuguese navigator serving the Spanish Crown</note> was led by his information to look for the large southern continent he was searching for toward the south. He believed he found it in what he named the **Southern Land of the Holy Spirit** <note>original: "Tierra Austral del Espiritu Santo"</note>. This island, now commonly known as **Santo**, has the native name of **Marina**. This was not the first land in the New Hebrides seen by Quiros; after apparently seeing the light of a volcano in the night, he found himself in the morning in view of three islands. One is the present **Aurora** <note>now Maewo</note> of the New Hebrides, and two belong to the **Banks Islands**: the volcanic cone, **Merlav**, called by him **Our Lady of the...** <note>original: "Nuestra Señora de la [Luz]" - Our Lady of the Light</note>

***

¹ I have personally witnessed the arrival of eleven canoes from **Tikopia** among the Banks Islands. The men said they had come to see the islands and were hospitably received. One man was shot at **Ureparapara**, and they departed. Shortly before this, a canoe from Tikopia had been driven by the wind to **Mota**, and the men in it were treated very kindly; the same thing has happened both before and since. The difference in size, behavior, language, and clothing between the Tikopians <note>who are Polynesians</note> and the Banks Islanders <note>who are Melanesians</note> was very noticeable. The true name is almost certainly **Chikopia**, since the Mota people learned the name **Sikopia** from their visitors; two Fijian islands are named **Cikobia** <note>pronounced Thikombia</note>.

² **Chicayana** is **Sikaiana** (Stewart Island); **Guaytopo** is **Vaitupu** (Tracy Island) of the Ellice group <note>now Tuvalu</note>; **Taukalo** is **Tokelau**; **Nupani** and **Pileni** are **Reef Islands** of Santa Cruz; **Manicolo** undoubtedly stands for **Vanikoro**. Bishop Patteson in 1866 found that the Reef Islanders of Santa Cruz visited **Taumako** and Tikopia. It is understandable at first glance to mistake the **Pouro** mentioned by Quiros for **Bauro** in **San Cristóbal**, but in my opinion, the attempt to identify them must completely fail. In the first place, Pouro and Bauro do not sound the same when the confusion of English spelling is removed; Quiros would never have written "ou" to represent the sound "au." Secondly, Bauro is not, and never was, the native name for the whole of San Cristóbal; it is a name picked up by Europeans—I believe by Bishop Selwyn <note>George Augustus Selwyn, the first Anglican Bishop of New Zealand</note>—and adopted for European convenience. Gallego <note>Hernán Gallego, Mendaña’s Chief Pilot</note> correctly calls only one part of the island **Paubro**. Thirdly, arrows with points shaped like knives (a fair description of some arrows from **Lepers' Island** <note>Aoba or Ambae</note>) are completely out of place in the Solomon Islands. Fourthly, the confirmed identifications of the other named islands do not lead in that direction. In the same way, when it is understood that the name of the island in the Malay Archipelago is **Buru** (spelled *Boeroe* in Dutch), there is very little reason to identify it with either Bauro or **Bulotu** <note>the Tongan spirit-world or paradise, spelled "Bourotou" in French</note>.

# Discoveries.

...Light <note>original Spanish: "Luz"</note>, and Santa Maria. After visiting the latter, he made his way to a larger island seen to the south and remained for a month in the great Bay of St. Philip and St. James on the island of Espiritu Santo. Merlav was renamed *Pic de l’Étoile* <note>original French: "Peak of the Star"</note> by the French explorer Bougainville, and is now known as Star Island. The eight islands of the Banks group are:

1. Star Island (Merlav)
2. Sainte Claire (Merig)
3. Santa Maria (Gaua)
4. Sugarloaf Island <note>named for its conical shape resembling a "loaf" of refined sugar</note> (Mota)
5. Great Banks Island (Vanua Lava)
6. Saddle Island (Motalava)
7. Bligh Island (Ureparapara)
8. Rowa¹

One of these, named Saddle Island by Captain Bligh, has no single native name for the island as a whole; another, the Reef Island of Rowa, has no standard geographical name. The Torres group consists of four islands—Hiw, Tegua, Lo, and Tog—and is now collectively known as Vava, though there is no original native name for the entire group. The native names of the three islands which, along with Espiritu Santo, make up the northern New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note> are: Maewo (*Aurora Island*), Araga (*Pentecost Island*), and Omba (*Lepers’ Island*). These last two names present a difficulty, and—

***

¹ Quiros named seven islands before he reached Espiritu Santo: *San Raymundo* <note>Saint Raymond</note>, *Los Portales de Belen* <note>The Gates of Bethlehem</note>, *La Vergel* <note>The Orchard</note>, *Las Lagrimas de San Pedro* <note>The Tears of Saint Peter</note>, *El Pilar de Zaragoza* <note>The Pillar of Zaragoza</note>, *Santa Maria* <note>Saint Mary</note>, and *Nuestra Señora de la Luz* <note>Our Lady of the Light</note>. Only the last two names are still recognized today. Bligh named Ureparapara after himself, while Saddle Island and Sugarloaf Island (which was probably Quiros's "Pillar") were named after their natural physical features. He named the largest island Great Banks Island, and the entire group the Banks Islands, after Sir Joseph Banks. 

In addition to these geographical names, most of these islands have three distinct sets of names. First, an island has its name in the local dialect and also in the Mota dialect, which has become a common language through the work of the Melanesian Mission. For example, Vanua Lava, Gaua, Ureparapara, and Meralava are the Mota versions of the local names *Vono Lav, Gog, Norbarbar,* and *Merlav*. 

A second set of names was used by natives when sailing between the islands to hide their destination from enemies. Mota was called *Ure-kor*, meaning "the place full of dried breadfruit"; Ureparapara (which means "full of slopes") was called *Ure-us*, "full of bows"; and Meralava was *Ure-kere*, "full of clubs," because the best bows and clubs were sourced there. Other islands were named after the specific foods or natural products that characterized them. 

Errors in mapping have also occurred: the rock Vat Ganai was misspelled and misread, appearing on maps as the island *Vatu Rhandi*. Similarly, a misreading of "Gaua" (the native name for Santa Maria, which inhabitants call "Gog") led traders to call it *Ganna*. The Torres group acquired the name "Vava" (sometimes recorded as *Avava* or *Ababa*, meaning "at Vava") from a specific part of one of the islands that the people of Ureparapara frequently visited. Traders also assigned the name *Pukapuka* to the island of Tog, a name originally unknown to the local people. Finally, the Mota name for Lepers’ Island—*Opa*, a variation of Omba—has become widely known.

...bring in a point of much interest. In the native name of Pentecost, the *a* is actually the preposition "at." *Omba*, when used with the same preposition, appears on charts as *Aoba*. It would be reasonable, therefore, to write *Raga* as well as *Omba*, but we must allow established custom to prevail in these matters. 

The interest of this point lies in the connection shown by the common use of this preposition in place-names across Melanesia, the Malay Archipelago, and Madagascar. Ethnological and historical questions are inseparable from the study of place-names; for example, the question of whether the *Bauro* of the Solomon Islands is the same as the *Bouro* (properly *Buru*) near the Moluccas, or whether *Futuna* of the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note> is named after *Futuna* (Horne's Island). 

About one thing, however, there should be no disagreement: however difficult it may be to determine a native name and its correct spelling <note>original: "orthography"</note>, European names should be written in the language to which they belong. We should write *San Cristoval* or *Cristobal*, not *Christoval*; *Espiritu Santo* <note>Spanish: "Holy Spirit"</note>, not *Spirito Santo* or *St. Esprit*; and where French names are retained, we should use *Contrariété Island* and *Cape Zélée*.

Between the time the Solomon Islands were discovered by Mendaña <note>Álvaro de Mendaña de Neira, a Spanish explorer who reached the Solomons in 1568</note> and the modern era—within the last thirty or forty years—when visits from whalers, traders, and missionaries have become frequent, Europeans did very little, if anything at all, to influence the character of native life. It is very interesting, therefore, to investigate in what specific details the Spaniards' account of what they discovered differs from what would be recorded by recent visitors. 

The place-names mentioned by the Spaniards—often recorded with more accuracy than is common today—are those still in use: *Malaita* for *Mala*, *Uraba* for *Ulawa*, *Paubro* for *Bauro*, and *Aguare* for *Owarii*. The names of people mentioned are also similar to those in use today. One of the few words that are not names found in the narrative of Gallego <note>Hernando Gallego, the chief pilot of Mendaña's expedition</note>—specifically *benau*, *panale*, or *panay*—is clearly *pana*, a type of yam with prickles on the vines. However, there are three points where it can be observed that Gallego reports things that would not have been seen in recent times. For instance, he describes the natives as attacking the Spaniards with bows and arrows everywhere,

The probable conclusion is that, once we account for lapses of memory on one side and exaggeration of facts on the other, the people, language, customs, and conditions of the Solomon Islands have not changed significantly since Mendaña’s discovery in 1567.

The account of Mendaña’s visit to Santa Cruz in 1595 and the Spanish attempt to form a settlement is extensive and detailed. It was remarked by Bishop Patteson <note>John Coleridge Patteson, the first Bishop of Melanesia</note>—who was likely the first European after Mendaña’s party to walk through the native villages—that what he observed corresponded closely with the Spanish records. It is only within the last ten years that, through the courage and enterprise of the current Missionary Bishop, John Selwyn, the island of Santa Cruz has again become open to friendly—and unhappily also to harmful—encounters <note>the author refers to "mischievous approach," likely a reference to the "blackbirding" or forced labor trade</note>. 

The present writer has reviewed the account of Mendaña’s visit with the natives of Santa Cruz, and their comments were certainly interesting. One point may be mentioned: when the Spaniards failed to get the people of the main island to learn their language, they resorted to kidnapping—a practice that seems to have come naturally to European visitors from the very beginning. They seized some boys from the neighboring Reef Islands, whom they had observed to be more intelligent...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of initial contact between Europeans and Melanesians, moving from historical records to the oral traditions and perceptions of the islanders themselves regarding the first arrivals of "white men."</meta>

<page-num>11</page-num>
<header>Discoveries.</header>

For later explorers <note>original: "discoverers"</note>, it was a matter of course that previously unknown countries would be found and that they would be inhabited by people unlike themselves. However, to the natives, it was a shocking thing that there should be any men unlike themselves, or any unknown land for them to come from. There are still natives in these islands who remember when a white man was first seen and what he was thought to be. In the Banks Islands <note>a group of islands in northern Vanuatu</note>, for example, the natives believed the world consisted only of their own group, the Torres Islands, the three or four northern New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>, and perhaps Tikopia. They believed the ocean spread out around these islands until it was hemmed in by the foundations of the sky at the horizon. 

The first ships they remember seeing were whalers, which they did not believe came from any country in the world. Indeed, they were quite certain they did not, but must have been built out at sea, because they knew that no men in the world possessed such vessels. Similarly, they were sure that the voyagers were not men; if they were, they would have been black <note>meaning dark-skinned like themselves</note>. What were they then? They were ghosts, and being ghosts, they were necessarily the spirits of men who had once lived in the world. 

When Mr. Patteson <note>John Coleridge Patteson (1827–1871), the first Anglican Bishop of Melanesia</note> first landed at Mota—the Mission party having been seen the previous year at Vanua Lava—the natives were divided in opinion. Some said that the brothers of Qat <note>the central hero-spirit and creator figure in the mythology of the Banks Islands</note> had returned, referring to certain supernatural beings of whom legends are told; others maintained that they were ghosts. Mr. Patteson retired from the heat and the crowd into an empty house, the owner of which had lately died. This settled the question for the locals: he was the ghost of the deceased householder and clearly recognized his own home. 

A very short acquaintance with white visitors shows that they are not ghosts, but it certainly does not prove that they are men. The theory then becomes that they are beings of another order—spirits or demons <note>original: "demons"; here used to mean supernatural spirits, not necessarily "evil" in the modern sense</note> who are undoubtedly powerful but also mischievous. A ghost would be received in a peaceful and respectful manner, which is how European visitors have always been received in the first instance. However, a being who is neither a living man nor a ghost possesses wonderful things to see and trade for, but he likely also brings disease and disaster. To the question of why the Santa Cruz...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the initial reactions of Melanesian islanders to European visitors, shifting from their supernatural interpretations to the tangible negative consequences of colonial contact, such as kidnapping and disease.</meta>

When the people shot at Bishop Patteson’s party in 1864, at a time when—as far as can be determined—they had not yet suffered any injuries from white men to avenge, the natives later explained that their elders warned that these strange beings would bring nothing but harm, and that it was best to drive them away. As for shooting at them, they believed the visitors were not truly human, and therefore the arrows could not do them much damage. It is tragic to consider how often those elders have been proven right, at least from their own perspective. Access to iron, tobacco, cloth <note>original: "calico"</note>, and a broader knowledge of the world has not compensated the native people for the arrival of new diseases and the weakening of their social bonds¹. While white visitors may not have intended to do the natives wrong, they have in fact caused them harm and have generally failed to earn their moral respect. 

From the beginning of their interactions with Melanesians, Europeans have kidnapped them, often convincing themselves that they were doing the natives a service by bringing them into contact with what is called "civilization." The natives, however, have from the start resented the kidnapping of their sons. Even if those sons wished to leave and valued what they learned and acquired abroad, no impartial observer would say they brought any benefit back to their communities upon their return. Nevertheless, some people seem to believe that a native learning to speak a bit of "pidgin English" <note>original: "pigeon English"</note> for the convenience of traders constitutes a great improvement.

To a traveler among these Melanesian islands who lacks specialized geological knowledge, the overall volcanic character of the land is—

The fact that there are no native names for this and other diseases is, to some extent, proof of their recent introduction. In my own memory, syphilis—or the venereal disease mistaken for it—was unknown in the islands visited by the Melanesian Mission, except at San Cristoval <note>now Makira in the Solomon Islands</note>, where contact with whalers and traders had been significant. <meta>This page continues the physical description of the islands, specifically focusing on their volcanic nature and geological activity. It follows from the previous page's introduction to the Melanesian environment.</meta>

islands, the volcanic origin of them cannot fail to be apparent. The high terrain of **Guadalcanal** <note>original: "Guadalcanar"</note>, rising to a height of 8,000 feet, and the towering mountains of **Espiritu Santo** and **New Caledonia**, might be thought by a traveler to have some other origin; but he cannot miss the still-active volcanoes, or fail to observe that many islands have the shape of active volcanoes in a more or less perfect or weathered condition. 

The massive cone of **Lopevi** in the **New Hebrides** <note>now the nation of Vanuatu</note> rises to a sharp point at a height of 5,000 feet and has been seen erupting smoke and ashes. **Tinakula**, near **Santa Cruz**—the native name of which is *Tamami*—is a well-formed cone 3,000 feet high. When the Spanish explorer **Mendaña** <note>Álvaro de Mendaña de Neira (1542–1595)</note> was attempting to establish a settlement in 1595, the peak of the cone was blown away; the volcano is now very active, discharging glowing masses of lava which roll down into the sea. 

The enormous crater of **Ambrym**, at a height of 2,500 feet, is the center of vast, rugged fields of lava that have so far been inaccessible. Around this main volcanic mass, there rise side cones that are no longer active; these are covered in forest up to their peaks and offer perhaps the most beautiful of Melanesian landscapes. When the **Solomon Islands** were first discovered by Europeans, the volcano on **Savo** was active. Some years ago, an eruption was expected by the natives because the elders remembered—or had been told of—considerable activity some fifty years prior. Rumblings were heard at that time and smoke was seen at **Florida Island** <note>also known as Nggela</note>; the steaming pool and the hot stream flowing from it are often visited. 

In the **Banks Islands**, **Vanua Lava** is always steaming from its sulfur springs. Large side cones on the north and east of this island are now extinct, but the streams that rise in the central mass run warm and foul-smelling to the sea, coating the rocks with sulfur. In **Santa Maria** <note>now Gaua</note>, above **Lakona**, there are steaming vents on the ridge of the ancient crater, which is now filled by a lake. <header>Introductory. [CH.</header>

**Ureparapara** is a remarkable example of the island type found at **Amsterdam** or **St. Paul's Island** in the Indian Ocean; the sea enters the ancient crater, and on its ridge—which rises to nearly 2,000 feet—there is a steaming vent. Star Island, or **Meralava**, is a massive cone rising so steeply to a height of 3,000 feet that it surprises strangers that it should even be inhabited. From below, the cone appears to end in a cup with a broken rim, but Bishop Selwyn and Mr. Palmer, who reached the top in 1881, found a more recent crater. This was undoubtedly active when the explorer Quiros <note>original: "Quiros"; Pedro Fernandes de Queirós (1563–1614), a Portuguese navigator</note> discovered the island; however, there is now no local memory of such activity ¹.

In the **New Hebrides** <note>now the nation of Vanuatu</note>, volcanic activity has not yet exhausted itself on **Lepers' Island** <note>now known as Ambae</note>. It is probable that, besides the very prominent volcanoes of **Ambrym**, **Lopevi**, and **Yazur** on **Tanna**, there are many sulfur springs <term>solfataras</term> and steam vents <term>fumaroles</term> as yet unnoticed in this group.

All these volcanic islands—whether still in active operation, fuming with hidden fires, or long ago extinct—have dead and living coral around their bases. Most of the islands exist as a ruined mass, in contrast to the perfect cones of **Lopevi** and **Tinakula**; in some, the volcanic form is hidden or

> A pool sluggishly bubbling and steaming is known as the "Old Woman"; another briskly active one is the "Stranger's Wonder." Another, the "New Vuro"—though clearly not very recent—is very active and noisy. In the largest pool, some twenty feet across, two jets of steam raise the water to a height of a couple of feet, and after rain, much higher. When I was there in 1875, a new vent had been lately opened by an earthquake.

<header>Introductory. [CH.</header>

[Volcanic] discharges stand upon a broad coral base that has been uplifted some 200 feet above the sea. On this raised surface lie blocks of volcanic stone. The ravines, cut deep through the land by mountain torrents, reveal the <term>madrepore</term> <note>A type of stony, reef-building coral</note> and other corals that compose the base. On the beach, water-worn fragments of both coral and volcanic rock lie among the living coral. In the Torres Islands, terraces formed by successive geological upheavals are very noticeable; here, nothing is seen but coral. In at least one of these islands, the natives must dig to find volcanic stone that can withstand the heat required for their cooking ovens. In the Banks Islands, it appears the land is still rising; a patch of sea between Mota and Motalava has become much shallower in the last few years.

Florida Island in the Solomon group is divided into three parts by two channels called *utuha*. This geography brings to mind the mainland of the Aru Islands, as described in Mr. Wallace's *Malay Archipelago*. Although the northernmost channel is quite wide, the natives consider the land to be a single island, which they call Nggela; none of the three individual parts has a name of its own. A similar channel divides *Mala masiki* from *Mala paina*—that is, Little Malaita from Great Malaita <note>original: "Malanta"</note>. In Florida, overlooking the wider channel known as the *utuha ta na vula* <note>original: "Moon Channel"</note>, there is a cliff as white as chalk. In the Banks Islands, small barren patches of coarse grass called *rea* appear here and there. In Florida, large barren spaces of this kind are very prominent, just as they are on the opposite slopes of Guadalcanal <note>original: "Guadalcanar"</note>. These spaces change the look of the landscape for anyone arriving from the heavily forested islands to the east.

<meta>This page continues the physical and geological description of the Melanesian islands, moving from the structure of larger islands like Florida and Malaita to the formation of atolls, lakes, and the regional distribution of wildlife.</meta>

<page-num>17</page-num>
<header>Reef Islands. Lakes. Zoology.</header>
<sig>1.] C</sig>

It is a matter of debate whether there are any true <term>atolls</term> <note>Ring-shaped coral reefs or islands that surround a lagoon</note> in this part of Melanesia. There are, however, two kinds of lagoon islands. The Reef Islands of the Santa Cruz group consist of flat patches of sand and coral resting on the reefs; one such island is Nukapu, where the lagoon is two miles wide. The Matema group, part of the same Swallow group, consists of several sand islets resting on the edge of a very large and irregular reef. Two of these islets, which are separated only at high tide, are inhabited in a very characteristic way: Nutilole is home to about twenty or forty Melanesians, while *Fenua loa*—as the name implies <note>original: "Fenua loa" is Polynesian for "Long Land"</note>—is inhabited by Polynesian colonists from the East. On the other hand, Rowa in the Banks Islands consists of five tiny islets on the curve of an irregular reef five miles long; the main islet is formed upon a jagged point of volcanic rock, which appears to be a fragment of the edge of a sunken crater.

The *Tas* <note>A local word for "lake" or "sea"</note> in the middle of Santa Maria <note>now known as Gauua</note> in the Banks Islands is the only lake of significant size known in Melanesia. It is about five miles long, occupying the hollow of an ancient crater into which the steaming hill of Garat <note>Mount Garet, an active volcano</note> has been pushed; the waters pour out in a magnificent waterfall. There is a much smaller lake on Vanua Lava that feeds two fine cascades, and another on Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae</note> with a volcanic vent on its edge. Bishop Selwyn <note>Likely Bishop John Selwyn, who served in the 1870s-80s</note> found the lake at Tikopia covered with large water-lilies in 1888; the *Tas* of Santa Maria will surely reward its first scientific visitor.

A few words may be ventured regarding the natural history of this part of Melanesia. The <term>cuscus</term> <note>A cat-sized, tree-dwelling marsupial</note> common in the Solomon Islands does not reach as far as Santa Cruz; it is believed to exist on Espiritu Santo, where the explorer Quiros reported seeing goats <note>Pedro Fernandes de Queirós, a 17th-century navigator; his "goats" were likely misidentified native animals</note>. The white cockatoo, which is abundant throughout most of the Solomon Islands, does not cross the two straits that separate Guadalcanal from San Cristoval <note>now Makira</note>, and Malaita <note>original: "Malanta"</note> from Ulawa. While Ulawa does not appear to a casual visitor to have different wildlife than Malaita, the birds of San Cristoval seem few and strange. Frogs also stop short of Santa Cruz, despite being abundant in the Solomons. A remarkable <term>megapode</term> <note>A "mound-builder" bird that uses volcanic heat or decomposing vegetation to incubate its eggs</note> is found in all these island groups, existing as one or perhaps several species.

...different habits. At Savo, where these birds <note>The malau or megapode, a bird that uses environmental heat to incubate its eggs</note> have become private property without any attempt to domesticate them, they lay eggs in a carefully divided and claimed patch of sand. They come out of the forest, as the locals say, twice a day to lay and look after their eggs. In the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>, they lay their eggs in the hollow of a decayed tree or in a heap of debris they have scratched together. In the Banks Islands, these birds are called *malau*, just as they are known as *maleo* in Celebes <note>now Sulawesi, Indonesia</note>¹. The native breed of chickens still thrives in Santa Cruz; however, imported chickens seem to have destroyed and replaced them in all the most commonly visited places, though they were common thirty years ago². 

Crocodiles are numerous in the Solomon Islands and Santa Cruz. They are sometimes seen in the Banks Islands, and one was recently killed in the Torres Islands; they are known and named in the Northern New Hebrides. The name for them is the same throughout the region: *vua* or *via*, which relates to the Malay word *buaya* and the Malagasy word *voay*. The people of Santa Isabel island claim that crocodiles have four eyes: two for seeing in clear water and two for seeing through mud. 

Snakes are not common everywhere. At Mota in the Banks Islands, there are no land snakes, and the locals claim that if any were brought there, they would not survive. On Vanua Lava and Saddle Island <note>Motalava</note> of the same group, the snakes that live among the massive roots of the banyan trees are said to reach an enormous size. The eels in the *Tas* <note>lake</note> of Santa Maria <note>Gauua</note> sometimes measure more than thirty inches around. It is frustrating for those who currently suffer so much from mosquitoes in the islands to know that Mendana <note>Álvaro de Mendaña de Neira, the Spanish explorer who reached the islands in 1595</note>, who spent two months at Santa Cruz,

<page-num>19</page-num>
<header>Zoology.</header>
<sig>C 2</sig>

...and Quiros <note>Pedro Fernandes de Queirós, a 17th-century Portuguese explorer</note>, who stayed for a month in the great bay of Espiritu Santo, both declared that in their time there were no mosquitoes. However, it is likely they were actually referring to the small housefly. The variety of mosquitoes found today is interesting, despite the suffering they bring. On Mota, there is only one kind, which bites only during the daylight hours. On Vanua Lava, during the rainy season, they are so relentless that they drive the locals to bury themselves in the sea sand to get some sleep. The same name for the mosquito is used from the Asian continent all the way to Fiji, and the repulsive blowfly carries the same name and habits throughout all the islands. 

Dr. Guppy <note>Henry B. Guppy, a surgeon and naturalist who visited the Solomon Islands in the 1880s</note> recommends that residents of the Pacific Ocean observe the habits of the *robber crab* <note>original Latin: *Birgus latro*; also known as the coconut crab</note>. The description of it in Hazlewood's Fiji Dictionary explains how the *ugavule* <note>the Fijian name for the coconut crab</note> climbs coconut trees, pierces and drinks from young nuts, and husks and breaks open mature nuts to eat the meat. It also describes how the crab is caught by tying a bundle of grass around the trunk of the tree it has climbed. When the crab descends backward and reaches the grass, it mistakenly believes it has reached the ground; it lets go of the tree, falls, and is stunned. The account also claims the crab throws dirt and stones into the faces of those chasing it. 

The same crab (or lobster) is called *ugair* in the Banks Islands. The locals there claim that when it grabs something, such as a person's hand, with its smaller left claw, it will not let go until sunset. Because of this, that claw is known as "sundown," or *loaroro*. They also say that when an *ugair* drops a coconut from a tree onto a stone to break it, it will only eat the fruit if the break is smooth; if the shell is jagged, the crab will not touch it. 

The people of Wango on San Cristoval <note>now Makira</note> tell stories that go beyond likely facts. They relate that on moonlight nights, they paddle over to the small island of Biu and quietly creep up the beach. There, they find these crabs engaged in a dance: two large, old crabs stand in the center, beating time by striking one claw against the other, while the rest circle around them and wave their claws just as the local people wave their clubs during a dance. While the crabs are thus distracted, they are captured in great numbers¹.

¹ The locals do not believe in the existence of great apes <note>original: "anthropoid apes"</note>. They do believe in the existence of "wild men," and for many years, Europeans have interpreted this belief to mean that apes exist there. See Chapter 18.

# CHAPTER II.

->SOCIAL REGULATIONS. DIVISIONS OF THE PEOPLE.<-

->KINSHIP AND MARRIAGE CONNECTION.<-

There will be no attempt made here to deal with the ethnology <note>original: "Ethnology"; the branch of anthropology that compares and analyzes the characteristics of different peoples and the relationships between them</note> of Melanesia. The origin of the Melanesian people, in their various locations and divisions, can be considered unknown; as they themselves apparently have no traditions and no opinions about the matter. In the stories that circulate among them, they represent themselves as having been created exactly where they are. 

The variety of their languages—and, to a much lesser extent, their arts and customs—shows <note>original: "shews"</note> that they did not arrive as a single group in the islands they now inhabit. However, an examination of their languages reveals a very significant underlying similarity. This book may perhaps be taken as evidence of a large general resemblance in the religious beliefs and practices, the customs, and the ways of life that prevail in the islands that are included here in a common view. 

As knowledge expands and detailed information is gathered from all sides, a connection will no doubt be traced with regions beyond Melanesia. For example, the loom—which is unique to Santa Cruz <note>an island group in the Solomon Islands archipelago</note> among the islands discussed here—may connect the people of that group with those of the Caroline Islands. Many similarities between Fiji and Madagascar, beyond just language, may bring those countries and much of the region that lies between them into whatever ethnographic category Madagascar is held to belong to. However, attempting to trace such connections is beyond the present purpose, which is limited to presenting the Melanesian people as they currently exist.

<summary>This page introduces the social regulations of Melanesia, noting that while the people lack traditions regarding their ancient origins, their languages and customs suggest both a shared heritage and distinct regional connections.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from a discussion on the general ethnology and linguistic similarities of Melanesians to their specific myths of origin and the fundamental "exogamous" social divisions that define their society.</meta>

<page-num>21</page-num>

# Exogamous Divisions

<margin>Actual origins</margin>
There are several myths of origin that now appear, beyond the stories of creation told about the figures Koevasi, Qat, or Tagar <note>mythological figures or "culture heroes" in Melanesian religion; Qat is central to New Hebrides (Vanuatu) stories, while Tagar is prominent in the northern islands</note>. For example, it is said in Saa, on the island of Mara Masiki <note>now part of Malaita in the Solomon Islands</note>, that humans sprouted spontaneously from a particular kind of sugar-cane called *toku nunu*. Two knots in the cane began to sprout, and the cane burst open beneath each shoot; from one came a man and from the other a woman, who became the parents of all humanity. 

It is of greater importance, however, to observe the meaning of the words the people of various islands use to describe themselves as human beings. It is sometimes said that people found living in isolation call themselves simply "men," without a specific name for their race or nation, as if they believed they were the only people in the world. In Melanesia, when natives were first asked who they were, they answered "men." By this, they meant they were living humans rather than demons or ghosts. They said this because they did not believe their visitors were human, but rather ghosts, demons, or spirits belonging to the sea.

In the native view of humanity, almost everywhere in the islands discussed here, nothing seems more fundamental than the division of the people into two or more classes. These groups are exogamous <note>original: "exogamous"; meaning individuals must marry someone from a different group rather than their own</note>, and descent is counted through the mother <note>this is a matrilineal system, where children belong to the mother's social group rather than the father's</note>. This division appears to be the primary way a native views his fellow humans. Knowledge of this system is likely the first social concept to take shape in the mind of a young Melanesian of either sex. It is not an exaggeration to say that this division is the foundation upon which the entire structure of native society is built. 

There are no "tribes" among these natives, at least not if the word is used as it is for the Maori people of New Zealand or in Fiji. No portion of territory, no matter how small, can be said to belong to just one of these divisions. No single family can consist of members from only one division; both divisions (where there are two) or all divisions (where there are more than two) are intermixed in their housing and property. Whatever political organization exists can never be described as a "tribe" grouped around a hereditary or elective chief. It is probably true...

<summary>This page explores Melanesian myths of origin and introduces the fundamental social structure of exogamous, matrilineal divisions, which differ significantly from the "tribe" models found in New Zealand or Fiji.</summary>
<keywords>myths of origin, Saa, Mara Masiki, toku nunu, exogamy, matrilineal descent, social structure, tribes, ghosts vs. men</keywords>

--- Page 51 ---
<meta>This page discusses the common misconception of "tribes" in Melanesia and highlights a unique exception in the Solomon Islands where descent is traced through the father rather than the mother.</meta>

<page-num>22</page-num>

<header>Social Regulations. [CH.</header>

<margin>See page 10</margin> In every account of Melanesian affairs presented to the world, "tribes" are mentioned. However, the belief that every indigenous people is organized into tribes is simply part of the assumptions brought by a Western visitor. When one reads about "coast tribes" or "bush tribes," nothing more is meant than the people who live on the coast or in the inland parts of an island.

There is, however, one very remarkable exception to this general rule of social division in the Solomon Islands. It is found in Ulawa, Ugi, and parts of San Cristoval <note>now Makira</note>, Malanta <note>now Malaita</note>, and Guadalcanar <note>now Guadalcanal</note>. This is a region where the languages also form a distinct group, and where a difference in the people's decorative art and physical appearance—though they remain thoroughly Melanesian—can hardly go unnoticed. In this region, the boundaries of which are currently unknown, there is no division of the people into matrilineal groups as found elsewhere; instead, descent follows the father. This is so unusual that for a time it seemed incredible to me. Nothing but the repeated declarations of a native who was well-acquainted with the social divisions in other island groups was enough to establish it for me as a verified fact. The specific or local causes that created this exceptional state of affairs are unknown, but the fact of the exception itself is valuable to note$^1$.

Generally speaking, it may be said that to a Melanesian man, all women of his own generation at least are either "sisters" or "wives." To a Melanesian woman, all men are either "brothers" or "husbands." <note>This refers to kinship categories: "sisters/brothers" are those within one's own social group whom one cannot marry, while "wives/husbands" are those in the opposite group who are potential partners.</note> An excellent illustration of this is found in the story of Taso from Aurora <note>Maewo</note> in the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>. In this story, the hero Qatu discovers and brings to his wife twin boys, who are the children of his deceased sister. His wife asks, "Are these my children or my husbands?" Qatu answers, "Your husbands, to be sure; they are my sister's children." In that island, there are two social divisions. Qatu and his wife could not belong to the same group, but Qatu, his sister, and her children must belong to the same group. Therefore, the boys were potential husbands for

L. Fison.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Melanesian social divisions, specifically how these kinship groups (moieties) regulate marriage and sexual relationships, using the example of the mythological figure Qatu and local customs in the Solomon and Banks Islands.</meta>

<page-num>23</page-num>

<header>II.] Restriction of Intercourse. 23</header>

Qatu’s wife; but had they belonged to the other division, their age would have made her count them her children rather than her brothers. It must not be understood that a Melanesian man regards all women who are not of his own division as his actual wives, or that he believes he has rights over any unmarried woman in those groups. However, the women who *could* be his wives through marriage and those who *cannot* possibly be so stand in a very different relation to him. It may be added that all women who are eligible to become wives and are not yet married are, to a certain extent, viewed by eligible men as being available for more or less legitimate sexual relations. 

In fact, the "appropriation" of specific women by their own husbands <note>meaning individual monogamous marriage</note>, though established by every sanction of native custom, does not have nearly as strong a hold on native society—nor likely as deep a foundation in their history—as the separation of the sexes into divisions. These divisions strictly limit the interaction of men and women to those belonging to the section or sections to which they do not themselves belong. 

Two proofs or examples of this are particularly notable: 

(1) There is probably no place where the common opinion of Melanesians approves of sexual relations between unmarried youths and girls as a good thing in itself, though it is tolerated as something to be expected and excused. However, intercourse within the group that is forbidden for marriage—where two members of the same division are involved—is a crime; it is considered incest. 

In Florida <note>now the Ngela Islands, Solomon Islands</note> in the old days, the man would have been killed and the woman forced into prostitution. Now that the severity of ancient customs has relaxed, the offense can be settled with money and pigs, but the fine is much higher than what is required if a man is found sinning with a woman who could have legally become his wife. 

In the Banks’ Islands <note>a group of islands in northern Vanuatu</note>, where the people are divided into two groups, if it became known that two members of the same group had been guilty of this disgraceful crime, as they considered it, the people of the *other* division would come and destroy the gardens of everyone belonging to the group in which the offense was committed. Those whose gardens were destroyed would offer no resistance or complaint. It was

The same was true on Lepers' Island <note>now Ambae, Vanuatu</note>; there, the offending man also had to make a large payment to the close relatives of the woman with whom he had committed the offense. This was done to appease their anger and to "fence against" <note>original: "fence against"; meaning to compensate for or protect oneself from the consequences of</note> the fault. Cases of this kind of incest were always rare across all the islands because the feeling against sexual intercourse within the kinship group was so strong. 

(2) On the other hand, the feeling that sexual relations were natural when the man and woman belonged to different divisions was shown by a specific feature of native hospitality: providing a guest with a temporary wife. Whether this is still practiced now or was practiced recently is quickly denied in the Solomon and Banks Islands, but it is not denied in the Northern New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>; there can be little doubt that it was once common everywhere. However, the woman provided to the guest was necessarily someone who was eligible to be his wife; the companionship of a woman from his own kinship group could never be allowed.

In providing a more detailed treatment of this subject, it will be convenient to first take examples from the Banks Islands and Northern New Hebrides, where the people are divided into two kinship groups <note>moieties</note>, and then from the Solomon Islands, where there are more than two divisions. The same two divisions exist throughout the Banks Islands, the Torres Islands, and the Northern New Hebrides. A Banks Islander knows his own kin wherever he goes within his own island group, and if he travels to Aurora <note>now Maewo</note> in the New Hebrides, he finds the same system. The men of Aurora know well who their kin are on Pentecost and Lepers' Island; the people of Lepers' Island know theirs on Espiritu Santo. Therefore, as strange as the language may be to a man from Mota visiting Pentecost, or to someone from Lepers' Island visiting Motalava, each feels "at home" in a way that would be impossible for him in the Solomon Islands¹. In neither the Banks Islands nor the New Hebrides is there a specific name to distinguish the division or kinship group; nor is there any badge or emblem belonging to either one. In these small communities, every neighbor is well known. Each of the divisions is in—
