<page-num>25</page-num>
<header>11.] Banks' Islands. Divisions. Adoption.</header>

In Mota, this division is called a *<term>vere</term>*, and in Motlav it is called a *<term>rev</term>*, a word that simply signifies "division." Those who belong to one *<term>vere</term>* are said to be *<term>tarala ima</term>* to the others, which means they are "from the other side of the house." When a woman marries, she does not join her husband's side of the house; she is said to be *<term>ape mateima</term>*, or "at the door" (since the doors are located at the ends of the native houses). Similarly, the husband does not move to the wife’s side. The children always belong to the mother’s side. 

All people who belong to the same "side of the house" are considered *<term>sogoi</term>* <note>original: "sogoi"; meaning kinsfolk or members of the same maternal descent group</note> to one another. Consequently, a man’s own children are not his *sogoi* or his kindred; his closest relations are actually his sister's children. There is no serious historical account given for the origin of these two divisions in the Banks Islands. 

Within these two *<term>vere</term>*, there are certain specific families among the Banks Island people whose members possess a degree of family pride and attempt to maintain their family connections through intermarriage. The most famous of these is the Lo Sepere family, from the area of that name on Vanua Lava, where the legendary figure Qat is believed to have lived ¹. 

Adoption is a common practice and generally carries no special ritual significance. Parents who have no children of their own will naturally adopt a child who is a relative of the wife, so that the adopted child holds the same social position as one born into that house. However, if an orphan from the husband’s side of the family is adopted out of pity—as sometimes happens—the child is raised as if they were a relative of the wife, and the parents take great care to hide the fact of the adoption. If the child grows up and happens to discover that they have been raised on the "wrong side of the house," they will often abandon their foster parents to go and live with their true *<term>sogoi</term>*. Such a discovery often leads to much grief and bitterness.

In Aurora (Maewo), which is the island in the New Hebrides <note>modern Vanuatu</note> closest to the Banks Islands and which maintains frequent communication with Merlav, the members of the two divisions—

These family groups exist within the *<term>vere</term>*, but they do not encompass the entire *<term>vere</term>*; neither side of the house is entirely divided into these specific family groups.

They speak of one another as being "of the other side," or *<term>ta tavuluna</term>*. They have a legend that the first woman was a cowry shell that transformed into a human. She called the men to her and divided them into her husbands and her brothers, fathers, and maternal uncles, according to the current social arrangements. The presence of specific families within these broader kinship groups on this island is very remarkable. There are several in the northern part of the island, mostly named after the places where they were established. There is one, however, named after the octopus, or *<term>wirita</term>*, which originally belonged to Bugita, a place on the shore. 

The connection between this family and the octopus is unclear; they have no belief that they are descended from the *<term>wirita</term>*, and they eat it as freely as other natives do. However, if a man from another family wanted to catch an octopus for food, he would take someone from the *wirita* family with him to stand on the beach at Bugita and cry out, "So-and-so wants an octopus!" Then, plenty would be caught. It seems more likely that the family’s residence in a place where octopuses are abundant—where the beach would naturally be their private fishing ground—gave rise to the name and the belief in a special connection. Another family, named "At the Wotaga" after their home near a certain fruit tree, would not raise a light-colored child; if such a child were born among them, they believed they would all die¹.

In Araga (Pentecost Island), although illicit sexual relations between members of the same kinship group are punished by the destruction of the offending side’s gardens by members of the other side, marriages within the same kin group are not unknown. Those who enter into such marriages are despised and even hated, but once money and pigs have been given and received, the marriage remains valid. In Lepers’ Island (Omba), the two divisions are called "bunches of fruit," or *<term>wai vung</term>*, as if all the members hang from the same stalk. Their story is that when the deity Tagar first created humanity, he made two people, both male, and then one of these...

<page-num>27</page-num>
<header>II. *The Question of Communal Marriage.*</header>

...took a tuber of *qevu* <term>a specific variety of yam</term>, and threw it at the other person, who at once turned into a woman and cried with a loud voice that many men should die because of women. This woman had two daughters, who had a falling out; from one of these daughters sprang one *wairung* <term>kinship division or "bunch"</term>, and from the second sprang the other. 

In cases where a child is adopted by a foster-mother who belongs to the other "bunch," the secret of their true kinship is carefully kept. The true state of the case is never mentioned by those who know it until the time for marriage comes. This is done out of consideration for the feelings of the adopting parents; however, the social repugnance toward marriage within the same kin is too great to allow for permanent concealment.

The system of dividing the people into strictly exogamous kins <term>social groups where members are required to marry outside of their own group</term> is undoubtedly best observed and analyzed where the division is simple and separates the entire population into one "side of the house" or the other. Two questions may, therefore, be suitably raised here: 

1. Whether there are traces of a communal system of marriage <note>a 19th-century anthropological theory, now largely discredited, suggesting that early human societies practiced "group marriage" where all men of one group were married to all women of another</note> within this division.
2. Whether the system is sufficient to prevent that which it seems intended to prevent—namely, the marriage of persons too closely allied by blood. 

In regard to the first question, it must be said, on the one hand, that the people have no memory of a time when all the women of one side were, in fact, common wives to the men of the other side. Furthermore, there is no occasion on which the women become common to the men who are not of their kin. While it is admitted that the sexual license at a large feast is great, such behavior is confessed to be disorderly and illegitimate; it is not defended on the grounds of tradition or ancient right. 

If a great man hosting a feast suggests that he will not allow the harmony of the gathering to be spoiled by jealous quarreling about women, it is taken as a temporary festive concession. However, if he announces that people are to behave well, they know that anyone who takes liberties will have to answer for it—not only to the injured husband, as is the case on ordinary occasions, but also to the powerful master of the feast. Additionally, the stories of the creation of mankind, and particularly of the first woman, consistently represent marriage as an individual arrangement between two people.

<header>Social Regulations. [CH.</header>

When Qat <term>a legendary hero and creator figure in Melanesian mythology</term> wove Iro Lei from flexible rods and brought her to life, it was so she could be his own wife. His brothers tried to kidnap her for themselves—one woman among eleven of them—but the stories say they were "stealing" her, rather than claiming a legitimate social right. When Qat created other human beings, both male and female, he assigned each man his own specific wife. 

On the other hand, there is strong evidence to the contrary found in the study of language. This evidence is found in the plural forms used for the terms "mother," "husband," and "wife." In the Mota language <term>the primary language of the Banks Islands</term>, this structure is very clear. The word *ra* is a plural prefix. The kinship division or "side" is called the *veve* <term>literally "division" or "kin"</term>, and the word for mother is *ra veve* <note>original: ra veve; literally "the kin" in plural form</note>. The word *soai* refers to a member of a group, such as a limb of a body or a component part of a house or tree; however, the term for either a husband or a wife is *ra soai* <note>original: ra soai; literally "the members" or "the parts"</note>. 

Some might argue that *ra* is simply a prefix used to show respect or dignity, but the native speakers themselves are fully aware that it expresses plurality. The kinship group is the *veve*; therefore, a child’s mother is referred to as "they of the kin"—his relatives. A man’s relatives are not called his *veve* simply because they are his mother’s people; rather, she is called his *veve* in the plural—his "kindred"—as if she were the collective representative of the entire kin group. It is as if he were not the child of the specific woman who gave birth to him, but the child of the entire kinship group for whom she brought him into the world. 

Following this same logic, a plural form is used for the Mota word for child: *reremera* <note>original: reremera; a word containing a doubled plural sign</note>. Even a single boy is not called "child" but "children," as if his individual identity were not distinguished from the collective offspring of his *veve*. This same plural prefix is found in other languages of the Banks Islands for the word "mother": *rave* in Santa Maria, *retne* in Vanua Lava, and *reme* in the Torres Islands. 

On Whitsuntide Island <term>Pentecost Island</term>, the mother is called *ratahi*, and on Lepers’ Island <term>Ambae</term> she is called *ratahigi*. These terms translate to "the sisters" or "the sisterhood." This is because the mother represents all the sister-members of the *waivung* <term>kinship division</term>, who are considered the mothers of the children in a general sense. Similarly, the single word used for either husband or wife is plural. In Mota, a man does not call his wife his "member" or his "component part," but rather his "members" or "parts"; a wife speaks of her husband in the same way. It is not that the man and his wife together form one composite body, but rather that the men on one side and the women on the other make up a

<header>II.] Testimony of Words. Descent through the Father's Line.</header>

...a composite married body. The Mota people know that the word they use refers to this collective group; one man admitted this to me with a blush—a Melanesian blush—while protesting that the word no longer represented a modern reality. The word used in Motlav <term>an island in the Banks group, part of Saddle Island</term>, provides similar confirmation for this interpretation of the Mota word, even though it does not have a plural form. In Motlav, the word *ignige* has the same meaning as the Mota word *soai* <note>meaning a "member" or "component part"</note>. A man says of his leg or his arm, "*ignik*"—"my member," or "one of my parts"—and he also calls his wife "*ignik*," while she calls him the same.

Regarding the second point in question, it is clear that the strict rule of exogamy <term>the custom of marrying outside one's own kinship group</term> technically leaves marriage open to those who are very close in blood. Under these rules, a man is not considered "of kin" to his own children, nor is he "of kin" to his brother's children <note>Because children belong to their mother's kinship group, not their father's</note>. But although it is only the intermarriage of *sogoi* <term>members of the same "vere" or kinship division</term> that is strictly forbidden, and descent is always counted through the mother, the biological connection to the father and the father’s close relatives is never ignored. 

Consequently, the marriage of those who are closely related by blood is discouraged, even if they are not *sogoi* and could lawfully marry. In Mota, for example, the children of a brother and sister are thought too closely related to marry. The brother and sister both belong to the same *vere* (let’s call it Division A), as they are children of the same mother. The children of the sister also belong to her *vere*, Division A. However, the brother’s children belong to *vere* Division B, following their mother, who must necessarily come from the other side of the community. It appears, then, that these two cousins—the children of a brother and sister—are not *sogoi*, since one is in Division A and the other is in Division B, and they could legally marry. But they will not; the match will not be made. If they did marry, people would say they were "going wrong¹." We can see that the inheritance of property shows the same tendency—perhaps a recent one—toward recognizing agnatic descent <term>descent and relationship traced through the father's line</term>.

These divisions are called *kema*, and each has its own distinguishing name. These are the Nggaombata, the Manukama (or Honggokama), the Honggokiki, the Kakau, the Himbo, and the Lahi. However, these six *kema* likely evolved from a much simpler original system. Two of them have names tied to specific locations: Nggaombata from Guadalcanal, and Himbo from Simbo (an island located somewhat vaguely to the west), from which these two *kema* are known to have originated. The Nggaombata and the Himbo are grouped together, perhaps because they arrived as outsiders, and the Lahi—a small division—is said to be so closely connected with the Himbo that their members cannot intermarry.

It is a matter of debate whether Honggokama and Manukama are different names for a single *kema*, or if they are two branches into which one group is currently splitting. The Honggokama and the Honggokiki—meaning "the great" and "the little"—are clearly parts of one original group. In Florida <term>the island of Nggela</term>, the situation is not simply a matter of an original double division splitting repeatedly; rather, the settlement of outsiders has made the arrangement so complicated that few locals claim to be able to fully understand it¹. Yet, these outsiders undoubtedly brought with them a distinct sense of kinship with one or another of the local *kema*. 

The strict rule of exogamy <term>the custom of marrying outside one's own clan</term> is not the only restriction on marriage. Here, as in the eastern islands, it is supplemented by a strong public opinion regarding what is proper. A notable example of this occurred a few years ago when Takua, a powerful chief, married the daughter of one of his other wives. Technically, the girl was not part of his own *kema*, so he was within his legal rights. However, the community’s sense of decency and propriety was outraged, and the man’s influence as a chief was greatly diminished as a result. In Bugotu on the island of Santa Isabel, there are three *vinahuhu* <term>the local term for clan divisions</term>: Dhonggokama, Vihuvunagi, and Poso—

### 11. Florida and Bugotu

...mogo <note>A clan or kinship division in Bugotu.</note>, not one of which now corresponds exactly with either of the Florida *kema*. But the *Dhonggokama*, they say, is the same as the ancient *kema* which has split into the *Honggokama* and *Honggokiki* in Florida; and the other two may well be believed to be the divided members of the original pair. The meanings of the names of three of the Florida *kema* (besides the two named after locations) are known: *Honggo* means "cat's-cradle," *Manukama* means "eagle," and *Kakau* means "crab." It is evident that when the divisions of a people multiply, names must be given to them. Where there are only two "sides of the house," no specific name is needed for either. however, when a man may have wives and children from three or four different kins that are not his own, a name for each kin is necessary to maintain the matriarchal system of descent through the mother.

It adds significantly to the distinction between these *kema* that each has one or more *buto* <term>a taboo; a thing or animal that is forbidden</term>. Members of the clan must keep clear of their *buto*, abstaining from eating, approaching, or even looking at it¹. One of the very first lessons learned by a child in Florida is what its *buto* is—its "abomination"—and that to eat, touch, or see it would be a dreadful thing. In only one case is this *buto* the living creature from which the *kema* takes its name: the *Kakau* kin may not eat the *Kakau* crab. The *Nggaombata* may not eat the giant clam; the *Lahi* may not eat white pig; and the *Manukama* may not eat the pigeon. The *Kakau*, in addition to their namesake crab, may not eat the parrot *Trichoglossus Massena* <note>The Coconut Lorikeet</note>. Interestingly, the *Manukama* are allowed to eat the eagle, the very bird from which they take their name. If you ask any member of these *kema* about this, they will likely answer that their *buto* is their ancestor; a *Manukama* member will say that the pigeon he refuses to eat is his ancestor. However, an intelligent native, describing this local custom, writes:

> "This is the explanation of the *buto*. We believe these *tindalo* <term>spirits of the dead or objects of worship</term> to have once been living men. Something that was with them, or which they had dealings with, has become a forbidden thing, *tambu* <note>taboo</note>, and abominable."

¹ For example, in the story of 'Percy Pomo,' a man is horrified at the sight of blue trousers because the color matches a part of the internal organs of the shark, which was his *buto*.

<margin>is</margin>
...is a taboo <note>original: buto</note> to those to whom the ghost <note>original: tindalo</note> belongs." He gives the example of the clam of the Nggaombata clan. The ghost <note>original: tindalo</note> of a famous ancient member of that clan <note>original: kema</note> named Polika haunted a beach opposite Mage. A large snake, a *poli*, was believed to represent him there. The Nggaombata could not approach that beach; Polika was their taboo <note>original: buto</note>¹. On another beach, where they catch fish to sacrifice to Polika, there is a giant clam <note>original: gima</note> which they call Polika. They used to believe it was, in some way, Polika himself; therefore, the giant clam <insert>is</insert> their taboo <note>original: buto</note>.

The question immediately arises whether we are seeing totems here. But we must ask: where are the totems? Are they the living creatures that give two of the divisions their names, or are they the creatures that members of those divisions are forbidden from eating? It is true that the Kakau kin group may not eat the *kakau* crab, but the Manukama kin group may eat the *manukama* bird. If there is a totem, it must be found in the taboo <note>original: buto</note>—for example, the pigeon of the Manukama or the giant clam of the Nggaohata, which are said to be ancestors. 

However, it must be noted that the object considered an abomination to eat is never believed to be the actual ancestor—and certainly not the eponymous ancestor <note>the ancestor for whom the clan is named</note> of the clan. Instead, it is said to represent some famous former member of the clan from a generation earlier than the fathers of current members—a grandfather or ancestor <note>original: kukua</note>. The object represents him so much that showing disrespect to it is the same as showing disrespect to him. The most likely explanation for these taboos <note>original: buto</note> might shed light on how totems began elsewhere, but it does not suggest that true totems exist in the Solomon Islands. The taboo <note>original: buto</note> of each clan <note>original: kema</note> is likely a relatively recent development in Florida; it was introduced to Bugotu within the memory of people still living. It is most likely a variation of a custom found on Ulawa, another island in the Solomons. It was observed with surprise when a Mission school was established—

On that island, the people of the place would not eat bananas and had ceased to plant the tree. It was found that the origin of this restraint was recent and well remembered; a man of great influence had, before his death not long ago, prohibited the eating of bananas after his passing, saying that he would be "in the banana." The elder natives would still give his name and say, "We cannot eat So-and-So." When a few years had passed, if the restriction had held its ground, they would have said, "We must not eat our ancestor." This represents a practice that is also common in Malanta <note>now Malaita</note> near Ulawa, where—as in Florida—a man will often declare that after death he will be seen as a shark.

These divisions, called *kema* <note>clans or kinship groups</note>, are not political divisions^1. Unlike the Banks' Islands, where every house must necessarily contain members of both divisions, not every *kema* will be represented in every village, as one or two of the smaller clans may have no members there. However, every man's wife (or wives) and all his children must belong to a *kema* different from his own <note>this reflects a matrilineal system where children belong to their mother's clan</note>, and every village must have a mixed population. The property of the members of each *kema* is intermixed with that of the others. In a large village, the principal chief is the head of the *kema* that predominates there, and he exercises his authority over everyone, while the leading men of the less numerous *kema* serve as lesser chiefs. 

It is evident that the dominance of any single *kema* cannot be permanent. Because of their kinship rules, a chief's sons are never of his own kin <note>his own clan</note>; and, as will be shown, he passes on as much of his property and authority to them as he can. If one kinship group is the most numerous in a certain district today, it cannot remain so in the next generation, because the children of those who are currently the most numerous will naturally be many more in...

Thus it was that twenty years ago the Nggaombata was the dominant *kema* <note>clan</note> in Florida <note>Nggela</note>, and it was said that to be a great chief, a man had to be Nggaombata. Now, however, the Manukama are rising to the leading position and providing the chiefs in many of the island's districts.

The system where the Melanesian people are divided into exogamous <note>marrying outside one's own group</note> groups, in which descent follows the mother's line, is naturally called a matriarchal system. However, it must be understood that the mother is by no means the head of the family. The family home belongs to the father, the garden is his, and the rule and government of the household are his. It is into the father’s house that a young bridegroom brings his wife, unless he already has a home of his own prepared. 

Despite this, the closest relationship according to native views is that which exists between a man and his sister’s son <note>maternal nephew</note>. This is because the mother, who transmits the kinship line, is unable to provide the social and protective services that a man can give. A man’s sons are not considered his own kin, even though he fulfills a father’s role for them. Instead, the tie between a man and his sister’s children carries the weight of the traditional bond of all native society: kinship through the mother. 

As a youth begins to have social needs beyond the food and shelter his father provides, he looks to his mother’s brother as the primary male representative of his kin. It is well known that in Fiji, the *vasu* <note>the sister's son</note> holds extraordinary rights and privileges regarding his maternal uncle. While this right is much less obvious or significant in the Melanesian islands west of Fiji, it is still taken for granted that a nephew should look to his mother’s brother for help of every kind, and that the uncle should view his sister’s son as his special responsibility. The closeness of this relationship is fundamental. 

The connection of kinship through the mother to the large exogamous group, and the connection of blood through the father to his family, are both clearly recognized. To a certain extent, these two ties necessarily conflict with one another. The connection created by marriage between members of different groups and—

# II. The Banks Islands System

In these families, there is a third relationship that is equally felt and expressed in words. The terms used to describe various degrees of relationship fall into three classes: the first concerns kinship through the mother; the second concerns the family generally on both the father's and mother's sides; and the third concerns those relationships resulting from marriage.

While a complete overview of the system of relationship and the terms that express it in one specific Melanesian area cannot be taken to show what prevails everywhere, it serves as a valuable representative example. The Mota system, which effectively represents the entire Banks Islands group, can be shown here completely and exactly.

(1) As previously mentioned, all members of each of the two <term>exogamous</term> <note>original: "exogamous divisions"; referring to the social rule where one must marry someone from a different clan</note> divisions of the people are ***sogoi***—that is, they are kin to one another. The only other relationship belonging specifically to this maternal kinship is that between the maternal uncle and his sister's children (both male and female), expressed by the terms ***maraui*** and ***vanangoi***. The uncle is ***maraui*** to his sister's child, and the nephew or niece is ***vanangoi*** to the mother's brother; however, the nephew is also called ***maraui*** in relation to his uncle. This relationship extends to the second generation: the children of a man's sister's daughters are his ***vanangoi***, and they are still considered his kin. However, his sister's son's children belong to the other ***veve*** <note>clan or division</note>, and the special tie of kinship is broken; they are instead called his "children," as they are raised to be in the same generation as their parents. For social purposes, a man's sister's child (his ***vanangoi***) stands as if he were in the same generation as the man himself.

(2) Aside from connections by marriage and the special relationship of the ***maraui*** and ***vanangoi***—which follows the rule of tracing kinship through the mother—general relationships can be arranged into four successive generations: grandparents, parents, children, and grandchildren. Consider the current generation, the ***tarangiu***, consisting of young married men and women; they are brothers and sisters. The generation above them are their fathers and mothers; the generation below them are their children; and the generation below that will be their grandchildren, to whom all those who came before...

It explains specific terms like "sogoi" and the unique social standing of the maternal uncle (maraui) and his nephew (vanangoi).</summary>

# Kinship and Marriage Connections

The parents of these parents are grandparents and ancestors. The terms ***tamai*** and ***veve*** must be translated as "father" and "mother." These are used generally for everyone in the same generation as the parents who are "close" kin and belong to the family circle. A child, whether a son or daughter, is called ***natui***. A grandparent and grandchild, or an ancestor and descendant, is called ***tupui***$^1$. 

The terms equivalent to "brother" and "sister" are used according to a different principle than the one we are familiar with, where the sex of the person being referred to determines the word used. In Melanesia, as in many other places, one word describes the relationship between people of the same sex, and a different word describes the relationship between people of different sexes. Men are ***tasiu*** to other men, and women are ***tasiu*** to other women. However, men are ***tutuai*** to women, and women are ***tutuai*** to men. 

There is a further distinction: when the individuals are of the same sex, the elder man or woman is ***tugui*** to the younger, and the younger man or woman is ***tasiu*** to the elder; however, ***tasiu*** is the more common term. In this system of kinship terms, it can be observed that everyone in one generation, within the family circle, is called "father" or "mother" to all the children who make up the generation below them. A man's brothers are called "fathers" of his children, and a woman's sisters are called "mothers" of her children. A father's brothers call his children their own, and a mother's sisters call her children their own. 

Regarding this, it must be noted that this broad use of the terms "father" and "mother" does not imply any lack of clarity regarding actual biological paternity and maternity. They are simply content to use one word for both "father" and "uncle," or "mother" and "aunt," provided the specific role of the maternal uncle does not apply. The speaker has no confusion in his mind regarding biological paternity; he will correct any misunderstanding with the explanation, "my own child, ***tur***... <note>The text cuts off here; "tur" likely begins the word for "true" or "actual" in Mota.</note>

---

$^1$ It may be observed that the primary terms for kinship are generally the same, not only in the Melanesian islands discussed here, but throughout the languages related to the Melanesian family; the word for "mother" is an exception. However, common words are not always applied in the same way; for example, the word ***tubu*** used in Florida <note>referring to the Florida Islands in the Solomon Islands</note> is undoubtedly the same as the Mota word ***tupu***.

(3) A general term, ***qaliga***, encompasses everyone on the other "side of the house" who has been brought into the family through marriage. This includes fathers-in-law, mothers-in-law, sons-in-law, and daughters-in-law, along with all their brothers and sisters. A man and his wife's brother call each other ***wulus***, and a woman and her husband's sister call each other ***walu***. However, the man is also called ***walu***, and both terms are extended to include the cousins of the husband or wife. A woman does not call her husband's brother her "brother-in-law"; socially, she has no specific relationship to him, even though her children—being his brother's children—are addressed as his own. A man calls his daughter-in-law ***tawarig***. 

Additionally, there is a term for a marriage relationship that has no English equivalent: parents whose children have married each other call one another ***gasala***, which may be translated as "fellow travelers" or "wayfarers."

A genealogical table or family tree of a Mota family (see page 38) provides examples of these various relationships and clarifies how these terms are used. The two ***vere*** <note>the two "sides" or moieties of the society</note>, or the two sides of the house, are distinguished in the diagram by the letters *A* and *B* for males, and *a* and *b* for females. All those labeled *A* and *a*, or *B* and *b*, are ***sogoi*** <note>members of the same kinship group</note> to one another, as they belong to the same side of the house. Because they are also "near" to one another by blood, they will call each other ***tasiu*** <note>sibling of the same sex</note> and ***tutuai*** <note>sibling of the opposite sex</note> even when the strict biological relationship described by those words is absent. The prefix **Ro** indicates a feminine name. ...level with his maternal uncle <note>original: *meraui*</note>, as if he stood in the place of his mother. Thus, Leveveg is in fact the great-uncle of John and Agnes, but he counts only as an uncle because they are the grandchildren of his sister. The grandchildren of his brother are considered his own grandchildren <note>original: *tupui*</note>—that is, his great-nephews and great-nieces. 

For the same reason, Leveveg—who is technically the maternal great-uncle to Dudley—counts as his maternal uncle <note>original: *meraui*</note>, because Dudley "ascends" into his mother’s genealogical position. Similarly, Pantutun is the first cousin to the mothers of Tavrowar and Mowur. Since he is of the generation above them, he would typically be called "father" or "uncle" <note>original: *tamai*</note> and they would be his "children," if not for the fact that he is a cousin to their mothers through his own mother. He therefore takes his mother's place on the second ascending step of the family tree and becomes a "grandfather" or great-uncle <note>original: *tupui*</note>. 

Thus, he is the "father" <note>original: *tamai*</note>—meaning the uncle—to his first cousins Ariaqoe and Marostuwale; likewise, his sister Maututun is their "mother" or aunt. This is because he moves into his mother’s position, and she was their father’s sister. 

The same rule technically makes Dudley the "father" or "uncle" to his first cousins John and Agnes. However, because they are from the same biological generation and are older than him, he refers to them incorrectly as "brother" and "sister." This is "incorrect" because they are not his clan-mates <term>sogoi: members of the same moiety or maternal descent group</term>, and in theory—though not with public approval—he could actually marry Agnes. 

It is even more remarkable that John is officially the "father" or "uncle" to his second cousins Tavrowar and Mowur, who are much older than he is. But because his father, Pantutun, is their great-uncle <note>original: *tupui*</note>, John is therefore their uncle <note>original: *tamai*</note>, or as it naturally sounds to us, their "father."¹

The case of Matevagqoe and Ro Tapermaro is distinct from this: he married her brother's daughter. To do that, he must have been from her "side of the house"—that is, her clan-mate <note>original: *sogoi*</note>. If he had married her sister's daughter, she and her niece’s husband would be in-laws <term>qaliga: a specific relationship between in-laws, often involving social avoidance or strict protocols</term>. However, that relationship cannot exist between clan-mates <note>original: *sogoi*</note>, so they instead call themselves cousins, or "brother and sister."

<page-num>40</page-num>
# Kinship and Marriage Connection

The system of kinship existed in its early stages, and one might ask whether the terms of relationship would undergo some change in certain cases. For example, would the sons of the same father by two different mothers be distinguished from the sons of the same father and mother? The answer is that no difference is made. A man’s wives, if he should have several, must all be *sogoi* <term>sogoi: members of the same moiety or maternal descent group</term>—meaning they are from the same "side of the house." They call one another "sisters," and each woman considers the other’s children to be her own, regardless of whether the children share the same father or have different husbands. 

This does not, however, completely exclude the relationship of step-father and step-mother. If a man has a son by a wife who has died, he does not technically bring in a "step-mother" for the boy if he marries another woman while his other wives are still living; the new woman simply enters the family as another "mother," and the boy would not treat her any differently. 

However, if a woman with children loses her husband and then becomes the wife of a man who is not a close relative <note>original: "near"</note> to her previous husband—though he is, of course, *sogoi* but with no recent blood relation—that man is considered a step-father. The term *usur* <note>original: *usur*, meaning "successor"</note> is applied to him, and the connection is called *usur-gae* <note>original: *usur-gae*, meaning "bond of succession"</note>. 

Even a looser connection than this is enough to create an *usur*. For instance, if a boy’s father had a wife (who was not the boy's biological mother) and that woman becomes a widow and marries another man, the boy will treat that man with great familiarity because he has stepped into the father's place. The boy might even go so far as to take yams from the man's garden without asking. 

There is also a specific custom regarding sneezing: when a step-father sneezes, the step-son will cry out, "May a sneeze draw out a worm for you!" <note>original: *Matia revereve gam o sulate!*</note>. The idea behind this is that the deceased husband might hold a grudge against his successor and send a "worm" <note>a spiritual affliction or curse</note> from a point of land where ghosts congregate.

In places like Florida <note>The Florida Islands, now known as Nggela, in the Solomon Islands</note> and neighboring parts of the Solomon Islands, the social divisions of the people are more complex, numbering three, four, or six. In these systems, a man may take a wife or wives from any division except his own. This would seem to make it more difficult to keep an accurate count of the various degrees of relationship between people. It is probable that, while the native system is precise in following every genealogical step and connection, the people do, in fact, content themselves com...

# Florida Terms
<sig>11.]</sig>

...commonly with general terms. The special relation of the sister's son to his mother's brother is, of course, prominent; each calls the other *tumbu* <term>tumbu: a reciprocal term for a maternal uncle and his nephew</term>. This term is also applied to the father's mother's brother by his great-nephew, and by the great-uncle to his sister's grandchild. Within a generation of members of the same *kema* <term>kema: a maternal clan or social division</term>, all members of the same sex call one another *hogo*. Depending on the closeness of their blood relation, they use terms for brothers and sisters: an elder brother or sister is *tuga* to someone of the same sex, while a younger brother or sister is *tahi*. A brother or sister is called *vavine* by a sibling of the opposite sex.

With the exception of the mother's brother, all blood relations of the preceding generation (the parents' generation) are called father and mother, *tama* and *tina*. In the generation above that, with the exception of the father's mother's brother mentioned earlier (who is *tumbu*), all males and females are called *kukua* <term>kukua: grandparent or elderly relative</term>.

Looking at the next generation down, a man's sons and daughters, along with his brother's and cousin's children, are called *dale*. These are distinguished as *dale mane* (son) and *dale vaivine* (daughter) according to their sex. As noted, a man's sister's child is called *tumbu*. Similarly, a woman's children, her sister's and female cousin's children, and her husband's brother's and sister's children are all considered her own children: *dale mane* for males and *dale vaivine* for females.

In the following generation, everyone is again *kukua* to their grandparents, great-uncles, and great-aunts, and everyone above them. The only exception, as previously stated, is the *tumbu* relationship that exists between a great-nephew and his father’s mother’s brother. Husband and wife are called *tau*. A father-in-law, mother-in-law, son-in-law, or daughter-in-law is called *vungo*; this term is applied broadly to people connected by marriage who belong to different generations. Brothers-in-law and sisters-in-law, and generally people of the same generation connected by marriage, call one another *ira* <gloss>¹</gloss>.

<page-num>42</page-num>
# Kinship and Marriage Connection
[CH. 11.]

The family relationships there are very different from those described as prevailing in the Banks Islands and in Florida. To a very considerable extent, this is undoubtedly true; however, it is unlikely that the special closeness of the relationship between a man and his sister's son would disappear entirely. I have little evidence to offer regarding this <note>original: "Of this I have little evidence to offer"</note>; families are organized around the father, and the only restriction on marriage is biological closeness. 

Regardless of the extent to which patrilineal descent (tracing ancestry through the father) removes that characteristic feature of the Melanesian family system—the special bond between the maternal uncle and his sister's child—it is certain that the fundamental structure remains the same as elsewhere. That is to say, there are no specific terms corresponding to uncle, aunt, nephew, niece, or cousin. Everyone on the same generational level is considered a brother or sister if they are the children of brothers, sisters, or cousins. These individuals look upon the children of their brothers, sisters, and cousins as their own children, and those children call them all "father" and "mother." Ancestors above the father and mother, and descendants in the second and lower generations (such as grandchildren), are all grouped under one general term which covers both ancestry and posterity alike. 

At Wango in San Cristoval <note>now known as Makira</note>, where the population has been maintained by the adoption of children from the interior <note>original: "from the bush"</note> due to low birth rates and infanticide, adopted children take the same position in the family they would have held if they had been born into it. Although no biological relationship exists, they are forbidden from marrying those who are closely related through the adoptive father. Traders often call these children "slaves" because they are purchased, but the people themselves refer to them as their children.

The subject of marriage relations is incomplete without mentioning the remarkable social avoidance <note>original: "reserve"</note> practiced toward the persons and names of those who have become related by marriage. This custom is very prominent in the Banks Islands but is less noticeable in the Solomon Islands. On Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae</note>, a...

# Reserve and Avoidance
[II.]

A remarkable degree of social distance <note>original: "singular reserve"</note> is clearly shown, as it is in Fiji, by brothers and sisters, and also by mothers and sons. However, while the existence and causes of this distance might shed light on the behavior between those related by marriage, it is not the primary focus here. In Florida <note>now known as Gela</note> in the Solomon Islands, there is no difficulty regarding meeting or mentioning the name of a father-in-law, mother-in-law, or any of a wife’s kindred, and no extraordinary marks of respect are shown. It is the same at Saa <note>on the island of Malaita</note>. The extraordinary separation of the sexes in Santa Cruz and the neighboring islands—however instructive to observe in this connection—does not result from marriage relationships. 

In the Banks Islands, the rules of avoidance and reserve are very strict and detailed. Regarding the avoidance of a person, a man will not come near his mother-in-law; this avoidance is mutual. If the two happen to meet on a path, the woman will step off it and stand with her back turned until he has gone by, or perhaps if it is more convenient, he will move out of the way. At Vanua Lava, in Port Patteson, a man would not follow his mother-in-law along the beach, nor she him, until the tide had washed out the footsteps of the first traveler from the sand. At the same time, a man and his mother-in-law may talk to each other from a distance. 

A man does not avoid his father-in-law, nor does a woman avoid hers. A man does not avoid his wife’s brother, but he will not sleep with him. He also does not avoid his son’s wife or his own wife’s sister. Boys and girls who are engaged generally avoid one another, but this is through shyness rather than by rule. In cases where the persons mentioned above do not avoid one another, they are careful to show respect by not taking anything from above someone's head or stepping over the legs of a father-in-law or a wife’s brother. It is disrespectful at all times for a young man to take anything from above an older man’s head, for there is something naturally sacred—<term>rongo</term> <note>a term implying something is set apart, forbidden, or sacred</note>—about the head, and no one will take the liberty of stepping over the legs of anyone except a brother or an intimate friend. To avoid mentioning a name shows a lower degree of respect than avoiding a person. A man who sits and talks with his wife’s father will not mention his name, much less his...

# Kinship and Marriage Connections

...his wife’s mother’s name. A man will not speak his wife’s brother’s name, but he will say his wife’s sister’s name, as she has no formal social status relative to him. A woman will not say her husband’s father’s name, although she does not have to avoid him physically; however, she will never, under any circumstances, speak the name of her daughter’s husband. Two people whose children have married each other—who are known as *gasala* <term>gasala: parents-in-law of the same couple</term>—will not speak each other’s names. 

This caution regarding names extends to the use of the name itself, or even any part of it, in ordinary conversation. On one occasion, a man spoke to me of his house as a "shed" <note>original: *paito*</note>. When I did not understand, he went and touched the house with his hand to show what he meant. When I still seemed confused, he looked around to make sure no one was nearby and whispered—not the actual name of his son’s wife, but a respectful substitute for her name: *amen Mulegona* <note>meaning "the one who is with Mulegona," his son</note>. Her real name was Tawurima, which means "Back of the House" <note>original: Hind-house</note>. 

Thus, referring to the Mota family tree given on page 38, a man named Leveveg could not use the common words *mate* (to die) or *qoe* (pig), because of his son-in-law’s name, Matevagqoe. Another man, Virsal, could not use the common words *panei* (hand) or *tutun* (hot) because of his wife’s brother’s name; he could not even use the number *tuwale* (one), because it was part of his wife’s cousin’s name. 

To deal with the difficulty caused by this limited vocabulary, a word might be used slightly incorrectly, such as calling a "house" (*ima*) a "shed" (*paito*). Or a knife might be called a "cutter" and a bow a "shooter." However, there is also a specific set of words kept for this very purpose. Using these instead of the common words is called to *un* <term>un: the practice of using substitute vocabulary to avoid taboo names</term>. For example, the *un* words used in the cases mentioned above would be *karwae* instead of *qoe* (pig), *saproro* for *mate* (to die), *lima* for *panei* (hand), and *val* for *tuwale* (one) <note>These substitute words often preserve older linguistic forms or links to other dialects</note>. The natives themselves explain this avoidance of both the person and the name as stemming from a feeling of shyness and respect—a certain "inward trembling."

# Reserve in the New Hebrides

...which they say prevents them from mentioning their own names as well. To blurt out a name is seen as taking an improper liberty; avoiding its use shows delicate respect, and people will often extend this respect to more distant relatives rather than applying it too strictly. When a local person is asked the name of someone else, they will often turn to a bystander who answers for them, and the explanation is provided in a single word: *qaliga* <term>qaliga: a Mota term for a relative by marriage subject to avoidance taboos</term>. Respect is also shown in Mota by using a dual pronoun <note>a grammatical form referring to exactly two people</note> when addressing or speaking of a single person. For instance, "Where are you two going?" is asked of a *qaliga*, as if both husband and wife were present.

In the New Hebrides, the practice is much the same. On Lepers’ Island <note>original: "Lepers’ Island," now known as Ambae</note>, a man and his mother-in-law may speak to each other, but they will not approach one another; when he speaks to her, she turns away. A mother-in-law or father-in-law does not mind using the name of a son-in-law or daughter-in-law when speaking about them to others, but they cannot use the name when addressing them directly. When a woman calls to her son-in-law, she addresses him as *mim* (the plural form of "you"). When she sends a message to him, she uses his name but phrases it in the third person: "They want *Tanga* to go to them," which actually means, "I want *Tanga* to come to me." 

A daughter-in-law does not avoid her father-in-law; a man will send his wife with messages to his father. However, a man will never speak the name of his wife’s brother. When speaking of him, he says, "my brother-in-law"; when speaking to him, he uses "you" in the plural. If he meets him on a path, he turns aside and asks, "Where are you (plural) going?" In this specific case, it appears the name is never spoken at all. Generally, the reserve among relatives by marriage is much less strict than the reserve between brothers and sisters. No one will step across another person's legs or reach over their head to take something—especially if it is a brother's head. Such actions are considered a serious sign of disrespect. 

In the neighboring island of Araga (Pentecost), social interaction between parents-in-law and their children-in-law is very little restricted. The main, if not the only, linguistic reserve is practiced by engaged couples before the payment of the bride-price <note>original: "giving of property for the girl"</note> is complete; this practice is called *lalag*.

## CHAPTER III.

### SOCIAL REGULATIONS. CHIEFS.

It has been shown that the social organization in these Melanesian islands is not based on tribes. It will have been observed, then, that there can be no political system held together by the power of tribal chiefs. However, chiefs do exist and still hold significant status and power on most islands, though perhaps they are never quite as important to the local people as they appear to European visitors, who bring with them the conviction that "savage" peoples are always ruled by chiefs.<insert>/</insert> A trader or other visitor looks for a chief and finds exactly what he expects to see. In this way, a very minor individual might come to be called—and to call himself—the "king" of his island; naturally, his reputation among his own people is greatly boosted by the status white people give him. 

Furthermore, the policy of naval commanders to hold local chiefs responsible for their people's behavior, and to treat them as if they had significant authority, definitely increases their standing; this outcome is not necessarily a bad thing.<insert>/</insert> In reality, the power of chiefs has traditionally rested upon the belief in their supernatural power <note>The author is referring to *mana*, a central concept of spiritual efficacy in Melanesian culture.</note> derived from the spirits or ghosts with whom they communicated. As this belief has faded—for example, in the Banks Islands some time ago—the position of a chief has tended to become less clear. Since this belief is now being generally eroded, a new type of leadership must emerge if a period of anarchy is to be avoided.<insert>/</insert> It is probably best to begin with accounts of a chief’s power and governance in the Solomon Islands, the Banks Islands, and the New Hebrides, as provided by the locals themselves.

<summary>This page introduces the concept of Melanesian chieftainship, explaining that while "chiefs" exist, their power is traditionally rooted in supernatural influence rather than a tribal political structure, and is often exaggerated by European visitors.</summary>
<keywords>social regulations, chiefs, Melanesian politics, Solomon Islands, Banks Islands, New Hebrides, supernatural power, mana, European influence</keywords>

#### Power of Chiefs

...of those groups respectively, who well knew what they were speaking about. A Florida <note>Florida Island is now known as Nggela in the Solomon Islands.</note> *Vunagi* <note>local term for chief</note> kept order in his place, directed common operations and industries, represented his people with strangers, presided at sacrifices, and led in war. He inflicted fines and would order anyone to be put to death. At Saa in Malanta <note>now Malaita</note>, the chief, *Maelaha*, holds his position by virtue of descent; a remarkable difference exists in many points between these people and Melanesians generally. The people work in his gardens, plant for him, and build a house or canoe for him at his word. He inflicts fines and can order a man to be put to death. In the Banks Islands, the *Tavusmele* or *Etrusmel* <note>titles for high-ranking individuals in the graded society</note> in former days kept order, gave commands about the common concerns of the place, and arranged difficulties with neighboring villages. He could order an offender (one, for example, who had bewitched or poisoned another) to be put to death or to pay a fine of pigs. In Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae in Vanuatu</note>, the *Ratahigi* <note>chief</note> commands or forbids in such matters as fishing, voyaging, and building; he can order an offender to be shot or clubbed, or to pay a fine of pigs. In each of these cases, it may be added that the chief has with him young men who have attached themselves to him and carry out his commands, and that the chief has no more property in or dominion over land than any other man. Further details as to the position and power of chiefs in the various islands will be given hereafter.

A point of difference between the Polynesian and Melanesian sections of the Pacific peoples is the conspicuous presence in the former, and the no less conspicuous absence in the latter, of native history and tradition. In the Melanesian islands, with one notable exception, the researcher seeks in vain for antiquity. The memory of the past perishes quickly where all things soon pass away, where every building soon decays, where life is short, and no marked change of seasons makes people count by longer measures of time than months. While anyone lives who remembers some famous man of the past, his fame lingers, but it dies with that personal remembrance. A man's ancestry goes back only as far as living memory extends; historical tradition can hardly be said to exist...

### Social Regulations

Historical records of where people originated are generally scarce. It is true that in Motlav <note>Motalava</note>, part of Saddle Island <note>Mota Lava</note> in the Banks Islands, the people who now live on the islet of Ra and the opposite coast know where their families came from—neighboring islands such as Mota, Vanua Lava, or other parts of Saddle Island. However, they say it was only recently that they moved to their current location. In Araga (Pentecost Island in the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>), they show their original ancestral seat at Atabulu, a village that still exists and is held in high respect. However, what little history remains—supported by a multitude of grave stones—is lost in the legend attached to a sacred, wing-shaped stone lying in the village square. It is called *Vingaga*, meaning "Flyer with webbed wings," and represents a figure named Vingaga who supposedly floated to shore in a canoe and founded the town. People, called *ata* <note>original: *ata*; person/people</note>, gathered and lived with him, called *bulu* <note>original: *bulu*; to be together</note>; after some time, he flew back to heaven. Ancient house sites, raised perhaps a yard above the ground, can be seen at Atabulu and nearby Anwalu, with stones marking the graves of forgotten chiefs. In Maewo, great heaps of stones mark the graves of great men of ancient times, the likes of whom have not been seen lately. In Motlav, near a famous and enormous *natu* tree <note>original: *natu*; a type of fruit-bearing tree, *Burckella obovata*</note>, there is a house-mound five feet high where no houses now stand. Men say it was passed down from ancestors to the last man whose house stood upon it; this is a rare local equivalent of the *yavu* <note>Fijian term for an ancestral house-foundation</note> of a high-ranking Fijian family.

The remarkable exception to this lack of history or tradition is found at Saa in Malanta <note>now Malaita in the Solomon Islands</note>. This history is so remarkable and characteristic of native life that the story must be told at length. The larger and principal part of the current inhabitants of "Saa by the sea" <note>original: *Saa ani menu*</note> came from "Inland Saa" <note>original: *Saa haalu*</note>, which is not very far off, eleven generations ago. The migration took place under the following circumstances: there were four brothers at the ancient Saa, of whom the eldest was the chief. Two were named Pau-ulo: the eldest was Pau-ulo *paina* <note>original: *paina*; the Great</note>, and the second was Pau-ulo *oou* <note>original: *oou*; the Champion</note>.

***

<margin>Mr. Fison writes, "The higher the house-mound, the higher its occupant's rank: 'their house-mound is high' <note>original Fijian: *sa cere na nodra yavu*</note> is still used to express that a family is of high rank." The *yavu* is described as the ancestral town-lot on which the house is built.</margin>

### III. History of Saa

The two youngest brothers had the same name: Ro Ute, also known as *oo'u* <note>original: *seu oo’u*. The footnote explains this title refers to "Bonito-gutter champions," a term for a hero, favorite, or fine fellow</note>. The chief, Pauulo Paina, was a quiet man, but the two youngest brothers, assisted by the second-born brother, were constantly fighting and damaging their neighbors' property. All of Pauulo Paina’s money <note>This refers to traditional shell money used for fines and social transactions</note> was spent paying compensation for the injuries they caused and in making peace. Finally, he told them he had to leave them and go away. 

The neighboring people, however, were determined to put an end to their troubles. They gathered their forces and began to surround the village of Saa as night fell. Before the circle was complete, the people of Saa realized they were in danger. They gathered their women and children and escaped undetected and unheard in the darkness, carrying three drums with them. These drums remained at the current village of Saa within the memory of old men who are still alive. 

Once they were clear of the enemy and safe outside their lines, they realized they had left behind a bunch of areca nuts <note>Often called betel nuts; they are chewed as a stimulant</note>. Pauulo Paina had already taken some from the bunch to chew with his betel leaves. This was dangerous, as the nuts would provide the enemy with the means to cause his death through charms <note>This refers to sympathetic magic, where an item a person has touched or consumed—"leavings"—can be used by a sorcerer to cast a lethal spell</note>. 

The two brothers named Ute agreed that one of them must go back for the nuts to save their elder brother, even if it cost him his life. The younger of the two took the risk upon himself because he was the youngest. By now, the enemy had completely surrounded the village, but it was still dark. Knowing nothing of the escape, they sat waiting for dawn to begin their attack. The young Ute took a seat among them, pretending to be part of their group. After a while, he told them he would sneak into the village to see if the people of Saa were still safely in their houses and could be taken by surprise. 

In this way, he passed through to the empty village. He climbed the palm tree using a rope around his feet, gathered all the remaining nuts on the tree, and as he climbed down, he twisted the stem so violently that when his feet touched the ground, it split into four and fell onto a house with a crash. Hearing the sound, the enemy thought the people of Saa were not yet asleep and remained still. Ute managed to pass back through their lines undetected with his nuts and rejoined his friends. Thus they escaped and climbed down toward the coast.

### Chiefs

When they reached a fork where the path divided, Pauulo Paina made a speech, declaring that no fighters, bullies, thieves, or sorcerers <note>original: "wizards"</note> were to follow him. One party then branched off with Pauulo Oou; further down, a second split occurred, so that in the end, three settlements were formed by people who considered themselves relatives. 

The inhabitants of what is now Saa ani menu welcomed the fugitives who were with Pauulo Paina, and his descendants in the male line have been the hereditary chiefs ever since <note>The eleven generations from Pauulo to the current chiefs are kept in memory by reciting their successive names during sacrifices.</note>. The descendants of the original inhabitants are now few in number and belong to the lower social classes, but they are still the legal owners of the land. It never occurred to the Saa immigrants to seize the land from them; the newcomers—even the chiefs—remain landless, except for the small amount of land that has been given or sold to them. They have always been allowed whatever land they needed for their gardens and have been satisfied with that. When the migration first happened, there was no great difference in their speech, and there is still no difference in their vocabulary today; however, the older race speaks very slowly and can still be distinguished by that slow habit of speech.

In Saa, and in the two other settlements founded by the refugees from the ancient Saa, there is a family of chiefs with a known history and a system of descent through the male line. All members of that family are, in a sense, born as chiefs. The eldest son succeeds to his father's position as the principal chief unless he is judged incompetent. If he turns out to be a bad or immoral man, he loses respect and power, and his brother gradually replaces him. Sometimes a man will retire because he recognizes his own unfitness <note>At the time of writing this, there were three chiefs of high rank at Saa. The acting chief was Dorawewe, but he is only the third son of the late head chief. The son and heir of the eldest son was not yet an adult; while he was respected for his birth, he had little power, especially because he had a bad character and was known for chasing women, so he did not gain personal respect. Watehaaodo—the young man’s maternal uncle and a member of the chief's family himself—was his guardian and was therefore an important man. It should be observed that this established a particularly close relationship...</note>. The chief's power, therefore, [is determined by both birth and character.]

### III. The Hereditary Element

In Saa, a chief's power comes from his birth and his personal qualities, rather than from his closeness to supernatural beings or his knowledge of magic. He may possess these traits—and in fact, he almost certainly will—but if someone, like Dorawewe today, performs sacrifices for the family, he does so not because he is the chief, but because the specific knowledge of how to perform the ritual was passed down to him. Similarly, when a chief places a curse in the name of a *lio'a* <note>original: "powerful ghost"</note> to forbid an action under penalty of death, he imposes these taboos because of his ancestral connection with that *lio'a*. He inherits wealth from his father and increases it through the fines he imposes and the gifts he receives from the people; however, no amount of wealth or success in war could make a man a chief in Saa if he were not born into the chiefly family.

The hereditary principle is also present in the succession of chiefs on other islands, though it is not always as influential as it might seem. A story to be told later illustrates how a man becomes a chief in Santa Cruz. The most prominent chief in Florida at the time Europeans first encountered the island was Takua of Boli; it is safe to say that his status was never as high in the eyes of the local people as it was in the eyes of foreign visitors. He was not a native of Florida, but of Malaita <note>original: "Mala"</note>, and his greatness originated from a victory in which he played a leading role as a young man, when a confederation of enemies attacked the people of Ta na ihu in Florida while he was staying there. His reputation for *mana* <note>spiritual or supernatural power</note> was established then. From that point on, as a member of the powerful Nggaombata family, along with his brothers Sauvui and Dikea, his—

This shows that in the native mind, a chief is essentially a warrior. It is customary in both Saa and Arosi (on San Cristoval) to adopt a boy who shows promise as a strong warrior into the chief’s family by purchasing him. He is then raised to be the town's champion and fighting man. I remember seeing such a person at Ubuna in Arosi: he was a dwarf whom his purchasers had mistaken for a remarkably strong and sturdy child, when he was actually much older than they realized. He turned out to be a true *mwaraba* <note>a champion or warrior</note> who refused to use a spear any shorter than those used by full-grown men.

# Chiefs

Thus, according to a native account of the matter, “the origin of the power of chiefs, *vunagi* <note>original: vunagi; a chief in the Florida Islands</note>, lies entirely in the belief that they have communication with powerful ghosts, *tindalo* <note>original: tindalo; ancestral spirits or ghosts of power</note>, and possess that *mana* <note>spiritual or supernatural power</note> through which they are able to bring the power of the *tindalo* to bear.” A chief would pass on his knowledge of how to approach and use the power of the *tindalo* to his son, his nephew, or his grandson, to whom he also bequeathed his possessions as much as possible. In this way, he was able to transfer his power to a chosen successor among his relatives, and a semblance of hereditary succession appeared.

Once a man’s position was obtained in this manner, his own character and success enhanced it, while weakness and failure caused him to lose it. Public opinion supported his claim to general obedience, alongside the dread universally felt regarding the *tindalo* power backing him. For example, if he imposed a fine, it was paid because his authority to do so was recognized, and because it was firmly believed that he could bring calamity and sickness upon those who resisted him; as soon as any considerable number of his people began to lose faith in his *tindalo*, his power to impose fines was shaken. 

However, a chief also had a band of retainers around him—mostly young men, some from different parts of the island and from various *kema* <note>original: kema; maternal clans or social divisions</note>. These men hovered around him, living in his canoe house, where they were always ready to do his bidding. They fought beside him and for him, executed his orders for punishment or plunder, received a share of his wealth, and did everything they could to please him so they might grow great and wealthy alongside him. If they were strangers to the area, they would marry and settle around him. Thus, a chief and his retainers were by no means always the representatives of the people over whom they ruled, and those people sometimes suffered for the group's misdeeds <margin>1. ### Chiefs in Florida.

The system of fining was a very active one. A chief forbids certain actions under the penalty of a fine, which is a form of <term>taboo</term> <note>original: taboo; a sacred prohibition or ban</note>. He orders anyone who has done wrong or who has offended him to pay a specific sum of money to him. For example, Takua imposed a heavy fine on a man who had proposed to marry someone within the prohibited degrees of kinship <note>The "prohibited degrees" refer to rules against marrying within one’s own maternal clan or close family circle</note>. The offender had to hire an advocate to state his case discreetly, apologize, and beg for a reduction of the fine. 

To collect the fine, the chief sends women or boys. These messengers sit at the man’s door and *dae* <note>original: dae; to dun or persistently demand payment by one's presence</note> him until he pays. If he refuses, the chief sends his retainers to destroy or carry away his property. It is evident that a chief with good sense, energy, and character will use his power, on the whole, to the great advantage of the people. However, the abuse of a chief's power is naturally common, resulting in oppression, the seizing of land and property, increasing his collection of trophy heads, and gaining a terrifying reputation. For example, a man who had a private enemy would give money to a chief to have him killed, as someone did not long ago to Dikea. Dikea would then send one of his young men to kill the enemy. But sometimes the intended victim would learn of his danger and send even more money to the chief to save his life. Dikea would take both sums of money and then do as he pleased.

The power of a chief naturally diminished in old age due to inactivity, stinginess, and a loss of reputation. To the credit of the people, his power also faded if he did something they considered to be wrong—such as when Takua married the daughter of a woman who was already his wife. In any case, there was always someone ready to gradually take the place of a leader whose influence was waning. A chief who expected his death would prepare his son, nephew, or a chosen successor...

He said he could have the man killed easily and it would cost him only a trifle to get it done, but to catch a man and keep him captive for ten months would be very difficult and very expensive. 

Things have now changed in Florida. Dikea of Ravu accused two men of taking scraps of his food to use in a magical charm against him. The men fled to Olevuga. Dikea sent money to Lipa, the chief of that place, to have them killed, but Lipa sent the money back. Dikea then sent money to Tambukoru of Honggo, asking him to attack Olevuga; that chief refused the request but kept the money anyway.

Without a chief, a village would fall apart.¹

The very significant role played in the native life of the Banks Islands by the secret societies—which will be described later, such as the *Suqe* <note>A prestigious male society where men advanced through ranks by providing feasts and money</note> and the *Tamate* <note>A society associated with "ghosts," often used to enforce social taboos</note>—has always made it difficult to see the kind of power one would expect a chief to exercise. Any man whose influence was notable was certainly high-ranking in these societies, and it would be completely inconsistent with the social customs of the people for a man with an insignificant position in the *Suqe* to have any considerable power. Because of this, missionaries working in these islands have hardly recognized "chiefs" as such, though traders have claimed to find "chiefs" and "kings." When Mala, many years ago, forbade the use of bows, it was understood that he did so through the power he held in all the secret societies.

### III. Chiefs in Banks Islands

...in Vanua Lava and Mota. Still, there was a name meaning "chief," *etvusmel* or *tavusmele*. A native of Motlav who lived for some weeks on the island of Florida <note>also known as Gela in the Solomon Islands</note>, in the district where Takua was considered a great chief, testified that he saw no great difference between that *vunagi* <note>chief</note> and the *etvusmel* of his own home¹. 

The succession of the *Etvusmel* is declared by him to have been from father to son for as long as can be remembered. This is an important point to notice, as family descent normally follows the mother's line. It is also said that the chief was always of the "great clan" or kin, the *vere liwoa* <note>literally "great group"</note>, an expression which also requires explanation. 

The explanation is that in practice—just like the inheritance of property and the passing down of religious and magical rites—a man always tried, as much as he could, to put his son into his own position. A rich and powerful man would secure a high rank in the *Suqe* <note>a prestigious male society where men advanced through ranks by providing feasts and money</note> for his son during his very early years. Thus, the great man’s son would succeed to his position and become, to some extent, an hereditary chief. 

The father and the son would always belong to different "sides of the house" <note>because the son belongs to his mother's clan, not his father's</note>. On the island of Florida, the chiefs were generally from the *kema* <note>maternal clan</note> which happened to be the most numerous at the time. Similarly, in the Banks Islands—where there are only two main social divisions, and each becomes more numerous in alternate generations—the chief man was regularly found on the most powerful side of the house. Thus, it can be said that the succession of *Etvusmel* at Motlav has been from father to son for as long as can be remembered, and it will continue to be so, though with less influence than in the past. Besides those who were truly chiefs, many men were called "great men" and had considerable influence in their villages; these were men who had been...

A man’s charms and amulets made him a great warrior, and his spells and sacred stones caused his pigs and yams to multiply, enabling him to pay for his advancement in the society. The cleanliness and order of a Banks Islands village are no longer what they once were, as the authority of these "great men" has decreased with the growing education of the younger generation.

In the northern New Hebrides <note>now part of Vanuatu</note>, the position of a chief is more prominent—though perhaps only because the first Europeans to visit those islands always assumed such men were very important people. A man of high rank in the **Suqe**, or a successful leader in war, held authority in his village in the northern part of Aurora <note>modern-day Maewo</note>, but he does not seem to have had a specific title as a "chief." 

In Araga <note>Pentecost Island</note> and Omba <note>Lepers' Island, now Ambae</note>, the remarkable title for a chief is ***Ratahigi***. This is the same word used for "mother" on those islands and is undoubtedly identical to the Mota word *ratasiu*, meaning "brothers" <note>original: *ratasiu*</note>. The likely reason for using a word meaning "brotherhood" or "sisterhood" as the term for "mother" has already been suggested (page 28); its use to designate a chief certainly seems to indicate that the chief is viewed as the representative of the brotherhood—the kin or clan. 

As has been pointed out, in societies where there are two distinct clans and a son does not belong to his father’s clan, it is natural for each clan’s influence to fluctuate. Because one clan may be more numerous in one generation and the other in the next, leadership often alternates. As a son succeeds his father, one belonging to this clan and the next to that, each in turn belongs to whichever clan is most powerful at the time. Consequently, people say that chiefs are hereditary—with a son succeeding a father or a nephew succeeding an uncle—as a general matter of fact, though not by a strict rule of law. The son does not strictly inherit the office of chief; instead, if the father can arrange it, he inherits what *grants* chieftainship: his father’s ***mana***, his charms, magic songs, sacred stones and ritual tools, his knowledge of how to communicate with spiritual beings, and his physical property. The current chief will teach his son his knowledge of the supernatural...

Several years ago, **Mairuru**, the chief of **Walurigi**, was a very influential man. It was immediately understood that a Christian education—which excluded the belief in and practice of ***mana*** <note>spiritual power or efficacy</note>—disqualified the boy from succeeding his father as chief. If this son had settled in his father’s village before the old man died, he would undoubtedly have inherited some of his property and social status, but he was away. 

When **Mairuru** died without an obvious successor, a certain man tried to take his place. He entered the late chief’s sacred retreat, his ***tavleu***, where the chief used to communicate with the ***vui*** <note>spirits</note>, and he claimed that he heard someone whistle to him there. He also told the people that later that night, he felt something land on his chest. He took it in his hands and found it was a stone shaped like the reproductive organs of a highly valued type of pig¹. Then, he claimed, **Mairuru** himself appeared to him and gave him the ***mana***—the magic chant—with which he was to use the stone to produce an abundance of those pigs. 

When he showed the stone, the people believed his story. However, in the end, nothing resulted from his ***mana***, and **Mairuru** ultimately had no successor. It appears, therefore, that on **Lepers' Island** <note>modern-day Ambae</note> and in **Araga** <note>modern-day Pentecost Island</note>, as elsewhere, the true foundation of a chief's power is the belief in the ***mana*** he possesses, along with—
