## CHAPTER IV.

### PROPERTY AND INHERITANCE.

In the nature of property and the laws of inheritance, there is hardly any difference to be found across the Melanesian islands discussed here. In all of them, it may be said that property consists of land and personal possessions. There is a specific distinction between land that has been inherited and land that has been cleared from the wild <note>original: "reclaimed from the waste"</note>. Furthermore, there is no strictly communal property in land <note>meaning land owned collectively by the whole community without individual or family rights</note>. For both landed and personal property, the traditional right of inheritance belongs to the sister's children <note>a matrilineal system where a man's heirs are his nephews and nieces through his sister, rather than his own children</note>, except in the very unusual case of Saa, and instances where children inherit property that their father acquired for himself.

The land may be considered everywhere to be divided into three parts: (1) the town lots; (2) the garden ground; and (3) the bush <note>wild, uncultivated forest</note>. In Florida <note>Nggela Islands</note>, these are (1) *Na Komu*, (2) *Na Matanga*, (3) *Na Leiau*; in Santa Cruz, (1) *Matalia*, (2) *Nabalo*, (3) *Nabaneqabo*; in Mota, (1) *O Vanua*, (2) *O Utag*, (3) *O Mot*; in Lepers' Island <note>Ambae</note>, (1) *A Vanue*, (2) *A Labute*, (3) *A Labute virogi*, which in Araga <note>Pentecost Island</note> are (1) *Vanua*, (2) *Lolgae*, (3) *Ute rono*. These categories correspond to the *Yavu*, the *Qele*, and the *Veikau* of Fiji^1. Of

---

^1 Land ownership <note>original: "tenure"</note> in Fiji has been described by the Reverend Lorimer Fison in a paper printed in the *Journal of the Anthropological Institute*, February 1881, summarized as follows: "The ownership of land is distinctly tribal, and the title is held by all full-born members of the tribe. The land is of three kinds: the *yavu* or town lot, the *qele* (pronounced *ngele*) or farmable <note>original: "arable"</note> land, and the *veikau* [forest]..."

<summary>This chapter introduces the uniform systems of property and inheritance in Melanesia, highlighting a matrilineal succession model where nephews inherit from their maternal uncles and land is categorized into residential, agricultural, and wild areas.</summary>

<keywords>property rights, inheritance, land tenure, matrilineal succession, Florida Islands, Santa Cruz, Mota, Fiji, Lorimer Fison, Melanesian customs</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of land ownership, focusing on the distinction between uncultivated "bush" and private garden land, as well as the limits of a chief's authority regarding property.</meta>

Of these three divisions of the land, the bush—the uncleared forest—is not considered private property. As far as I am aware, the natives do not fix any specific limits to define which part of the bush belongs to a particular district or group of villages where they live, though they would likely resent anyone cutting down trees too close to their own grounds. 

The gardens and the village sites are all held as private property and pass through inheritance. Therefore, every piece of land has an owner at any given time who holds it as his share of the family property; however, he cannot sell or transfer it <note>original: "alienate"</note> as if it were simply his own private possession. 

No matter how powerful chiefs may be in certain places, they have no more property rights over the land or more authority over it than any other man. They often use their power tyrannically to drive away the owners of gardens they want, and they are quite willing to exploit the common European belief that a chief is the "owner of the soil" by accepting payment for land that is not actually theirs to sell. However, the true ownership of every piece of land is remembered and will be asserted when the opportunity arises. The remarkable case of the landless chiefs at Saa (page 50) shows how firmly the right to land property is established. 

Before the arrival of Europeans, the sale of land was not unknown—at least at Saa—but it was certainly uncommon. Lately, especially in the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>, much land has been sold to Europeans. Some of these sales were honest and effective, while others were mere transactions where the "seller’s" only title to the land was their willingness to receive some calico and guns. In a legitimate sale, the consent of everyone who has an interest in the property must be obtained, and the exact boundaries of each parcel of land must be defined. Then, the value of each piece of land and every fruit tree must be determined, and the claim of—

---

> —or forest. The *reikau* <note>Fijian: forest/wilderness</note> is common to all members of a community, but the *yavu* <note>Fijian: house site/foundation</note> and the *qele* <note>Fijian: arable soil/land</note> are divided and subdivided. Each owner, however, holds the land for the household to which he belongs; the household holds it for the clan, the clan for the tribe, the tribe for the community, and the community for future generations <note>original: "posterity"</note>. Each generation only has the right to use the land and its fruits <note>term: "usufruct" — the legal right to use and enjoy the advantages of another's property without destroying it</note> and cannot sell or transfer it <note>original: "alienate"</note>. The chiefs have overridden this rule, but most unjustly.' This description applies to the islands west of Fiji, with the important distinction that these islands lack a tribal structure.

every single individual involved has been consulted and satisfied. A fruit tree planted on another person's land, with their consent, remains the property of the person who planted it and of his heirs. ¹ It is also important to observe that property—whether in the villages or in the gardens—is not held in large sections corresponding to the social divisions used for marriage (the various kinship groups or clans, such as the *kema* of Florida, the *vere* of Mota, or the *wai rung* of Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae Island</note>). Instead, all these holdings are intermixed. It is likely that during the original formation of each settlement, the various divisions of the people worked together to clear their gardens; as it stands now, families have formed within those divisions, and the land is held by these individual families. Sons work in the gardens of their fathers, even though the sons belong to a different kinship group than their fathers. <note>In these matrilineal societies, children belong to their mother's clan, meaning they are technically not the "kin" of their father.</note> It is unlikely that there is any family or married couple in which at least two different kinship groups do not have a shared interest in the land.

It is truly remarkable how similar the nature of property rights is across the Solomon Islands, the Banks' Islands, and the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note> regarding land reclaimed from the wild bush. In all these places, a similar effect has been produced: a growing tendency for a son to inherit his father's property, rather than the traditional right of inheritance passing through the mother’s line. This will be shown, along with the very general agreement on the nature of landed property and its inheritance, as the subject is treated in detail with examples from the various island groups—beginning with Florida in the Solomon Islands and passing eastwards through Santa Cruz and the Banks' Islands to the New Hebrides.

In Florida, the house sites in the *komu* <term>village or cluster of houses</term>, like the gardens of the *matanga* <term>cultivated land</term>, are hereditary property; and, though there do

# Property and Inheritance.

Although there do not appear to be any ancient village sites currently occupied, these old sites are well remembered and their owners are known. Members of the various *kema* <gloss>clans or kinship groups</gloss> who live intermixed on their property in the village also have their gardens intermixed in the *matanga* <gloss>garden land</gloss>. Because a village is not inhabited by a single local tribe, it naturally happens that some villagers have no property of their own in the village or in the neighboring garden grounds. In these cases, their neighbors accommodate them with what they need. 

Ownership of *matanga* property is never held absolutely by an individual, but rather by the *kema*. It is viewed as having been originally cleared by the clan; portions are occupied in hereditary succession by families within the *kema* through an original agreement that has now become a legal right. These ancient family lands pass by right to members of the same *kema*—ordinarily the sister's children <note>In this matrilineal society, a man's heirs are his sister's children because they belong to his clan, whereas his own children belong to their mother's clan.</note>. 

The entire *matanga* area near a town is rarely under cultivation at the same time. If a place is deserted, some parts may return entirely to bush, but it is never strictly considered *leiao* <gloss>wild, unowned bush land</gloss>, because its history and ownership are remembered. Near a prosperous village, a man and his sons working with him will often clear a piece of wild bush land and turn it into *matanga*. This land then passes to his sons without question, as it is held to be his own. As long as it is clearly remembered how the land was acquired, it passes from father to son. However, after some time, the original circumstances of the property may be forgotten; then, the nephews of a deceased owner will claim it from his sons, supported by their *kema*. Serious quarrels often arise in this way. 

A chief (*vunagi*) has no more right to property in the *komu* <gloss>village site</gloss> and *matanga* than any other man.<sup>1</sup> If a man plants a coconut tree, an areca palm tree, or another useful tree on a friend's ground, the tree belongs to the planter's son; if the landowner remains friendly, this arrangement will continue without dispute.

---

<sup>1</sup> Dikea, the chief at Ravu, drove away Logana and his family from that place on the pretext that Logana's brother-in-law had set fire to his canoe house. In reality, he did this to gain possession of Logana's *matanga*, which was large and of good quality. The dispossessed family at Olevuga is keeping a close watch on the property, waiting for Dikea's death to reclaim it.

# IV. Personal Property. 63

A man can also plant fruit trees in his own *matanga* <gloss>garden land</gloss> and specifically declare them to be the property of his sons. At his death, the ground will pass to his nephews (his own blood kin <note>In these matrilineal societies, a man's "kin" refers to those of his own clan, such as his sister's children, while his own children belong to their mother's clan.</note>), but his sons will own the trees. However, the people of Florida (Solomon Islands) are very reckless about destroying fruit trees.

The inheritance of personal property in Florida is traditionally handled by the members of the *kema* <gloss>clan or kinship group</gloss>, the relatives of the deceased. These relatives will assemble after a death, and if the deceased was not very wealthy, they will eat all of his pigs and food. A chief will sometimes take whatever he likes, though he has no legal right to do so. Before his death, a man may direct that his canoe should go to his son, and the son will receive it; otherwise, both the son and the nephew will claim it, and the stronger individual will take it. 

A wealthy man’s money is divided among his brothers, nephews, and—if they can manage to get any—his sons. This is a frequent source of quarrels. However, a man’s wife, in anticipation of his death, would often hide a significant amount of his money. After the crowd that gathered for the division of the inheritance had dispersed, she would bring it out for herself and her sons. Chiefs used to hide their money and valuable property and place a *tambu* <gloss>taboo or sacred prohibition</gloss> on the location. Now that the fear of the *tambu* has faded, the young people search for these hoards and take what they find. These customs in Florida may be seen as representative of those in the surrounding Solomon Islands. 

In Saa and its neighborhood, property naturally descends entirely through the patriarchal line <note>In a patriarchal or patrilineal system, inheritance passes from father to son, rather than through the mother's line.</note>. In Santa Cruz, a man’s nephews usually inherit his property—including land, pigs, money, and other items—though sons also inherit in some cases. There, a man also owns property in the form of trees that are not located on his own land.

In the Banks Islands, the town land (the *vanua*) and the garden grounds (the *utag*) are considered private property to the extent that an owner can be identified for every piece. The owner is the person who holds life-long possession of the portion of family land he has inherited. The lands and houses of the two *rere* <gloss>moieties or primary kinship divisions</gloss> are intermingled, and the land is rightfully inherited by the sister’s children. Here, the *utag* is also divided into ancient, hereditary cultivated ground and...

<summary>This page describes the complex rules of inheritance for personal property and land across the Solomon and Banks Islands, highlighting the conflict between matrilineal clan rights and a father's desire to provide for his own sons.</summary>

...land that has been reclaimed from the *mot* <gloss>uncleared forest</gloss> by the present owner or his recent predecessors. In the first case <note>Referring to ancestral land that has been in the family for generations.</note>, the nephews on their mother’s side of the previous owner occupy the ground; each takes the piece he wants for his own garden, and all have a collective ownership of the whole property. 

Land of the second character <note>Land newly cleared from the forest.</note> passes to the children of the man who cleared the forest from it; his own kin <note>In this context, "kin" refers to his maternal relatives, who would normally be his heirs under the matrilineal system.</note> have no claim to it. The children divide it into separate lots and do not hold the property in common in any way. The eldest son will take the oldest plantation, and the youngest will have the latest one that has not yet produced a crop.¹ In this instance, patriarchal succession is firmly established; in the other case, it is beginning to be introduced and has a recognized footing. 

It is common to make arrangements where a man's children succeed him with the consent of the legal heirs. For example, when the father of a man named Woser died, he had held an *utag* <gloss>garden ground</gloss> at Motlav in common inheritance with his brother. Woser gave a pig to his uncle, who then gave up his claim to half of the garden property, which he was not using. The heir of the deceased—and also the prospective heir of the deceased’s brother—was the son of their sister. Woser gave money to this cousin to settle and "quiet" his claim. Because of this, Woser, along with his two brothers and two sisters, took possession of the *utag* as if they had inherited it; that is, they held the whole property in common while maintaining separate individual gardens. 

If a similar transaction were to occur after the death of these current owners (who are not of their father’s kin <note>Because they belong to their mother's clan.</note>), the land would go to their children, who will not be of their father's kin but of their mother’s. In this way, the property will revert to the *veve* <gloss>maternal kinship group or clan</gloss> to which it belongs. Sometimes, before his death, a man begs his brother not to disturb his son in his garden; the brother agrees, and the son takes his father’s place.

Daughters inherit by right equally with sons, but in practice, they tend to transmit the inheritance to their children. As noted in Fiji: "Daughters can hardly be said to inherit land. Land is given *with* them at their marriage, but it is not given *to* them. If they hold it at all, it is only a means of passing the land to their children."—Rev. L. Fison.

# IV. Redemption. Trees. Houses.

The father held the land by right, but the son strictly has no right to it. Therefore, the son gives money to the natural heirs—his father’s sister’s children. In order to make a transaction of this kind secure, the son will place the money for the redemption of the garden upon his father’s corpse when he is laid out for burial. The nephews and heirs of the deceased take the money from their dead *maraui* <gloss>maternal uncle</gloss> in the presence of the assembled people, and they can never afterward deny that they have surrendered their right ^1. If a man’s children are not wealthy enough at the time of his death to redeem the whole *ulag* <gloss>garden plot</gloss>, they redeem only a portion. 

It is part of the acknowledgment of the rights of the sister’s children, and part of the satisfaction for those rights, that they are allowed to take fruit and other produce from the garden for a certain time. This is because these crops were the result of the labor of the deceased, whose heirs are his nephews and nieces of his own kin; however, they will not claim the produce resulting from the new owner’s work. 

Ownership of trees is distinct from ownership of the land, and trees go to the planter’s children. Consequently, in the case of a land sale, there is a great variety of titles for different parcels of ground and different owners for the fruit trees; the knowledge of these details is incredibly minute and accurate. The exact limits of every small piece of property are known, and the value of the right to be settled is discussed and decided by common consent ^2.

The village lots in the *vanua* <gloss>village</gloss>—specifically the house sites, or *tano ima*—are held in the same way. When a young man establishes his own home, he builds on the property of his own kin, such as his mother’s or his maternal uncle’s. It naturally happens that the elder sons...

<header>Property and Inheritance. [CH. IV]</header>

They have left their father’s house upon marriage before his death, or do so sequentially after his death; the youngest son then remains with his mother and keeps the house. In a flourishing village, a new house is built on an old site, which therefore rises over time into something of a mound; however, villages are seldom permanent. When a new village is established, it may occupy an ancient site that has been recently unused—in which case the ownership of the town lots is well remembered—or it may be a new occupation of ground for building. The *vanua* <gloss>village</gloss> at Losalav in Motlav was formed around a house built by the great-uncle of Woser, who gave two *rawe* <note>original: "rawe"; these are highly prized pigs with circular tusks</note> pigs to the owner of the *utag* <gloss>garden land</gloss> for the ground, and thus became the landlord. His daughter afterward, though she received nothing in the way of rent, was treated with respect by the householders because they were not living on property of their own.

Personal property—the highly valued pigs, the money, canoes, ornaments, weapons, and the various implements used in native life—generally goes to the children; however, the rights of the sister’s children <note>the matrilineal heirs</note> are still maintained. When a man dies, his brothers and kinsmen, or *sogoi* <gloss>members of the same lineage</gloss>, will come and carry off his pigs unless the children buy them off. But if a man, before his death, makes a sort of testament or will, *vatavata varvarnanau* <note>literally "an ordering of instruction"</note>, declaring that he gives his property to his children and distributing it, they will not be disturbed in their inheritance. 

A great man often buried quantities of shell money, which was never found. In Lakona, part of Santa Maria, it is said that "a man will hide some of his money; then, if he has a good son who helps him well in his garden or always gives him food, the father will make his hoard known to him so that it may be his; if not, it is gone forever." In that place, a man’s money at his death is carefully distributed in short lengths among his children and his kinsmen, and his pigs are distributed in the same way. The children give money and pigs to the kinsmen so that the children may keep his personal belongings, his land, and his fruit trees, which are then completely surrendered by the kinsmen. <header>iv.] New Hebrides. 67</header>

In particular, his sister’s son has a right to go and take whatever the deceased may have left behind. However, this is generally settled by the payment of a sum of money called <term>tulag</term> <gloss>a compensatory payment to satisfy a claim</gloss>. After this payment is received, no further claims can be made. In such cases, there is very often a suspicion or accusation that poisoning or witchcraft caused the death, for which additional compensation is demanded¹.

In the New Hebrides, the ancient tradition of the sister's son succeeding to his uncle's property appears to be strictly maintained in Araga (Pentecost Island). There, the nephew inherits his uncle's house, garden, and pigs, while the son receives nothing except what his father gave him during his lifetime. Even if a man clears a new garden for himself out of the bush, it must eventually go to his sister's son. 

It is very different, however, on Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae or Aoba</note>, where the rights of the sister's son are barely recognized. In that location, property in the villages and gardens is held by individuals as their own, rather than belonging to the <term>wairung</term> <gloss>the maternal kinship group or clan</gloss>. The town lots are fenced in, so the houses stand within private enclosures. A man's son inherits his house property, but the son will not live in the house as long as his mother and sisters are there, due to the social restrictions on family intercourse mentioned previously. Houses are rebuilt in the same general area, though not always on the exact same spot, and villages are often moved, though the ownership of the ground is always remembered. 

A man's garden ground, or <term>labute</term>, goes to his sons, who arrange how to divide it among themselves unless their father expressed his specific wishes before his death. Women do not inherit land, but they have a right to a share of the produce from their father's gardens; indeed, their brothers are expected to hold the land partly for their sisters' benefit. A man can also create a new garden for himself out of unappropriated ground suitable for cultivation, known as <term>labute virogi</term>—land that is "loose" or not yet tied to a specific owner.

When the traveling party returned and the cause of death was revealed, Wete shot his sister with his gun because her husband was held responsible for his son’s death. The entire event was treated as a matter of course; the woman was not seriously hurt, and Wete remained on the best of terms with his neighbors and relatives.

<header>Property and Inheritance.</header>

and there cannot be any difference between this and his hereditary property. Gardens are all fenced. Fruit trees planted on another man's land remain the property of the planter and his heirs. The rights of kinship are most clearly seen in the inheritance of a man's personal property. Upon a man's death, his sons distribute his pigs, money, and other possessions among the members of his *waivung* <gloss>maternal kinship group or clan</gloss>. A prize pig and a larger share of other goods are given to the sister's son, because his special relationship is highly respected. A man, however, will often make his will before his death, expressing his wishes regarding the distribution of his property. Inheritance is a frequent source of quarrels, and it is natural that personal interest often outweighs established rights when the rightful heirs are not present.

Throughout these islands of Melanesia, there appears to be a remarkable general tendency toward replacing a man's sister's children (and other maternal kin) with his own children as the heirs to his property. This shift seems to begin with property created by the man's own hard work—usually with the help of his sons—such as gardens newly cleared from the forest, his money, his pigs, and his canoes. The traditional right of a man's own maternal kin, especially his sister's sons, to be his heirs—not only to hereditary lands passed down through the clan but also to personal property—is still strongly defended. This is true even on Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae</note>, where the move toward a patriarchal system <note>a system where descent and inheritance follow the father's line</note> has progressed significantly. It is likely that even at Saa <note>a village on the island of Malaita</note>, some traces still survive of what must have been the original customs of that people's ancestors, as well as those of the rest of the Melanesians. It is evident that this newer form of inheritance depends on the recognition of fatherhood. As it sometimes arises when new ground is occupied, this trend may be strengthened by the formation of new settlements after a family has established itself within the larger kinship group.

## CHAPTER V.

### SECRET SOCIETIES AND MYSTERIES.

Nothing is certainly more characteristic of Melanesian life than the presence of societies that celebrate "mysteries" strictly concealed from the uninitiated <note>those who have not been formally admitted to the group</note> and from all women. Members wear a costume with a mask or hat to disguise themselves if they appear during the day; they also use strange cries and sounds to make their presence known when they are hidden from view. In some cases, such as on the islands of Florida <note>now known as Nggela</note> and Aurora <note>now known as Maewo</note>, they make a public display of items said to be the handiwork of ghosts, with whom the members pretend to have been associating. 

Such societies include the *Dukduk* of New Britain (described by Mr. Brown and Mr. Romilly), the *Matambala* of Florida, the *Tamate* of the Banks Islands, and the *Qatu* of the northern New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>. A photograph from New Caledonia shows a figure that can hardly be distinguished from a *tamate* from the Banks Islands, and Mr. Romilly mentions an institution similar to the *Dukduk* in New Guinea. It is clear, therefore, that this institution extends very widely through Melanesia. Even the *Nanga* of Fiji, though different in some respects, cannot be considered entirely distinct from it. Yet, it is remarkable that nothing of the sort has yet been found in Santa Cruz or in the Solomon Islands east of Florida$^1$.

---

# Secret Societies and Mysteries.

The Florida <note>modern name: Nggela</note> mysteries were believed to have been brought from Ysabel <note>Santa Isabel Island</note>, where nothing of that kind has yet been observed. This belief, however, serves to point to a connection with the *Dukduk* of New Britain; a further connection may probably be found in that name. In all these societies, the ghosts of the dead were supposed to be present. In the Banks Islands, their name is "The Ghosts"; in Santa Cruz, a ghost is called *duka*; in Florida, one method of consulting the ghosts of the dead is called *paluduka*. It is very likely, therefore, that in New Britain, the *Dukduk* are also "The Ghosts."

<image-desc>A detailed engraving of a "New Caledonia Masker." The figure is entirely enveloped in a voluminous, layered costume made of dark shaggy fibers or dried grasses. The head is covered by a large, bulbous mask with simplified facial features, including large circular eyes and a wide mouth. The figure holds a long, thin stick or spear in each hand.</image-desc>

->NEW CALEDONIA MASKER.<-

One very important point of difference separates these societies from the *bora* <note>an initiation ceremony for young men</note> of Australia. In the *bora*, the grown youth of the tribe are "made young men" and have some knowledge of the religious beliefs and practices of the elders shared with them. In contrast, grown men and infants, married and unmarried, are equally admitted to the societies of Florida and the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>. While in the Banks Islands it is not customary to admit very young boys, there is certainly no age limit regarding admission. It is undoubtedly the case that where these societies flourish, a youth who has not become a member of one of them does not hold a position of full social equality with the other young men.

The *Nanga* <note>a stone ritual structure and associated secret society</note> appears to be limited to only a part of Viti Levu in Fiji and escaped notice there for a long time. It is therefore reasonable to expect the discovery of many secret societies in Melanesia that have not yet been observed.

<summary>Codrington establishes a linguistic link between various secret societies across Melanesia based on the word for "ghost" and notes that, unlike Australian maturity rites, these societies are often open to males of all ages.</summary>

### v.] Absence of Religious Character.

...who are members; it is also likely that such a young man has no wife. A young man like this has been unable to meet the expense of initiation or of marriage <note>original: "matrimony"</note>. His friends, whether through carelessness or poverty, have allowed him to grow up without making proper provision for him; he remains uninitiated and unmarried for the same reason. However, initiation is by no means a required preliminary step to marriage. 

Given the strict secrecy and solemnity of these mysteries, it is difficult to believe that no religious knowledge is shared during initiation. The outside world of women, children, and the uninitiated—the *matakonokono* <note>literally "those whose eyes were closed"</note>—undoubtedly believed that the initiated members entered into association with the ghosts of the dead. To their ears, the strange cries and terrifying sounds that came from the association's sacred and forbidden lodge, or from the forest when members were out, were more than human; the figures that appeared did not seem to be men. 

Occasionally, an accident would surely make it obvious that a "ghost" was actually a well-known and recognized man; however, the belief was maintained that his disguise was not the work of mortal hands. While someone might shrewdly guess that all the others were just as much neighbors and men as the one whose fall revealed him, it would have been dangerous to express such a thought. It was only when a newcomer <note>original: "neophyte"</note> was admitted into the mysterious grounds that he found only his daily companions there. He learned that there was nothing to be taught to him except how the sounds were produced, how the costumes and decorations were made, and, in some cases, a specific song and dance. No secret articles of belief were revealed, and no secret forms of worship were practiced. The ordinary forms of prayer and sacrifice were performed just as they were elsewhere, though here they were done in connection with these mysteries. There were no forms of worship unique to the society, and no objects of worship that were unknown to those outside the group.

It is also remarkable that, as far as I have been able to determine, there is very little, if anything, that is obscene or morally objectionable, beyond the element of deception <note>original: "imposture"</note>...

<summary>Codrington explains that despite the terrifying sounds and ghostly disguises used by secret societies to awe the uninitiated, these groups lack a truly "secret" religious doctrine or unique form of worship.</summary>

...along with a certain amount of tyranny and intimidation. In some places, the initiates <note>original: "neophytes"</note> had to endure hardships or even tortures; however, these were absent in the Banks' Islands, where these societies are very numerous. The property of the uninitiated was looted, and they themselves were beaten and oppressed when the mystery rituals were active; all order and industry were disrupted. At the same time, vile and immoral excesses <note>original: "hideous and obscene orgies"</note> were absent. A native convert to Christianity might enter his lodge and find nothing there to offend him that he would not also find in the village. A European visitor might enter and find nothing more mysterious to be revealed to him than the hats, dresses, and the tools used for producing unearthly sounds.

The Fijian *nangu* <term>nangu: a sacred stone enclosure used for initiation ceremonies in Fiji</term> as described by Mr. Fison and Mr. Joske—to which the presence of women immediately gives a different character—must be taken as representing these secret societies in that group. It is reasonable to suppose a direct connection in origin between this and those that flourish in the islands further to the west. The institution in Fiji, however, is so subtle <note>original: "little conspicuous"</note> in the life of the people—likely because it is so limited in its distribution—that it escaped the observation of Mr. Fison himself for many years. 

In the Banks' Islands, the *tamate* <term>tamate: literally "ghost" or "dead man," referring to the secret societies and their masked members</term> would very soon be noticed. If no special celebration of the mysteries was being carried out, a visitor would soon become aware that there were retreats near every village frequented by most of his native companions and unapproachable by some. The members of the societies would be proud to show him these retreats and the wonderful works of art they contained. Very few days would pass without the appearance of some masked figures, or the sound of some strange noise or cry. 

In that island group, the number of these societies is surprising: some are very insignificant, local, or recently started by individuals; some are select and respected; and one is found everywhere, acting as the principal and apparently original institution of its kind. In the Northern New Hebrides, this "Great Tamate" of the Banks' Islands is not found, but others of a similar character appear. I have seen a mask and...

# Secret Societies and Mysteries. [Chapter V]

...to believe in their supernatural character. The uninitiated boys from the Banks Islands, while at school on Norfolk Island, heard from their classmates from Florida <note>Florida: The colonial name for the island of Nggela in the Solomon Islands</note> what they had seen, and the sacredness of the <term>salagoro</term> <note>salagoro: the secluded meeting place or lodge of a secret society</note> was lost for them. The secret was revealed many years ago, although in Florida, the power of these mysteries was maintained until Christianity became dominant in the only part of the island where the institution was established.

In the Banks Islands, the <term>tamate</term> <note>tamate: literally "ghost"; refers to both the secret society and the masked figures representing spirits</note> has survived the introduction of Christianity. All belief in the supernatural nature of these associations has long since disappeared. All women and children now know that the *tamate* are simply men dressed in disguises they have made themselves, and that the strange sounds and cries they hear are produced by natural means. However, these societies held such an important place in the social structure of the people that they have maintained their position as social clubs. 

It is not only in the Banks Islands that secrecy and costumes are attractive. The secrecy of the lodges is still maintained; the *salagoro* remains off-limits to women and the uninitiated, and the new member must still undergo a period of probation and seclusion. Furthermore, the authority of the society is still sometimes enforced through the same kind of heavy-handed control used in the old days¹. In truth, the social power of these societies was too deep-seated to be easily broken up, and in the—

***

¹ It was a matter of principle for Bishop Patteson <note>Bishop John Coleridge Patteson (1827–1871): The first Anglican Bishop of Melanesia</note> not to interfere in an arbitrary or dictatorial way with the people's institutions. Instead, he left it to their own sense of right and wrong, and their own understanding of their actions, to decide whether to condemn or tolerate customs that their growing enlightenment might lead them to question. 

Consequently, a doubt arose among his early pupils as to whether it was right for them, as Christians, to remain members of the *tamate* societies, to seek admission into them, or to frequent their lodges. The Bishop suggested that they should inquire and consult among themselves about the true nature of these societies: did they offer worship and prayer to ghosts or spirits? Were they required to take part in anything indecent or cruel? Did membership require a profession of belief or the practice of superstitions unique to the members? 

After consulting with one another, they reported to him that they could not find anything inherently wrong, except for the pretense of associating with ghosts (which had already stopped being taken seriously) and the practice of beating and robbing those who were not initiated. They believed it was entirely possible for them to refuse to participate in these actions and to oppose them. Therefore, the Bishop did not condemn the societies. In the Banks Islands, they continue to exist and, in fact, flourish more than is perhaps desirable.

<page-num>75</page-num>

<header>v.] Banks' Islands. 75</header>

In the absence of any strong political organization, the social status of a member in the largest and most exclusive of these societies has been very significant. Many years ago, I clearly remember how, in the early morning on the island of Mota, a strange cry was heard repeated from every direction—shrill, prolonged, and unmistakable. It was the cry of the <term>tamate</term> <note>original: tamate; literally "ghost," the term for both the society and its masked members</note>. The members of the Great *Tamate* were all out and in possession of the island; <note>original: o ranua we gona; "the country was occupied" or "under restriction"</note>, the country was under their control. No one could move about, and all the business of ordinary life came to a standstill until the society was satisfied. 

Upon inquiry, we were told that the evening before, a man in a fit of anger had taken up his bow. In accordance with the teachings of Bishop Patteson <note>John Coleridge Patteson (1827–1871), the first Anglican Bishop of Melanesia</note> and the authority of the island's leading men, the Great *Tamate* society had forbidden the use of bows and arrows in private quarrels, under penalty of a fine paid to them. On this occasion, the man who had committed the offense hurried to make amends by offering a pig, and everything became quiet again. It is not surprising that membership in such a powerful society should be highly valued and not easily given up.

## I. The Banks Islands

The Banks Islands, along with the neighboring Torres group, are undoubtedly the primary center for these societies. There, they are universally called "The Ghosts" (<term>o tamate</term> in Mota or <term>netmet</term> in the Torres Islands). In the Torres Islands alone, there are a hundred such groups, and every man belongs to four or five of them. The most important society, the <term>tamate liwoa</term> <note>literally "Great Ghost"</note> of Mota, is present everywhere, though in some places it is not as influential as a more exclusive society of local origin. 

Another association is distinguished by its unique dance and differs from the others because it has no permanent lodge or clubhouse; this group, the <term>Qat</term> <note>named after Qat, the central hero-spirit of Banks Islands mythology</note>, is found throughout the Banks Islands but not in the Torres Islands. All these *tamate* associations have a specific leaf or flower as their particular badge. The many distinct varieties of the <term>croton</term> <note>a tropical shrub with brightly colored, variegated leaves</note>, which all have specific native names, provide these leaves. The flowers used are those of the many varieties of hibiscus, which are also specifically named. It is very common to stick flowers in one's hair (<term>rou</term>); the specific part of the head where the flower is placed...

...decorated with the specific flower that identifies a member of that particular *tamate* <note>original: tamate; literally "ghost," the term for both the society and its masked members</note>. Wearing this badge without being a member of the society is considered an offense, and the punishment depends on the power and status of the group that was offended. In the Torres Islands, for example, one of the three major *tamate* societies is called *Nipir*, and its badge is a hibiscus flower worn on the forehead. If a non-member is seen wearing the flower in this way, the society places a bundle of flowers and leaves in a public space; the offender then knows he must pay a fine of one pig. He brings the pig, ties it in the village square, and stands beside it. A member of the society then beats him for his arrogance, after which he must undergo the formal initiation and pay the required entrance fees.

Unlike in Florida <note>Florida Island (Nggela) in the Solomon Islands</note>, no local traditions explain the origins of these societies in the Banks Islands; therefore, they are assumed to be very ancient. One legend tells of a woman who encountered a ghost in a tree. The ghost gave her a figurine wearing the hat and cloak of a *tamate*, which she kept hidden behind a partition in her home. Word spread that she had a marvelous secret, and she allowed men to see it privately for a fee. Once enough men had shared the secret, they took control of it from the woman and built a meeting house (lodge) for themselves. They were taught by the figurine—which was actually a ghost itself—how to make the costume. In this way, they established the first *tamate* association, which has strictly excluded women ever since. This story, however, offers little real insight into how such a widespread institution actually began.

The many smaller associations, which are usually named after birds, are mostly local and are likely more modern. Anyone could start a new society by gathering a group of co-founders and choosing any object that caught their interest as the foundation and symbol of their group. For example, a man who visited Norfolk Island saw a bird there that was unfamiliar to him; upon returning to <term>Mota</term> <note>an island in the Banks group</note>, he founded a society called "the Norfolk Island Bird." Other new groups...

<page-num>77</page-num>
# Banks' Islands. Lodges.
<sig>v.]</sig>

Some of these societies will succeed and flourish, while others will fail; however, the total number of them in the Banks Islands and the Torres Islands must be very large. Three or four might be common to the entire island group, a few may be shared by two or more islands, and the rest are more or less strictly localized. Some societies are exclusive, requiring large entrance fees, and are attended by older men of high social standing; others are inexpensive and easy to join. I think it likely that in places where the Great Tamate <note>The most powerful and prestigious of the secret societies</note> is dominant, all members of the other societies also belong to it and cooperate with it—except for the younger members of the least important groups, whose privacy is relatively less respected.

The lodge, or secret meeting place, of the Great Tamate is called the *salagoro*. These are established in secluded spots, usually among tall trees, near every significant village or group of villages. The path leading to it, where it branches off from the public road, is marked by bright orange-colored fruits placed on reeds, bouquets of flowers, fronds of the *cycas* <note>a palm-like tropical plant</note>, and the traditional *soloi*—taboo signs that forbid entry. These markers are repeated at intervals along the winding path until it opens into the clearing where the building stands. These signs are quite effective at preventing trespassing because they represent the collective power of the association, not because they rely on any specific religious penalty. The location is not considered inherently "sacred" (*rongo* <note>original: rongo; meaning holy or spiritually charged</note>); rather, it is "set apart" (*tapu* <note>original: tapu; the root of the modern word "taboo," meaning restricted by authority</note>) by a recognized power. 

No woman or uninitiated person would ever think of approaching the area. Foreigners, however, are admitted without difficulty—specifically those from distant islands where the society is not known to exist, such as people from the Solomon Islands. If no initiation or special celebration is currently taking place, a visitor will find only a few members present: some who use the lodge as a club for their meals, and newly admitted members whose duty it is to prepare those meals, keep the grounds swept, and remain inside for a fixed number of days. It is quite possible that a coconut will be pointed out to you, representing a member who has been excused from attending in person. The hats and costumes worn during the most recent dance or public ceremony may also be inspected. These hats are truly ingenious, and when they are new, they are...

<page-num>80</page-num>
<header>Secret Societies and Mysteries. [CH. V</header>

This secret was once—or until very recently—not easily revealed. It concerns the apparatus used to produce the peculiar and certainly very impressive sound which outsiders believed to be the cry or voice of the ghosts. This device consists of a flat, smooth stone upon which the base of a palm-leaf fan's stalk is rubbed. The vibration of the fan produces an extraordinary sound, which the performer can adjust in strength and tone at will. When this sound emerged in the stillness of daybreak from the mysterious depths of the *salagoro* <note>original: salagoro; the secluded, sacred meeting place of the secret society</note>, it may well have convinced people of a supernatural presence and power. 

The origin of this invention is told in the following story. Two members of the Great *Tamate* <note>original: Tamate; the name of the secret society, literally meaning "ghosts"</note> in Vanua Lava were walking along the shore when they heard a strange and unearthly sound as they approached a point of land that was a common haunt for ghosts. They found the sound was being made by an old woman sitting on the beach. She was grinding down shells to make money upon a stone; she had figured out how to do her work while also sheltering herself from the sun by using the handle of her palm-leaf umbrella as the stick to hold the shell. The men realized how valuable this discovery would be for their secret rituals, so they attacked and killed the woman and stole both the stone and her umbrella. This apparatus serves the same purpose as the "bull-roarer" <term>bull-roarer</term> <note>a ritual musical instrument made of a slat of wood tied to a cord, which makes a roaring sound when whirled</note>, which is too well known in the Banks Islands to be used for secret mysteries, though it is used for that purpose elsewhere.

To seek admission into any of these societies is called *tiro*. Before admission to the Great *Tamate* can be granted, the candidate or his friends must *usur* <note>make a formal payment or offering</note> with a pig of the highly valued variety called *rawe*. There is also a period of fasting that must be completed. When the candidate is finally admitted, he is brought into the *salagoro* and must deposit money at successive stages of his progress, which are marked by *soloi* <note>stone piles or markers</note> beside the path, until he comes—

<note>This text continues the footnote from the previous page regarding the linguistic connection between masks and hats.</note>
...a mask worn in one of these societies has the same name as the society itself: *tamate*, meaning a ghost. Furthermore, *tamate* has long been established as the local name for any European hat or cap. Therefore, it is more natural to refer to these ritual disguises as "hats" rather than masks; this is also useful to distinguish them from the masks designed to cover the face which are used in other places.

In the village courtyard, there was a group of children—all boys, including some babies carried in their fathers' arms. These were the candidates for admission into the *Salagoro*. We waited for a short time until someone gave a signal, and one of the men let out a long, loud cry with all the strength of his lungs. Then, a strange figure I had seen earlier getting dressed for the occasion came rushing from a path inland. This was the *tamate wasawasa* (the 'harmless ghost') who was to lead the children into the *Salagoro*. He approached with a light, springy step, holding two white rods in his hands which he waved up and down. All you could see of the man were his two legs. On his head was a strange kind of hat or mask—a *tamate*; it is a mask with holes or slits in it for him to see through. Long fringes of bleached coconut leaves covered his body entirely, forming a kind of Inverness cape <term>Inverness cape</term> <note>a sleeveless overcoat with a long cape attached, popular in the 19th century</note> through which his hands poked out. The figure has a very striking appearance because of the peculiar, high-trotting way he runs, which makes his leafy coat fly around him with a rustling noise. He came leaping into the *tinesara* <note>original: tinesara; the open village square or dancing ground</note> over a stone wall with a springy bound and danced round and round the group in the middle. Then, all at once with a shout, he rushed into the midst of them and struck his two white wands together over the heads of the group until they were broken to shreds. One little boy got frightened and ran away, but he was soon brought back. Then the *tamate* retired into the enclosure, and the group walked in a single-file procession around the *tinesara*, where a number of pigs were tied to stakes. Each child gave the pigs a slap; then they all went in single file into the tall enclosure. As we watched them, the same little boy who had been frightened before rushed back out from behind the screen, and after hiding for a moment, jumped up and ran away into the woods, accompanied by a roar of laughter from the crowd. I heard later that he ran all the way home, a distance of some five or six miles. This was only the preliminary ceremony. These children will have to remain in the enclosure for forty or fifty days, until all the money and pigs are paid for the privilege of belonging to this club."—Island Voyage, 1879.

...days <note>This continues the description of the hundred-day seclusion mentioned on the previous page</note>, and after that he must attend to the cooking oven for another hundred days. During his first hundred days, he does not wash and becomes so dirty that when he eventually emerges, he is not recognized; he is so dirty, they say, that he cannot even be seen. In this island <note>referring to Ureparapara</note>, the Great *Tamate* <note>original: Tamate; the "Ghost" society</note>, though it keeps the name, does not even have a *salagoro* <note>original: salagoro; a sacred enclosure or private retreat</note>. Instead, a chamber for initiation is made in the *gamal* <note>original: gamal; the communal men's house</note>, the house of the *Suqe* <note>original: Suqe; a graded social club or rank system</note> Club. The entrance fee is small, and even infants are admitted. 

In the Banks Islands, the lesser societies also have no *salagoro*, whether they are exclusive like the *Oviovi* or minor like the *Meretang*; their lodge is called the *sara* <note>original: sara; a meeting place or open precinct</note>. Women and the uninitiated—the *matawonowono* <note>original: matawonowono; literally "those whose eyes are closed"</note>—are strictly excluded from all these lodges alike. Women may venture to stand near the entrances to the retreats of the lesser clubs, which are often barely secluded from the public road, but the *salagoro* of the Great *Tamate* and the *sara* of the more important societies are very carefully respected. The croton <note>A tropical plant with brightly colored leaves used as a ritual symbol</note> leaves, which serve as the badge of each society, are well known. A member of any society will mark a fruit tree or a garden he wishes to reserve for a specific purpose with such a leaf, and the prohibition will be observed. He has the support of the entire *tamate* society¹ behind him, with whom any offender would have to settle the matter.

For most of the year, the *salagoro* or the *sara* is used as a kind of club. The newly admitted members have the duty of preparing a daily meal, which attracts those who have no other business; it provides a convenient and somewhat prestigious place to relax during the heat of the day. A Western visitor will likely find any man he wishes to see there; he may even find a meal there himself if he wants one. A yam from the *salagoro* oven will be sent to him as a gesture of respect, though no one whose "eyes are still unopened" <note>meaning those who are uninitiated</note> would dare to eat any of it. From time to time, the members rouse themselves...

They spring into activity to make their presence known, attract recruits, impress the people with a sense of their importance, and enjoy a festival. During this time, they begin making new masks and costumes within their lodge, and the solemn sound of the <term>linge tamate</term> <note>original: *linge tamate*; a sacred song or ritual sound</note> warns everyone outside that the mysteries have begun. The land is then said to be "closed" or "forbidden," <term>o vanua we gona</term>, and no one dares to travel along the paths without the risk of being beaten by the <term>tamate</term> <note>original: *tamate*; the masked members acting as "ghosts"</note>. These members take total liberty in seizing whatever they want, raiding gardens and stripping fruit trees for their feasts; furthermore, anyone who has spoken or acted without due respect toward the society will be made to suffer. The "ghosts" in their disguises rush into the villages, chasing the terrified women and children and beating anyone they can catch. The disadvantage of remaining an outsider—one of the <term>matawonowono</term> <note>original: *matawonowono*; literally "those whose eyes are closed," referring to the uninitiated</note>—is made very apparent. 

Many of the smaller societies, composed of men who are also members of the "Great Tamate" (and who have that greater power at their backs), practice the same kind of tyranny. However, there are some societies that do not terrify or beat people, but instead come out simply to show off their finery and dance. It is a beautiful and pleasant scene when two or three figures dance out into the sunshine of the village square. Their heads are concealed in masks shaped like the pointed hoods of Italian <term>becchini</term> <note>original: *becchini*; Italian corpse-bearers or gravediggers, who traditionally wore peaked hoods during times of plague</note>, which come down to a point on the chest. These masks have round eyes painted on the sides and are white, glistening with scarlet seeds and the fresh green of <term>cycas</term> <note>a palm-like tropical plant often used in rituals</note> fronds. Their bodies are hidden in golden-brown cloaks made of sago leaves.

They were adorned with hibiscus flowers and croton leaves, their faces smudged with charcoal, and a leaf held in the mouth, each carrying a stick. Two or three of these wore a <term>tamate</term>—a hat and mask with a long fringe of leaves reaching down to the heels." ...each holding a <term>cycas frond</term> <note>original: *cycas frond*; a leaf from a palm-like cycad tree</note> in each hand, much like a martyr in a painting holds a palm branch. The women and little children crowd around, full of admiration mixed with awe, saying, "These are good <term>tamate</term> <note>original: *tamate*; masked "ghost" members of a secret society</note>; they never beat or chase us." On the island of Ureparapara, it is not the custom to beat outsiders, but the members are still very strict about enforcing their rules. When an initiation into their <term>menmendol</term> <note>original: *menmendol*; a specific local secret society</note> is taking place, there must be no smoke from any fire. If smoke is seen anywhere, the society sets up their <term>sagilo</term>—a ritual bundle of flowers and leaves—and a pig must be given as a fine for the offense.

In the parts of the New Hebrides <note>now the nation of Vanuatu</note> that are closest to the Banks Islands, these *tamate* societies are not as common. However, on the islands of Aurora <note>Maewo</note>, Araga <note>Pentecost Island</note>, and Ambrym, there are mysterious associations that maintain retreats that are off-limits to the uninitiated, as well as their own masks and costumes. In the southern parts of Araga, there is said to be a group called a *tamate*, but there is little information available about it. On Ambrym, I have been taken into a secret place and shown a mask fashioned upon a human skull; it was fitted with a wig of hair and decorated with the tusks of a boar. In any case, the Araga *tamate* is different from the <term>Qeta</term> <note>another type of society described later in this book</note>.

The institution of the <term>Qat</term> <note>original: *Qat*; a society and ritual named after a legendary Melanesian hero-figure</note> is found throughout the entire island group. It differs from the *tamate* societies of the Banks Islands because it does not have a permanent meeting place, yet it closely resembles them in almost every other important way. The great distinction of this group, however, is the dance. While the *tamate* will prepare and perform very elaborate versions of their local island dances, the *Qat* is essentially defined by the dance itself. 

For the initiation, whenever a sufficient number of candidates are ready, a secluded enclosure is built with a fence made of reeds. The two ends of the fence overlap to create an entrance called the "shark's mouth," through which it is impossible to see. Here the <term>neophytes</term> <note>new initiates</note> remain for a set period of time—unwashed and blackened with ashes—learning the dance and the songs that regulate the dance steps. To obtain admission is, as with the *tamate*, called to <term>tiro</term> <note>original: *tiro*; to seek entry or pay the entrance fee</note>, and money...

...has to be paid. Children too young to dance have their fees paid for them so they can enter; when they are old enough, they enter again to learn the dance. Nothing could better represent the scene of an initiation into religious mysteries to a visitor than this jealously guarded enclosure. From it, in the dead of night, strange sounds and loud calls emerge. Its name associates it with Qat, who might be mistaken for a god they worship¹. However, the name *Qat* actually refers to the hats and not to the <term>vui</term> <note>original: *vui*; a spirit or supernatural being</note>, and inquiry reveals no religious meaning in the initiation itself. The <term>neophytes</term> <note>beginners or new initiates</note> learn a dance that is difficult to perform and requires much practice—not because of a complicated pattern, but because of the speed and precision with which the steps are stamped. 

The steps, as in other dances, follow a song and the rhythmic tapping of a bamboo instrument. The Mota song is as follows: "Mother! Bring a bow here, that I may shoot a bird, a flying bird; Mother, bring a bow here, that I may shoot a bird." <note>original Mota: *Veve! la us mae, na ven toa, to salsal, to salsal, Verae, la us mae, na ven toa*</note> A similar song, with slight changes in wording, is used on Santa Maria and likely on the other islands as well. While they dance, they follow this song silently or sing it in a low voice. There are other songs learned and sung in the <term>nin</term> <note>original: *nin*; the sacred enclosure or dancing ground</note> that are unknown to those who haven't been initiated. I have one from Gaua on Santa Maria that begins, "Oh! Make the fire and blow it into flame, we will finish covering our oven." It contains nothing that wouldn't be found in any other common song. 

It might be thought that the simple words of the song used for the *Qat* dance hide some mysterious meaning, but the initiated insist they do not. When the appointed time comes, the newly instructed dancers and the initiated emerge wearing lofty hats. These hats, which were undoubtedly what the *Qat* was originally danced in, correspond to the masks of the <term>tamate</term> <note>masked members of a secret society</note>, but are

The hats are high and pointed, resting on the shoulders; they are now so tall that they require support ropes on either side to hold them up, and it is impossible to wear them while dancing. The Qat dance is wonderful indeed. The open space in the middle of a village on a moonlight night is lined with spectators; the loud report of bursting bladders <note>Bladders were likely used to create a popping sound like a drum or firecracker to signal the start.</note> is heard from the surrounding woods. One after another, the performers enter the ground with a surprisingly rapid stamping motion of their feet and come to an equally surprising sudden halt. The leader carries a length of bamboo made into a drum, which he uses to direct and control the dance; the rest carry their bows in their hands. When the dancers are numerous and expert, the force and accuracy with which they beat the ground is remarkable; the island seems to shake beneath their feet. In Santa Maria, whether at Gaua or at Lakona, the Qat is more elaborate and difficult than in Mota or Motalava; the boys at Norfolk Island <note>The site of St. Barnabas’ Mission School, where many Melanesian students were educated.</note> will never even attempt it. A practice period of three or four months is needed before newly initiated performers can venture to come out and dance. In former times, when the newly taught dancers made their first appearance, the old members who were past their dancing days would gather from far and near with their bows in their hands and jealously watch the steps. If they saw an error, they would shoot an arrow; if anyone was hit, the blame was placed entirely on the faulty dancer. There was no quarrel with the shooter, and no compensation <note>original: "no compensation to be made"; refers to the lack of "blood money" or legal retribution usually required for injuries.</note> was required.

II. *The New Hebrides.* In the Northern New Hebrides, the *Qatu*, along with other institutions of the same kind, has its place in Maewo, Omba, and Araga. In Omba (Lepers' Island), I know only that there is a *Qatu* and that the hats for it are made in the shape of a shark; however, information from the other two islands is abundant. In Maewo (Aurora), there is more than one *Qatu*, but one called the *Qatu lata* <note>The "Great Qatu."</note> is the most important. In all of these, there is an initiation involving trials of endurance through physical suffering and hardships, but there is no "secret" shared other than the knowledge of the song and dance and how to create the decorations. For the initiation, an enclosure is made with reeds near a group of...

The neophytes <term>neophyte: a new initiate or beginner</term> are gathered into these enclosures, where they remain unwashed and with very little food and water until the appointed time has expired, which may be as long as thirty days. During this time they learn a dance and various songs, but they do not follow a song as they dance as they do in the Banks Islands. Little boys are not initiated because they could not endure the hardships and physical trials <note>original: "tortures"</note> they would have to undergo; however, they can enter by proxy. A man who has already been initiated will go through the formal initiation ceremony on their behalf. There is no age limit and no specific period of life that is considered more appropriate for initiation than another; it is entirely a matter of payment—specifically, giving pigs. A wealthy man will provide pigs for his son or brother; consequently, an infant and a grown man are equally eligible for admission.

The mark of a member of the *Qatu* is the flower of the *nalnal*, a ginger-like plant <term>original: "scitamineous plant," an archaic botanical term for plants in the ginger, banana, or arrowroot families</term> which no outsider is allowed to wear. Those who enter these societies assume a new name, though this does not replace their old name as it does on the neighboring island. They become known as *Tari* or *Vula*. The young men, though commonly called *Tileg* and *Gao*, are referred to as *Tari-koli* and *Vula-ngoda* within the *Qatu*. 

While the initiation is in progress, if women assemble—as they often do—to hear the singing from outside the enclosure where the neophytes are being taught, it is an accepted custom for men to carry them off and sexually assault <note>original: "ravish"</note> them. For a woman to see the newly initiated members before they have returned to ordinary life is a capital offense. The initiates emerge black with dirt and soot and must not be seen until they have washed. Not long ago, a girl from *U'ta* (inland) accidentally saw this washing ceremony. She fled to Tanoriki, where the Mission school is located, seeking refuge, but they were unable to protect her. The people of *U'ta* sent for her, and she went, knowing she was certain to die. They buried her alive, and she did not resist.

The great secret of the society is the construction of the *Qatu*, from which the group takes its name. This corresponds to the *qatu* hats of the Banks Islands, as it is actually a hat or mask. It is made from the trunks of tree-ferns, featuring a pointed upright section large enough for a man to stand inside and carry it, and a cross-piece that is pointed at the ends. This cross is smeared with...

The white grated root of the caladium <term>caladium: a tropical plant with large, heart-shaped leaves and edible roots</term> is used, and it is painted with pigments known only within the society. The pointed top is adorned with a tuft of dracaena leaves; the ends are connected and kept firm by sticks decorated with sago-palm frondlets. Two large eyes are painted on the front, and the back is covered with the hairy fiber <note>original: "plexus"</note> from the sago fronds. Once completed and the appointed day arrives, a man inside the structure carries it out, supported by three other men. In the past, outsiders believed these were the work of ghosts. The similarity between this and the *tindalo* <term>tindalo: a spirit or ghost of a deceased person in Solomon Islands culture</term> work of the Matambala society on Florida Island <note>Florida Island: an island in the Solomon Islands, also known as Nggela Sulia</note> is as remarkable as it is complete.

An account of his initiation into the chief *Qatu*, called the *Qatu ta Gobio*, was written for me by a native youth while his memory of the event was still fresh. He was likely sixteen years old when he and two others underwent the experience he relates here:

> “Father, let me tell you how I joined the *Qatu*. I did not know what it was when my brother said to me, ‘Now you are going to enter the *Qatu*.’ Then I went, and there was a very large crowd in the place where they were celebrating the *Qatu*. My brother asked me, ‘Are you strong?’ and I answered him, saying, ‘It is all right! If I should die, it is all right!’ After that, I went to a building—a *gamal* <term>gamal: a communal men's house or clubhouse used for ceremonies</term>—put up for this purpose not far from the village. My *malo* <term>malo: a traditional loincloth or dress</term> and ornaments were taken off, and I went inside. The *gamal* was narrow, low, and very long. Inside, they had placed two rows of *kalato* leaves (from the nettle tree) sprinkled with salt water, which met together about a yard above the ground. I bent my knees and ran through it. Those *kalato* leaves they had put in the *gamal* sting <note>original: "bite"</note> intensely. They had heated the salt water before pouring it on the leaves—there were no stalks, just leaves—and they sting terribly. When I came out from that thing, I cried as I never had before or since, and I nearly fainted from the pain. I neither ate nor drank water; I did nothing but cry for two days. Only then did I eat food. As for the pig (one of his brother’s which had been given as an entrance fee), they...”

> cooked in an oven; and they gave me some before it was finished, and I ate it. After that, I was thirsty. If I had refused, they would have beaten me to death; but I did not refuse, and I ate that food which they had made so repulsive for me. As for my mashed food, they mashed it directly on the ground; they also grated unripe bananas to make *loko* <term>loko: a traditional dish of grated and cooked starchy plants</term> and stirred it together with dung. However, the three of us did not finish all the *loko* they made. Then we were forced to pick up glowing embers in our hands; they stood around us with guns, and we grasped that burning fire. They commanded us to do it, and we held the fire. Then we lay down on the ground and they trampled on us; they all ran over us, with one man taking the lead, and after he had stamped on us while running, everyone else stamped on us too. After that, when we rose from the ground, one man took a bow and pretended to shoot us. We were not allowed to sit down properly; we had to lie on the ground to eat our food, and we also lay down to drink our water. Regarding that *Qatu* <note>original: "Qatu" — here referring to the ritual structure or mask</note>, it is made of tree-fern pieces put together like planks, and we grated the *qeta* (**caladium**) and built the *Qatu* with it. On the night after that, we danced, and the next morning we performed the *Qatu* dance for the first time. After we had spent thirty days in that *gamal* <term>gamal: a communal men's house used for rituals</term>, we sacrificed a pig; then we went back into the village, stayed in the village *gamal*, and cooked that pig. If a person wishes to stay forty days in that initiation house, he then comes out; but the effects of that nettle will not leave him for a long time.'

> "...which we call the *Taputae*, and it is exceedingly bad. It is right that I should tell you the story of what they did to me. It went like this: They dug a hole—not a very deep one—and brought a great quantity of dung <note>original: "dung"; refers here to animal or organic waste used to degrade the initiate as a test of humility and endurance</note> and put it in the hole until it was full of that very nasty waste. They also poured water into the hole so that a man would sink into it. That hole was not like the well here; it was dug like the drainage ditch by the *kumara* house <term>kumara: the sweet potato, a staple crop in the Pacific</term> beside the road. That is what it was like, and I got into it. My whole body was covered in dung, and my hair was also covered in it. There was one man who poured a great quantity of dung over me. Then I got out and washed myself in clean water. But those others, the adult men, did not get into that; they did nothing but shout. Then some went away, and we danced through the night until morning, and then we performed the *Qatu* dance. After that, we killed a pig. Women cannot eat that pig, nor can some men, because they have not yet been initiated; that pig is eaten all at once. None of it will be saved; it must be completely eaten."

He adds that the bark of the *varu* (a type of hibiscus) is beaten until it turns white to be used for the decoration of this *Qatu* ritual. An initiated member will take a bit of this bark, catch a fish with it, and burn the bark while he cooks the fish. He believes that by doing this, he will obtain *mana* <term>mana: a pervasive supernatural or magical power that can be concentrated in objects or persons</term> for catching that specific kind of fish. If, while carrying this bark, he meets an outsider on the path who sees it, he will either kill the person on the spot or take a pig from them as a fine. If a pig is given, the members of the *Qat* society will agree to eat the pig and allow the outsider to live.

There is another institution on the same island of a similar character called the *Welu*. In this society, the initiate <term>original: "neophyte"; a person who is new to a subject, skill, or belief—in this context, a person undergoing initiation</term> lies face down in a hole in the ground that has been cut exactly to his shape, and lighted coconut fronds are thrown onto his back. He must not move, and he will not cry out. The scars remain on his back as a permanent mark of membership. While the initiation into the *Welu* is ongoing, there are certain trials or games. A bundle of sticks is tied together with a length of vine, and one of the initiates strikes at it with an axe. If he severs it with one...

If the older members prevail, the new ones have to wait.

There are two things here worth noting. First, the expression 'dancing the Qat,' and the fact that each secret society <term>mystery: used here in the classical sense of a "mystēria," or a secret religious rite</term> has its own specific dance—learning which is the primary part of the initiation—reminds one of the dances in the ancient Greek mysteries and the Southern African San people's <note>original: "Bushman"; a 19th-century term for the San people</note> use of the word 'dance' as a synonym for 'mystery.' (Referencing Andrew Lang's *Custom and Myth*.)

However, it seems certain that in these *Qatu* and *Welu* societies, there is no secret knowledge conveyed and no hidden <term>esoteric: intended for or likely to be understood by only a small number of people with specialized knowledge</term> religious instruction given. There is no 'mystery' other than the construction of the *Qatu* figure and the specific movements of the *Qatu* dance. 

Secondly, the question arises: if no advantage is gained other than the status of an initiated member, why are the islanders willing to pay the entrance fee...

<header>Secret Societies and Mysteries. [CH. V.]</header>

Members must pay fees and suffer through the rituals just as their predecessors did. However, while it is certain that these rituals are not a formal "making of young men" <note>original: "making of young men"; referring to a general puberty rite or rite of passage into adulthood</note> and that initiation is not a required step toward marriage, it is equally certain that a native person's social standing depends heavily on membership in the most important of these clubs. An outsider could never be an influential person. A man of high social status would consider it his duty to secure that same position for his son by enrolling him early in the clubs to which he himself belonged. 

The practice of receiving a new member with tests of endurance, allowing him to achieve equality only through pain and insulting treatment <note>original: "contumely"</note>, has been—and may still be—the tradition of Universities and Schools. There is no reason why the appeal of a mysterious secret, which attracts civilized men, should not also influence the savage. Before his initiation, the native initiate <term>neophyte: a person who is new to a subject, skill, or belief</term> also expected that he would truly join the company of the ghosts of the departed. Once he was fully informed <note>original: "illuminated"</note> of the secrets, he enjoyed participating in the deception of those who followed him, and he was quite satisfied to eat their pigs and take their money.

In the island of Araga (also known as Pentecost or Whitsuntide), located immediately south of Aurora, the institution is called the <term>Qeta</term>. I have received a description of it from someone who was made a member as an infant but has witnessed all the proceedings in recent years. The rites are celebrated at irregular intervals whenever there are enough candidates available from a group of villages—perhaps every six or ten years. Some influential man (or two or three together) presides over the event, manages the arrangements, and teaches the songs and dances; the <term>Qeta</term> is said to belong to him or them. 

The meeting takes place at a <term>ute gogona</term>, a place on which a <term>tapu</term> <note>original: "tapu"; a sacred prohibition or taboo</note> has been placed. Many small houses are built there, where the boys live during the first part of their seclusion. Boys of all ages are initiated, generally around the time they begin wearing the <term>malo</term>, the traditional dress worn by men. All are initiated sooner or later, and none grow up without undergoing the rite; putting on the <term>malo</term> and entering the <term>Qeta</term> are considered necessary steps in life. The entrance payment is a mat provided by the father or guardian—one for each boy.

It also introduces the Qeta society of Pentecost Island, noting its sacred locations and the requirement of initiation for all men.</summary>
