## New Hebrides: Pentecost Island

When the designated day for the Qeta ceremony arrives, all the initiated men assemble at the site, and the women must stay away. There is no formal fenced enclosure, but when the ceremony begins, a stick is laid upon the ground to mark the entrance. Two groups of the initiated men stand singing inside this boundary, leaving a space between them. The boy being initiated steps over the stick; as he does so, if he is already wearing a *malo* <term>malo: a traditional loincloth or belt made from plant fibers</term>, the men unexpectedly break his belt string. The *malo* falls off, and he enters the space naked. 

If a boy is too young to walk, he is carried over the mark by his father or the friend who is paying his entry fees. The boys do not remain naked for the entire duration of their seclusion; a new *malo* is eventually given to each of them. My source, who was himself initiated while being carried in his father's arms, began his account by saying that the Qeta was "exceedingly bad." When I asked him at the end of his story to point out exactly what was so "exceedingly bad" about the entire proceeding, he referred to this specific act: he believed that exposing a boy naked who had already earned the right to wear the *malo* was a very shameful thing to do <note>original: "very bad indeed"</note>.

Once they have entered, the <term>neophytes: new initiates</term> stay inside the houses, except when they come out to eat, sing, and dance. They have their bodies blackened with charcoal and wear no ornaments. Long rows of seats are constructed for the boys to sit on while eating. The initiated men feed them, giving each boy only a single bite of food. The boys receive nothing else to eat, even though the initiated men bring in plenty of food for themselves and eat it in private. 

The boys are taught a specific dance and song, singing aloud and dancing around the seats. The meaning of the song is trivial; its primary purpose is to keep time for the dance steps. There is absolutely no secret knowledge or any other information communicated during this time other than the song and dance; there is nothing else involved in the initiation. 

The duration of this seclusion is flexible. After the first three days, the majority of the initiated men leave. Food supplies run low, even though the boys are only given tiny portions. Eventually, the groups begin to scatter slightly; they do not return to the villages but instead live in small houses near the gardens, where the men look after and feed each small group of boys. The entire period of seclusion lasts about five months—typically starting when the yams are planted and lasting until the harvest. In the latter part of this period, the food restrictions are relaxed, though no fish or shellfish is [permitted]...

During the entire time of their seclusion, the boys are not allowed to wash, and their bodies have become quite black <note>Likely from the charcoal used to blacken their skin mentioned on the previous page</note>. The conclusion of the entire process occurs when the first yams are harvested; the group gathers together and goes down to the beach to wash and eat. The women then come to look at them. After this, they return to their villages, and having achieved the rank of *tari*, they take on a name using that prefix, such as Tariliu or Tarisuluana. In all of this, there appears to be no intent to communicate with ghosts or spirits; however, the master of the <term>qeta: a secret society on Pentecost Island</term> undoubtedly offers prayers and sacrifices for the success of the rite.

### III. **Solomon Islands.**

Moving from the New Hebrides <note>Modern-day Vanuatu</note> to Florida Island <note>Also known as Nggela</note> in the Solomon Islands is a significant distance, but in the Matambala society, another form of the Qatu appears very clearly. Its center is a district of Florida called Belaga, which was the only place where the rites were celebrated; men from other districts traveled there to be initiated. The origin of the institution is attributed to a figure named Siko, who came from Bugotu on Santa Isabel Island. Sacrifices were made to him in their assemblies by a line of men who held the office until the year 1883, when the last office-holder embraced Christianity and the Matambala came to an end.

The mysteries were celebrated at irregular intervals of six or ten years, but the initiated formed a permanent organization. A certain part of the beach at Belaga, along with the forest behind it, was always <term>tambu: sacred or forbidden; the root of the word "taboo"</term>, so that no uninitiated person could enter the grounds, and no woman could even walk along the beach. Within this sacred region, there were twelve <term>vunutha: sanctuaries</term>, and in each one, a sacred <term>vovoko: ritual house</term> was built. However, the two sanctuaries at Materago and Volotha were far more important than the rest. The houses built there were so sacred that no man entered them or even approached them. Inside, there were images of birds, fish, crocodiles, sharks, the sun, the moon, and human figures. The construction of these two houses marked the beginning of the most important part of the proceedings. In everything they did, the members believed they were retracing the actions of Siko.

I have received a written account of these proceedings sent from Belaga by an old friend and pupil of mine. It was explained to me in great detail on Norfolk Island by a native from a neighboring district who remembered his own initiation perfectly well. I have also been provided by Bishop Selwyn with an account given to him at Belaga—the headquarters of the Matambala—by men who had been initiated. It is not easy to connect the two accounts in every detail, and some particulars are described with unnecessary minuteness, but the general progression and character of the proceedings are clear¹. 

The month in which the entire process begins is when the *canarium* almonds <note>original: *canarium*; these are common Pacific almonds</note> become ripe. The first step in the ceremony is the *bigo*, which is the gathering of the first-fruits (to be described later). The cracking of the nuts begins at Gole and proceeds through twelve specific locations, ending at Buthinigai. When the new moon of the *bigo* season is seen, the women and children set baskets in rows along the road; the men then gather almonds from morning until nightfall and fill the baskets with them. 

The next moon is known as the "moon of sweeping." During this time, they sweep the paths from Gole to Buthinigai, signifying that these paths are now reserved exclusively for the Matambala. This is followed by a period of strict *tambu* <term>tambu: sacred or forbidden; the origin of the word "taboo"</term>, during which the entire district becomes sacred. Finally, there is the *Teimbelaga*, the time when everyone assembles at Materago to watch the *sasale* dance of Siko during the night.

On the following morning the Matambala, those already—

¹ The native account begins: "This is the story of *Siko*, the man from across the sea who started it. *Siko* lived in ancient times and was a countryman from *Bugotu* <note>A region on Santa Isabel Island</note>. He and *Doriki* separated because *Doriki* said *Siko* should not be chief, and *Siko* said *Doriki* should not be chief. *Doriki* gained the upper hand, so *Siko* fled in secret and made his way here to *Belaga*. He first came ashore down at *Siota* and liked the place, but when he looked back, he could still see *Bugotu*. So, he put his men and property back into his canoe and traveled to *Materago*, where he could no longer see *Bugotu*, and there he lived. The initiated members go down to occupy houses that have been built upon the beach and remain there until the proceedings are over. Those from each village who are already initiated take their friends who are to be admitted with them, but they do not yet let them enter the *vunutha* <term>vunutha: a sanctuary or sacred lodge located in the bush</term>, where the members themselves are busy making the bamboo structures called *tindalo* <term>tindalo: spirits or ghosts, or the physical structures representing them</term>. 

These structures took several forms. One, called the *Voi*, was described to the Bishop as a screen about ten feet long and nine feet high, made of painted and decorated bark. Several men carried it out into the open while hiding behind it, where it could be seen by the women, children, and uninitiated, who firmly believed it was not so much the handiwork of ghosts as an actual appearance of the ghosts themselves. Another structure, the *Koitaba-vunutha*, was so large that eighty or a hundred men inside were required to carry it down to the beach for the general population to gaze at. There was also another ritual object, the *Kuku*, which was a wooden club shaped like a bird's head. One of the first tasks of the Matambala men, after the paths were swept and the country was "made close" <note>This refers to the period of ritual seclusion and restricted travel described on the previous page.</note>, was to cut down tall bamboos for these structures, tie them in bundles, and lay them in the sun to dry.

> "After a while, they brought these down to the *vunutha* and joined them together until they were extremely long. Then they took vines and sago spathes <note>original: *spathes*; the large, leaf-like sheaths that protect the flower of the sago palm</note> and fastened them to the prepared bamboos. Next, they took coleus and turmeric; they chewed the coleus for its juice and mixed it with squeezed wild oranges to create a red dye, and they pounded the turmeric in a wooden pot. Then they used these mixtures to paint the sago spathes they had fastened to the bamboos, making them colorful and dazzling—a very fearful sight for us to behold."

The *tindalo* figures, of which thirty or forty were made in one place, must have resembled the *Qatu* masks or hats of the Banks Islands, though they were much taller. Like the *Qatu*, they were conical in shape and were moved by men hidden inside them.

> "And when all was finished, they set a day for the spectacle. All the women and boys came out in the evening and viewed the *tindalo*, and all the men in the *vunutha* held up and brought—"

...they brought the *tindalo* <term>tindalo: spirits or ghosts, or the physical representations of them</term> images down to the beach. After that, they scheduled another display for the day after tomorrow; when that day arrived, the women again gathered in the open for the spectacle. Once the show performed in that manner was over, the men took the *tindalo* images back into the *vunatha* <term>vunatha: a sanctuary or sacred lodge</term> and burned all those images in a fire. When this was finished, all the men returned to their villages from the sanctuary. It was impossible to reveal things of this kind to women and boys; but at last, when the Gospel reached us, the truth came out, so that all the women, boys, and uninitiated finally understood the reality of these matters.

The uninitiated were called *telegai*, while the neophytes were known as the "new Matambala." As in the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides, no secret knowledge was actually communicated, except for the fact that everything done was the work of men and not of ghosts—which was undoubtedly a surprising revelation. Still, we can be sure that the Matambala members, both new and old, firmly believed that the art of making the images and the entire course of their proceedings had been taught by Siko (who was now a *tindalo*). They believed they were guided and empowered by the supernatural assistance of Siko and his companions, and by the ghosts of their eminent predecessors in the Matambala society, all of whom—including Siko—were invoked with sacrifices. 

However, there was no secret doctrine taught, nor any secret shared beyond the method of making the images. On this point, the testimony of the initiated is as clear in Florida as it is in the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides. There was, however, a specific rite or mark of initiation: the candidate clasped a tree and was touched in six places with a fire-stick—on the shoulders, loins, and buttocks. When they were branded in this way, they were told they were now "Siko's men" or "Siko's messengers." In admission to these mysteries, there was also no age limit, and no stage of life was considered more appropriate than another. Grown men were admitted, who generally came from other parts of the island; at Belaga...

In the village and the surrounding area, boys were initiated whenever the ceremonies took place. Even young children—including nursing infants—were made Matambala. For the infants, the men would go into the villages to beg milk from the women, because the babies could not leave the sacred precincts and the women were forbidden from entering. The children were branded with the slender midribs of coconut leaflets. No fee was paid to join the Matambala. The initiation of new members was not performed until they had lived for some time in houses on the beach, while mysterious figures were being constructed in secret locations within the woods. As part of their preparation, they were intentionally frightened by bird-headed clubs called *kuku*, and they were threatened with death if they revealed any secrets. Altogether, they remained away from their homes for three months.

During this entire time, the Matambala used the terror of their supposed association with ghosts to their advantage. By closing off the paths, they spent their time playing tricks and robbing the surrounding countryside. They would travel as far as Gaeta to steal pigs to sacrifice to Siko <note>Siko: A powerful spirit or ancestor-god (tindalo) associated with the Matambala society</note>. They would fell trees across the roads, and no one dared to remove them. At night, they used ropes to pull down coconut palms and large trees as "proof" that ghosts were roaming about, for it was assumed that no mere mortal could be strong enough to topple them. From time to time, they offered sacrifices to Siko. Occasionally, they also made an appearance in the villages. "When the bamboos have been cut down, they set aside a three-day period for the 'ghosts' (meaning the Matambala) to travel inland. After those three days have passed, around ten o'clock at night, the ghosts go up. All the women in the villages have been preparing *tutu* and *gola* <term>tutu and gola: traditional mashes of food</term> since morning. When night falls, the Matambala men down at the beach take *buro* <term>buro: bull-roarers, instruments whirled to create a roaring sound</term> and *seesee* <term>seesee: bundles of coconut fronds used to beat against a stick</term>. They travel inland with these items and approach the village, beating the *seesee* and whirling the *buro* as they enter."

# Florida 'Matambala'

...they whistle and make clucking sounds, and all the women in the village lock their houses tightly and are very afraid, because they think the visitors are certainly ghosts. The women take the *tutu* and the *gola* <note>original: mashed food and pudding</note> and give them to the "ghosts" outside. Then all the men cry out "*mluemlue*" <note>a ritual shout</note> and go back down to the shore. After that, they set a day for the "ghosts" to return, usually choosing the fourth day. When the fourth night arrives, they once again take the *seesee* <note>a split bamboo instrument</note> and the *buro* <note>a bull-roarer</note> as they did before. They go out and beat the *seesee*, whirl the *buro*, and whistle and cluck. Again, the women give them *tutu* and *soisombi* <note>food mash</note> mixed with almonds, and then all the men cry "*mluemlue*" and return to the beach. 

The women prepared small holes in the walls of the houses through which to push the food to the Matambala. This was a device to prevent the women from accidentally feeling the hands of the men. When the women heard the whistle, they would ask, "Who are you? Are you Siko?" and the man would whistle in answer before taking the food. Great care was taken to ensure the men were not seen when the ghosts were believed to be nearby. When appearing as ghosts, the Matambala were covered, as they were in other regions, with a cloak of leaves. However, during the daytime, the men went among the women to give notice of what the "ghosts" planned to do next or to call attention to what the "ghosts" had already accomplished.

The collapse of this superstition and deception has been complete. It had long been undermined by the fact that boys and young men from Florida <note>Florida: An island in the Solomon Islands, also known as Nggela</note> were allowed to join the *salagoro* <note>a similar secret society</note> in the Banks' Islands, where they learned the truth of how these "ghostly" mysteries actually worked. No Matambala celebration had taken place for several years; all the young people knew how the tricks were performed, even though the elders did not entirely give up their belief in Siko or the idea that there was something supernatural about it. At length, as previously mentioned, the man who held the knowledge of how to sacrifice to Siko became a Christian. Consequently, the sacred grounds were explored, <term>bull-roarers</term> <note>original: buro; a wooden slat swung on a string to create a roaring or whistling sound</note> became toys for the boys, and the old men sat and wept over the desecration of their secrets and their loss of power and privilege ¹.

# Secret Societies and Mysteries

I am aware of no other *Matambala* or similar institutions in the Solomon Islands. However, in *Malaita* <note>original: Malanta</note> and *Ulawa*, there is a period of seclusion for a boy as he grows up; to an inhabitant of the *Banks Islands*, this appears to be an initiation into the *salagoro* <note>a sacred or forbidden place associated with secret societies</note>.

# CHAPTER VI.

### SOCIETIES. CLUBS.

**In** every village and cluster of houses in the Torres Islands, the Banks Islands, and the Northern New Hebrides, there is a prominent building that does not appear to be a regular dwelling-house. In a large village of the Banks Islands, this building is very long and low, with entrances at intervals along the sides below the wall-plate <term>wall-plate</term> <note>original: "wall-plate"; the horizontal timber at the top of a wall that supports the roof rafters</note>. It features stone seats or a stone platform at the main entrances at either end, and low stone walls nearby are planted with dracænas and crotons <note>ornamental tropical plants with vibrant, colorful leaves</note>. The jawbones of pigs and backbones of fish hang under the eaves; very often, the clatter of pounding sticks in wooden vessels and white clouds of steam signal the preparation of a meal. This is a *gamal* <term>gamal</term> <note>a communal clubhouse or men's house that serves as the center of social and political life</note>. The same name, and a building of the same general character—though with some differences in form—is found in the New Hebrides at least as far south as the Shepherd Islands. The buildings called "chiefs' houses" in New Caledonia probably represent the same institution.

In some of the Banks Islands, a visitor entering a village might see one or more square stone platforms with tall, pointed little structures built upon them, open at the front like shrines. Below these are the embers of a fire, and above is an image carved in a human form. A visitor would naturally take these for shrines of idols with altars for making sacrifices to them; but these, too, are *gamal*. The little structure is the eating-place of a man of rank; the fire has cooked his food, which no one but he can eat in that place, and the image is the emblem of his social degree <term>degree</term> <note>a specific rank or level attained within the graded social hierarchy of the club</note>. In another island of the same group, a *gamal* may be seen with 

<summary>This page introduces the "gamal," a prominent communal building or men's clubhouse found throughout the Banks and Torres Islands, describing its physical appearance and its role as a place for social rank and ritual eating.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the description of the gamal (clubhouse) and introduces the Suqe, a social hierarchy and club prevalent in the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides. It distinguishes these clubhouses from general public buildings found elsewhere in Melanesia.</meta>

...one end might be newly built and taller than the rest, or perhaps one end is in ruins while the remainder is in good repair and fully occupied. Here again, one might find a man—perhaps two or three—who has recently been promoted to a new rank <term>degree</term><note>original: "degree"; a level of social standing within the Suqe club, achieved through rituals and payments</note>, for whom a special eating area has been prepared. In other cases, the men of high rank in a village may have all passed away, and because no one of lower rank can legally take their place, that section of the building sits empty. 

Inside, these long buildings are divided by log fences called *tingtingiav*, or "fire-boundaries." Each division contains its own oven along with the necessary cooking tools; log pillows and mats make up the rest of the furniture. The *gamal* is a clubhouse, and the club itself is called the *Suqe* in the islands where I am most familiar with it.

In all Melanesian island groups, it is the standard rule that every village has a building of a public nature. This is where the men eat and spend their time, where the young men sleep, and where strangers are hosted. In the Solomon Islands, these buildings are also where canoes are kept and religious images are displayed, and women are generally excluded from them. These buildings have various names: the *kiala* of Florida Island, the *oha* of San Cristoval, the *madai* of Santa Cruz, the *tambu* <term>tambu</term><note>taboo or sacred</note> house of the traders, and the *bure* of Fiji. All of these undoubtedly correspond to the *balai* and other public halls found in the Malay Archipelago. However, these are not "clubhouses" in the same sense as the *gamal* houses of the *Suqe*. While the *gamal* houses certainly serve public purposes—since almost every man is a member of the club—they are actually the homes of a specific society where every member has a designated place according to his rank.

The name *Suqe* is the same as that of the *Vui* <term>Vui</term><note>a spirit or supernatural being that has never been human</note> known as Supwe in the New Hebrides. However, it is doubtful whether any real connection exists between the two. In the Banks Islands, where the society is very active, there is no known spirit called *Vui Suqe*. Conversely, in Whitsuntide <note>Pentecost Island</note> in the New Hebrides, where the spirit *Vui Supwe* is recognized, the club society goes by a different name. Nothing is known about the origins of this club. It is not connected to the secret societies involving ghosts, nor is it a secret society of that type. The clubhouse stands in the open, and everyone—except for women—can see it.

<meta>This page continues the description of the Suqe, the central social club and hierarchy of the Banks Islands, explaining how members advance through its ranks and how it functions as a form of government.</meta>

<page-num>103</page-num>
<header>VI.] Banks' Islands 'Suqe.'</header>

When new members are admitted, the general public can see what is going on, though women are most strictly excluded. It is a social institution rather than a religious one; yet, because religious practices are woven into the common life of the people, and all success and advancement in life is believed to be caused by *mana* <term>mana</term><note>original: "mana"; a pervasive supernatural power or influence that can be possessed by people, spirits, or objects</note>, the aid of unseen powers is sought through fasting, sacrifices, and prayers in order to mount to the successive levels of the society. 

To rise from step to step, a person needs money, food, and pigs. No one can acquire these unless he has the *mana* to do so; therefore, just as *mana* helps a man advance in the *Suqe* <term>Suqe</term><note>the hierarchical male social club or "graded society" of the Banks Islands</note>, every person who reaches a high rank in the *Suqe* is certainly a man with *mana*. He is a man of authority and a great man—someone who may be called a chief, and whom foreign traders might call a king. A man who has reached the very top and "emerged" (*me wot*) is a very great man indeed. He holds the title of *Weluka* <note>original: "Weluka"; a title indicating one has reached the highest possible status, metaphorically reaching the sky</note>, as if he had reached the sky. He holds a rank that very few have ever attained, and no one can be promoted at all without his consent, which must be obtained through a substantial payment. 

In the stories of the Banks Islands, the "poor lad" or orphan who becomes the "Fortunate Youth" rises to greatness through the *Suqe*; he achieves the highest grade in this club instead of marrying a king's daughter as he might in European fairy tales. Given the absence of any more direct political arrangements among these people, it is clear that the *Suqe* provides a valuable social bond. It unites the male population and grants a considerable power of control to the older and wealthier men, who can admit or reject candidates for the higher ranks as they see fit. 

The great mass of the natives never rise above the middle rank, and many never even reach that level. However, almost everyone—exceptions are very rare—is brought into the society while they are still boys. A man who has never entered the club is given the nickname *luna* <note>original: "luna"; a species of flying fox (fruit bat) that does not fly in flocks like common bats, used here as a metaphor for a social outcast</note>. To enter and to take every successive step, money must be paid to those who have already reached that rank, and a feast must be given, which becomes more costly depending on the rank being sought. Consequently, while almost no boy is so friendless that he cannot enter the lowest division, hardly anyone lives long enough to rise to the very highest place.

...unless, of course, they joined at a very young age, had their initial steps purchased for them by family, and have been very successful in their ventures. Reaching the higher ranks provides an occasion for large public gatherings and feasts, complete with songs and dances; these events are similar to the *kolekole* <term>kolekole</term><note>original: "kolekole"; ceremonial festivals or performances involving music and dancing, often used to celebrate status</note> which will be described later. There are also specific hats and carved images reserved for those in these highest ranks.

The number of "ovens" and ranks varies across different islands. Each community believes their own version of the *Suqe* <term>Suqe</term><note>the central male social club and status hierarchy of the region</note> is the correct one, yet they all recognize the value of the different ranks, even though the requirements to reach them may vary significantly.

In the Banks Islands, the *Suqe* on the island of Mota has many levels and "ovens," all of which are considered *av-tapug* <term>av-tapug</term><note>literally "sacred fire" or "holy oven"; this refers to the ritual separation of cooking fires, where members of different ranks must eat food cooked at their own specific fire</note>. (1) *Won*, (2) *Arrig*, (3) *Qat tagiav*, (4) *Artagataga*, (5) *Luwaiav*, (6) *Tamasuria*, (7) *Tavasuqe*, (8) *Tarasuqelara*, (9) *Kerepue*, (10) *Mele*, (11) *Tetug*, (12) *Lano*, (13) *Poroporolara*, (14) *Wometeloa*, (15) *Welgan*, (16) *Wesukut*, (17) *Wetaur-o-meligo*, (18) *Tiqangwono*.

The lowest ranks are commonly skipped over or taken together; on the other hand, there are three degrees under the eleventh name, and two under the twelfth. Some of the names carry a specific meaning: *arrig* means "the little fire"; *kerepue* means "the bottom of the bamboo water-carrier"; *mele* is the cycas <term>cycas</term><note>original: "mele"; a palm-like plant with spiritual significance</note>, which possesses a certain sanctity; *poroporolara* means "great joking"; *wometeloa* means "the face of the sun"; *wetaur-o-meligo* means "catches the clouds"; and *tiqangwono* means "shoots and completes." 

The *lano* rank wears a very tall conical hat, like that of the legendary *Qat* <term>Qat</term><note>a folk hero and spirit in Melanesian mythology</note>, though it is sometimes forked; the *poroporolara* has an image of a man painted with black and white rings; the *wometeloa* has an image of a man carrying a disk on his head with outstretched arms, representing the firmament with heavenly bodies painted upon it. These images are carried about at the feast that celebrates the promotion in rank and are afterwards set up in the little *gamal* <term>gamal</term><note>the communal men's house where cooking and socializing occur according to rank</note> in which the high-ranking man cooks his food. The hat is worn by the new *lano* at the feast he hosts and is afterwards seen leaning against the *gamal*. 

At Gaua in Santa Maria, there are not as many "ovens" (ranks); boys begin their membership much higher up the scale, so that a Gaua boy often holds a rank equal to a gray-haired man from Mota. Those who reach the higher ranks there build a *gamal* on a lofty platform of stones for every "oven" or step, whereas at Mota, they are content to simply raise the end of the *gamal*. In the Torres Islands—or at least in one of them—there are only seven ovens and degrees of rank in the *Huqa*, as the *Suqe* is called there. In their *gamal*, the first rank is the *arlar*, or "big fire," which is located on the threshold of the *gamal* rather than inside it. Young boys do not enter the club there. In all these islands, the distinction between each successive stage is strictly marked; anyone stepping over the boundary to an oven above his rank would be trampled to death by those on whom he had intruded.

In the first place, his introducer is by right his maternal uncle <note>original: "mother's brother"; in many Melanesian societies, the maternal uncle holds a more significant disciplinary and social role than the father</note>. The uncle's goodwill must be secured several months in advance with the gift of a pig, which is formally handed over to him with a slap upon its back. Having undertaken to sponsor the candidate for the *suqe* <term>suqe</term><note>the graded social club or secret society</note>, the patron organizes a feast and a dance for him. He decorates the village square with male pandanus flowers and sets out money for the candidate. The participants of the feast, including the candidate, give the patron a small amount of money, and he provides a return gift to them; they *vene* <term>vene</term><note>literally "to shoot," meaning to invest or pay money into the rank</note>, and he *sar* <term>sar</term><note>to compensate or repay the investment</note>. 

For the lowest grade in Mota, the *vene* money is only half a fathom <note>a measurement of shell money reaching from fingertip to fingertip</note>, which is returned with a full fathom. For the higher grades, a great deal of money is required, and sometimes when money is scarce, pigs are used instead. A boy who has no property of his own is supplied by his father or a friend with the resources necessary to secure the patronage of his uncle, upon whom the primary expense falls. In the higher grades, the candidate seeking advancement still has a patron, but the expenses fall upon the candidate himself. He is aided by his friends with gifts, or *mategae* <term>mategae</term><note>contributions or supplementary gifts given to help someone meet a social obligation</note>, of pigs and money; his father-in-law is also expected to be generous in this. The candidate then repays the patron as liberally as possible for everything done on his behalf. 

The formal entrance into the society, or into a higher rank within it, consists of two parts. When the time comes and a day has been appointed and announced, the women leave the village before nightfall, and the members gather in the *gamal* <term>gamal</term><note>the communal men's house</note>. The candidate enters the specific division containing the fire and oven to which his new rank belongs. His patron breaks the string of some shell money and pours it into a basket. The other members place a garland over the money—made of bamboo leaves for the lower degrees, and of cycas leaves for the *mele* <term>mele</term><note>the rank named after the cycas palm</note> rank and all those above it. This ritual is called *soso makomako*, or "filling the garland." 

The new member then sits down, and someone chosen for his eloquence delivers a discourse to him. He is told that it is his duty to work for his designated oven and not to complain even if his duties are difficult. They then give him a piece of an almond, and every member takes a piece in his hand; they all hold the almond to their lips, and at a specific word they *negneg* <term>negneg</term><note>to eat together in a ritualized, simultaneous fashion</note>, eating together. The declaration is simply this: "I give you food from my fire." Then the money in the basket is distributed; the participants perform the *sese makomako* <term>sese makomako</term><note>literally "tearing the garland"</note>, pulling apart the decorative garland. The *gana tapug* <term>gana tapug</term><note>the ceremonial eating</note> is thus finished during the night. In modern times, the *wol tapug* <term>wol tapug</term><note>the formal "buying" or payment for the rank</note> follows the next morning, whereas in the past there was a ten-day interval. 

The new member then breaks his strings of shell money and touches the various types of food he has provided. He was previously forbidden from touching these because he had been fasting for several days. He then distributes his money and food to every hearth in the *gamal* <term>gamal</term><note>the men's communal clubhouse</note>. A general feast follows. He must then *goto* <term>goto</term><note>to observe a period of ritual seclusion</note>, staying in the clubhouse and eating only food cooked over his *av tapug* <term>av tapug</term><note>the ceremonial fire designated for his specific rank</note>. This seclusion lasts for a set number of days according to his rank: five or ten days for the middle ranks, and significantly longer for the highest ranks. 

The feast held when someone enters a higher rank is a public event. Throughout the celebration, the distinction between food cooked on the ceremonial *av tapug* fire and regular food is strictly maintained. In the highest ranks, where very few people are eligible to eat food from the newly attained level of the oven, portions are sent to men of the same rank living elsewhere. 

The pigs—the primary provision and sign of great hospitality—are not actually slaughtered and eaten at the feast. Instead, they are sent to various locations after being given a ritual slap by the new member (or the person acting on his behalf) who provided them. Occasionally, their death is represented through a ceremonial performance rather than an actual killing. 

For the lower ranks, or in wealthy families where a boy’s advancement is expected, the feast is a local celebration for the neighbors. However, massive crowds gather for the dances and feasts associated with the highest ranks, when the initiate wants to fully display his new social status. There was once a specific garment called a *malo-saru* <term>malo-saru</term><note>a ceremonial cape</note> worn exclusively for these occasions, though it is no longer seen. It was a type of cape made of four oblong sections of beautifully crafted colored matting, representing the pinnacle of Banks Island artistry. A candidate for these high ranks would remain unseen for many days beforehand, secluded and fasting in an inner chamber of the *gamal*. He trotted back and forth before the <term>palakos</term>, with his new companion following at his heels, modestly covering his face. His speech was interpreted to this effect:

Then the pigs were brought out one by one and smacked by the host of the feast as he handed them over to another high-ranking man who decided where they were to go. There were four or five large, fat beasts, each with its own name, and several more of lesser importance. As each pig was smacked, three other high-ranking men blew a loud blast on conch shells. Then the new member laid out his money on the ground, and the conchs were blown again. The last act of the ceremony was the appearance of another high-ranking man with a bow and arrows. He and the modest host, with the palm leaf still over his face, capered about for a while, and then the man made a speech to this effect:

> "The man who undertook to introduce this new member to his current position is dead; but I have taken his place instead. He has done generously—pigs, money, and everything that is proper."

Although women are completely excluded from the men’s *Suqe*, they have a similar institution of their own, which is sometimes incorrectly called by the same name. They are admitted to various grades of honor by paying money and hosting a feast, thereby becoming *tavine motar* (<term>tavine motar</term><note>literally, "women of distinction"</note>). Through their *Suqe*, they acquire wealth in the form of shell money, which they use to help their husbands advance in rank; they also plant their own gardens for the feasts. In this way, they earn the right to be tattooed, to wear shell bracelets, to wear an ornamented *pari* (<term>pari</term><note>a woman’s traditional short garment or loincloth</note>), and to decorate their faces with red earth. The *tavine worawora* (<term>tavine worawora</term><note>literally, "common" or ordinary women</note>) can have no share in any of these honors. However, this system is more like a *kolekole* than a *suqe*; these are two things that become so interconnected in the higher ranks of men that an account of one is incomplete without an explanation of the other.

A *kolekole* is a feast involving dancing and singing held in connection with a specific object, which grants a certain rank marked by its own specific ornament. A man hosts such a feast for himself, or for his son or nephew. When someone has reached the highest position in the *Suqe*, they can still advance their social standing through *kolekole*; indeed, they often pair these festivals with their regular progress through the *Suqe* ranks. The story of the "Little Orphan" illustrates native grandeur and success through a succession of these festivals. 

When a man builds a new house, he will *kole* it (consecrate it with a feast), and a *nule* (<term>nule</term><note>a carved, often grotesque, memorial image</note>) will remain at the door as a memorial. When a new *gamal* (<term>gamal</term><note>the men's clubhouse or graded society house</note>) for the *Suqe* is built, or when a man adds a new compartment to the oven to which he has recently risen or is about to rise, a *kole-gamal* is held. A stone is brought up from the beach and placed near the *gamal*, or a *wona* (<term>wona</term><note>a platform made of stones</note>) is built, and a feast is held to *kole* it. The host of the feast, or the youth in whose honor it is held, dances on the stone and is afterward entitled to wear on his ankle a *wetapup*, an ornamental...

Another kind of feast grants the right to wear a pig’s tail in one's hair; I have seen a man at Maewo wearing twenty-five of them. If a man possessed a wonderful or rare object, perhaps brought from foreign places—such as a white cockatoo from the Solomon Islands—he might *kole* (<term>kole</term><note>to host a feast for the purpose of display</note>) this; or, more likely, he would take advantage of another man’s feast to dance about and exhibit it. 

Orators mounted on the roof of the *gamal* (<term>gamal</term><note>the men’s communal clubhouse</note>), or on a newly built house, would harangue the crowd, praising the virtues of the feast's host. Others would go about with baskets of his money, proclaiming his liberality. Decorated *palako* logs, heavy with *mana* (<term>mana</term><note>spiritual power or efficacy</note>), would be carried in. Pigs would be sent off to distant villages with a slap from the host. Crowds gathered from all directions; dancers and drummers exerted themselves in anticipation of the next day’s payment, and women competed with new songs for prizes and honor. 

It was a great achievement for a man to have a large gathering at his feast, and it gave his enemies great satisfaction to prevent it; therefore, each would use charms to further his purpose. A man would rub the leaves of a scented ginger plant, or a strong-smelling *erythrina* (<term>erythrina</term><note>the coral tree</note>), in his hands overnight and hang them over the fire. He would chop the twigs and leaves while singing a charm over them; he would chew and puff all night to acquire *mana*. In the morning, he would blow his shell trumpet to spread the influence of his leaves, which would *avul* (<term>avul</term><note>to magnetically attract or draw a multitude</note>), drawing a crowd to the feast. Conversely, a counter-charm from an adversary would make people feel unwilling to go. 

Another decoration to be obtained by hosting a dance and feast is the *urai non Qat* of Mota, or *noran Qat* of the Torres Islands (where perhaps it is now most commonly practiced), which is the head-anointing of Qat (<note>Qat is the legendary hero and central figure in the mythology of the Banks Islands</note>). The head is smeared with a mixture of dust from a specific tree, the juice of *coleus* leaves, native oranges, and salt water, which produces a brilliant red color. ...yellow color. The *Vui Ro Som* <note>a legendary figure</note> in the Story of Ganviviris was adorned in this way when she appeared with all the ornaments that wealth could grant her the right to wear.

A feast of the same kind, called a *Vovo* feast, is held to commemorate a deliverance. For example, when the famine and suffering that followed a devastating hurricane had passed at Mota and food was once again abundant, the people celebrated a *Vovo* feast. A similar feast was held by a native of the same island when he had fully recovered from a slight wound received at Santa Cruz; he danced about, showing off his hat with the arrow still stuck through it.

In the northern part of Maewo (also known as Aurora) in the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>, the *Suqe* <term>Suqe</term><note>the men's graded society or club</note> is now almost extinct. The older members still use the *gamal* <term>gamal</term><note>the men’s communal clubhouse</note> as a convenient place to gather, but no one else cares about joining. This is largely because, in the old days, a high rank in the *Suqe* was valued for the advantages it provided after death. A native writer explained that "the reason for the *Suqe* is this: so that later, when a man dies, his soul may remain in happiness in that place called *Panoi* <term>Panoi</term><note>the underworld or land of the dead</note>. But if anyone should die who has not sacrificed a pig, his soul will simply stay in a tree, hanging from it forever like a flying fox <note>a large fruit bat</note>. For this reason, no man wants his son to be left without these rituals being performed; it is a matter of the highest importance that he should obtain many pigs and seek wealth (meaning ceremonial mats), so that later, when everything is prepared, he may give that wealth to those who have already sacrificed pigs, and thus ensure his own well-being."

Consequently, at the birth of a son, a man’s first priority was to give a pig in the child's name to begin his progress in the *Suqe*. Furthermore, rank in the *Suqe* carried the same social status and respect here as it did in the Banks Islands. Even among children, a boy whose father had not provided a pig for his admission would be looked down upon. Once a man had properly sacrificed pigs on his own account later in life, his position in society was secure. "He can adorn himself with pigs' tusks, and with the white shell-money that we have, and with the most highly-regarded leaves—croton, dracaena, or cycas—and he thinks to himself, 'Now I am free of trouble; there is nothing weighing upon me now.'" > "There are some now who have realized that there is no truth in this; and they say these things are the deceits and vanities of the world." <note>This likely refers to the spiritual claims about the afterlife mentioned on the previous page.</note>

On Omba <note>also known as Lepers' Island or Ambae</note>, the *Hunge* <term>Hunge</term><note>the local version of the graded men's society</note> is in full vigor. A *gamali* <term>gamali</term><note>a men’s communal clubhouse</note> is a necessity for a man to eat in, even if there is only a single dwelling-house nearby. There are not many ranks or ovens; a Lepers' Island *gamali* appears short and lofty to a visitor from the Banks Islands. There are only four ranks in the society, and therefore only four divisions (*diringi*) in the *gamali*: the lowest is the *toa* (the fowl); the second is *moli*; the third is *levusi* (meaning "many"); and the highest is *vire*, which means "having fruited" or "flowered."

However, there is more than one oven for each rank, and a member must "eat his way" through them before he can pass to the next division. For example, in one *gamali*, there are five ovens for the *moli* rank and two for *levusi*. When a man has reached the highest rank of *vire*, he can continue to advance within it, holding another feast and taking another name as often as he pleases, becoming a greater man every time. The lowest step does not grant a title, but a new name is assumed with the higher ranks to show one's status. These names, however, are not commonly used in everyday speech. No one, for example, calls Tangamben by the name *Molimbembe* ("Moli-butterfly"), which is the name belonging to his *moli* rank. Nevertheless, a man who has passed through all the ranks and become a *Vire* many times over will possess a great number of these names.

Age has nothing to do with entering the society or rising in the ranks; it is simply a matter of providing pigs and mats, which serve as money. There is no formal initiation ritual; all males, except for very small boys, are members and eat in the *gamali*. Friends help the boys at first, but the great aim of everyone is to rise and gain social position. A boy is given a fowl (*toa*) to start him in life, and that fowl "buys" him his first step, also called the *toa*. As his fowls multiply, he trades some of them for a young sow; thus his property increases, and as he grows richer, he desires to take each further step. The higher ranks of the *Hunge* provide great power and authority because those who have reached them can always obstruct those who wish to rise.

...and the goodwill of each member must be secured. There is less strictness here than in the Banks Islands regarding the rule that keeps each man to his own oven; a man can descend from his own higher rank to eat in a lower division. However, if someone encroaches on a rank above him, he must pay a fine of pigs. 

The system for entering the society is the same as in the Banks Islands: a patron introduces the new member and makes his *huge* <term>huge</term><note>original: "huge"; a ceremonial payment or gift made upon entering a rank</note> for him—gifts which are, to a large extent, reciprocal. The patron is usually a member of the same family division, such as a maternal uncle or a brother. For example, in the case of a boy whose wealthy father paid for him to reach the rank of *moli* <term>moli</term><note>a high social rank</note> during early childhood, the first step was to give a pig to the members of the boy’s *waivung* <term>waivung</term><note>his mother's kin group</note>. This served as an acknowledgment that he was intruding on their territory—that is, the patriarchal (father's) lineage was intruding on the matriarchal (mother's) system. 

Afterward, his father gave him a pig for a feast held in the boy's name. Every person who took a piece of the pig gave a mat in return; the man who took the head gave a mat one hundred fathoms long. Of these mats, the boy gave fifty back to his father to repay him for the pig. Then, mats were given in the boy's name to the *moli* members he was joining, and when he first ate at their oven, they held a small feast for him. Finally, his mother's relatives gave a pig to his father in his name and hosted a feast for him.

At Whitsuntide Island (Araga), the word *Loli* <term>Loli</term><note>the local name for the graded society</note> is used instead of *Suqe*, but the institution is the same. In fact, the entire male population are members of the society; wherever there is a dwelling-house, there is also a *gamal* <term>gamal</term><note>a men’s communal clubhouse</note>. There are twelve divisions with their respective ovens, called *matan gabi* <term>matan gabi</term><note>literally 'the face of the fire,' the individual ovens for different ranks</note>: 
1. *ma langgelu*, the stage of youth; 
2. *gabi liv hangvulu*, the oven of ten tusks; 
3. *ma votu*; 
4. *gabi rara*, the oven of the erythrina leaf <note>the leaf of the coral tree, which serves as a badge of rank</note>; 
5. *woda*, the stone-wall seat at the front of the *gamal*, on which no one below this rank may sit. 

These first five are the lower steps; fathers ensure their sons take these as soon as possible, advancing them as quickly as they can afford to pay for their promotion. Although the lowest rank is nominally for grown youths, no...

### VI. New Hebrides: Whitsuntide Island

A child who is too young to be admitted may still have his entrance payments and gifts of pigs and mats provided by his father or, more appropriately, his maternal uncle. Here, too, although in principle the mother's kin should take charge of the boy's social advancement, in practice the father usually takes this responsibility upon himself. 

The sixth step, <term>moli</term><note>a significant intermediate rank in the Loli society</note>, is the first one of major importance; the youth takes the "great <term>loli</term>" <term>ma loli gaivua</term><note>a major ceremonial step or feast</note> and assumes a new name with the prefix *Moli*. There are three distinct levels within the *moli* rank. The ninth rank is <term>udu</term>, the tenth is <term>nggarae</term>, the eleventh is <term>livusi</term>, and the final rank is <term>vira</term>. 

When a youth achieves the rank of *moli*, his patron or father gives him some of that beautiful white shell-money. Although this is not used as common currency, it is highly valued as an ornament. It is worth many pigs and is worn on the arm or wrist on a string, or woven into an armlet. These family jewels remain as heirlooms and are reassembled for each successive wearer. 

Discipline within the society is severe; anyone who dares to intrude into a division of the <term>gamal</term><note>the communal men's clubhouse</note> higher than his own rank would be clubbed or shot. To rise to the higher *moli* levels and the steps beyond is the ambition of every young man, and his friends are obligated to help him. To achieve this, sacrifices are made and <term>mana</term><note>supernatural power or influence</note> is sought from <term>Tagar</term><note>a high deity or spiritual being in New Hebrides mythology</note>. 

To gain new steps in rank, many pigs, many mats, and abundant supplies of food are required. Such resources are believed to come to a man supernaturally; he must possess *mana*. The rank of <term>Vira</term> is seldom reached. A man of that rank, such as Viradoro is now, is effectively the chief. He must possess great *mana* and the favor of Tagar, or he could not have risen to such a position. His authority is absolute within the <term>Loli</term><note>the name of the secret society or club</note>, for no one can rise in rank without his consent, and every man is a member of the society and hopes to advance. He has likely been fortunate in war, or he would not have survived; he comes from a family of wealthy and influential men who purchased his first steps when he was a child, and using their wealth, he has purchased the higher ranks. He is the "great man," the <term>Ratahigi</term><note>the paramount leader or chief</note>.

# CHAPTER VII.

## RELIGION.

The religion of the Melanesians is the expression of their understanding of the supernatural and covers a very wide range of beliefs and practices, the boundaries of which are very difficult to define. It is equally difficult to determine exactly what these beliefs are. The ideas of the local people are not clear on many points, as they are not accustomed to presenting them in any formal system among themselves. 

An observer who sets themselves the task of making systematic inquiries will find themselves confused from the start by the variety of languages they must deal with. Even if the researcher uses a language that they and their informants can use easily for the daily purposes of life, they find that language fails when trying to understand the real meaning of expressions that an informant must use in their own native tongue—simply because there is no equivalent for them in the common language being used. Or, if the informant provides what they suppose to be an equivalent word, it will often happen that the researcher and the speaker do not understand that word in the same way. 

A missionary faces their own difficulty in the fact that much of their communication is with the young, who do not themselves know or understand very much of what their elders believe and practice. Converts are often inclined to speak poorly <note>original: "blacken"</note> and unfairly of their own former state, and they describe the current practices of others with even greater zeal. There are some things they are truly ashamed to speak of; and there are others which—

### Difficulties.

...they think they ought to consider wrong, because they are associated in their memory with what they know to be really bad. Many native Christians will completely condemn native songs and dances; however, when questioning begins to clear their minds, they acknowledge that some dances are quite innocent. They explain that none they know have any religious significance at all, and say that many songs also have nothing bad in them, even writing out one or two as examples. Natives who are still practitioners of their traditional religion <note>original: "heathen"</note> will speak with reserve about what they still consider sacred, and a thoughtful missionary will respect such reserve. If he does not respect it, the native may very likely lose respect for him and amuse himself at the missionary's expense.

Few missionaries have the time to make systematic inquiries; if they do, they are likely to make them too soon, and for the rest of their career, they try to make whatever they observe fit into their early theories about the native religion. Often, it is feared, missionaries manage things so that neither they nor the first generation of their converts really know what the old religion of the native people actually was. 

There is always the difficulty of language for missionaries. A man may speak a native language every day for years and have reason to believe he speaks it well, but it is a poor sign of his real acquaintance with it if he does not eventually find out that he makes mistakes. Resident traders, if they are observant, are free from some of a missionary's difficulties, but they have their own. "Pidgin English" <note>original: "pigeon English"</note>, which is sure to be used, carries its own deceptions. The phrase "plenty devil" is used to convey a great deal of information: a chief's grave is called "devil stones," the dancing ground of a village is a "devil ground," the drums are called "idols," and a dancing club is a "devil stick."<insert>¹</insert> The most intelligent travelers and naval officers...

The word was certainly not introduced in the Solomon or Banks Islands by missionaries, who in those regions have never used the word "devil." Yet, most unfortunately, it has happened that the religious beliefs of European traders have been conveyed to the natives through the word "devil," which the natives now use without knowing what it means. It is much to be hoped that educated Europeans would not use the word as loosely as they do.</note>

...carries its own set of misunderstandings. Naval officers spend their brief observation periods in this atmosphere of confusion. Besides, everyone—missionary and visitor alike—carries with him some preconceived notions; he expects to see idols, and so he sees them. Images are labeled as "idols" in museums, even though their makers carved them merely for amusement. A Solomon Islander might fashion the head of his lime-box stick <note>A stick used for applying lime to the mouth while chewing betel nut.</note> into a grotesque figure, and it then becomes the subject of a woodcut illustration labeled "a Solomon Island god." 

It is extremely difficult for anyone to begin inquiries without some prejudices <note>original: "prepossessions"</note>, which affect how he understands the answers he receives, even if he can communicate with the local people in their own language. The questions he asks guide the native person toward the answer he thinks he is expected to give. The native, whose own beliefs and notions are floating like a vague, cloudy solution in his mind, finds that the European’s questions provide a thread upon which these ideas can suddenly crystallize <note>original: "precipitate themselves"</note>. Thus, without any intention to deceive, he avails himself of the opportunity to clear his own mind while he satisfies the questioner.

Some statement like this regarding the difficulties in obtaining reliable knowledge is a necessary introduction to this account of Melanesian religion. It is also important that the author should not claim to be perfectly accurate or complete. The general view presented here must be considered alongside the specific examples of Melanesian beliefs and religious customs that follow.

The notion of a Supreme Being is altogether foreign to them—or indeed the idea of any being occupying a very elevated place in their world... # VII. ‘Mana’

This power is beyond the ordinary ability of men and outside the common processes of nature. It is present in the very atmosphere of life, attaches itself to people and to objects, and is revealed through results that can only be explained by its influence. When a person has acquired it, they can use and direct it, though its force may suddenly emerge at some new point. Its presence is confirmed by practical proof. 

For example, a man might happen by chance upon a stone that catches his eye because its shape is unusual; it resembles something specific and is certainly not an ordinary stone, so he concludes there must be *mana* in it. He reasons with himself and puts it to the test: he places it at the root of a tree whose fruit the stone resembles, or he buries it in the ground when he plants his garden. An abundant harvest from the tree or the garden shows <note>original: "shews"</note> that he was right—the stone is *mana*¹, meaning it possesses that power. Having that power, the stone becomes a vessel to transfer *mana* to other stones. 

In the same way, certain sequences of words—usually in the form of a song—have power for specific purposes; such a verbal charm is also called a *mana*. However, this power, though impersonal in itself, is always connected with a person who directs it. All spirits possess it, as do ghosts <note>The author distinguishes "ghosts" (disembodied human souls) from "spirits" (supernatural beings that were never human).</note> generally, and some living men. If a stone is found to have supernatural power, it is because a spirit has associated itself with it; likewise, a bone from a deceased man has this power because his spirit is connected to it.

> **This is Mana.** I believe this word is common to the entire Pacific, and people have tried very hard to describe what it signifies in different regions. I believe I understand what the people here mean by it, and that meaning seems to cover everything I hear about it elsewhere. It is a power or influence—not physical, and in a way supernatural—but it shows itself in physical force or in any kind of power or excellence that a man possesses. This **Mana** is not permanently fixed in any one thing and can be carried in almost anything; however, spirits—whether they are souls separated from bodies or supernatural beings—possess it and can grant it. It fundamentally belongs to personal beings to originate this power, even though it may act through the medium of water, a stone, or a bone. In fact, all Melanesian religion consists of obtaining this **Mana** for oneself, or having it used for one's benefit—that is, all religion in terms of religious practices, such as prayers and sacrifices.

***

<note>¹ The word *mana* functions as both a noun and a verb. The transitive forms of the verb—*manag*, *manahi*, and *manangi*—mean to grant *mana* or to influence something with it. An object containing *mana*, or a spirit that naturally possesses it, is described as being *mana* (using the word as a verb). A person "has *mana*," but it is grammatically incorrect to say a person "is *mana*."</note>

<summary>This page defines "Mana" as the central supernatural force in Melanesian belief, explaining how it is identified through success, transferred through objects like stones or bones, and directed by spirits or certain men.</summary>
<keywords>Mana, Melanesian religion, supernatural power, spirits, ghosts, charms, ritual objects, linguistic definitions</keywords>

--- Page 149 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of "mana," explaining how this supernatural power is perceived as the source of all success, influence, and effectiveness in Melanesian life, whether in war, agriculture, or daily tasks.</meta>

...with it *mana*, because the ghost is associated with the bone. A person may have such a close connection <note>original: "connexion"</note> with a spirit or ghost that they possess *mana* within themselves as well, allowing them to direct it to achieve what they desire. A charm is powerful because the name of a spirit or ghost—when spoken in a specific set of words—brings into that charm the power that the ghost or spirit exercises through it.

Thus, all obvious success is proof that a person has *mana*. Their influence depends on the impression they make on the minds of others that they possess it; indeed, one becomes a chief by virtue of this power. Consequently, a man's power—even if it is political or social in nature—is his *mana*. This word is used naturally according to the native understanding that all power and influence are essentially supernatural. 

If a man has been successful in battle, it is not attributed to his natural arm strength, his quick eyesight, or his resourcefulness. Rather, he has certainly obtained the *mana* of a spirit or a deceased warrior to empower him. This power might be carried in an amulet—perhaps a stone worn around his neck, a tuft of leaves in his belt, or a tooth hung on a finger of his bow-hand—or it might come through the specific words he uses to call supernatural assistance to his side. 

If a man’s pigs multiply and his gardens are productive, it is not because he is hard-working or looks after his property well, but because he possesses stones full of *mana* specifically for pigs and yams <note>A starchy tuber that is a staple crop in Melanesian agriculture.</note>. While it is well known that a yam naturally grows when planted, it will not grow very large unless *mana* is involved. Similarly, a canoe will not be swift, a net will not catch many fish, and an arrow will not inflict a fatal wound unless *mana* is applied to them.

(2) The Melanesians believe in the existence of beings who are personal, intelligent, and full of *mana*. These beings have a visible bodily form, though it is not made of flesh like a human body. They are believed to be more or less actively involved in human affairs, and people invoke or otherwise approach them. These may be called spirits, but it is vital to distinguish between spirits—who are beings of a higher order than humanity—and the disembodied spirits of deceased humans, which have become (in the common sense of the word) ghosts.

<summary>This page explains that "mana" is seen as the underlying cause of all success, from victory in war to the growth of crops. It also begins to distinguish between "spirits" (higher beings) and "ghosts" (deceased humans).</summary>

# VII. Spirits and Ghosts

A great deal of confusion and misunderstanding arises from neglecting this distinction, and it is highly desirable that missionaries, at the very least, should carefully observe the difference. European observers tend to label any personal object of worship among indigenous peoples in all parts of the world as a "spirit," a "god," or a "devil." However, among Melanesians, it is very common to call upon deceased relatives and friends and to perform religious rites dedicated to them. 

Therefore, when a man approaches his deceased father with a ritual—believing his father’s spirit still exists and is pleased by this act of piety—he is often thought by outsiders to be worshipping a "false god" or a "deceiving spirit." The man is then likely told that the being he worships does not even exist. The confused native hears with one ear that there is no such thing as the departed spirit he honors as a "ghost" (but which his instructor mistakes for a "god"), while hearing with the other ear that the soul never dies and that his own spiritual interests are of supreme importance and eternal. 

The Melanesians themselves make a clear distinction between the existing, conscious, powerful, disembodied spirits of the dead and other spiritual beings that were never human at all. It is true that these two types of beings can become blurred in native language and thought, but the confusion starts from different directions. The locals think so constantly of ghosts that they begin to refer to beings who were never human as "ghosts." On the other hand, Europeans mistake the spirits of the recently dead for "gods," while less educated Europeans bluntly call them "devils." 

All Melanesians, as far as my acquaintance with them extends, believe in the existence of both spirits that were never human and ghosts, which are the souls of deceased people. To maintain this distinction as clearly as possible, supernatural beings that never inhabited a human body are referred to here as ***spirits***, while the spirits of people who have left the body are called ***ghosts***¹.

# Religion [Chapter VII]
->122<-

There is, however, a very remarkable difference between the people of the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note> and the Banks Islands to the east, and the people of the Solomon Islands to the west. The religious ideas and practices of the former are directed toward **spirits** <note>beings that were never human</note> rather than **ghosts** <note>the souls of the dead</note>; the latter pay very little attention to spirits and address themselves almost entirely to ghosts. 

This shift toward ghost-worship in the west coincides with a much greater development of a sacrificial system, as well as a certain advancement in the "arts of life" <note>technological and social organization</note>. Not enough is known about the people of Santa Cruz, who live between these two areas, to speak with certainty, but they appear to align themselves—as they do geographically—more with the Solomon Islands. 

In Fiji, it is the established custom to call the objects of traditional worship "gods." However, Mr. Fison <note>Lorimer Fison, a missionary and ethnologist</note> was inclined to think that all the spiritual beings of Fiji, including the gods, were simply what the Mota language calls *tamate* <gloss>ghosts</gloss>. The words of Mr. Hazelwood, quoted by Mr. Brenchley in *The Cruise of the Curaçoa*, confirm this view. A chief named Tuikilakila <note>a powerful mid-19th-century chief in Fiji</note> once told one of the first missionaries how he proposed to treat him: "If you die first," he said, "I shall make you my god." 

The same Tuikilakila would sometimes say of himself, "I am a god." It is added that he truly believed it, and his belief was surely correct. It should be observed that the chief never said he was or should be a "god" in English, but that he was or should be a *kalou* <gloss>a spirit or deity</gloss> in Fijian. A *kalou* he no doubt became; that is to say, upon his death, his departed spirit was invoked and worshipped just as he knew it would be. In his own language, he used no verb for "am" or "shall be," but simply said, "I a *kalou*." 

In Fiji, this worship of the dead—rather than of beings that were never in the flesh—is accompanied by a more significant advancement in the arts of life than is found in, for example, the Banks Islands. It is plain that the natives of the southern islands of the New Hebrides, though they are said to worship "gods," actually believe in the existence and power of spirits other than the disembodied...

# VII. Misuse of Terms. Spirits.
->123<-

...spirits of the dead, as well as the ghosts of men. When a missionary visiting Anaiteum <note>modern-day Aneityum in Vanuatu</note> reported that the people "lived under the most abject bondage to their *Natmuses*" and called these "gods," he was clearly referring to ghosts—the *Natmat* of the Banks Islands—as the word is undoubtedly the same. 

The belief in other spirits that are not ghosts of the dead is equally clear in accounts of sacred stones and places. These correspond to those found in the northern islands of the same group, as well as the "minor deities" described as the offspring of Nugerain. Called "gods of the sea, the land, the mountains, and the valleys," these represent the *vui* <gloss>spirits that were never human</gloss> of Lepers’ Island <note>modern-day Ambae</note> and Araga <note>modern-day Pentecost Island</note>. 

There does not appear to be a belief anywhere in Melanesia in a spirit that animates a natural object—such as a tree, waterfall, storm, or rock—in the same way a soul is believed to animate a human body. While Europeans often speak of "spirits of the sea," "spirits of the storm," or "spirits of the forest," the actual indigenous concept is that ghosts haunt the sea and the forest, possessing the power to raise storms or strike a traveler with disease; alternatively, supernatural beings who were never human perform these actions. 

We can say, then, that Melanesian religion divides the region into two groups. In the first group, such as the Solomon Islands, worship is directed toward the ghosts of the dead, though there is also a belief in spirits that were never human. In the second group, such as the New Hebrides <note>Vanuatu</note> and the Banks Islands, both ghosts and spirits play important roles, but spirits receive more worship than ghosts.

(3) In the Banks Islands, a spirit is called a *vui*. One native man, when asked to explain the original meaning of the word as used by the elders, gave this definition after careful reflection: "What is a *vui*? It lives and thinks; it has more intelligence than a human; it knows secret things without seeing them; it is supernaturally powerful with *mana* <gloss>spiritual power or efficacy</gloss>; it has no visible form; and it has no soul, because it is itself like a soul."

In the Solomon Islands, it is difficult to find a definition of a "spirit" except that they are beings who were never men and do not possess the physical nature of a human. In San Cristoval <note>modern-day Makira</note>, such a being is called a *Figona* or *Hi’ona*. One such being was Kahausibware, a female who was also a snake. The name *hi’ona* is also known in Malanta <note>Malaita</note>, though it is used without a very clear meaning; the people there also believe in the *urehi*—beings who are neither living men nor the ghosts of the dead, but who haunt large trees in the forest and snatch away human souls. These are seen as ghosts are, but they are not offered sacrifices or invoked in prayer. 

The name *vigona* is also known on Florida Island <note>Nggela Islands</note> and is applied to beings whose power manifests in storms, rain, drought, calms, and the growth of food. However, the natives refuse to admit that these are simple spirits, believing they must have once been men; undoubtedly, some who are called by this name were indeed living men not long ago. Only one being there is asserted to be superhuman—never having lived a human life and therefore not now a ghost. This being currently receives no worship but is the subject of stories only, without any religious devotion. This is Koevasi, a female figure. 

No one knows how she came into existence. She created things of all kinds and became the mother of a woman from whom the people of the island descend. She was the author of death by putting back on her cast-off skin <note>a common Melanesian myth suggests humans were originally immortal and renewed their youth by shedding their skin like snakes until an ancestor failed to do so correctly</note>. She was also the originator of the various dialects of the surrounding islands; while on a voyage, she was seized with ague <term>ague: a fit of shivering or fever, likely malaria</term> and shook so much that her speech became confused. Wherever she landed, the people caught from her an almost unintelligible form of speech. The chill of this fever remains in the Kakambona River in Laudari, Guadalcanar; Koevasi washed in it, and the water is now so cold that wading into it makes a person ill.

These spirits, as they are, hold no real position in the religion of the Solomon Islands. Instead, it is the ghosts—the disembodied spirits of the dead—who are the objects of worship. <page-num>125</page-num>
<header>VII.] Ghosts of Worship. Example.</header>

A ghost becomes an object of worship. A man in danger may call upon his father, his grandfather, or his uncle; his close family relationship is sufficient grounds for it. The ghost who is to be worshipped is the spirit of a man who, during his lifetime, possessed *mana* <note>supernatural power or influence</note>. The souls of ordinary men are just the common crowd of ghosts—insignificant both before and after death. The supernatural power that resided in a powerful living man remains in his ghost after death, with even greater strength and more freedom of movement. 

Therefore, after his death, it is expected that he should begin to work, and someone will typically come forward and claim a special acquaintance with the ghost. If his power shows itself, his status is assured as one worthy of being invoked and receiving offerings. This continues until his cult <note>original: "cultus"; the system of religious veneration</note> is replaced by the rising importance of someone more recently deceased. In time, the only memorial of him that remains is the sacred place where his shrine once stood and his relics were preserved. If no proof of his activity appears, he is forgotten immediately. 

An excellent example of how the worship of a *tindalo* <note>a powerful ghost of a deceased person who is worshipped</note> was established on Florida Island <note>Nggela Islands</note> is found in the story of Ganindo, which was shared with me by Bishop Selwyn. A group of men gathered at Honggo to go on a head-hunting expedition led by Chief Kulanikama (who himself later became a ghost of worship), and Ganindo was their greatest warrior. They went to attack Gaeta, and Lumba of Gaeta shot Ganindo near the collarbone with an arrow. Having failed in their mission, they returned to Honggo and said, "Our friend is dead." 

But since he was still alive, they took him over to Nggaombata on Guadalcanal, brought him back again, and placed him on Bonipari Hill, where he eventually died and was buried. Then they took his head, wove a basket for it, and built a shrine <note>original: "house"</note> for it, declaring that he was now a *tindalo*. "Let us go and take heads," they said, and they set out on an expedition. As they traveled, they stopped paddling in a calm spot and waited until they felt their canoe rock beneath them; then they said, "Here is a *tindalo*!" To find out who it was, they called out the names of various *tindalos*, and when they called the name of Ganindo, the canoe shook again. In the

Following this solemn procession, the relics were placed upon a bamboo platform, and sacrifices to the new *keramo* <term>a ghost powerful in war</term> began. These were led first by Nisi, then Satani, and finally Begoni. After Begoni’s death about four years ago, the sacrifices ceased, and the shrine fell into ruin as Christian teachings spread. To the people of Florida Island, Ganindo was a *tindalo* (a ghost of worship) and a *keramo* (a ghost powerful in war). Some Europeans today would call him a god, while others would call him a devil; indeed, the natives who speak Pidgin English <note>original: "pigeon-English"</note>, believing "devil" to be the English word for *tindalo*, use that term themselves. 

In Florida and the surrounding areas, it is a firm belief that every *tindalo* was once a living man.
