### VII. Prayers and Offerings

(4) Taking the islands of Melanesia as a whole—at least as many as are discussed here—it is found that *prayers* and *offerings* are made everywhere to spirits, to ghosts, or to both. In some cases, these prayers are "constraining charms" <note>formulas or spells intended to force a spirit to act</note>; they are certainly often specific forms of words believed to be pleasing to the being addressed, and known only to those who have special access to that being. However, there are also natural, spontaneous calls for help during times of danger and distress. 

The offerings or sacrifices, whether made to spirits or to ghosts, differ significantly between the eastern and western islands and are made for various reasons. Some are propitiatory <term>intended to regain favor or appease</term>, substituting an animal for a person who has caused offense; some are deprecatory <term>intended to ward off evil or bad luck</term>; some are offered to win favor and gain benefits; and some are given simply to show proper attention, respect, or even affection. However, the concept of propitiation—the idea of appeasing an angry deity—is not actually very common. 

There is no formal order of priests, and no people who can properly be called priests in the Western sense. Any man can have access to an object of worship, and in fact, most men do—either by discovering a method on their own or by receiving knowledge passed down from those who have used it before. If the object of worship is common to a whole community (as is the case with some sacrifices), the man who knows the correct way to approach that object acts, in a sense, as their priest and performs sacrifices for everyone. But he only holds a sacred character regarding that specific ritual. Furthermore, it is often because of this religious function that a man becomes a chief; he does not perform the sacrifice simply because he is already the chief. Women and children are generally excluded from religious rites. Closely connected with these religious observances are the various practices of magic, witchcraft, healing, and weather-control <note>original: "weather-doctoring"</note>, because all of these things are believed to be done with the assistance of ghosts and spirits.

# CHAPTER VIII.

## SACRIFICES.

The simplest and most common sacrificial act is throwing a small portion of food to the dead; this is probably a universal practice in Melanesia. A fragment of food ready to be eaten—such as yam, a leaf of mallow <note>original: "mallow"; a common edible plant or herb</note>, or a piece of betel-nut—is thrown aside. In places where they drink kava <term>a ceremonial drink made from the roots of the kava plant</term>, a libation <term>a liquid offering poured out to a spirit or deity</term> of a few drops is made as a share for departed friends, or as a memorial to please them. This is done while perhaps calling the name of someone who recently died or is specifically being remembered at the time; otherwise, it is done out of general respect for the ghosts of former members of the community. It is not really thought that this literally becomes the food of the departed, but somehow it is to their advantage, or at least it pleases them. At the same time, the living like to feel and show remembrance of the dead who once sat with them around the oven; it is also an opportunity to seek help from ghostly power, for which prayer is made. 

In the New Hebrides <note>now known as Vanuatu</note> and the Banks Islands, this domestic rite has not, as far as I know, developed into any formal sacrifice, as it has in the Solomon Islands. It is very likely that the sacrifices in the Solomon Islands originated from these simple offerings to the dead. To place food on a burial place or before a memorial image is common; doing this is a type of sacrifice, even if—as in Santa Cruz—the offering is soon taken away and eaten by the living. However, the natives do not call either of these offerings a sacrifice, and they do not use the specific words for which...

In English, no other translation can be found <note>original: "no other translation"; referring to the difficulty of finding a single English word that captures the various Melanesian concepts of sacrifice</note>. The sacrifices, in the more restricted sense, of the Solomon Islands are widely different from those of the New Hebrides and Banks Islands. In the western islands, the offerings are made to ghosts and are consumed by fire as well as eaten; in the eastern islands, they are made to spirits, and there is no sacrificial fire or meal. In the former, nothing is offered but food; in the latter, money <note>referring to traditional shell money</note> has a prominent place.

(1) A Solomon Island sacrifice has been excellently described by a native of San Cristoval <note>now known as Makira</note>.

> "In my country," he wrote, "they think that ghosts are many—very many indeed—some very powerful, and some not. There is one who is the leader in war; this one is truly mighty and strong. When our people wish to fight with any other place, the village chiefs, the sacrificers, the elders, and the younger men assemble in the place sacred to this ghost, whose name is Harumae. When they are thus assembled to sacrifice, the chief sacrificer goes and takes a pig. If it were not a barrow pig <term>a castrated male pig</term>, they would not sacrifice it to that ghost; he would reject it and not eat of it. The pig is killed—it is strangled—not by the chief sacrificer, but by those he chooses to assist him near the sacred place. Then they cut it up; they take great care of the blood so that it does not fall upon the ground. They bring a bowl and set the pig in it, and when they cut it up, the blood runs down into it. When the butchering is finished, the chief sacrificer takes a bit of flesh from the pig and a coconut shell to scoop up some of the blood. Then he takes the blood and the bit of flesh and enters into the house (the shrine) and calls to that ghost, saying: 'Harumae! Chief in war! We sacrifice to you with this pig, so that you may help us to strike down that place; and whatever we carry away shall be your property, and we also will be yours.' Then he burns the bit of flesh in a fire upon a stone and pours the blood onto the fire. Then the fire blazes high toward the roof, and the house is full of the smell of pig—a sign that the ghost has heard. But when the sacrificer went in, he did not..."

To sacrifice in this way is called *hoasi*, and the ghost to whom the sacrifice is made is called an *'ataro* <term>a ghost of a deceased person worshipped as a spirit</term>. It should be noted that Harumae had not been dead for many years when this account was written; the elders remembered him when he was alive. He was not a famous warrior, but a kind and generous man who was believed to possess much *mana* <term>spiritual power or efficacy</term>. His shrine was a small house in the village where his relics were kept. Since his death, no one else had died whom the people considered worthy of such worship; if someone had, Harumae would have been neglected in their favor.

In Florida <note>the Nggela Islands</note>, as has been said, the objects of worship are *tindalo* <term>powerful ghosts of the dead</term>, to whom food consumed in the fire is offered as their portion. Some are well-known by name, while others are known only to specific individuals who have discovered or been taught how to approach them; such a person calls each *tindalo* his own, or *nagana*. We are concerned here with sacrifices: public ones, offered to well-known *tindalo* who are powerful in matters concerning the general well-being; and private ones, offered by individuals to the *tindalo* of whom they have particular knowledge¹. In every village, there was a *tindalo* accepted at the time, and the chief acted as the sacrificer. He had received from his predecessor the knowledge of how to "throw" the sacrifice to this *tindalo*, and he passed this knowledge to his son or nephew, whom he intended to leave as his successor. The place of sacrifice was near the village—either an ancient site or a newly made one, depending on how long that *tindalo* had been popular. It was an enclosure containing a small house or shrine where relics were...

preserved. When a public sacrifice was performed, the people of the village assembled—boys, but not women, being present—near but not inside the sacred place. Food is prepared but not eaten until the sacrifice has been offered. The sacrificer enters the sacred place or shrine alone, taking with him his son or the person he has trained. He makes a fire of small sticks, muttering words of *<term>mana</term>* <note>spiritual power or efficacy</note>, but he must not blow on it. He takes some of the prepared food—perhaps a mash of yam or something of that kind—in a basket lined with *dracaena* <note>a tropical plant often used in rituals</note> leaves and others specific to this *<term>tindalo</term>* <term>the ghost of a person who has become a powerful spirit</term>. 

Part of this food he throws upon the fire, calling the name of the *<term>tindalo</term>* and the names of others with it; he tells the spirit to take its food and makes a petition for whatever is desired. The fire blazes up, which is a favorable sign that the *<term>tindalo</term>* are present and are blowing on the fire; the piece of food is consumed.¹ What remains the sacrificer takes back to the assembly and eats, giving some of it to his assistant. Then the people receive their portions of the prepared food from him and eat it or take it away. While the sacrifice is going on, there is a solemn silence. If a pig is killed for the occasion, the heart (in Florida) or the gullet (at Bugotu) is burned upon the sacrificial fire. 

One *<term>tindalo</term>* commonly known, whose worship is not restricted to one locality, is Manoga. At sacrifices offered to him, little boys are present, and sometimes even women partake of the sacrificial food. The one who presents the sacrifice, when he invokes this *<term>tindalo</term>*, swings the offering all around and calls to him. First, he turns to the east, where the sun rises, saying, "If you dwell in the east, where the sun rises, Manoga! Come here and eat your *<term>tutu</term>* <term>pounded yam</term> mash!" Then turning, he lifts it towards where the sun sets and says, "If you dwell in the west, where the sun sets, Manoga! Come here and eat your *<term>tutu</term>*!" There is no direction toward which he does not lift it up. And when he has finished lifting it, he says, "If you dwell in heaven above, Manoga! Come here and eat your *<term>tutu</term>*! This Manoga belongs particularly to the Manukama or Lahi division of the Florida people. Each division, or *kema* <term>clan or social group</term>, has a *tindalo* <term>the ghost of a person who has become a powerful spirit</term> whom they worship as peculiarly their own, and whom they vaguely call their ancestor. These include: Polika of the Nggaombata, Barego of the Kakan, Kuma of the Honggokama, and Sisiro of the Himbo. The Honggokiki division worships *Tindalo lamba* <note>original: "Great Spirit"</note>, whose personal name is not known. 

As these clans are intermixed in the villages—though one is generally more largely represented in any one village than the others—sacrifices are offered in each village or group of villages to each of these *tindalo*. The person who performs the sacrifice is the man who knows the particular leaves, creepers, species of *dracaena* <note>a tropical plant often used in rituals</note>, ginger, tree shavings, and words of *mana* <term>spiritual power or efficacy</term> with which that specific *tindalo* is approached. This is knowledge he has received from his predecessors. Therefore, the sacrificer of the dominant family division in a place is, in fact, the ostensible chief; the sacrificers of the less numerous divisions are minor chiefs. 

With the worship of these *tindalo* who have a larger and wider following, the sacrificer also combines the worship of lesser and more private *keramo* <term>spirits associated specifically with fighting</term> that he knows. Local *tindalo* who are currently in vogue, such as Ganindo, occupy a middle place between the general and particular objects of sacrificial worship. There are also *tindalo* known to everyone who are particularly powerful in certain spheres, such as Daula in the sea, Pelu (one of the *vigona* <note>spirits associated with nature rather than human ancestors</note>) in gardens, and Hauri in fighting. However, only those who know the proper way to approach them can sacrifice to them before a voyage, a planting, or a fight.

There were two general sacrifices in the year in which the people of a village took part. The first, the *bigo*, was held when the *ngali* <note>the Canarium nut, a staple in local cooking</note> was ripe.¹ No one could eat these nuts until the sacrifice of the "first-fruits" was offered. ### VIII. Florida First-fruits. Private Sacrifices.

The authority to open the harvest season was handed down through the generations along with the specific ritual knowledge of the *tindalo* <term>the ghost of a person who has become a powerful spirit</term> involved. The man who holds this knowledge observes the timing of the season, and early one morning, he is heard to shout. He climbs a tree, picks some nuts, cracks them open, eats some, and places others on the stones in his sacred place as an offering to the *tindalo*. 

After this, the community is permitted to gather nuts for themselves. The chief then performs a sacrifice using food mixed with the new nuts on the stones of the village sanctuary; meanwhile, every man who has a personal *tindalo* performs a similar ritual in his own private sacred place. About two months after this, another general sacrifice is held called the *sukagi karango* <note>a harvest festival for root crops</note>, marking the time when the general food crops have been harvested. When a man digs up his yams or gathers whatever harvest he has, he makes a private sacrifice as well. At the general communal sacrifice, pig or fish is offered.

Individual private sacrifices are performed in the same manner. A man may have acquired for himself—or had someone teach him—the knowledge of which leaves, bark, and vines a particular *tindalo* prefers. With these items, he approaches the spirit in his own private sacred place, known as a *vunutha* <term>a personal shrine or altar</term>, and makes an offering to maintain the spirit's favor or to request a specific favor. There, he invokes his familiar *tindalo*, along with several others, and burns a small portion of food in a fire. 

A man will commonly have his own *keramo* <term>a spirit specifically associated with killing or warfare</term>, who assists him in battle or in slaying a personal enemy. Before a fight, he will pull up a ginger plant and judge his future success by how easily it comes out of the earth. He then makes his sacrifice and attaches the ginger and ritual leaves to his shield, his belt, and his right armlet before heading into combat. 

He curses his enemy in the name of his war spirit, saying, "Siria <note>Siria is the name of a specific war spirit</note> eats you, and I shall slay you!" If he succeeds in killing the man, he cries out, "This man is yours, Siria! Now, give me *mana* <term>spiritual power or efficacy</term>." 

Killing someone without the protection and help of a *tindalo* would be considered very dangerous for the slayer. It is believed that the ghost of the slain man would have power over his killer unless the *mana* of the *keramo*—a stronger ghost—was on the killer's side. In cases of failure, it is believed that the ghostly power on the enemy’s side was proved to be stronger. Every man felt it was necessary to have his own *keramo*, even if he had to buy the ritual knowledge from someone else; if...

# Sacrifices

...If what his father or uncle taught and gave him did not succeed, he tried another method. A relic of the *keramo* <term>the ghost of a powerful warrior</term>—who was himself lately a fighting man—such as a tooth or some hair in a little bag, was hung around the neck; or the contents of the bag might be only a stone. These amulets, called *bomboso*, were kept in the house and were referred to as a man’s *keramo*, just as other relics were called *tindalo*. 

The *vigona* <term>spirits associated with natural phenomena rather than ancestors</term>, as has been said, have influence over the weather and in gardens. If a man himself knows a specific spirit, he can perform the ritual for himself; otherwise, he pays a *mane nggehe vigona* <term>a ritual specialist who works with these spirits</term> to do it for him. Such a person goes into the middle of the garden with mashed food in the palm of his left hand, and he strikes it with his right hand as he calls on his *vigona* to come and eat. He says:

> "You shall eat this produce; give *mana* <term>spiritual power or effectiveness</term> to this garden, so that food may be good and plentiful."

He digs holes at the four corners and buries the leaves appropriate to his *vigona* to give spiritual power to the garden, ensuring it is fruitful and guarded; stones are also used for the same purpose. As the yams, or *pana* <note>a specific variety of prickly yam</note>, grow, they are entwined with a special creeper and fastened with the wood which the *vigona* spirit favors. 

These *tindalo* spirits of the gardens must not be offended by the entrance of men who have eaten pig’s flesh, fish, the flesh of the *kandora* <note>original: "kandora cuscus," a type of tree-climbing marsupial</note>, or shellfish. Three or four days after they have eaten such things, they may approach; once the food offensive to the *vigona* has left their systems, the crop will not be harmed. While the yam vines are being trained, the men sleep near the gardens and never approach their wives; should they do so and then step into the garden, it would be ruined. 

A man who has his own *vigona* can also use his power to damage another man’s garden, whether moved by his own grudge or because he was paid to do so. Supported by his own *vigona*, he offends the spirit of the garden he intends to spoil by laying putrid things there. If the crop is still good after this, the first spirit has been shown to be stronger than the other. The names of sixteen of these *vigona* are generally known. When the crop is harvested, a portion of the fruit is burnt in sacrifice to the spirit involved.

# VIII. Human Sacrifices

There was no sacrificial feast upon the flesh as there was when a pig was offered; instead, only small pieces were eaten by those who wished to obtain fighting *mana* <term>spiritual power or effectiveness</term>, by young men, and by elders for specific purposes. Such sacrifices were thought to be more effective than others. Often, a crime—or a perceived crime—was used as an excuse to take a life and offer the victim to a *tindalo* <term>the ghost of a deceased person of influence</term>. For example, within the memory of men who are still young today, Dikea, the chief of Ravu, sentenced a man named Gisukokovilo to death for stealing tobacco, and the young men of Handika ate portions of him cooked in the sacrificial fire. 

The same Dikea offered a human sacrifice in the year 1886. Dikea had suffered two misfortunes: one of his wives had been unfaithful, and he had sent her away, swearing she would not return until he had made a sacrifice to Hauri <note>Hauri is a powerful and often demanding spirit or tindalo</note>. Additionally, his son had died, and he vowed to kill a man in the boy's honor. Some people expected him to kill a man to be buried alongside the boy, but he did not do so. Instead, he exhumed his son’s body to see him one last time; then, following common practice, he took the skull and placed it in his sacred shrine. 

It was widely known that Dikea had made this vow and was willing to pay handsomely for someone to kill. The people of Savo had purchased a captive boy from Guadalcanar who was lame and nearly blind; they brought him to Dikea and sold him for twenty coils of money <note>original: "twenty coils of money," referring to shell money, a traditional currency made from polished shell beads</note>. The boy, who did not understand the local language, was unaware of his fate. Dikea placed his hand on the victim’s chest and cried, "Hauri! Here is a man for you!" His followers then killed the boy with clubs and axes. The boy's head was taken to be added to Dikea’s collection of skulls, and his legs were sent away to announce what had been done, but none of his flesh was eaten. Thus, "Dikea sacrificed to Hauri with that boy."

In Bugotu on Ysabel Island, these sacrifices—known as *haruyagi*—are the same as those in Florida. Only the coastal inhabitants practiced human sacrifice, and they claimed, as they did in Florida, that the custom had reached them from further west. When the head of an enemy killed in a fight was brought back in triumph, small pieces were cut off and burned as a sacrifice. A captive would be taken to the sacred burial ground of the *tindatho* <term>the Bugotu term for a tindalo, or ancestral spirit</term> to whom the sacrifice was to be made, and there they were bound hand and foot. Then the men of the place, following the chief who led the

In a sacrifice, each person beat the victim on the chest with their hands, calling on the *tindatho* <term>the ghost of a deceased person of power</term> and giving the victim to him. This beating was sometimes enough to cause death; if not, they cut his throat. Then the sacrificer burned a small piece of the victim in the fire for the *tindatho*. Did the men who were gathered there eat the sacrifice? Bera, the high chief, used to do so until Wadrokal <note>Wadrokal was an influential Melanesian Christian teacher and missionary</note> went there to teach. Bera would cook an arm in an oven and eat it, having first made a sacrificial offering with a portion of it. 

Only six years ago, Soga at Mang-gotu sacrificed a man. He accused some visitors from Bugotu of using charms to kill one of his friends. He killed eight of them, but one he bound and took to the place where his friend was buried. There, he offered the man to the ghost—now a *tindatho*—of the man supposed to have been bewitched; however, he did not eat the sacrifice. In these instances, as well as in smaller sacrifices, the idea of propitiation <term>an act to appease a spirit or deity</term> or substitution is not commonly present. When misfortune is believed to follow an offense, as in the case of Dikea, the offended *tindalo* <term>spirit/ghost</term> is propitiated by the sacrifice, and this is also done in cases of sickness. But generally, the goal is simply to gain the favor and keep the goodwill of the deceased spirit.

In Sa'a, near Cape Zélée on the island of Malaita <note>original: "Malanta"</note>, some sacrifices involve a distinct substitution of the victim for the person on whose behalf the offering is made. The ghost of a departed warrior or otherwise powerful man becomes a *lio'a* <term>a powerful, active ghost</term>. If the ghost of a warrior is found through experience to be active, he is known as a *lio'a ni ma'e* <note>original: "lio'a ni ma'e," meaning a ghost of battle or killing</note>, similar to the *keramo* of Florida Island. The names of many such ghosts, such as those of recent chiefs, are generally known, but some are known only to those who have learned the specific means of contacting them. 

There is no single word used for "sacrificing." Instead, there are seven rites which an educated native of the area classifies with the sacrifices of other islands. 
(1) The simplest is called *tau taha* <note>original: "Tau taha," meaning "to put food"</note>. This is done when someone returning from a voyage places food near the case containing the relics of his father, as Ara'ana did. During a voyage, when landing on an uninhabited islet, they will also throw food and call on their father, grandfather, and other deceased friends; they do the same in any danger...

### VIII.] Seven Sacrifices at Sa’a.

...will do the same. There are three other types of sacrifice that share many similarities; the choice of which to use depends on the person who is called in and consulted.

(2) One is called *'unu qo*, which means "burning a pig." This is offered during a sickness, or when a failing garden crop shows that some *lio'a* <term>the ghost of a deceased person of power</term> has been offended. A man known to be skilled in sacrifice is called in; he will typically claim to know which *lio'a* has caused the trouble. A small pig is sent to him to take the place of the person whom the ghost is tormenting. He takes the pig to the sacred place of that *lio'a*—usually under a tree—strangles it, and burns it whole in a fire lit on sacred stones or on the ground. Along with the pig, he burns grated yam and coconut mixed with fish. Then, standing, he calls out loudly to the *lio'a* of that place. He also calls upon the names of all the ghosts of his family and ancestors, including deceased children and women, naming the person who provided the pig as the one offering food to these *lio'a*. He leaves a small piece of the mixed food unburnt, wraps it in a *dracaena* <term>a tropical plant with colorful leaves often used in rituals</term> leaf, and places it by the relic case of the person to whose ghost he has been sacrificing. He is then rewarded for his work with a gift of food.

(3) Another sacrifice is called *toto 'ukalo*, or "clearing the soul." This is performed in the house of the sacrificer, who cooks a small pig or a dog. He recites the names of the *lio'a* who are causing the trouble, calling upon them to *toto* <note>original: "toto", meaning to clear away or cleanse</note>, to clear away the mischief—whether it is sickness, a magical charm, or a curse—and to make the afflicted person "clean." Afterward, he takes the animal out and either throws it into the sea or places it on a stone in the sacred place belonging to the *lio'a* he addressed. He will not place it in a common area because it is considered holy; it has "taken away the mischief" and "made clean."

(4) The third of these is called *toto epa hanua*, or "thoroughly clearing the place." This is performed in the house of the sick person for whom it is offered. They cook a pig or dog in an oven, cut it up, and arrange all the parts in order. Then the sacrificer sits at the head of the arrangement and calls out the names of the deceased members of the *lio'a*'s family in order from oldest to most recent, saying, "Help, deliver this man; cut short the line that has bound him." (5) When the yams are ripe, some are brought from every garden to be offered to the *lio'a* <term>the ghost of a powerful ancestor</term>. All the family members who look to a specific line of ancestors as the *lio'a* concerned with their harvest gather at their sacred site; women are excluded from this assembly. One person enters the sacred area with a yam and cries out in a loud voice to the *lio'a*, “This is yours to eat,” and places the yam next to the skull kept in that place. The others softly invoke the names of all their ancestors and present their yams. These are many in number, because one yam from every garden is given to every *lio'a*. They also include *awalosi* <term>the edible flower of a reed</term>. This offering of first-fruits is made in the early morning. If anyone keeps a relic in their house—such as a head, bones, or hair—they take a yam back with them to set beside it. 

(6) First-fruits of flying fish. Like the bonito, catching these fish is believed to require a specific supernatural power; therefore, not every canoe is used to hunt flying fish. When the season arrives, the men prepare their floats, while the women go into the gardens to dig up new yams and prepare grated food. The men then catch a few flying fish and use them for sacrifice. Some *lio'a* take the form of sharks, and the first-fruits are offered to them. Some of these spirits have sacred sites on land where figures of sharks are displayed, and cooked flying fish are laid before them. Other ghost-sharks have no sacred place on shore; for these, the fish are taken out to sea. There, the spirits' names are called out, and the fish is shredded into the water as food for them. 

(7) The new canarium almonds <term>also known as Galip nuts</term> cannot be eaten until the first-fruits have been offered to the *lio'a*. A similar offering, which includes flying fish, is made with dried almonds before they are consumed.

A sacrifice in San Cristoval <note>original: San Cristoval; modern Makira Island in the Solomon Islands</note> has been described previously. In cases of illness where a certain malignant ghost named Tapia is believed to have seized a person’s soul and bound it to a banyan tree, a “sacrifice of substitution” is offered. A mediator who has a connection with Tapia is hired to intercede; he takes a pig or a fish to the sacred place and offers it, saying, “This is for you to eat in place of that man; eat this, and do not kill him.”

<header>Santa Cruz Sacrifices.</header>

At Santa Cruz, when a man of high status dies, his ghost becomes a *duka* <term>the ghost of a deceased person</term>. A wooden post is set up in his house to represent him. This remains, and is periodically replaced, until the man is eventually forgotten or the post is neglected because attention has shifted to a newer and more successful *duka*. When the post is first erected, a pig is killed, and two strips of meat from along the inside of the backbone are placed before the post as food for the *duka* it represents. These do not stay there long; they are soon taken away and eaten by the living. 

When the posts are renewed, the same ritual is performed again. From time to time, offerings of food are made to the *duka* before the post, left there for a short period, and then taken up and eaten. In the event of danger at sea, a *duka* is called upon by name—perhaps a man’s father, a deceased chief, or a certain figure named Lata, who is not remembered as having been a mortal man—and a small piece of food is thrown out with the words, "This is for you to eat." 

Betel nuts <term>the seed of the areca palm, often chewed as a stimulant</term> are placed on sacred stones for the *duka*. When a garden is planted, they spread feather-money <term>a traditional form of currency made from the red feathers of the honeyeater bird</term> and red native cloth around it for the *duka*, later taking it away again. A patient who has recovered from illness under the care of a native doctor gives a pig for the *duka* involved in the cure; when the pig is killed, a piece of meat is placed before the post representing that ghost. Offerings of the first-fruits of the yam harvest are made in the same way, in the form of mash or pudding. These "economical" offerings in Santa Cruz may be explained by the belief that the *duka*, being immaterial themselves, consume only the immaterial essence of the gifts. Therefore, the physical material remains and may be consumed by mortal men.

(2) The nature of what might be called sacrifices in the Banks' Islands and Northern New Hebrides differs significantly from those in the Solomon Islands in two ways: the offerings are generally made to spirits <note>original: *vui*</note> rather than ghosts, and fire is not used to consume the offerings. While it is true that fragments of food are thrown for the ghosts of the recently deceased—an action undoubtedly closely related to the sacrifices of the western islands—this is not associated with the same ritual fire.

<summary>This page describes the ritual veneration of ghosts (duka) in Santa Cruz through wooden idols and food offerings, noting that the physical food is later eaten by humans. It also begins to contrast these practices with the spirit-focused, fireless rituals of the Banks' Islands.</summary>

<page-num>140</page-num>
<header>### Sacrifices. [Chapter VII]</header>

They do not have the same notion of a sacrifice as the people further to the east understand it. In the Banks’ Islands, the word that has been taken as the equivalent to "sacrifice" is *oloolo* <note>original: *oloolo*; a term describing the act of ritual offering</note>. It is important to observe that this word is not used in reference to the spirit to whom the offering is made, but rather to the man himself who presents the offering to the spirit. This indicates that the word *oloolo* does not mean "to sacrifice" in the strict sense. Nevertheless, a sacrificial offering does exist; it is used as a means of appeasing a spirit after an offense, as well as a way to obtain a desired outcome. Food is not commonly the thing offered; in the Banks’ Islands, perhaps nothing but native money is used for the offering.

The spirits who are approached with these offerings are almost always connected with stones upon which the offerings are made. Some of these stones have been sacred to a spirit since ancient times, and the knowledge of how to approach the spirit connected with them has been passed down to the current owner. However, any man may find a stone for himself if its shape catches his fancy. He might also find another object—such as an octopus in its hole, a shark, a snake, or an eel—that seems unusual to him and therefore connected with a spirit. He then takes money and scatters it around the stone, or on the place where he saw the object that caught his interest, and then goes home to sleep. He dreams that someone takes him to a place and shows him the pigs or money he will receive because of his connection with the thing he has found. In the Banks’ Islands, this object becomes his *tano-oloolo* <term>place of offering</term>, the site where offerings are made to obtain pigs or wealth. His neighbors begin to realize he possesses this power when they see his wealth increasing. They then come to him to seek the assistance of the spirit he has discovered through his mediation. He eventually passes this knowledge down to his son or nephew. If a man is sick, he gives money to another person who—

<gloss>A man is said to make an offering with money to the person who knows the stone; that person then makes the offering on the stone on behalf of the first man. ...is known to have a stone of power—it being suggested that the sick man has offended the spirit connected with it—he brings a short string of money and a bit of the pepper root, <term>gea</term> <note>original: *gea*; the local name for the plant *Piper methysticum*</note>, which is used for <term>kava</term> <note>original: *kava*; a ceremonial and social drink made from the roots of the pepper plant</note>. The sick man is said to <term>oloolo</term> <note>original: *oloolo*; to perform a ritual offering or sacrifice</note> to the owner of the stone. The owner takes the offerings to his sacred place and throws them down, saying, "Let [this person] recover." When the sick man recovers, he pays a fee to the owner. 

If a man desires to gain the benefit of a stone (or any other sacred object) owned by someone else—perhaps to increase his wealth in money, pigs, or food, or to ensure success in battle—the owner of the stone will take him to his sacred place. There, he likely keeps many stones, each serving its own specific purpose. The applicant provides money, perhaps a hundred strings only a few inches long. The guide shows him one stone and says, "This is a big yam," and the worshipper places money down. Of another, the owner says it represents a boar; of another, a pig with tusks; and money is offered to each. The belief is that the spirit, or <term>vui</term> <note>original: *vui*; a spirit that was never human, often associated with natural objects</note>, attached to the stone appreciates the money, which is left to remain upon or beside the stone. If the <term>oloolo</term> sacrifice succeeds, the person who benefited pays the man who owns the stones and spirits. 

If a man performs a sacrifice for success in fighting, he takes great care that nothing sharp pricks or scratches him, and that no stone bruises him. In their belief, if he were scratched, he would later be shot in battle; if he were bruised, he would be clubbed.

Some of these objects of sacrificial worship are well known, but they can only be approached by the person who has inherited the right of access to them. There must be a mediator between the worshipper who desires a favor and the spirit who bestows it: not only the physical medium of the stone (or whatever other object the spirit is connected with), but also the man who has established a personal acquaintance with that spirit through the stone. 

On the island of <term>Vanua Lava</term>, at <term>Sarewoana</term> near <term>Alo Sepere</term>—the legendary home of the hero-spirit <term>Qat</term>—there is still the stump of a tree that <term>Qat</term> is said to have cut down to make his canoe. It is an ancient stump with young shoots springing from it. Men who are building a canoe make sacrifices at this stump, throwing down money there so that their canoe may be swift and strong and never

...shipwrecked. It does not appear that anyone acts as a mediator between the person making the offering and Qat in this instance, perhaps because Qat is a figure known to everyone. 

There is no doubt that a sacrifice, or <term>oloolo</term> <note>original: *oloolo*; a ritual offering or sacrifice to a spirit</note>, is often made as a way of seeking favor or forgiveness; however, a <term>vui</term> <note>original: *vui*; a spirit that was never human</note> is not considered a malicious spirit that will cause harm unless it is constantly appeased. If a man has accidentally entered a sacred place and fears he has offended the spirit residing there, he will make an offering to the man who owns that sacred place so that the owner may appease the spirit on his behalf. In cases of sickness, there is always a working assumption that some spirit has been offended. 

A man whose "familiar spirit" is associated with a snake, an eel, an owl, a crab, or some similar creature, will visit that animal and make offerings to remain in its favor. He may also do this to obtain the spirit's favor for someone else who has paid him to make an offering. 

It is said that a man who has a <term>mae</term> <note>original: *mae*; an amphibious snake considered to have a sacred or awe-inspiring nature</note>—an amphibious snake with a fearsome reputation—as his familiar will go to the sacred place it haunts and call it until it appears. He sits down, and the snake crawls over him, putting its tongue into his mouth, which the man then sucks. He scatters money for the spirit, because he is not making the offering to the snake itself, but rather to the spirit, or *vui*, that resides within and is manifested through the snake. 

The man does not invoke or pray directly to the spirit, but he may pray to the ghosts of his predecessors who previously practiced this specific secret ritual. When a man visits his familiar spirit in this way, no one else is present. Because of this privacy, some local people have doubted whether there is actually a snake there at all. It is a fact that when a man who was known for receiving money to offer to the snake dies, and his successor (who received instructions from him) goes to reopen this profitable connection, the creature is often not found. However, people simply conclude that the man and the snake died together. 

Money used in this form of sacrifice—if it can be called that—is scattered into deep holes in a stream or into pools among the rocks on the beach. Wherever the natural environment inspires a sense of awe in the mind of a local person, they perceive the presence of a haunting *vui* and feel moved to perform an act of worship. However, the offering is not made to the stone, the stream, the tree, or even to the "spirit of the object" itself; instead, the *vui* is regarded as a personal being, like a...

### VIII. New Hebrides Sacrifices

...the man is, and its presence makes the place sacred. In the past, many men had a personal sacred place with a familiar spirit of their own; in fact, most grown-up men likely had one. There was no formal priestly order, no dedicated sacred buildings, and nothing designed for public spectacle.

In the Northern New Hebrides <note>now known as Vanuatu</note>, spirits are very commonly approached at specific stones. Offerings are made upon these stones to secure the spirits' favor or to appease them if they have been offended. This appears to be the only form of sacrifice practiced on Maewo (Aurora Island). They do not use any word that can be translated as "sacrifice," except perhaps *turegi* <note>original: *turegi*</note>, which simply means to lay an offering upon a stone. 

However, a specific type of offering is made to a ghost. If a man loses his pig, he will go to the grave of a relative and place a <term>qaru</term> <note>original: *qaru*; a tuft of leaves from a dracaena or croton plant</note> on the stones above it, saying, "Bring my pig back to me." It is believed the ghost will then drive the pig back to the village. Making this kind of offering is called *malai o qaru* <note>original: *malai o qaru*</note>. 

On Pentecost Island <note>original: Whitsuntide or Araga</note>, there are stones associated with spirits in sacred places known only to those who discovered them or were introduced to the spirits by their predecessors. Sacrifices are made at these stones. For example, a young man might wish to advance in the <term>Loli Society</term> <note>a graded secret society or social hierarchy</note>, to become wealthy, or to live a long life—the primary goal being to achieve high status within the Loli. 

Such a person gives an offering of a pig or mats to the man who is familiar with the spirit—this is called *ma dugu boe lalainia* <note>original: *ma dugu boe lalainia*</note>. As in the Banks Islands, they say the offering is not given directly to the spirit, but to the man who "knows" the spirit. This mediator keeps the pig for himself. He takes the petitioner to the sacred place and mutters to the spirit, Tagaro: "This man has given the two of us a pig; let him be great; let him become a man of status." After this, the petitioner is allowed to go to the sacred place and make his own requests. 

Sometimes a very young coconut is broken and the juice is poured over the man's head as a sign of his admission. They also place a young coconut on the stone as an offering. These sacrifices are performed to request sunshine, rain, and plentiful harvests. Offerings are also made to the ghosts of powerful men who have recently died, either at their graves or...

# Sacrifices

...where they <note>referring to spirits</note> are supposed to haunt. Men who know these locations and have access to them take mats, food, and pigs—either living or cooked—into the sacred place and leave them there. At Lepers' Island <note>modern-day Ambae</note>, they *drugv* <note>original: *drugv*; to make a sacrificial payment or offering</note> to the men who have access to spirits, known as *vui*, who are associated with specific stones. They give money and pigs to these mediators for their intercession; however, offerings are not commonly made directly to *vui* or to ghosts. 

Offerings are also made at sea near certain dangerous rocks. A tuft of pig’s hair or a fowl’s feather from the cargo, or perhaps a small piece of food, is thrown into the sea for Tagaro <note>a prominent creator-deity or hero-figure in Melanesian mythology</note>, so that he may grant the canoe a safe passage. Bishop Patteson <note>John Coleridge Patteson, the first Anglican Bishop of Melanesia</note> noted during his final voyage that on the island of Ambrym, it was the practice for high-ranking men to burn a pig entirely, without any accompanying prayer, within their <term>Suqe</term> <note>a graded social and religious secret society</note>. This was done with the goal of obtaining <term>mana</term> <note>spiritual power or efficacy</note>. This practice must be considered a sacrificial act.

**NOTE.**—The sacrifices of the Solomon Islands can likely be traced to a desire to keep the deceased as participants in the shared family meal; what is offered and burnt is simply common food. At Saa and San Cristoval <note>modern-day Makira</note>, they go a step further by begging an offended ghost to take the offering and spare the life of a sick person. 

It should be noted that there is no connection between these sacrifices and the *buto* <note>see page 32; a creature or object a person must avoid or respect</note>, which may be regarded as a <term>totem</term> <note>a natural object or animal believed by a particular society to have spiritual significance and a symbolic relationship to a clan</note>. In the Banks' Islands, it is much harder to connect the offering of money to a spirit (who is never the ghost of a human, nor the animating spirit of a natural object) with the idea of sharing a meal with the deceased. If there is such a thing as a Melanesian sacrifice to a god, it is an offering to a *vui*. To offer money is apparently to give what humans value most, and what it is assumed the spirit also loves.

Codrington argues that while some sacrifices represent a "shared meal" with the dead, others involving money or spirits (vui) represent the surrender of something valuable to the divine.</summary>

## CHAPTER IX.

### PRAYERS.

When a Melanesian is in danger, difficulty, or distress, they will naturally call upon the beings in whose power to help they believe. On occasion, they will do this with exclamations that express their feelings. From their point of view, this would not be considered "prayer" because it lacks a formal character. There are also songs, incantations, and charms which possess inherent power because of the names or words they contain. These are not addressed directly to the beings whose power they invoke and would not be called prayers.

There are, however, invocations that may be called prayers—that is, formal addresses used to beg for help or aid. Yet, it is certainly very difficult, if not impossible, to find a word in any Melanesian language that directly translates to the word "prayer," because the concept of effectiveness <note>original: "efficacy"</note> is so closely tied to the specific form of words used. In the Solomon Islands, addresses that may be called prayers are, of course, made to the beings from whom they seek supernatural aid: the <term>tindalo</term> <note>ghosts of deceased men who are believed to have become powerful spirits</note>. The invocations used during sacrifices are prayers, as are those used at sea. For example, in Florida <note>the Nggela Islands in the Solomon Islands</note>, a prayer is offered to **Daula**, a *tindalo* who is widely known and associated with the frigate-bird:

> "Pull the canoe so that it may reach the land; speed my canoe, grandfather, so that I may quickly reach the shore where I am going. Daula, lighten the canoe so that it may quickly reach the land and come up upon the shore."

They also invoke **Bagea** as their grandfather; the word *bagea* meaning...

...sharks, and any <term>tindalo</term> <note>a powerful spirit of a deceased person</note> that has taken up residence in a shark, or is represented by one, is called *Bagea*. They also call upon their immediate ancestors when in danger at sea. One person might call to his grandfather, another to his father, and another to a deceased friend, addressing them with reverence and saying:

> "Save us on the deep sea, save us from the storm, and bring us to the shore."

**Daula** <note>a spirit often associated with the frigate-bird</note> is invoked for help with fishing:

> "If you are powerful and possess <term>mana</term> <note>supernatural or spiritual power</note>, O Daula, put a fish or two into this net and let them die there."

After a good catch, the spirit is praised:

> "Powerful and full of *mana* is the *tindalo* of the net."

They rub their fishing lines with leaves dedicated to such a *tindalo*. In San Cristoval <note>now known as Makira</note>, the <term>'ataro</term> <note>ghosts or spirits</note> are asked for help in battle, during sickness, and for good harvests. However, the word they use, *lihungai*, suggests the idea of a charm rather than a simple prayer. These formulas are passed down from father to son or taught in exchange for payment. Similarly, at Saa, a man who has no special connection with a <term>lio'a</term> <note>a ghost of the dead</note> will call on his father or grandfather when in danger at sea. But a person who knows a specific *lio'a* will use a specific set of words he has learned, which is believed to hold power over the elements. After doing this, he calls upon the deceased person who first introduced him to that *lio'a* and taught him the incantation, followed by calls to his own father and grandfather.

The <term>tataro</term> of the Banks Islands, which might be called a prayer, is strictly an invocation of the dead. It is likely named this because the ritual begins with the word *tataro*, which is clearly related to the *'ataro* of San Cristoval—meaning a powerful ghost. The people of the Banks Islands are certain that a *tataro* is properly directed only to the dead; however, the spirits known as <term>vui</term> <note>beings that were never human</note>, such as **Qat** and **Marawa**, are addressed in the same manner. A man in danger at sea will call on deceased friends, especially someone who was a skilled sailor in life. However, if he merely cries out as he would in daily life, it is not considered a *tataro*, which requires a specific form of words. 

The use of *tataro* on the island of Motlav is described this way: a man falls ill, and it is suggested that the cause of his sickness is an offense against a sacred place where he remembers trespassing. Then the man to whom the sacred place belongs...

<page-num>147</page-num>
<header>IX.] Banks' Island Prayers.</header>

[The person to whom the sacred place] belongs will, for payment, go and perform a <term>tataro</term> <note>a prayer or invocation to a spirit</note> for him there morning and evening. He calls aloud the name of the sick man and listens for an answering sound, such as the cry of a kingfisher or another bird. If he hears a sound, he calls "Come back" to the life or soul of the sick man, runs back to the house where the man lies, and cries, "He will live!"—meaning that he has brought back the person's life.

If it happens that a lizard runs onto him on his way to the sacred place, that is considered enough of a sign; he has captured the life and returns with it. If a man who possesses a sacred stone is going to it to perform an <term>oloolo</term> <note>a sacrifice or offering</note> and sees a rat, crab, iguana, or lizard on the way, he scatters a little loose money for it and says a *tataro* that he knows.

When the oven is opened for a meal, one of the men will break off a bit of food and throw it against the side wall of the house with a *tataro*. In the same way, when water is poured into the oven to create steam, a *tataro* is used against an enemy, or to try to bring rain or sunshine. Some examples from the Mota language are as follows. On opening an oven, when a leaf of cooked mallow is thrown for a deceased person:

> "Prayer—this is a lucky portion for you to eat. May those who have charmed your food or clubbed you (as the case may be) be seized by the hands; drag them away to the place of the dead <note>original: "hell," referring here to the Melanesian underworld</note>; let them die."

If, after this, it is heard that the person the curse was directed at met with an accident, the other says, "Aha! My curse while eating has worked on him; he is dead." When water is poured into the oven:

> "Prayer—pour it on the head of that person down there who has plotted against me, clubbed me, shot me, or stolen this thing of mine (as the case may be). He shall die!"

On making a <term>libation</term> <note>a ritual pouring of a liquid as an offering</note> of kava <note>a ceremonial drink made from the roots of a pepper plant</note> before drinking:

> "Prayer—Grandfather! This is your lucky drop of kava. Let boars come to me; let wealth <note>original: *rare*, a specific type of valuable shell money</note> come to me. Let the money I have spent return to me; let the food that is gone come back here to our house."

L. Fison.

<header>Prayers. [CH. IX]</header>

On starting a voyage: 
> 'Invocation—Uncle! Father! I offer many boars to you, many tusked pigs <note>original: rawe; a castrated boar with circular tusks, highly valued in Melanesian culture</note>, and much money; <term>kava</term> <note>a traditional ceremonial drink made from the roots of a pepper plant</note> for you to drink, and lucky food for you to eat in the canoe. I pray to you with these offerings: look down upon me and let me travel on a calm sea.' 

Or when the canoe struggles with a heavy load: 
> 'Remove your heavy burden from us, so that we may travel quickly on a safe sea.' 

Another prayer was used over the oven in the <term>gamal</term> <note>the men's communal clubhouse</note> of the <term>Suqe</term> club, specifically at the pit where the fire is made: 
> 'Grandfather! May it be so—Father! My Uncle! My Great-uncle! the two of us will proceed with a hundred fathoms of your shell money; look down upon us and do not look upon us with disfavor. Let money be plentiful for the two of us, along with boars, tusked pigs, and food; let our progress in the <term>Suqe</term> <note>a hierarchical social and religious society</note> reach its end successfully; do not let our outrigger be broken; sit and watch over the two of us; let us proceed well, without receiving looks of disfavor; let us two come straight to the oven pit shared by the three of us, into the hot <term>Suqe</term> oven of us three; let the <term>Suqe</term> ceremony emerge and move forward.' 

There is no difference between these and the invocations of the spirits, or <term>vui</term> <note>supernatural beings that were never human</note>, such as <term>Qat</term> and <term>Marawa</term>. However, the following invocations are not strictly called <term>tataro</term> <note>invocations to the dead</note> because they are not addressed to deceased ancestors. These three were used at sea: 

> 'Qat! You and <term>Marawa</term> <note>a spirit companion of the hero-god Qat</note>, cover the blow-hole with your hands to protect me, so that I may reach a peaceful landing place; let the sea become calm for me. Let our canoe arrive at a quiet landing place.' 
> 'Qat! Marawa! Look down upon me; prepare the sea for us, so that I may travel on a safe sea. Beat down the crests of the waves for me; let the tide-rip subside and move away from me; beat the water level so it may flatten and roll away, so that I may reach a peaceful landing place.' 
> 'Qat! Marawa! May it be so—let our canoe transform into a whale, a flying fish, or an eagle; let it leap again and again over the waves; let it go, and let it reach my homeland.' 

In response to prayers like these, it was believed that Qat and Marawa would come and hold fast the mast and rigging of the canoe, protecting it from danger and speeding it on its course.

In the northern <term>New Hebrides</term> <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>, on the island of Maewo <note>original: Aurora</note>, they use the same word, *tataro*, for a ritual formula used, for example, in—

# CHAPTER X.

## SPIRITS.

Beings of a more or less spiritual nature—who, in any case, were never human—feature much more prominently in the beliefs and stories of the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides than they do in the Solomon Islands. Koevasi, who was mentioned previously, in Florida and Kahausibware in San Cristoval belong to this latter group, and they are likely the same figure known by different names. Neither was ever human, yet both were in some way the originators of the human race; both were female, and both were the subjects of stories rather than objects of worship. 

Kahausibware was a <term>Hi'ona</term> <note>a being of superhuman character</note>, dwelling on the mountain of Bauro—the central mass of San Cristoval—during the infancy of the human race. She took the outward form of a snake. In the same place lived a woman, a human being, who was somehow the offspring of Kahausibware. In those days, all the fruits of the earth grew without labor, and everything was of the highest quality. It was Kahausibware who created humans, pigs, and other animals, as well as coconuts, fruit trees, and all the food sources with which the island is now provided; at that time, death had not yet appeared. 

One day, the woman went to her work and left her infant in the house in the care of the spirit-snake. The spirit was so annoyed by the child's screaming that she coiled herself around it and strangled it. The mother returned while the serpent's body was still coiled around her child, and seizing an axe, she began to chop the snake into pieces. As she chopped it apart, the pieces joined back together again; but the

# Solomon Islands. Banks' Islands.

The snake finally could bear it no longer and cried out weeping, "I am going, and who will help you now?" Accordingly, she made her way down to the sea, and her track became a watercourse. Leaving the island, she swam across first to Ugi, but from there she could still see the Bauro mountain. She went on further to Ulawa, and from there again to the southeast end of Malanta <note>now Malaita</note>, but even there in clear weather she could see her former home. She therefore crossed to Marau, the southeast part of Guadalcanal <note>original: Guadalcanar</note> nearest to San Cristoval <note>now Makira</note>, where the view of the mountain of Bauro is blocked by the nearer hills; there she remains to this day. Since her departure, all things in San Cristoval have worsened. Snakes upon the Bauro mountain are venerated as the offspring or representatives of Kahausibware; but they are simple snakes, while she was a <term>Hi'ona</term>, or <term>Figona</term> <note>a powerful spirit or deity that was never human</note>.

In the Banks Islands and in the northern New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>, the purely spiritual beings who have no physical bodies are innumerable and unnamed. These are the ones whose representative form is generally a stone, who haunt the places that are sacred because of their presence, and who connect themselves with certain snakes, owls, sharks, and other creatures. In these objects, there is a means of communication with them; they are powerful enough to assist those who can approach them, and also to injure men, though they are not of a malicious nature. They are certainly believed to have no body, yet it is impossible for the natives to conceive of them as being entirely without form. Men, therefore, have declared that they have seen something indistinct, with no definite outline—grey like dust and vanishing as soon as it was looked at—near a stone, and this must have been a spirit, a <term>vui</term> <note>a non-human spirit</note>. 

But the same word is used to describe beings who *do* have bodies and are individually known and named. The natives will deny that these have bodies as men do, and they assert that these beings are of the same nature as those which are incorporeal. However, in the stories told about them, they appear as men, though possessed of powers which humans can never have. Consistency can hardly be expected; indeed, the native mind aims high when—

# Spirits

The human mind conceives of a being that lives, thinks, knows, and has power over nature without having a physical body or even a distinct form. However, people struggle when trying to describe a specific individual of this kind. Because of this, stories represent a <term>vui</term> <note>a spirit that was never human</note> as a person with greater powers. For example, a native person seeing some new and wonderful foreign object will exclaim, "A spirit made it!" Or, when a boy returns home after growing up elsewhere, they might cry, "*Me vui gai!*" <note>original: "He is a spirit, to be sure!"</note>.

It is also remarkable that among these superhuman beings called <term>vui</term> or <term>wui</term> in the **Banks Islands** and the **New Hebrides** <note>now Vanuatu</note>, whose actions resemble those of humans, there seem to be two distinct classes or ranks. In the stories of the **Banks Islands**, <term>Qat</term>, and in the **New Hebrides** stories, <term>Tagaro</term>, act as heroes or demigods living among a lesser group of dwarfs and trolls. These lesser beings are just as full of mysterious magical power as the heroes, but they are relatively crude and easily tricked. These beings remained on the islands even after <term>Qat</term>, <term>Tagaro</term>, and their brothers departed. In recent times, they have reportedly been seen in human form—smaller than the local people, darker-skinned, and with long, straight hair.

<term>Marawa</term>, the friend of <term>Qat</term>, was one of these. Only a few years ago, a man named <term>Manlepei</term> living on **Vanua Lava** went to the riverside early one morning and saw a little man with long, hanging hair. He followed him up the river valley until they came to a narrow gorge blocked by a rock. The <term>vui</term> rapped on the rock with his hand and it opened for him; as <term>Manlepei</term> followed closely behind, it closed again behind them both. They were inside a cave, which served as the spirit's house. He identified himself as <term>Marawa</term> and said he would appear to the man again if he returned to his village and brought back money.

<term>Manlepei</term> prospered ever after through <term>Marawa’s</term> help, and he did not hide the source of his wealth. He was always willing to accept money from his neighbors on <term>Marawa’s</term> behalf, promising to secure a share of the spirit's favor for them. It has also not been very long since a female <term>vui</term> with a child was seen on **Saddle Island** <note>now Loh or Motlav</note>, near the house of a man who often found a fine yam left for him on the bench by his door and who noticed that his money bag always remained full.

<summary>This page describes how Melanesians conceptualize spirits (vui) as being both formless and human-like, while categorizing them into higher demigods like Qat and lower, dwarf-like beings like Marawa who interact with humans.</summary>
<keywords>vui, wui, Banks Islands, New Hebrides, Qat, Tagaro, Marawa, Vanua Lava, Manlepei, Saddle Island, spirits, folklore, Melanesian mythology</keywords>

### x. Banks' Islands. 'Nopitu'

...after he had paid a debt. A few years ago, a woman lived in **Mota** whose father was a <term>vui</term> <note>a spirit that was never human</note>. Popular stories showed how these beings were believed to be closely involved in human affairs. For instance, a woman working in her garden heard a voice coming from a gourd fruit asking her for food. When she pulled up a <term>caladium</term> <note>a tropical plant with edible roots, similar to taro</note> or dug up a yam, another one immediately appeared in its place. However, when she stopped to listen to another *vui* playing his panpipes, the first spirit grew jealous and spirited away the garden and everything in it. In these stories, and likely in common belief, there was some confusion between these spirits and the ghosts of the deceased.

Certain *vui*—spiritual beings that were nonetheless physical in some way—appear strangely in the stories of **Mota** as <term>Nopitu</term>, and in **Motlav** as <term>Dembit</term> (another version of the same word). It is often difficult to understand what is said about them because the name *Nopitu* is used for both the spirit itself and the person possessed by the spirit. This possessed person performs wonders through the power and in the name of the *Nopitu* who possesses him. 

Such a person would call himself a *Nopitu*; or rather, when speaking of himself, he would not say "I," but "we two," meaning the *Nopitu* and himself. If he were possessed by many spirits, he would say "we." He would dance at a festival, such as a <term>kolekole</term> <note>a traditional celebratory feast and dance used to gain social prestige</note>, in a way that no man could possibly dance without being possessed by a *Nopitu*. He would scratch his arm or his head, and new shell money—not yet strung together—would fall from his fingers. A man named **Vetpepewu** told me he had seen bags full of money fall from a *Nopitu* during a *kolekole*. 

Another would shake himself over a mat, and unstrung money would pour down onto it. He would pick up a coconut to drink, but bystanders would hear money pouring out instead of juice, rattling against his teeth, and he would then spit the money out onto the ground. **Tursul** witnessed a woman in **Mota** vomit native money—she was a *Nopitu* possessed by such a spirit. To gain the favor of the *Nopitu*, men would make an <term>oloolo</term> <note>a ritual offering or sacrifice</note> to the possessed person. They would give him a red yam and almonds; he would eat the yam raw, and the sound of him crunching money with his teeth could be heard. If he were offered a young coconut, he would open the "eye" and drink, then return the shell completely full of money.

<summary>This page describes the 'Nopitu' and 'Dembit' spirits of the Banks Islands, focusing on how they possess humans and manifest physical wealth, specifically by miraculously producing shell money.</summary>

### Spirits

But a **Nopitu** <note>a type of spirit that could possess humans or manifest in small, physical forms</note> would also reveal itself in a different way. A group of people would be sitting around an evening fire, and one of them would hear a voice that seemed to come from his own thigh, saying, "Here I am; give me some food, I am hungry." He would roast a small red yam and, when it was finished, fold it into the corner of the mat on which he was sitting. In a short while, the food would disappear, and then the **Nopitu** would begin to talk and sing in a voice so small, clear, and sweet that, once heard, it could never be forgotten. It sang the ordinary **Mota** <note>Mota is one of the Banks Islands in Vanuatu</note> songs, while the men drummed an accompaniment for it. Then it would say, "I am going;" they would call out to it, but it would be gone. 

Sometimes a woman would feel the spirit come to her and sit upon her knee; she would hear it cry, "Mother! Mother!" She would recognize it and carry it in a mat on her back like an infant. Occasionally, a woman would hear a **Nopitu** say, "Mother, I am coming to you," and she would feel the spirit entering into her; it would afterwards be born as an ordinary child. A person like this, named **Rongoloa**, was still living at **Motlav** not long ago. The **Nopitu**, like other spirits, were the companion spirits <term>familiars</term> <note>spirits believed to attend and obey a particular person</note> only of those who knew them, and these were often women. If a man wished to know and become known to a **Nopitu**, he gave money <note>likely traditional shell money or currency</note> to a woman who was familiar with those spirits, and then one would come to him.

The place of **Qat** <note>the central figure in Banks Islands mythology, often credited with the creation of natural phenomena</note> in the popular beliefs of the **Banks Islands** was so high and so prominent that when the people first became known to Europeans, it was assumed that he was their god—the supreme creator of men, pigs, and food. It is certain that he was believed to have "made" things in a different sense than how humans make things. To this day, a mother might scold a sleepy, irritable <term>fractious</term> child, or one crying from hunger, with the words, "Do you think you are going to die? Don't you know that **Qat** made you this way?" If a pig comes indoors to sleep during bad weather, the man who drives it out says to it, "**Qat** made you to stay outside." These are not solemn sayings, but it was believed that **Qat** had created some creatures and determined the natural state of—

## x. Banks' Islands: Qat

...things in the world. The regular cycles of the seasons are attributed to him: the calm months from September to December, when the **un** <note>the Palolo sea-worm, which appears predictably in the reefs</note> emerges; the yearly storms; and the high tide in the month of **wotgoro**. However, unpredictable rains, winds, and calms are blamed on men who are believed to influence the **vui** <term>spirits</term> to produce them. 

The name of **Qat** is also given to remarkable natural objects and phenomena. When fish die in the sea from the intense heat of the sun, **Qat** is said to have poisoned them. A certain kind of fungus is called his basket; a mushroom coral <note>original: "fungia coral"</note> is his dish; and the sulphur found at the volcanic vents on the island of **Vanua Lava** is considered his sauce. A beam of light shining through a hole in a roof into the dusty air is seen as his spear, and the passing shadow of a lone cloud over the sea is called the shadow of **Qat**. 

Despite all this, it is impossible to take **Qat** very seriously or to grant him the status of a true deity. He is certainly not the ruler of all spirits. Instead, he is a folk hero—the ideal character for a good-natured people who believe deeply in magic and greatly admire cleverness and success in using it. **Qat** himself is kind-hearted and only playfully mischievous, and he thoroughly enjoys exercising his extraordinary powers.¹ When he is said to "create," he is merely adding to the "furniture" of the world into which he was born. In that world, there were already houses, canoes, weapons, and ornaments, as well as garden crops and the various skills of life that the islanders possessed when they were first visited by Europeans. Storytellers find it difficult to distinguish him from ordinary men, even though they always insist he was a **vui**; and while he certainly never was a human being, the people of **Alo Sepere** on **Vanua Lava**—the place where he was born—claim him as their ancestor.

It would be pointless to look for a single, consistent history of **Qat** from his birth to his disappearance. He is the central figure of a cycle of stories that vary across the different islands of the Banks group. All versions agree, however, that he was born on **Vanua**—

The story that follows is translated, with additions from other sources, from the Mota language version written by the late indigenous Deacon Edward Wogale, who was himself of the Sepere lineage.

*The Story of Qat.* Qat did have a beginning. He had a mother named Qatgoro (otherwise known as Iro Ul), and this mother was a stone that burst apart and brought him forth. He had no father, and he was born on the road. He matured and spoke immediately. He asked his mother what his name was, saying that if he had a father or a maternal uncle, one of them would have named him; then he gave himself the name Qat. 

He also had brothers. The first was Tangaro Gilagilala, Tangaro the Wise, who understood all things and could teach the others. The second was Tangaro Loloqong, Tangaro the Fool, who was ignorant of everything and acted like a fool. The others were Tangaro Siria, Tangaro Nolas, Tangaro Nokalato, Tangaro Noav, Tangaro Nopatau, Tangaro Noau, Tangaro Nomatig, Tangaro Novunue, and Tangaro Novlog. There were eleven of them, all named Tangaro—twelve in total including Qat. 

The names of the last nine are composed of the names of leaves from trees and plants—Nettle-leaf, Breadfruit-leaf, Bamboo-leaf, Coconut-leaf, and Umbrella-palm-leaf—added to the name Tangaro. This name is undoubtedly the same as the Tagaro of the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note> and the Tangaroa of the Polynesians. All of these brothers grew up as soon as they were born, and they settled in the village of Alo Sepere, where their mother can still be seen today in her stone form. 

There, Qat began to create things: men, pigs, trees, and rocks, whenever the whim struck him. However, even after he had made all sorts of things, he still did not know how to create night, and the daytime was always light. Then his brothers said to him, "Hey, Qat! This is not at all pleasant; there is nothing but day here. Can’t you do something for us?" Then, searching for what he could do with the daylight, he heard that there was night at Vava, in the Torres Islands <note>a small archipelago in northern Vanuatu</note>. So he took a pig and tied it up, and...

Qat put the night into his canoe and sailed over to Vava, where he bought night, *qong* <note>original: "qong", meaning night</note>, from "I Qong" (Night personified), who lived there. Others say that he paddled to the base of the sky to buy night from Night itself, and that Night blackened his eyebrows, showed him how to sleep that evening, and taught him in the morning how to create the dawn. Qat returned to his brothers with the knowledge of night, bringing a rooster and other birds to signal the time when the light should return. 

He then told his brothers to prepare their beds; they plaited coconut fronds and spread them out in the house. For the first time, they saw the sun moving and sinking toward the west, and they called out to Qat that it was crawling away. "It will soon be gone," he said; "and if you see a change on the face of the earth, that is night." Then he let the night go. 

"What is this coming out of the sea," they cried, "and covering the sky?" 

"That is night," he replied; "sit down on both sides of the house, and when you feel something in your eyes, lie down and be quiet." 

Soon it was dark, and their eyes began to blink. "Qat! Qat! What is this? Are we going to die?" 

"Shut your eyes," he said; "this is it—go to sleep." 

When night had lasted long enough, the rooster began to crow and the birds began to twitter. Qat took a piece of red obsidian <note>a sharp, glass-like volcanic rock</note> and cut the night with it. The light over which the night had spread itself shone forth again, and Qat’s brothers awoke. <note>The author notes that this myth explains the local expressions *o maran me tere* ("the morning has cut") and *o mera ti lamagag* ("the dawn strikes upon the sky"), where *mera* is a common word for red.</note> After this, he occupied himself once more with creating things.

According to the story told at Lakona, on the island of Santa Maria, Qat and Marawa (another *rui* <term>a type of spirit or supernatural being</term> who corresponds here to the spirit Supwe of Maewo and Araga) lived at Matan, near the mountain Garat, where volcanic fires still smolder. The two of them created humans in this way: Qat carved wood from dracaena trees into shape; he formed legs, arms, trunks, and heads, and added ears and eyes. He fitted the parts together, working on them for six days. After this, he set a period of six days for them to come to life. For three days he hid them away, and—

But Marawa the spider—for this was he, another very powerful spirit <note>original: "vui" – a supernatural being or spirit in Melanesian mythology</note>—pleaded with Qat, "Oh, friend, do not kill me, and I will fix your canoe for you." He then went to work and soon finished it using only his fingernails <note>Hence, when iron was first seen in the form of nails at Mota, it was called Marawa’s fingernails (*pis Marawa*); *pismarawa* is now a widely accepted name for nails in the region.</note>. 

When all the canoes were finished, Qat told his brothers to launch their own. As each one was pushed into the water, he raised his hand, and one by one, they sank. Then Qat and Marawa appeared in the canoe they had built together, paddling swiftly around to the astonishment of the brothers, who had not even known Qat had started working. After amusing himself with their embarrassment, he recovered their canoes for them during the night.

Following this, his brothers tried many tricks to kill Qat so they could take his wife and his canoe for themselves. One day, they led him to the hole of a land crab beneath a large stone. They had already dug underneath the stone so it was ready to topple over. Qat crawled into the hole and began digging for the crab. His brothers tipped the stone onto him and, thinking he was crushed to death, ran off to seize Ro Lei <note>Qat's wife</note> and the canoe. But Qat called out to Marawa by name, "Marawa! Take me back to Ro Lei!" and by the time his brothers reached the...
