Back at the village, the brothers were astonished to find Qat sitting by the side of his wife. On another occasion, they partially cut through the branch of a fruit tree and persuaded Qat to go out onto it to gather the nuts. When the branch broke and he fell, they thought he had surely been killed. However, Marawa <note>The spider spirit who acts as Qat's companion and protector.</note> saved him once again. When the brothers ran to seize Qat’s wife, they found him already there, lying with his head in her lap.

Qat was always ready to play tricks on his brothers in return, though never out of malice. One moonlight night, he convinced them to go out and shoot flying foxes <note>original: "flying foxes" — large fruit-eating bats common in the Pacific islands.</note>. While they were getting ready, Qat covered himself with wooden boards and flew up into a pandanus tree, where he hung upside down like a bat. His brothers spotted him, shot their arrows, and hit him. Qat spat blood onto the ground, and the brothers, certain they had wounded him, climbed into the tree one after another to capture the "bat." As each brother shot at him and climbed up, Qat flew off and returned to hang in a different spot. Once all the brothers had shot their arrows and climbed the tree, Qat flew home, pulled the arrows out of his wooden armor, and hung them up in the *gamal* <term>the men’s communal house or clubhouse</term>. When his brothers returned, he asked them what luck they had. When they described how they had hit a wonderful, giant bat, he made them look at the arrows in the *gamal* and identify them as their own.

Iro Lei <note>Also referred to as Ro Lei; the prefix "Iro" or "Ro" often denotes a female name or title in the Banks Islands.</note> also took part in these tricks. One day, while Qat and his brothers were sailing in their canoes, they saw a woman standing on a rocky point. She called out to each brother as he passed, inviting him to come and share her food. As each brother drew near and saw that she looked like an old woman, they rejected her offer. However, when Qat approached, he took her into his canoe. The brothers had rejected the very woman they so greatly desired, for this was actually Qat's wife, Ro Lei, in disguise.

Again, the brothers consulted on how they might destroy him and decided to entrap him while they were out snaring birds. They each prepared a station for themselves in a nutmeg tree. Each brother chose a tree further and further away from the village, with the tree intended for Qat being the furthest of all. They took Qat out and showed him his place. Qat climbed up into his tree, and as soon as he was busy with his bird snares, the brother nearest to him climbed down from his own station, ran to the base of Qat’s tree, and shouted, "My nutmeg tree, swell!"

### Adventures of Qat

The nutmeg tree instantly grew so large in the trunk that Qat’s arms could never wrap around it, and all its boughs and branches grew equally thick. But Qat did not at first discover this, because he was busy setting his snares. His brother, who had cast the spell upon the nutmeg tree, ran back, collecting the others as he went into the village. They seized and carried off Ro Lei <note>Qat's wife</note>, dragged the canoe down into the sea, and paddled away at once. The island had already sunk out of their sight when they blew their shell trumpet <note>original: "shell trumpet" — a conch shell used for signaling.</note> to let Qat know that they were gone. 

When he heard it, he knew what had happened and would have followed them, but the size of the swollen branches of the nutmeg tree made it impossible for him to descend. He tried and tried in vain, and then he raised his voice and wept. His friend Marawa, the Spider, heard his cries and came to ask him what was the matter. "I can’t get down," said he; "my brothers have played me this trick." "Down with you," said Marawa, whose hair was exceedingly long and loose; and he sent his hair up to Qat, who descended by it and ran into the village. 

There he found only the rollers <note>Logs used to slide a canoe into the water.</note> of his canoe remaining. He sought his wife in vain, for his brothers had taken off both his wife and his canoe to be their own. Then Qat went inside his house and took his cock’s-tail plume, his string of the smallest shell-money <term>traditional currency made from tiny, polished shell discs</term>, his red earth <note>A pigment used for ritual or decorative purposes.</note>, and his shell hatchet, and asked his mother for his bananas. "They have plucked them all," she answered, "except these little ones at the end of the bunch." "Pluck them all off," said Qat. 

Then he took a coconut-shell bottle and stored all his things and his food within it. He made himself small and took his seat inside it, and commanded his mother to count three waves, and at the fourth small wave to throw it into the sea. So Qat floated on and on in the bottle until he came up to the canoe in which his brothers were, for they had not yet reached land. Then he floated along before the bow of the canoe, and wherever he drifted they were forced to follow. By and by he took one of his bananas and ate it, and threw the skin into the sea where the canoe would pass. His brothers saw it and remarked that it was like those...

They had taken some of Qat’s bananas, and they asked among themselves who had been eating a banana. When everyone denied it, Tangaro the Wise spoke out: “You all,” he said, “it is Qat who has eaten this banana. He has thrown the skin here for us to give us notice that he is not dead, but has escaped and is following us.” But the rest of them would not listen to him, declaring that Qat was dead. 

The same thing happened again when he threw out another banana skin for them. After this, they saw the bottle itself in which Qat was floating, close to the canoe. One of them picked it up, thinking it was a good coconut, but when he smelled it and found the smell was bad, he threw it away again. Each of them did this one after another, except for Tangaro the Wise, who did not happen to notice it. 

Then Qat floated quickly to the shore of Maewo <note>An island in the northern part of Vanuatu.</note> and emerged from his bottle. He colored his hair with red earth, bound his small shell-money <term>traditional currency made from tiny, polished shell discs</term> around his head, stuck his cock’s-tail feather in his hair, and took his seat on the top of a male pandanus tree <term>a palm-like tropical tree with prop roots and sword-shaped leaves</term> on the beach. There he sat and waited for his brothers to come to land, as they were still in the canoe. 

Presently, they came through the reef and up to the shore. Then they looked up and saw him sitting in the pandanus tree, and they asked one another who it was sitting up there. “It is Qat,” said Tangaro the Wise. But his brothers argued that he could not have made his way there, seeing as he was already dead. “That is Qat, and no mistake,” said Tangaro the Wise, for he knew better than his brothers about this and all other things. 

So they brought their canoe to land, but they had no need to haul it up, for Qat made the rocks rise and carry it high and dry. Qat leaped down upon them with his axe and chopped the canoe to pieces while singing this song:

> “Chop, chop the canoe; whose canoe is it? Marawa’s <note>Marawa is the Spider, Qat's supernatural friend and helper.</note> canoe. My brothers tricked me about twisting a string—swelling the nutmeg tree—to draw the snare. I had one canoe, and my canoe slipped away from me.”

So he chopped the canoe to pieces before their eyes. After this, he made peace with them and told them to live in harmony together.

<page-num>163</page-num>

<header>X. Adventures of Qat.</header>

Another remarkable series of adventures involved Qat's encounters with Qasavara. This was a *vui* <term>a non-human spirit</term>, very strong, a great fighter, a tyrant, and a cannibal, who lived on the island that was the home of Qat and his brothers. One day the brothers went to bathe and found the fruit of a Tahitian chestnut, a *make* <term>the edible seed of the *Inocarpus edulis* tree</term>, floating down the stream. The others took it up one after another and rejected it, thinking it was not good; but Qat took it, found it was good, and gave it to his mother to cook. As each of the brothers returned from bathing, they went to their mother for food. She had nothing but Qat’s *make*, and they each took a bit of it; Tangaro the Fool finished it. 

Qat sent them to get some more, and by following the stream up which this fruit had floated, they came upon the tree. They climbed it to gather the chestnuts, and Tangaro the Fool dropped one onto the house of Qasavara, which sat beneath the overhanging branches. The ogre came out in a rage, seized and killed the brothers, and put them in his food-chest. 

Qat waited five days, then took his bow and arrows and his shell hatchet and went in search of them. Following the stream, he found the tree and, guessing what had happened, lured Qasavara out by dropping a *make* on his house. They fought, and Qat killed Qasavara. Then, searching for his brothers, he found their bones in the food-chest. He revived them by blowing through a reed into their mouths and telling them to laugh if they were truly his brothers. 

Another adventure, which is not very consistent with this one, is narrated as follows: Qasavara, happening to meet Qat and his brothers, invited them to his village and prepared a fire in his oven for them. When evening came, he told them they were to sleep by themselves in his *gamal* <term>a communal men's clubhouse</term>; but they, knowing they would be killed, were incredibly afraid. Night fell and they were very sleepy, and Qat called them to come to bed. He split open one of the rafters of the *gamal* with his knuckles, and they all climbed inside and slept. In the middle of the night, Qasavara and his men took clubs and bows and came to kill Qat’s party, but not finding them in the sleeping places, they went back disappointed. At the approach of day, the cock crowed, and Qat awoke his brothers,

"Qasavara," Qat said, "do me no harm; kindly take me as one of your household, and I will work for you."

"No, indeed," said Qat <note>Though the text attributes the first plea to Qasavara, the context suggests Qasavara is pleading for his life after being trapped in the tree, and Qat is responding.</note>, "instead I will take revenge for the mischief you have caused me."

His head struck against the sky, and he fell back to the earth; there he lay stretched out on his face and turned into a stone. Even now, they offer sacrifices at that stone for courage; if anyone desires to be valiant and strong in battle, he makes an offering at that stone, which they say is Qasavara himself¹.

The stone is apparently not located at Tatgan on Vanua Lava where it ought to be, so the people say it is in Gaua instead; however, it is agreed that Qat and his brothers made their home at Tatgan. Nevertheless, the story says it was from Gaua that Qat departed from the world. In the center of that island, where the great lake called the Tas <note>Now known as Lake Letas, the largest lake in Vanuatu.</note> is now located, there was formerly a large plain covered with forest. Qat carved a massive canoe there out of one of the largest trees. While he was making it, his brothers often mocked him, asking how he would ever get such a large canoe to the sea. He always answered that they would see in time.

When the canoe was finished, he took his wife and brothers inside. He collected the living creatures of the island—even those as small as ants—and shut himself in with them inside the canoe, for which he had built a covering. Then came a deluge of rain; the great basin of the island became full of water, which eventually burst through the surrounding hills where the great waterfall of Gaua now flows. The canoe carved a channel for itself out to the sea and disappeared. The people believed that the best of everything was taken away from the islands when Qat left them, and they looked forward to his return. 

When Bishop Patteson <note>John Coleridge Patteson (1827–1871), the first Anglican Bishop of Melanesia.</note> and his companions first went ashore at Mota, some of the natives still living remember people saying that Qat and his brothers had returned. It is very probable that Lata—who is said by the people of Santa Cruz to have created humans and animals—is viewed by them in the same way that Qat was viewed by the people of the Banks Islands. Furthermore, Tinota is a *duka* <note>original: *duka*; a term for a spirit or ghost of a deceased ancestor, or a supernatural being with creative powers</note> of the same type as Lata. A story told about Natei, who is currently the chief at Nelua in Santa Cruz, also demonstrates a belief in the same kind of beings that the Banks Islanders believe live among them, which they call *vui* <note>original: *vui*; spirits that were never human, often possessing great supernatural power</note>. This story is undoubtedly much older than Natei himself, just as the similar story of Manlepei in Vanua Lava was certainly told about someone else—and by someone else about himself—long before Manlepei’s time. 

The current younger generation in Santa Cruz, seeing that Natei is a powerful man and assuming his success must have come from supernatural help, tell this story about him. This person then led him along an excellent path up the valley, which narrowed into a steep ravine. This ravine opened up again into an area containing fine gardens and a village. Five days later, the people of Nelua saw some visitors coming to their village, whom they assumed were men from some place further inland, asking for Natei. They were shown his house and they entered it, but they were never seen again. When Natei arrived and entered his house, he found it draped with feather-money brought by his visitors. The nearest of the Banks Islands to the New Hebrides is Merlav (Star Island), and there Qat and his brothers are the subjects of stories common in the rest of the group. The northernmost of the New Hebrides and the closest to Merlav is Maewo (Aurora), and there Qat, though not unknown, is not recognized as a spirit. Instead, Tagaro takes his place. The people said that Qatu <note>A variation of the name Qat.</note> was a great man of ancient times, very high-ranking in the *suqe* <note>original: *suqe*; a graded secret society or social hierarchy central to Melanesian life</note>, reaching a status that men no longer achieve today. But Tagaro was a *wui* <note>original: *wui*; a spirit that was never human and possesses creative powers</note>. Regarding any *wui*, the belief in Maewo was that they had no bodily form; any old man there would describe one in that way.

Yet the stories of Tagaro, who was a *wui*, treat him much like the stories of the Banks Islands treat Qat. While nothing is told of Tagaro’s brothers, his companion was Suqe-matua, who was his opposite in all things. Tagaro wanted everything to be good and desired no pain or suffering; Suqe-matua wanted all things to be bad. When Tagaro created things, either he or Suqe-matua would toss them up into the air; whatever Tagaro caught is good for food, but whatever he missed is worthless. 

Tagaro lived at Mambarambara, and particularly at Hombio, not far from Tanoriki. He was not born there, but he lived there, made his canoe, built his house and his *gamal* <note>original: *gamal*; a large communal house or clubhouse used by men</note>, and created and grew his own food. His life was full of wonders; his coconuts increased as he ate them, and dry nuts from which he scooped the meat would fill up again. Finally, Tagaro became angry because someone stole his pig and went off to Mamalu (no one knows where that is). He turned the island upside down and went off eastwards in his canoe from the east coast of the island, taking the best of everything with him, never to return. He extinguished the fire but threw back a fire-stick; his shell trumpet lies on the beach in the form of a rock; Lepers' Island <note>Now known as Ambae or Aoba.</note> is said to be his canoe. His place at Hombio is considered very sacred; his yams still remain there, trailing over a *gamal* called the *gamal*...

...dam, the yam *gamal* <note>original: *gamal*; a communal clubhouse or men's house used by initiated men</note>. There is also one *vui* <note>original: *vui*; a spirit that was never human and possesses creative powers</note> named Gaviga, and some say there is another who rules over the dead; however, the vast majority of the purely spiritual, bodiless beings called *vui* are associated with sacred stones. In Araga (Whitsuntide Island), which lies immediately south of Maewo, Tagaro has ten brothers, in addition to Suqe, who stays with him and constantly thwarts his work. Tagaro descended from heaven, created humanity and other things, and then returned to heaven. 

Suqe, on the other hand, belonged to the earth. His head was forked, which meant he had two different thoughts inside it. Whatever Tagaro did or made was right, but Suqe was always wrong. For example, Suqe wanted humans to die for only five days <note>likely implying he wanted death to be temporary</note>; he wanted there to be six nights for every one day; and when he planted yams, he planted the scooped-out meat of the vegetable instead of the rind. Eventually, Tagaro sent him to a place where there is a bottomless chasm, somewhere in the interior of Araga, where Suqe now rules over the ghosts of the dead. 

When Tagaro lived on earth, even though he was a *vui*, he took a human form but possessed superhuman power. He created the flat plains by treading on the ground with his feet; the places where he did not step remained as hills. He had no wife or children of his own spiritual kind, but he became the father of a boy on earth. The boy repeatedly asked his mother who his father was, and she told him that his father lived in heaven. The boy insisted on going to heaven to see him, so his mother made him a bow and an arrow from an *ere* <note>original: *ere*; a type of flowering reed</note>. He shot the arrow upward and hit the sky; the *ere* then transformed into something resembling the hanging root of a banyan tree, which the two used to climb up to heaven. 

Once there, they found Tagaro sitting in a *salite* tree <note>a tropical fruit tree</note>, carving images of himself out of the fruit. He threw one of these images to the boy, who took it to his mother. She recognized the features and told the boy it was indeed his father. Tagaro agreed to return to earth with them; however, as they were descending, he cut the line above them and below himself. He returned to heaven, while they landed at Atambulu, the original home of humanity *on that island.*

There are also many other *vui*, all connected with stones and sacred places, whose names are known only to those who have the spiritual right to access them. These spirits may also be seen during the rain or as night falls, and they provide people with food. When they appear, they have long hair and sometimes long fingernails, and they wear an old *malo* <note>original: *malo*; a traditional loincloth made of bark cloth or woven fiber</note>.

One that Tapera saw not long ago was a *Sarivanua* <note>original: *Sarivanua*; a wild spirit of the hills</note> of the hills, standing in the rain by a banyan tree with bananas in his hand. He looked like a man with small legs; when spoken to he did not answer, and when struck he did not feel it. The multitude of *vui* <note>original: *vui*; spirits that were never human</note>, whose stones and haunts are sacred, are unknown by name and have no physical form.

In Omba (Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae</note>), a spirit, or *vui*, is defined this way: spirits are immortal; they have bodies, but they are invisible; they are like men, but they do not eat or drink, and they can be seen only by the dead. However, there are others that also appear in bodily shape. Some are known by name, the most remarkable being Nggelevu, who presides over the dead, and Tagaro and his brothers or companions. Suqe is not known in all parts of the island; his place is perhaps filled by Tagaro-lawua <note>Tagaro the Big</note>, who also corresponds to Tangaro-loloqong in the Banks' Island stories. 

It was Tagaro who made fruit trees, food, pigs, and lastly, men. He is still invisibly active in human affairs and is therefore invoked in times of sickness and all difficulties. Tagaro-lawua, the Big, was a boaster and incompetent; Tagaro-mbiti, the Little, was exceedingly clever <note>original: "knowing"</note> and powerful. If someone speaks of Tagaro, it is Tagaro-mbiti who is meant. Just as Qat <note>a hero-spirit from the Banks Islands</note> is represented by Tagaro-mbiti, so Merambuto, also a *vui*, corresponds to Qasavara. Merambuto, like Qasavara, tried to catch Tagaro’s party by night and kill them, but Tagaro made them all sleep inside a shell. The next morning Tagaro-lawua let out the secret, and Tagaro-mbiti made them sleep elsewhere. 

All sacred stones are connected with Tagaro, though other spirits are also involved; all charms derive their power from the name of Tagaro within them. There are also, as in the neighboring islands, spiritual beings (*vui*) who are not of the same order as Tagaro. They are superhuman in nature and power, and they can be seen. These women were *vui* whose power was connected to pigs; nevertheless, to this day, when the man's wives go down to the beach to fish, they find fish already caught and lying ready for them.

It is well worth noting that Merambuto and his companions are depicted not only as somewhat mischievous and unfriendly but also as easily deceived and ignorant. This appears clearly in the story of Merambuto and Tagaro-mbiti in the tree, where Merambuto did not recognize and was terrified of the unknown sound of a conch-shell trumpet. Similarly, a story from Motlav also describes a *vui* who was afraid of the sound of a drum.

On the side of Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae</note> nearest to Araga <note>Pentecost Island</note>, the story of Suqe is told, and he is portrayed as always being in the wrong, even though he shared the work of creation with Tagaro. The two of them created the land and everything on it. When they made trees, the fruit of Tagaro’s trees was good for food, but Suqe’s fruit was bitter. When they created humans, Tagaro said they should walk upright on two legs, but Suqe wanted them to move like pigs. Suqe wanted people to sleep inside the trunks of sago palms, but Tagaro said they should work and live in houses. They constantly disagreed, and in every case, Tagaro’s decision was final <note>original: "the word of Tagaro stood"</note>.

It was also Tagaro who went to Maewo and brought back night inside a shell. When he released it and darkness spread across the sky, people wept and beat their houses <note>likely out of fear or to drive away the unknown darkness</note>. Tagaro is also described as the father of ten sons, the last of whom was Tagaro-mbiti ("the Little"), who was incredibly small. His brothers went out to work, but he stayed home because of a sore on his leg. They planted the leaves of the edible caladium <note>a tropical plant with edible roots, similar to taro</note>, the top shoots of bananas, and the vines of yams; but when they were gone, he took the crowns of the caladium, the suckers of the banana plants, and the rinds of the yams,

<header>Spirits.</header>

...and planted them. His brothers scolded him for idleness, not knowing what he had done; but when the season came round and they had nothing to eat, he showed them his garden full of abundant food. It was Tagaro also (though called Qatu in the Maewo story) who married the winged woman—a *Banewonowono* or *Vinmara*, meaning "Web-wing" or "Dove-skin"—from heaven. This was not exactly a spirit, *vui* <note>original: *vui*; in Melanesian belief, these are spirits that were never human</note>, but one of a group of women with webbed wings like those of bats. These women flew down from heaven to bathe, and Tagaro watched them. He saw them take off their wings, stole one pair, and hid them at the foot of the main pillar of his house. He then returned and found all the women had fled except the wingless one; he took her to his house and presented her to his mother as his wife. After a time, Tagaro took her to weed his garden when the yams were not yet ripe. As she weeded and touched the yam vines, ripe tubers came into her hand. Tagaro’s brothers thought she was digging the yams before their time and scolded her; she went into the house and sat weeping at the foot of the pillar. As she wept, her tears fell, and by wearing away the earth, they pattered down upon her buried wings. She heard the sound, recovered her wings, and flew back to heaven.

Beings called *Tavogivogi* must be classed as spirits; they are certainly not human beings and correspond to the mysterious snakes called *mae*, which in neighboring islands are believed to assume the form of men. A *Tavogivogi* is not thought ever to take the appearance of a snake; instead, one of them appears in the form of a beautiful youth or woman in order to entice someone of the opposite sex, and any young man or woman who yields to the seduction dies. There is no outward sign of the real character of the *Tavogivogi*, but the test is to ask the name of a tree, and a wrong answer will show that there is deceit. Whether successful in their seduction or not, the *Tavogivogi* suddenly disappears "like a bird," taking the form of a bird or another creature. The young man goes home and sickens; he remembers the sudden disappearance, knows what has befallen him, and never recovers. The name means "changeling," from the word *wog* in the Banks Islands, meaning to change one's form.

# CHAPTER XI.
## SACRED PLACES AND THINGS.

It is almost certain that idols have no place in the account I am about to give regarding the sacred places and objects I have encountered in Melanesia. It is true that the word "idol" is frequently used to describe any kind of native-made image, regardless of whether it actually possesses a sacred character or not. The people of San Cristobal, Ugi, and Ulawa were notable for their love of carving and their technical skill. A man from these islands might amuse himself by shaping soft stone or a piece of wood into the figure of a person, a bird, or a fish, or by decorating functional objects with carvings. 

I saw a remarkably clever carving at Fagani (Ha’ani) in San Cristobal, positioned above the peak of a gable. it depicted a man climbing up to shoot an opossum, with the animal looking down at him from the top of a pole in a very life-like pose. This would hardly be mistaken for an idol, yet it is just as much an "idol" as many figures that have ended up in museums labeled as such. 

The canoe-houses, community halls, and public houses—known in those regions as *oha*—were filled with carvings used for both structural and decorative purposes. Some of these, such as the posts supporting the roof's ridge-pole and the purlins <note>Horizontal beams that support the rafters of a roof.</note>, are often shaped like human figures. The village leaders might loosely refer to these as ancestors, and they were treated with respect; occasionally, food and betel nuts <note>The seeds of the areca palm, which are chewed as a stimulant.</note> could be seen placed before them. However, these figures had no sacred character beyond being memorials of...

...deceased great men, whose ghosts, visiting their accustomed homes, would be pleased by signs of remembrance and affection, but irritated by disrespect. There was no idea that the ghost of the deceased resided within the image, nor was the image thought to have any supernatural power <note>original: "efficacy"</note> in itself. In any *<term>oka</term>* <term>community house; original: "oka"</term> in Malaita <note>original: "Malanta"</note>, one may see an image of a shark, a swordfish, or a bonito <note>A type of tuna important in local culture and ritual.</note>, before which portions of food are placed. These figures are said to represent the fathers, grandfathers, and ancestors of those who honor them. These are indeed containers for the dead—not for their spirits, but for their physical remains or relics. Therefore, they cannot be called idols. Although they also sometimes create other images and name them after the deceased as a way of remembering them, they do not pray or offer sacrifices to these images, nor are they considered holy. 

In Florida Island <note>The Nggela Islands.</note>, a roughly shaped image of a man could often be seen in a sacred place near a village or on the seashore, with coconuts tied to it or food laid at its feet. This would be a *<term>tindalo</term>* <term>the ghost of a deceased person of power, or an object representing them</term>, an image representing some influential man who had died. The food was intended for him to eat, and the image itself was considered sacred. That is to say, the image was a memorial to a *tindalo*, and was not believed to possess power of its own or to be inhabited by the ghost of the departed. Images representing a *tindalo* were also carved onto the posts of the canoe houses; these were merely memorials that were not highly regarded and were approached without any special reverence.

The wooden posts <note>original: "stocks"</note> set up in Santa Cruz to represent the dead are the simplest forms of memorials. In the Banks Islands, tree-fern trunks carved into very crude figures of men were often seen. These were memorials created for funeral feasts and possessed no sacred character at all. In those same islands, the images carried around during *<term>Suqe</term>* <term>a hierarchical secret society or social club</term> feasts—and later placed in the eating areas corresponding to the rank they represent—might easily be mistaken for idols by those unfamiliar with their meaning. The same could be said for the *<term>nule</term>* <term>a carved figure on a house post</term>, a figure carved into a house post when the building's completion is celebrated by a *<term>kolekole</term>* <term>a festival or feast marking a significant life event or achievement</term>. In the New Hebrides <note>Now the nation of Vanuatu.</note>, on the island of Ambrym, images of the deceased whose death feasts are to be celebrated are prepared with great detail. There is no attempt, however, to represent the...

# XI. Images Are Not Idols; Sacred Stones.

...figures of the specific deceased person, but created in a conventional style. These are sometimes carved out of tree-fern trunks, and other times fashioned with wickerwork and sago <term>spathes</term> <note>The leaf-like sheath that encloses the flower cluster of a sago palm.</note>, then painted and adorned. Some that are hidden from public view by bamboo screens likely belong to secret societies. On the same island, drums are set up for funeral feasts featuring elaborate faces carved into them; these remain as memorials to the deceased, though visitors often mistake them for idols or "devil-drums." Similar images are made in the neighboring islands.

Sacred places almost always contain stones; it is impossible to discuss sacred places and sacred stones separately. However, while some places are considered sacred because stones are naturally located there, the stones found in other places have been brought there as part of the fixtures <note>original: "furniture"</note> of a sacred site. The holiness of some places and stones originates from graves or the physical remains <note>original: "relics"</note> of the dead, having been designated as such by people. Others are sacred simply because the stones are there, with the stones themselves being holy because they are associated with a spirit. 

It is helpful here to remember the distinction—which is very important in this context—between **ghosts** (the disembodied spirits of deceased humans) and **spirits** (beings of a different order than human souls, which have never been connected to a human body). Generally speaking, the religion of the Solomon Islands is concerned with ghosts, while that of the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides <note>Now known as Vanuatu.</note> is concerned with spirits.

The sacred places and objects of the Solomon Islands will be described first, beginning with those related to burial <note>original: "sepulture"</note>. In Florida <note>The Nggela Islands in the Solomons.</note>, a sacred place is called a *vunuka*. These sites are sometimes located within the village, in which case they are fenced off so they are not accidentally stepped upon; other times they are in the garden grounds or in the wild bush. A *<term>vunuka</term>* is sacred to a *<term>tindalo</term>* <term>the ghost of a person who possessed great spiritual power</term>, and sacrifices are offered to the *tindalo* there. In some cases, the *vunuka* is the actual burial place of the man who became a *tindalo*; in other cases, his remains have been moved there. Sometimes there is a shrine, and sometimes an image. There are generally, if not always, stones in such a sacred place; some stones lying...

<page-num>176</page-num>

# Sacred Places and Things

The location usually catches the imagination of the man who began the worship of the *tindalo* <term>the ghost of a powerful person</term>; he considers it a probable place for the ghost to frequent. Consequently, other smaller stones and shells called *peopeo* are added to the site. Once a *vunuha* <term>a sacred precinct or shrine</term> has been established, everything within it is sacred, or *tambu* <term>taboo; set apart</term>, and belongs to the *tindalo*. If a tree growing in such a place were to fall across a path, no one would dare to step over it. 

When entering a *vunuha*, a man who knows the *tindalo* and performs the sacrifices leads the way, while those with him walk strictly in his footsteps. Upon leaving, no one will look back, fearing that their soul might stay behind. No one would pass a *vunuha* when the sun was low enough to cast their shadow into it, as it was believed the ghost would pull the shadow from them. If there were a shrine within the *vunuha*, only the priest performing the sacrifice would enter it. Inside were the weapons and other belongings used by the person who is now the object of worship while they were alive; some of these items were said to be of great antiquity <note>The *vunuha* of Pelosule at Olevuga contained an image thought to be very ancient; a club sent to me from there is of a design no longer in use. I also have an adze taken from the *vunuha* of Murini at Belaga, which still has soot from sacrificial fires on it. The Reverend A. Penny has other *tindalo* relics believed by the locals to be ancient.</note>. 

Modern schoolboys have now broken down these shrines and pelted the images, and the teachers have carried away the weapons. Dikea, a chief at Ravu, had ten *vunuha* of his own, one of which was close to a garden he wanted to enlarge. He was afraid to desecrate the sacred place himself, fearing the *tindalo* might harm him. Therefore, he sent for Gura and Kerekere, two young Christian teachers, to do it for him because he knew they would not be afraid. They took their students and went, while the other local boys did not venture near. In the *vunuha*, they found one large stone in its natural position, surrounded by smaller stones, *peopeo* shells, and ginger leaves, all of which they threw about. The two *tindalo* to whom the place was dedicated, Koli and Kukui, later appeared in dreams to the non-Christian men and threatened those who had desecrated the site. Dikea waited until it was clear that the teachers were unharmed, and only then did he enlarge his garden.

At Saa in Malaita <note>original: "Malanta"</note>, all burial places where ordinary people are interred are considered sacred enough that no one will go there...

# xi.] Solomon Islands: Shrines and Sanctuaries

...for no good reason; but those places where the remains of high-ranking people are placed, where sacrifices are offered, and which may be called family sanctuaries, are regarded with very great respect. Some of these are very ancient, as the *lio'a* <term>the powerful ghost of a remote ancestor</term> who is worshipped there lived long ago. It sometimes happens that the man who offered the sacrifices in such a place dies without fully instructing his son in the proper chant of invocation with which the *lio'a* should be approached. The young man who succeeds him is then afraid to go there often. Instead, he begins a new sacred place, taking some ashes from the old sacrificial fireplace to start the new sanctuary. It is not common in that part of Malanta <note>original: Malanta; now known as Malaita</note> to build shrines for relics, but it is sometimes done when the *oka* <term>canoe-house</term> is full. Such shrines are common in the villages of San Cristoval <note>original: San Cristoval; now known as Makira</note> and in the sacred places where great men have been buried. To trespass on these sacred places would always be likely to anger the ghosts, some of whom are also known to have a malicious nature. One such ghost is Tapia, whose haunt is at the mouth of a river near Ha'ani; the sacrifices made to him have already been described.

There are sacred places, however, in the Solomon Islands which are not burial sites, though there are probably none whose sacredness does not depend on the presence of a ghost. In Florida <note>The Florida Islands, or Nggela Islands</note>, the appearance of something wonderful will cause any place to become a *vunuhu* <term>a sacred place</term>, the wonder being seen as evidence of a ghostly presence. For example, a man once planted some coconut and almond trees in the bush near Olevuga and died shortly after. A white *kandora* <term>a cuscus; a type of marsupial</term>—a great rarity—then appeared among the trees. This was assumed to be the manifestation of the dead man, now a *tindalo* <term>ghost</term>, and the creature was called by his name. The place became a *vunuhu*; no one would gather the coconuts or almonds until recently, when two young Christian men took the sacred place and its trees for a garden. Through this same part of the forest ran a stream full of eels (which the people of Olevuga do not eat). Among them was one so large that it was thought to be a *tindalo*...

<header>Sacred Places and Things. [CH.</header>

...dwelling or representation of someone who has died; no one would bathe in that stream or drink from it, except for one pool along its course that was intentionally not considered sacred for the sake of convenience. In Boli <note>A district on the island of Florida, now Nggela</note>, there was also a sacred pool containing a *tindalo* <term>the spirit of a deceased person who has become a powerful ghost</term> eel. In Bugotu, on the island of Santa Isabel <note>original: Ysabel</note>, there is a pool that is the home of an ancient ghost. Enemies will throw scraps of a person's food into this pool if they wish to place a curse or charm on them. If the fish, which are numerous in the pool, quickly eat the food, the person is expected to die. If they do not, the person who knows the place and the ghost reports that the *tindalo* is unwilling to cause harm. In such cases, the person whose life was being targeted has likely already paid the guardian for his friendly intervention. 

To ensure a good harvest, food is placed on stones in these sacred places, and fragments of cooked fish are offered to ensure success in fishing. Small amounts of money are also left there. The guardian or "owner" of the *vunuha* <term>a sacred place</term>, who is personally acquainted with the ghost, makes these offerings on behalf of those seeking the ghost's favor. 

Stones therefore play a significant, though not always obvious, role among the sacred objects of the Solomon Islands. This occurs whenever their location or appearance has linked them to a powerful ghost. Stones in open areas are treated with such reverence that no one will go near them, let alone sit or step on them. Meanwhile, stones in hidden sacred locations serve as a kind of altar for sacrifices. However, as time passes and older ghosts are replaced by more recent ones, only a vague sense of respect remains for these older stones. Small sacred stones become even more powerful when they are included among the relics and tools of a powerful man who has died and become a spirit himself. In life, his sacrifices were directed toward a *tindalo* whose presence was tied to that stone; now, because his own ghost is believed to be attached to the same stone, the sacrifices offered to him near or on it are considered even more effective.

Living sacred objects in the Solomon Islands primarily include sharks, crocodiles <note>original: "alligators," though crocodiles are the species native to the Solomon Islands</note>, snakes, bonitos <note>a type of fish related to tuna</note>, and frigate-birds. Snakes that frequent a sacred place are considered sacred themselves, as they belong...

<header>XI.] *Solomon Islands. Snakes. Sharks.*</header>

...serving as an embodiment of a ghost. There was one such snake in Savo, and it was believed that looking at it would cause death. In San Cristoval <note>Now known as Makira</note>, there is a special reverence for snakes as representatives of the spirit-snake Kahausibware. Sharks, in all these islands, are very often thought to be the home of ghosts. This is because men will announce before their death that they will reappear as sharks; afterwards, any shark remarkable for its size or color that is observed to frequent a certain shore or rock is taken to be that person's ghost, and the name of the deceased is given to it. 

One such shark was Sautahimatawa at Ulawa, a dreaded man-eater to which offerings of porpoise teeth <note>A form of traditional currency</note> were made. At Saa, certain food—such as coconuts from specific trees—is reserved to feed such a ghost-shark. There are certain men who are known to become sharks after death, and they are therefore allowed to eat this sacred food in the sacred place while still alive. Other men will try to join their company; a man will speak as if with the voice of a shark-*lio'a* <term>the ghost of a deceased person</term> within him and say, "Give me some of that food to eat." If it appears that such a man is truly *saka* <term>possessed of supernatural power or "mana"</term>, he will be counted as a shark-*lio'a* himself after his death; however, it is possible for him to fail. 

In Saa and in Ulawa, if a sacred shark had attempted to seize a man and he escaped, the people would be so afraid of the shark's anger that they would throw the man back into the sea to be drowned. These sharks were also thought to assist in catching the bonito <note>A type of tuna, the catching of which was a highly ritualized activity</note>, for which supernatural power was considered necessary. 

Not long ago, near Makira in San Cristoval, there was a shark that was highly respected and fed with pig's flesh. It was believed to have grown so large within a circle of rocks where it lived that it was no longer able to pass through the narrow entrance. Sharks are very commonly believed to be the dwellings of ghosts in Florida <note>Now Nggela</note>, Ysabel <note>Santa Isabel</note>, and in Savo, where they are particularly numerous. Consequently, although not all sharks are worshiped, there is no living creature so commonly held sacred as a shark. Indeed, the *tindalo* <term>spirit or powerful ghost</term> of the shark, or *bagea* <note>original: bagea; a local term for shark</note>, seems to even form a special class of powerful supernatural beings. In Savo, not long ago, a man named Lodo had a shark that he used to feed, and to which he used...

...to sacrifice. He swam out to it with food, called it by its name, and it came to him. He had inherited his association with this shark from his ancestors, in the same way that the connection with other ghosts on shore and the knowledge of them was handed down from generation to generation; for this shark was a <term>tindalo</term> <note>the ghost of a deceased person that has become an object of worship</note>. 

There was the same association with crocodiles <note>original: "alligators"</note>; within my memory, a chief of Bugotu had such a connection with one, in which his son at Norfolk Island thoroughly believed. There was also a story circulating about a crocodile that would come out of the sea and make itself at home in a village on Florida Island <note>One of the Solomon Islands, not the American state</note> where the man whose ghost inhabited it had lived. It was called by his name, and though there was one man who had a special connection with it and was said to "own" it, the creature was friendly with everyone and would let children ride upon its back. However, it must be confessed that although its existence was everywhere asserted, the specific village where it could be seen was never actually identified. 

A lizard seen frequenting a house after a death was taken to be the ghost returning to his old home. The sacred character of the frigate bird is certain; its figure, however stylized, is the most common ornament used in the Solomon Islands and is even tattooed onto the hands of the Bugotu people. The oath sworn by its name, <term>daula</term>, is solemn and binding on Florida Island, where <term>Daula</term> is a <term>tindalo</term>; as the <term>kaula</term>, it is sacred at Ulawa. Just as many ghosts take up their home in sharks, many ghosts that are powerful to aid people at sea reside in these birds. 

The ginger plant has a certain sacred character on Florida and the neighboring islands; the same is true for various other objects, both living and inanimate, from which the respective divisions of the people abstain as a matter of religious obligation.

In Santa Cruz, there are stones about which stories are told connecting them with the <term>duka</term> <note>ghosts or other spirits</note>, which are the objects of worship; betel nuts are placed on these stones as offerings. Traveling eastward to the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides <note>Now known as Vanuatu</note>, one reaches a region in which religion concerns itself chiefly with spirits that were never human...

### XI. Banks Islands and New Hebrides: Sacred Stones

...embodied in men; therefore, sacred places and objects are generally considered holy because of their connection with spirits. Burial places are certainly held in high regard, especially the graves of men who were important during their lives. A certain sense of sacredness is attached to everything belonging to the deceased; however, the special quality of most sacred places and objects comes from the presence of a spirit, or <term>vui</term> <note>a non-human spirit, distinct from a ghost of a deceased person</note>. 

In the Banks Islands, the distinction between a "naturally sacred" character and a sacredness that results from an official separation from common use is marked by the use of two words: <term>rongo</term> <note>meaning naturally sacred or holy</note> and <term>tapu</term> or <term>tambu</term> <note>meaning forbidden or set apart by authority; the origin of the English word "taboo"</note>. The corresponding terms in the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note> are <term>sapuga</term> and <term>gogona</term>. A naturally sacred (<term>rongo</term> or <term>sapuga</term>) character is created by the presence of a spirit or an association with one. In the vast majority of instances, it is found that such a spirit is associated with a stone.

In the Banks Islands, a man might happen to find a boulder of volcanic or coral rock and be struck by the belief that a spirit was connected with it. The stone and the place where it lay then became <term>rongo</term>. The man would establish himself as the master of the sanctuary; it became his <term>marana</term> <note>a private sacred space</note> which no one could enter except for himself or those he invited in.

Some stones are known to everyone and are more publicly accessible. At Losalav on Saddle Island <note>now known as Motalava</note>, there is a natural ring of stones near the beach that has been a sacred place since time immemorial. The people call this ring a "fence," the space within it a "garden," and the stones lying inside it are identified as yams, bananas, kava pepper, and other roots and fruits they commonly plant. These stones were used for offerings of money and sweet-smelling leaves, based on the belief that the plants corresponding to the stones would flourish and grow in abundance. 

The character and influence of the spirit connected to any sacred stone was judged by the shape of the stone itself. If a man came across a large stone with a number of small ones beneath it—lying like a sow among her litter—he was certain that offering money upon it would bring him pigs. One such stone is called <term>Ro Tortoros</term> at Mota. Another man, named Merina, found a stone and named it "the Pig" because of its shape; his subsequent wealth in pigs was attributed to his discovery.

<summary>This page explains the Melanesian distinction between natural and declared sacredness, focusing on the role of "vui" (spirits) residing in stones. It describes how the physical shape of a stone is believed to influence its spiritual power, such as stones shaped like pigs bringing wealth in livestock.</summary>

A stone with little disks on it, such as a block of ancient coral, was considered good for bringing in money. Any imaginative interpretation of a mark on a stone, or of its particular shape, was enough to give a specific character to the stone and to the spirit associated with it; the belief was that the stone would not possess that mark or shape without a specific reason. 

Many of these stones had names of their own, as mentioned previously, such as *Puglava*, meaning "much money out at interest," at Luwai, and more than one named simply "Money." The spirits belonging to these stones are nameless, and their connection to their individual stone is not clearly defined. The people say that the stone is not the "body" of the spirit, nor is the spirit like the "soul" of the stone—for they believe a stone certainly has no soul. Instead, they say that the spirit is *at* the stone <note>original: "o vui ape vatu"</note>, or near the stone, and it is the spirit, not the physical stone, that acts. 

Some of these stones have an ancient, established sanctity. Only the few individuals who know how to approach the spirit will visit them to perform a sacrifice; all others pass by with awe and will not tread on the sacred ground surrounding them. If someone accidentally discovers that he has intruded on a sacred place, he quickly seeks the services of the man who "knows" the stone to make an offering to the spirit, fearing he might otherwise suffer from an accident or sickness. 

There are some stones that have a sinister reputation, such as those near which an accident has occurred, and there are some upon which it is considered dangerous for a man’s shadow to fall. It is wise to make offerings upon these to keep the spirit in a good mood. A stone that is believed to bring success in fighting is also likely to do harm if it is not treated with proper respect. Some stones have the name <term>galaqar</term>, suggesting they might spring up like a trap upon a trespasser. 

Large stones, in their natural positions, hold a high place among the sacred objects of the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>. In Aurora <note>Maewo Island</note>, some of these are believed to have been produced in the ancient era of universal darkness, <term>gong tali</term>. It is said that during that time, if two men were sitting even slightly apart, a stone would grow up out of the ground between them. Such stones can be seen in the forest today, as tall as a house and with strange shapes. These do not have individual names, unlike others that have been named since ancient times; the common name for all such sacred stones is <term>matiu</term>. Some are <term>vui</term> <note>non-human spirits</note> who have turned into stones; some in the sea are...

<page-num>183</page-num>
<header>XI.] New Hebrides: Stones.</header>

There were men from ancient times who turned into stones; others were never anything but stones, yet they have a *vui* <note>original: "vui"; a spirit or supernatural being, often without a human origin</note> connected with them. Certain stones located above a waterfall are called the "dwellers in the land"—the native inhabitants of the stream—and these all have their own names. They possess significant spiritual power because they are, in a sense, the physical manifestation of the spirits that own the stream. When people go eel-fishing, they ensure success by offering a small piece of the first fish they catch upon the appropriate stone. 

Sacred stones of all kinds possess spiritual power, or *mana* <note>supernatural power or influence</note>, to varying degrees as they belong to spirits; this power is obtained for various purposes. Some cause sickness of the soul; others have great power when used in a charm, such as when a fragment of the stone is taken with a prayer, pounded into powder, and mixed with a scrap of food belonging to a person against whom harm is intended. 

In Maewo <note>original: "Aurora"</note>, a stone is sometimes smeared with red earth. In Pentecost and Ambae <note>original: "Lepers’ Island"</note>, stones are anointed with the juice of a young coconut. On Ambae, no other offerings are made to stones; instead, men go to them in sacred places in the forest and call upon Tagaro <note>a prominent deity or culture hero in Melanesian mythology</note>. There are also stones in the sea near Ambae that belong to spirits; people in canoes will not approach them for fear that sharks will eat them.

The stones mentioned so far are those that remain in their natural positions. Their presence, because of their association with a spirit, makes the ground around them a holy place—a *tano rongo* or *ute sapuga*. However, small stones that could be carried about also played an active role in the daily life of the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides. 

The following are examples from the Banks Islands group: No garden was planted without burying stones in the ground to ensure a crop. A piece of *Astræa* <note>original: "Astræa"; star coral</note> coral-stone, worn smooth by the waves on the beach, often bears a striking resemblance to a breadfruit. A man who finds one of these would test its power by laying it at the root of one of his own trees; a good crop would prove its connection with a spirit that favors breadfruit. The happy owner would then, for a fee, take stones of a less distinct character from other men and let them lie near his own until the *mana* in his stone was transferred to theirs. A resemblance to other fruits or tubers would be the...

# Sacred Places and Things. [CH. XI]

...grounds for a belief in similar powers. Stones were frequently used by weather-doctors <note>individuals believed to have the power to control the weather</note>. To create sunshine, it might be enough to simply smear a standing stone with red earth. However, a more effective method involved taking a very round stone, a <term>vat loa</term> <note>original: "vat loa"; sunstone</note>, and winding red braid around it. The stone would then be stuck with owl feathers to represent rays of light. While singing the appropriate spell in a low voice, the practitioner would hang the stone on a tall tree, such as a banyan or a casuarina <note>a tree with slender, drooping branches, often called an ironwood</note>, in a sacred place. Alternatively, the stone representing the sun might be laid on the ground with a circle of white rods radiating from it like sunbeams.

In the Banks Islands, there are stones of a remarkably long shape called <term>tamate gangan</term> <note>original: "tamate gangan"; literally "eating ghost"</note>. These are considered extremely powerful because of the presence of a ghost <note>In this context, a ghost is the soul of a deceased human, whereas a spirit (vui) was never human</note>, rather than a nature spirit. If a person's shadow falls on one of these stones, it will draw the soul out of them, causing them to die. Consequently, such stones are placed in houses to guard them. Anyone sent to a house by the owner during his absence must call out the name of the person who sent him. This prevents the ghost from thinking the visitor has bad intentions and causing them harm.

Other stones, also connected with ghosts, possess such power that when the owner places one under his pillow and dreams of another man, that man will die. A person who owns such a stone might be paid by an enemy to destroy a man in this way; this practice is called "dreaming him to an end," or <term>ti qore mot</term>. These stones are exceptional because they derive their power from the dead.

Some stones are called <term>tangaroa</term>, a name which is undoubtedly the same as that of the brothers of the legendary figure Qat. A man might carry these with him in a bag or hang them in his house. If someone entered a house where these stones were hanging and interfered with the owner's property, and then later suffered an accident, it would be said that the <term>tangaroa</term> had caused it. 

Other stones, called <term>tarunglea</term> and <term>varasurlea</term>, were swung around in a place that was being attacked to demoralize the invaders. Others were hung as amulets, <term>soasoa</term>, around a man's neck to keep him safe in times of danger. Some stones were believed to sharpen a man's aim and strengthen his arm for shooting. There were even stones that women would take to bed with them in the hope of conceiving children. The stones upon which, or in relation to which, sacrifices are made are by no means always such as...

<header>XI.] Sacred Stones. Heaps.</header>

In some cases, small stones occur naturally *in their original place* <note>original: "in situ"</note>, but they are so small they might be lost. If this happens, the owner of the stone, believing that ghosts have hidden it, calls out to them and they return it. Even so, such a *tano-oloolo* <note>a sacred place or "place of offerings"</note> is considered sacred because of its association with spirits, not ghosts.

Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae</note> provides examples of how portable stones are used in the northern New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>. In addition to the stones that lie naturally in the bush within the *tauteu*—the sacred spot where the deity Tagaro is invoked—there are sacred stones that possess varying degrees of *mana* <note>supernatural power or spiritual influence</note> and are effective for various purposes. Some are kept in bags hanging in the house. Some of these are ancient heirlooms, while others are new. Some provide an advantage in battle, some help produce food, and others can even cause a crop to fail. However, none of these stones can guarantee a large general harvest for the entire year (which requires specific spoken spells), and none are used for fishing. They are also not used when planting a garden; instead, the juice of a young coconut is sprinkled on the ground along with charms, and the shells are placed at the sides. Each stone has a specific song or charm containing Tagaro’s name, which is sung over it when it is put to use.

Although superstitious respect for stones is very common and their uses are diverse, there are certain practices involving stones that the locals claim have no superstitious or religious meaning, despite what an outside observer might assume. One such practice is throwing stones onto a heap by the roadside. Such a heap can be seen at Valuwa on Saddle Island <note>now Mota Lava</note>; every traveler who arrives there adds a stone to the pile. The locals explain that their idea is that days accumulate just like stones; when a man adds his stone to the heap, he "places his day upon it." At Pun, on the same island, there is a heap made of the fruits of various trees. As a traveler passes by, they gather any fruit from the roadside and add it to the pile. In both cases, this is simply a local custom. The people there like to maintain these heaps because they show how many visitors they have received. Between Valuwa and Motlav, the path runs between two large stones; travelers going from Motlav to Valuwa kick the

This is another old custom that is not taken very seriously. Another practice common to the Banks Islands and the Solomon Islands is that of throwing sticks, leaves, or stones onto a heap at a steep descent or where a difficult path begins. They say they are "throwing away their fatigue"; they certainly do not admit that they are making a prayer or a religious offering <note>The author is noting that these acts are perceived as practical or superstitious charms rather than formal worship.</note>.

<margin>Sacred Pools and Trees</margin> Streams, or rather pools within streams, are considered sacred in the Banks Islands because of the presence of a spirit. At Valuwa, there is a deep hole that no one dares to look into; if a person's reflection should fall upon the surface of the water, they would die, as the spirit would seize their life through that reflection. Trees are also considered sacred when they are located in a sacred place. For example, a banyan tree often hides a sacred snake—which is actually a spirit—within the maze of its trunks and roots, and the tree itself is therefore considered sacred. 

There are, however, two trees that possess a certain inherent sacredness of their own: the casuarina <note>also known as the she-oak</note>, called *aru*, and the cycas, called *mele*. Nothing looks more eerie or ghostly than an old casuarina standing alone on a windswept beach or rising from a high cliff, with its bare gray trunk and shadowless foliage, never silent—whispering in a calm or shrieking in a breeze. The presence of one of these trees gives a certain sense of holiness and awe <note>original: "awfulness," used here in the traditional sense of "inspiring awe."</note> to a place. ¹ Many years ago, I noticed a small heap of sticks beside a path in a forest on Norfolk Island, evidently thrown there by Melanesian boys passing on their way to fish at the bottom of steep, difficult cliffs. I asked my companions about it, but they smiled and did not answer. Long after, having read Henry O. Forbes’s *A Naturalist’s Wanderings in the Eastern Archipelago*, I asked boys from the Banks Islands and from Florida <note>An island in the Solomon Islands, also known as Nggela Sule.</note> about it again. Both gave the same explanation: it was done to ensure a safe descent in that spot and was a common practice in their home islands. Both insisted there was no intention of sacrifice or offering, and no prayer; if anything was said at all, it was simply the words, "There goes my fatigue." Mr. Forbes mentions a similar practice twice: once in Sumatra (p. 166), where the porters placed handfuls of leaves on a stone and prayed for a dry day and good luck; and again in Timor (p. 481), where the natives laid leaves and twigs on a mound at the start of a steep and precipitous descent "to ensure a safe journey down."

<meta>This page continues the discussion of sacred trees from the previous page and shifts focus to sacred animals, specifically sharks and snakes, in the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides.</meta>

<page-num>187</page-num>
<header>XI.] Trees. Sharks. Snakes.</header>

The Mota word is *tano-aruaru*, meaning the place of casuarinas. The cycas is also sacred, or *rongo*, but the natives will cut it down without hesitation if it stands in their way. Crotons and dracaenas <note>ornamental shrubs with colorful foliage</note> possess a certain sacredness in connection with the dead. In Araga (Pentecost Island), there is a strange belief that the cycas tree can turn into a young man or woman, much like the snakes to be mentioned later; only the ear remains unchanged, as it still resembles a leaflet of the tree.

The living creatures most commonly held sacred in the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note> are sharks and snakes. All kingfishers are considered to have at least some sacred character, as do some owls, crabs, lizards, eels, and other creatures that haunt a place made sacred by the presence of a spirit. In the Banks Islands, a shark may be a *tangaroa*—a type of familiar spirit—or the vessel for one. Some years ago, Manurwar—the son of Mala, a leading man in Vanua Lava—possessed such a shark, for which he had paid money to a man from Maewo to send to him. It was very tame and would come up to him when he went down to the beach at Nawono, following him through the surf as he walked along the shore. Tursal, my informant, had seen this happen himself. This corresponds with what was related earlier regarding Lodo and his shark at Savo; the difference, however, is instructive: in the Banks Islands, the shark was a spirit <note>original: *vui*, a being that was never human</note>, whereas in the Solomon Islands, it was a ghost <note>the spirit of a deceased human</note>. 

In the New Hebrides, some men are believed by the natives to have the power to change themselves into sharks, as can be seen in the story of Tarkeke. A great deal of superstition is connected with snakes, not only because they are frequently seen around sacred places, but because the reptile is often thought to be otherwise connected with a *vui* (spirit) or to have a spirit near it. In Mota, there are no land snakes. In the other islands of the Banks group, snakes of enormous size are said to live in banyan trees and are held sacred. At Valuwa, there are snakes that strangers are not permitted to see, for fear that some misfortune might follow. Ordinary snakes are killed. Those held sacred are not generally fed or worshipped, but those that are the familiars of specific individuals who know them do receive sacrifices.

<page-num>188</page-num>
<header>Sacred Places and Things. [CH. XI</header>

In the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>, snakes are perhaps more highly regarded than they are in the Banks Islands. On Pentecost Island, if a native sees one in a sacred place or in a house, he will believe there is a specific reason for its appearance to him. He will pour the juice of a young coconut over himself and, from then on, expect his life to go well through the influence of the spirit—or perhaps the ghost—associated with the reptile. On Lepers' Island <note>now Ambae</note>, if a snake haunts a man’s house, especially if it is the home of an influential man, the people are convinced that it is a spirit. It is considered *gogona* <term>original: gogona; meaning sacred, forbidden, or dangerous to approach</term> and is not to be approached lightly. It is believed to bring good luck to the household and helps the owner rise in rank within the *huqa* society <note>a graded social hierarchy or secret society</note>. The house itself is treated with great respect; no one would throw a stone at it or climb upon it, as it is believed the snake would resent such disrespect and cause the offender to become ill.

There is an amphibious sea-snake marked with bands of dark and light colors which is always more or less dreaded whenever it is seen in the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides. In these islands, it is generally called a *mae* <note>likely the Banded Sea Krait</note>, and it is this kind of snake that becomes the "familiar spirit" of those who have, or claim to have, communication with it. In Araga (Pentecost Island), every *mae* is believed to possess the supernatural power of *mana* <term>original: mana; spiritual power or influence</term>. One of these snakes might harm people by carrying scraps of their food into a sacred place; if this happens, it is believed the person’s lips will swell and their body will break out in ulcers. 

The natives believe that some men can turn into these snakes, and these snakes, in turn, can transform into men. A *mae* does not behave like an ordinary snake; it shows it is something different—for example, by "washing" its young. In a certain *gamal* <term>original: gamal; a men’s communal club-house</term> in Araga, there is a hollow piece of wood from a tree they call *bugo*, which contains water. At night, a mother *mae* used to come and wash her young one in this water; the people sleeping there would hear it cry and knew what it was. They eventually made a pipe to imitate the cry exactly and still use it today. There is a very strong belief across all these islands that this snake can transform itself into a young man or woman—usually a young woman—to tempt someone of the opposite sex. To give in to this temptation is said to cause death.

<summary>This page details the spiritual significance of snakes in the New Hebrides, where they are viewed as powerful spirits or ghosts capable of bringing luck or illness. It specifically describes the *mae* (sea-snake), its association with *mana*, and the widespread belief in its ability to shape-shift into human form to tempt the living.</summary>

<page-num>189</page-num>
<header>XI. Changeling Snakes</header>

It is possible to uncover the trickery, but the discovery is often made too late. In Araga <note>Pentecost Island</note>, the transformed *mae* <note>original: mae; a species of sea snake, likely the Banded Sea Krait</note> can be recognized by the skin under the neck, which remains unchanged. It was only recently that a youth died at Vathuqe on that island after being lured away by a "changeling" girl. He saw the skin on her neck and returned to tell his people; they tried the proper remedy—using smoke—but it was in vain. There is another test used on that island: the suspected temptress is persuaded to sit on a nettle-tree <note>a tree with stinging leaves, likely Laportea</note>, and her true nature is proven by her ignorance of its stinging character.

In the Banks Islands, a young man once shared his experience with me. Returning from fishing on the rocks toward sunset, he saw a girl with her head decorated with flowers, beckoning to him from the slope of the cliff where his path led. He recognized the face of a girl from his own or a neighboring village. He stood and hesitated, thinking she must be a *mae*. Upon closer inspection, he noticed that her elbows and knees bent the wrong way. This revealed her true character, and he fled. If a young man can strike the temptress with a *dracaena* leaf, she returns to her original shape and glides away as a snake.

At Gaua, Santa Maria, a man met one of these "standing" or "variegated" snakes—as they call them, *mae tiratira* or *valeleas*—on the beach at night in the form of a local woman. Noticing by her reversed joints what she was, he offered to go to the village and bring her money. When he returned, he found her waiting for him in her true form as a *mae*. He scattered money upon her back, and she went off with it into the sea.

More recently in the same place, a young man who had just returned from "labor" in Queensland <note>referring to the system of indentured Pacific Island labor in Australia, often called "blackbirding"</note> saw one of these beings in the form of a young married woman from his village. She transformed into the stalk of a creeper <note>a climbing plant</note>, as people on that island believe these creatures can do. It is also believed that if a man can cut the creeper short, he will survive. Accordingly, this young man broke the vine off short and made it safely home. However, since then, something has been disturbing those who sleep in the same club-house <term>original: club-house; a communal men's house, often called a gamal</term> with him, and he has confessed that it is this snake-woman who comes to visit him in the night.

...and everyone believes him. Sometimes a young man will run home at night and lose his senses; the people are certain that he has been with a *mae* <note>original: mae; a snake-spirit or "changeling" snake</note>. Sometimes a man will come in, lie down, and fall ill; they question him closely, and he confesses what he has done and seen, and then he dies. Nothing seems to be more firmly fixed in the minds of the natives—even those who have received some education—than the conviction that all of this is true.

The sacred character of the kingfisher is remarkable, and the reason for it is hard to find. In San Cristoval <note>now known as Makira</note>, a kingfisher pecks the head of a recently departed soul that has not yet realized its condition, causing it to sink into the state of a ghost; the natives therefore kill the bird, but they believe young ones spring up from the blood of every one they kill. In the Banks Islands, every kingfisher (*sigo*) is sacred (*rongo* <note>meaning set apart or forbidden</note>); a spirit is connected with it, and not one is ever killed or eaten. It is a singular thing that they create "halcyon days" <note>A reference to the Greek myth of the Halcyon (kingfisher) bird, which was said to calm the seas</note>; it is the name of the kingfisher that carries the magic power in the charm for sunshine, for the *sigo* is thought to control storms and rain, and the charm calls on it to "eat" the rising waves and create a calm. 

They declare that there are kingfishers at sea as well as on land, including a species seen only at sea, far from land. If a man going out on a journey hears a kingfisher cry, he thinks it is angry and forbids his going; he therefore sings a charm: "Tagar <note>a spirit of influence or luck</note>, be favorable to me; let mischief pass beside me; let good luck come around before my face!" ¹

<meta>This page begins Chapter XII, introducing and defining the central Melanesian concept of "mana"—the supernatural force believed to be the source of all magical and spiritual power.</meta>

# CHAPTER XII.

->MAGIC.<-

That invisible power which the natives believe causes all effects beyond their understanding of the natural world is generally known as *mana*. This power resides in spiritual beings, whether in the souls of living people or in the ghosts of the dead. It is passed on by them to their names and to various objects belonging to them, such as stones, snakes, and indeed things of all sorts. Without some understanding of this, it is impossible to understand the religious beliefs and practices of the Melanesians; furthermore, this is the active force in everything they do and believe to be done through magic, whether "white" <note>beneficial magic, such as healing or good weather</note> or "black" <note>harmful magic or sorcery</note>.

By means of this power, men are able to control or direct the forces of nature: making rain or sunshine, wind or calm, causing or removing sickness, knowing what is far away in time and space, and bringing good luck and prosperity—or disaster and curses. However, no man possesses this power on his own; everything he does is achieved with the help of personal beings, such as ghosts or spirits. A person cannot be said to *be* "mana" himself (using the word as a quality or adjective), as a spirit can; rather, he is said to *have* "mana," or it is said to be "with him" (using the word as a noun). 

In the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>, the Banks Islands, and the Solomon Islands around Florida <note>now the Nggela Islands</note>, as well as in New Zealand and many other Pacific Islands, the word used is *mana*. In Santa Cruz, a different word, *malete*, is used, which carries the same meaning. At Saa on Malaita <note>original: Malanta</note>, all persons and things in which this supernatural power resides are said to be *saka*, which means "hot." Ghosts that are powerful are called *saka*; a man who has know-

<summary>This page defines "mana" as the fundamental supernatural power in Melanesian culture, explaining that it originates from spirits or ghosts and allows humans to influence nature and health. It also notes regional linguistic variations for the concept, such as "malete" in Santa Cruz and "saka" (hot) in Malaita.</summary>

<keywords>mana, magic, Melanesia, spirits, ghosts, malete, saka, Solomon Islands, New Hebrides, supernatural power</keywords>
