<meta>This page continues the discussion of supernatural power, focusing on the specific term "saka" used on the island of Malaita, and how this power underpins all forms of magic and religious practice.</meta>

[Know]ledge of the things which have spiritual power is himself *saka* <note>original: saka; possessing supernatural power, similar to mana</note>; one who knows a charm which is *saka* mutters it over water (*saru'e* <note>original: saru'e; the act of muttering a charm</note>), and makes the water "hot" (*ha'asaka* <note>original: ha'asaka; to make something spiritually active or powerful</note>). The people of Mala Masiki <note>Little Malaita</note>, the smaller part of the island—which is divided near its southeastern end by a narrow channel—believe that the men of the larger part, Mala Paina <note>Big Malaita</note>, are very *saka*. If one of these men visits the Saa people and points with his finger (*suisui*), there is a danger of death or disaster; if one of them spits on a man, that man dies at once.

By whatever name it is called, it is the belief in this supernatural power, and in the effectiveness of the various ways that spirits and ghosts can be persuaded to use it for the benefit of humans, that forms the foundation of all religious rites and practices. It is from this same belief that everything which may be called magic and witchcraft draws its origin. Wizards, doctors, weather-controllers, prophets, diviners, and dreamers alike, throughout the islands, all work through this power. 

There are many who practice these arts as a profession, gaining property and influence through them. Every significant village or settlement is sure to have someone who can control the weather and the waves, someone who knows how to treat sickness, or someone who can cause harm with various charms. Sometimes one man’s skill covers all these areas, but generally, one person knows how to do one thing and another person specializes in something else. This diverse knowledge is handed down from father to son, or from an uncle to his sister's son, in the same way that knowledge of the rituals and methods of sacrifice and prayer is passed down. Very often, the same man who knows the sacrificial rites also knows how to control the weather and create charms for many other purposes. 

However, just as there is no formal order of priests, there is also no formal order of magicians or medicine men. Almost every man of social standing knows how to approach some ghost or spirit and possesses some secret of occult practices. Knowledge of either kind can be bought, if the owner chooses to share it with someone other than his natural heirs.

There is no doubt that those who practice these arts really—

# XII. Native Belief in Charms

They believe in the power of these charms as much as the people for whom they perform them. In some cases, there is intentional trickery, as has been admitted many times by those who have since become Christians. A young woman I knew in the Banks Islands had a reputation for healing toothaches using a charm taught to her by a deceased elderly relative. She would place a certain rolled-up leaf on the inflamed area while muttering specific words. When the pain eventually subsided, she would take out and unfold the leaf to show the little white maggot that was supposedly the cause of the trouble. When Christian teaching began on the island, she had no problem disclosing her secret, and everyone laughed about the trick together. 

It is also quite likely that a weather-doctor <note>A specialist believed to have the power to control the elements, such as rain or wind.</note> observed the weather for himself—and was taught by his predecessor to notice the signs of change or stability—and performed his charms or held them back based on his observations. However, the methods he used seemed so naturally effective to him, and were so frequently followed by the results he aimed for, that he seriously believed in them. If they occasionally failed spectacularly—as happened on Santa Isabel <note>original: Ysabel</note> when a weather-doctor's own house was blown down by a storm on the very day he had guaranteed a calm—there was always the explanation that a stronger counter-charm had been at work. Such a logic tended to confirm the belief in the power of weather-doctors much more than it weakened it. It is not only in the Melanesian islands that people accept whatever confirms a belief while ignoring whatever contradicts it. Those who practiced various kinds of magic truly believed in their own craft.

Though those who practice these various arts cannot be divided into distinct classes or ranks, nor even be regarded as a separate social order—since they are mixed among the general population and practice as many or as few arts as they happen to know—it is necessary to categorize their practices. These may be arranged under the headings of Sickness, Weather, Witchcraft, Dreams, Prophecy, and Divination.

<header>Magic</header>

### Ordeals, Poison, and Curses

In all of these, whatever is achieved is believed to be caused by the <term>mana</term> <note>A Melanesian term for supernatural power or influence that can reside in people, spirits, or objects.</note> of spirits and ghosts. This power acts through various mediums and is triggered by secret formulas or chants. These words are given the power to work by the names of the spirits or ghosts, or by the living or inanimate things to which this mysterious influence is attached.

<margin>(1)</margin>
**Sickness.** Any sickness that is serious is believed to be caused by ghosts or spirits; common complaints, such as fever and chills <note>original: "ague"</note>, are accepted as occurring in the natural course of things. To say that "savages" are never ill without assuming a supernatural cause is not true of Melanesians; they decide as the sickness develops whether it is natural or not. The more important the individual who is sick, the more likely it is that their sickness will be attributed to witchcraft or the anger of a ghost whom they have offended. No person of high status would like to be told that they were ill simply due to natural weakness or the decay of old age. 

Sickness is almost always believed to be caused by a ghost, not by a spirit. It does happen—for instance, in the New Hebrides <note>A chain of islands in the South Pacific, now known as Vanuatu.</note>, where spirits are the primary focus of religious devotion—that a man knows he has trespassed on a sacred place belonging to some spirit, or has an enemy who is helped by a spirit; in such cases, he assumes that a spirit has brought the sickness upon him. But generally, in the eastern islands as well as in the western, sickness is attributed to the ghosts of the dead. People turn to these ghosts for help in both causing and removing sickness. 

Ghosts are believed to inflict sickness not only because an offense, such as a trespass, has been committed against them, or because someone familiar with them has sought their help with sacrifices and spells, but because there is a certain malice in the feelings of all ghosts toward the living, who offend them simply by being alive. All human powers that are not merely physical are believed to be enhanced by death; therefore, the ghost of a powerful, ill-tempered man is naturally thought to be ready to use his increased powers for mischief.

Thus, in Florida <note>An island in the Solomon Islands, also known as Nggela.</note>, it is a <term>tindalo</term>—that is, a ghost of power—that causes illness. It then becomes a matter of guessing which of the...

<header>XII. Florida. Sickness.</header>

...which known <term>tindalos</term> <note>original: "tindalos"; deified ghosts or ancestor spirits</note> it may be. Sometimes a person has reason to believe, or imagines, that he has offended his deceased father, uncle, or brother. In such cases, no special mediator is required; the patient himself or a family member will offer a sacrifice and beg the <term>tindalo</term> to remove the sickness. It is treated as a private family matter. 

Sometimes a sick man thinks the cause is his own familiar <term>tindalo</term> <note>A personal guardian spirit or ghost</note> and will leave his house to avoid it. If the cause of the illness is a matter of guesswork, a <term>mane kisu</term> <note>literally a "man of blessing"; a traditional healer or doctor</note>—someone who understands these spiritual matters—is called in. He will claim to know which ghost has been offended. If the patient is a child, the doctor will say the child has stepped into a <term>vunuha</term> <note>a sacred or forbidden place</note> belonging to a <term>tindalo</term> whom the doctor claims to be his own. Alternatively, the parents will try to guess or investigate where the child has been and will send for the <term>mane kisu</term> who has influence with the <term>tindalo</term> of that specific place. 

The doctor who is called in will bind leaves associated with his own <term>tindalo</term> onto the patient. He will then chew ginger and blow into the patient's ears and onto the fontanelle <note>The soft part of the skull, especially in infants</note>. He will call upon the name of the <term>tindalo</term> and plead with him to remove the sickness. When he makes this request, speaking in a low voice, it is called <term>kokoe liuliruti</term>—to speak, as the word is used today, in prayer. 

If the sickness continues, another <term>tindalo</term> or another <term>mane kisu</term> is consulted. If no one can guess which ghost has been offended, any <term>mane kisu</term> will, for a fee, undertake to have his own <term>tindalo</term> (who is expected to know the truth) intercede with the one who is causing the trouble. In some cases, it may be suspected that someone who holds a grudge against the sufferer has set their own <term>tindalo</term> to afflict—or as they say, to "eat"—the patient. This person might then accept money to call off the "eating" ghost. If he refuses to do this, a more powerful <term>tindalo</term> may be hired through another <term>mane kisu</term> to overpower the original assailant and drive him away. 

While these spiritual remedies are being tried, the patient either recovers or dies. If he recovers, the doctor whose treatment was active when he began to mend receives the credit and a generous payment. If the patient dies, it simply confirms the superior power of the <term>tindalo</term> that has prevailed. There is also something like the use of herbal medicine mixed into this treatment; however, its effectiveness is always believed to depend upon the power of the <term>tindalo</term>...

...engaged. The <term>mane kisu</term> <note>literally a "man of blessing"; a traditional healer or doctor</note> knows certain herbs and warms them in a coconut shell over the fire; the steam applied to the patient drives away the pain or the disease. For a cough, an infusion is drunk, and the leaves are thrown away. The doctors also practice massage, kneading, squeezing, and rubbing the body and limbs of the patient. In Ysabel (and no doubt also in Florida), the doctor called in will discover the <term>tindatho</term> <note>the local Ysabel term for a ghost or ancestor spirit; equivalent to the "tindalo" of Florida</note> who causes the complaint he has to treat. He does this by suspending a stone or heavy ornament at the end of a string which he holds in his hand and calling out the names of the recently deceased. When the name of the person who is causing the disease is called, the stone swings in answer. Then it remains to ask what shall be given to appease the anger of the ghost—a mash of yams, a fish, a pig, or even a man. The answer is given in the same way; whatever is desired is offered on the dead man's grave, and the sickness leaves.

In Wango, in San Cristobal, the natives not long ago believed that the ghosts, there called <term>adaro</term> <note>ghosts or spirits of the dead</note>, actually fought with one another over the sick person using spears. A man might have a grudge against another and pay a wizard to bring an *adaro* to "eat" <note>to consume the life force or cause spiritual harm</note> him or do him mischief. It would become known that he had given a pig, for instance, to that wizard; then the man whose life was targeted, or his friends, would go to another wizard and, by paying a larger fee, secure what they hoped would be a stronger *adaro* for their side. The two ghosts would fight it out, or probably more than one would be engaged on either side; the man would sicken, die, or keep his health according to the outcome of the unseen battle. 

Ghosts that haunt the sea are believed to shoot men on the reefs or in canoes with fish darted at them invisibly. If, as often happens, a flying-fish or garfish springs from the waves and strikes a man, they say that an *adaro* shoots it; it is no common fish, and the man will die. Sick persons are commonly treated with ginger and other roots and leaves, and with water over which a charm has been muttered to give it healing power from an *adaro*.

<header>Magic. [CH. XII.]</header>

The treatment for a local pain involves squeezing leaves and herbs onto the affected area; but it is the *malete* <note>spiritual power; the Santa Cruz equivalent to *mana*</note>, rather than the natural properties of these medicines, that performs the cure.

In the Banks Islands, the *gismana* <note>a traditional healer or magician</note> practiced the same arts as his colleagues in the west $^1$. He worked the cause of the pain and disease downward until he could extract it; he stroked the site of the pain and spat; he sucked or bit out a fragment of wood, bone, or leaf from the painful area. For swellings, he chewed specific herbs and leaves and blew—a practice called *pupsag*—upon the spot. He used warm compresses <note>original: "fomentations"</note> and poultices made of mallow leaves, for example, showing some knowledge of their natural healing and soothing properties. He also gave the patient water to drink from a hollow in a sacred stone, or water in which stones full of *mana* <note>supernatural power or influence</note> had been placed for this purpose. This is likely why European medicine eventually came to be called *pei mana* <note>literally "mana water"</note>. All of this was done by virtue of the *mana* conveyed through the charms sung over the remedy—songs which were themselves called *mana*—or through the muttered words, known as *wosag*, which drove the disease away. 

Women also shared in the practice of this art; some knew the charms to recall the soul of a sick child that was being drawn away by a ghost, and how to drive that ghost off. The woman would blow on the child’s eyes while calling out the name of the attacking ghost. The *gismana* did not limit himself only to the care of the sick; all methods of working through *mana* were within his line of practice. Women, however, did not

<header>XII.] Sickness in the New Hebrides. Weather.</header>

In the New Hebrides <note>the colonial name for the islands of modern Vanuatu</note>, the healing of the sick belongs in Aurora <note>modern Maewo</note> to the *gismana*, in Lepers' Island <note>modern Ambae</note> to the *tangaloe ngoro*, and in Pentecost to the *mata tawaga*. These are the individuals who possess the knowledge of the songs and charms believed to have been handed down from Tagaro <note>a major deity or culture hero in Melanesian mythology</note> himself, through which *mana* <note>spiritual power or influence</note> is conveyed and applied. In Aurora, those who experience dreams have the largest medical practice. 

In Pentecost and Lepers' Island, the juice of a very young coconut—upon which the doctor has blown while a charm is muttered or sung—is drunk by the patient or rubbed onto them. Water that has had *mana* imparted to it in the same way is also used. Sickness is generally supposed to be caused by ghosts <note>spirits of the deceased</note>, but since the sacred places and objects that may be profaned or used carelessly belong to spirits <note>supernatural beings that were never human</note>, these spirits are often believed to be angry and to inflict pain and disease. The power of a spirit can also be directed by a charm or curse to harm a person. It is natural, therefore, that in the treatment of the sick, people turn to spirits—and above all to Tagaro—rather than to ghosts. The name of Tagaro controls both ghosts and spirits. In Pentecost, the doctor will forbid the patient from eating certain kinds of food; when the patient recovers, the doctor brings them some of that food to eat as proof that they are well. 

In both islands, women know how to relieve pain. In Pentecost, the women use leaves as poultices. When they remove them, they claim to take away the cause of the pain with them—a snake, a lizard, or something from the beach. "But," says a native who has undergone the treatment, "no one sees the object except the women, and the pain remains." In Lepers’ Island, the female practitioner rubs the patient downward with a bunch of leaves that she knows to have the proper qualities, while singing and muttering her charms. She will work one day upon the head and continue working downward day by day, squeezing and—

(2) *Weather.* In all these islands, it is believed that spirits and ghosts have power over the weather. It follows, therefore, that the men who have close contact with these spirits and ghosts are believed to be able to persuade them to interfere—bringing wind or calm, sunshine or rain, as may be desired. The spirits and ghosts have also imparted power to specific spoken charms, stones, leaves, and other objects, which therefore affect the weather on their own. There is also a certain natural connection between some of these objects and the effects they produce, which seems to make them suitable vehicles for this power. The men who possess and know these things have *mana* <note>spiritual or supernatural power</note> which they can use to benefit or afflict friends and enemies, turning the weather in whatever direction they are paid to turn it. 

Everywhere in these islands, therefore, there are weather-doctors or weather-sellers who can control the aerial powers and are willing to supply wind, calm, rain, sunshine, famine, and abundance for a price. These men were generally also masters of other charms besides those affecting the weather; some knew one weather charm and some another, but there were generally enough practitioners in a community to meet all requirements. Their arts, once secret, are now quite well known. In Florida <note>modern Nggela, Solomon Islands</note>, the *mane nggehe vigona* <note>literally "the man who works the vigona spirit"</note>, when a calm was wanted, tied together the leaves appropriate to his *vigona* <note>a type of spirit associated with natural forces</note> and hid them in the hollow of a tree where there was water, calling upon the *vigona* spirit with the proper charm. This process was believed to bring down rain to create the calm. If sunshine was required, he tied the appropriate leaves and creeper-vines to the end of a bamboo pole and held them over a fire. He fanned the fire with a song to give *mana* to the fire, and the fire gave

In the seafaring life of the Solomon Islands, the maker of calms is a valuable citizen. The Santa Cruz people are also great voyagers, and their *mendleka* <note>weather wizards</note> control the weather on their expeditions. They take with them a wooden figure which represents their *duka* <note>an ancestral spirit or ghost</note> and set it up in the cabin on the platform of the canoe. With the presence of his familiar spirit thus secured, the weather-doctor will undertake to provide a fair wind or a calm sea. In the same island, to get sunshine, the wizard puts some burnt wood into a tree. To get rain, he throws down water at the foot of the wooden figure of Tinota, an ancient spirit. To make wind, he waves the branch of a tree that possesses power; in each case, he chants the appropriate charm.

The same things were done and similar methods were followed in the Banks’ Islands with *mana* songs and *mana* stones <note>Referencing page 184 of the original text.</note>. The art is the same in the New Hebrides. To get rain, the *gismana* <note>weather-doctor</note> of Aurora puts a tuft of leaves—which possess *mana* for this purpose—into the hollow of a stone. Upon this, he places some branches of the *piper methysticum* <note>the plant used to make the ceremonial drink kava</note>, which have been pounded and crushed. To these, he adds one of his collection of stones which has *mana* for rain. All of this is done while singing charms that invoke the name of Tagaro <note>a high deity or culture hero in Melanesian mythology</note>, and the entire arrangement is covered over. The mass ferments, and steam charged with *mana* rises to make clouds and rain. The wizard must be careful not to pound the pepper plant too hard, for fear that the wind might blow too strongly. All these charms derive their power from the inclusion of the name Tagaro <note>a creator deity or heroic cultural figure in the mythology of the New Hebrides and the Banks Islands</note>.

Weather charms are similar in category to those used in the Banks Islands to assist a sow with her first litter of pigs. These rituals include beating her back with branches of a pepper plant closely resembling the one used for *kava* <note>a ceremonial drink made from the roots of *Piper methysticum*</note>, scattering blossoms of the *wotaga* <note>original: *wotaga*; the *Barringtonia* tree, known for its large fruit and flowers</note> over her back, and laying coconut fronds upon her. They also break a bamboo water vessel over her back so that the salt water runs over her and hang a bag full of native almonds above her head—all while reciting the proper incantations.

Nets being used for the first time are also charmed with leaves and a song intended to grant them *mana*. On Lepers’ Island <note>now known as Ambae in Vanuatu</note>, when a large new canoe is finished and ready for its first voyage, a very young coconut is imbued with *mana* through a song. This chant commands the canoe to be swift, successful in trade, and victorious in battle. The coconut is then placed on the outrigger. After a short trial run of the new canoe, they set out with a conch-shell trumpet and a supply of mats to trade for pigs. 

It would be hard indeed to define the limits of such charms. Essentially the same in character, they are used to assist those who know the spells or pay for them, or conversely, to injure and obstruct their enemies. For example, in anticipation of a fight, a man in the Banks Islands—in addition to carrying his amulets and sacred stones—might strengthen his ability to shoot and kill by drinking an infusion of extremely bitter herbs and bark. He might also chew other leaves and blow out their magic influence to discourage an advancing enemy.

<page-num>203</page-num>
<header>XII.] Witchcraft. ‘Garata.’</header>

The men who heal illnesses are often the same men who cause them. The *mana* <note>spiritual or supernatural power</note> derived from spirits and ghosts is the agent employed in both cases. However, it often happens that the darker secrets of the magic art are possessed and practiced only by those whose power lies in doing harm, and who are sought out when someone desires to bring evil upon an enemy. Their secrets, like others connected with *mana*, are passed down from one generation to another and may be bought. 

The most common method of this malignant witchcraft is one frequently found in various cultures <note>original: "savages"</note>, in which a fragment of food, a bit of hair or a fingernail, or anything closely connected with the person to be injured is the medium through which the power of the ghost or spirit is directed. Some relic, such as a bone of the dead person whose ghost is being set to work, is very desirable—if not strictly necessary—for bringing that spirit's power into the charm. A stone may also have its own *mana* for doing mischief. 

What is required is a way to bring together the man who is to be injured and the spirit or ghost who is to injure him. This can be done when something pertaining to the man’s person can be used, such as a hair, a nail, or a leaf with which he has wiped the perspiration from his face. It is equally effective when a fragment of the food that has passed into the man forms the link of union. 

For this reason, in Florida <note>the Nggela Islands in the Solomon Islands</note>, if a scrap from a man’s meal could be secretly taken and thrown into the *vunuhu* <note>a haunted or sacred place</note> inhabited by a *tindalo* <note>the ghost of a powerful deceased person</note>, the man would certainly fall ill. Similarly, in the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>, when the *mae* snake carried away a fragment of food into a place sacred to a spirit, the man who had eaten that food would sicken as the fragment decayed. 

It was, therefore, a constant concern to prevent anything that might be used in witchcraft from falling into the hands of ill-wishers. It was the regular practice to hide hair and nail parings and to give the remains of food most carefully to the pigs¹. In the Banks Islands, the fragment of food, or what—

<page-num>204</page-num>
<header>Magic. [CH. XII]</header>

Whatever the object may be by which a man is charmed, it is called *garata*. This was prepared by a wizard using a piece of human bone and smeared with a magical liquid in which it would rot away. Alternatively, the *garata* would be burned, and while it was burning, the wizard would sing his charm. As the *garata* was slowly consumed—the wizard burning it by degrees day after day—the man from whom the fragment was taken <note>The "fragment" refers to the bit of food, hair, or personal item belonging to the victim mentioned on the previous page.</note> would sicken and eventually die. The ghost of the person whose bone was being burned would take away the victim's life. 

Therefore, if any man who knows he has an enemy has reason to think that something has been taken from him, or if his friends hear that a *garata* made from his belongings is in a wizard's hands, he or his friends will offer money to get the fragment back. Conversely, the enemy and his friends will offer even more money to ensure the charm continues. In Maewo <note>original: "Aurora"</note>, the fragment of food is prepared with certain leaves; as these rot and smell, the victim dies. In Ambae <note>original: "Lepers' Island"</note>, the *garata* is boiled in a clam shell along with certain magical substances and charms that call upon Tagaro <note>a high deity or creator-spirit in Northern Vanuatu</note>. 

It is evident that no one who intends to bring mischief to a man using a fragment of his food will eat any of that food himself, because by doing so he would bring the mischief upon himself as well. Consequently, a native offering even a single banana to a visitor will bite the end of it before giving it, and a European giving medicine to a sick native gains their confidence by taking a little bit themselves first^1^.

Another charm is common to both the eastern and western islands, which is called *talamatai* in the Banks Islands. A piece of human bone, a fragment of coral, a splinter of wood, or a piece of an arrow that has killed a man is bound together with leaves that possess *mana* <note>spiritual power</note> for this purpose, accompanied by a *mana* song. By this means, the power of the ghost is bound into the charm, and the *talamatai* is secretly planted in the path along which the intended victim will walk.

<header>XII.] 'Ghost-shooter.'</header>

The charm is placed on a path where the person at whom it is aimed must pass, so that its power may spring out and strike them with disease. The magic power comes from tying and binding the <term>talamatai</term> <note>a charm involving the tight binding of fibers</note> tightly while a charm is chanted. If the fibers used to make the string are rolled upon the skull of a former practitioner of the art, the charm's effectiveness will be even greater. A <term>talamatai</term> was made quite recently in Valuwa on Saddle Island <note>now known as Motalava in Vanuatu</note>; however, the wizard who tied the last one brought out all his magical apparatus before the people of his village and smashed it with an axe. In Ambae <note>original: "Lepers' Island"</note>, this same type of charm is called a <term>rango</term>.

Another remarkable engine of mischief is called in the Banks Islands the <term>tamaletiqa</term>, or "ghost-shooter." Since this is also used in the Nggela Islands <note>original: "Florida"</note>, it can be assumed to be common to all these islands. A piece of bamboo is stuffed with leaves, a dead man's bone, and other magical ingredients, while the proper <term>mana</term> <note>spiritual or supernatural power</note> song is chanted over it. In the Banks Islands, but apparently not in the Solomon Islands, fasting adds power to this and other charms. 

The man who has made or bought one of these holds it in his hand, keeping the open end of the bamboo covered with his thumb until he sees his enemy. Then, he lets out the magic influence and "shoots" his target. Some years ago in Mota, a man named Isvitag was waiting with his ghost-shooter in hand for the man he intended to shoot. However, he released the magic too soon, just as a woman with a child on her hip stepped across the path. The child was his sister’s child—his nearest relative—and he was certain he had hit the infant directly. To save the child, he placed the contents of the bamboo into water to prevent the invisible wound from becoming "inflamed," and the child suffered no harm. 

Another striking story was told to me by Edwin Sakalraw of Ara regarding what he saw himself. A man on that small island was known to have prepared a <term>tamaletiqa</term> and had declared his intention to shoot his enemy with it at an upcoming feast. However, he would not reveal whom he intended to kill, fearing that a friend of the victim might buy back the power of the charm from the wizard who had originally prepared it.

The man he aimed at fell to the ground at once, and the dancers stopped. Then the shooter saw that he had failed and that the wrong man had been hit, which caused him great distress. However, the man who had fallen and was at the point of death, once he was made to understand that no harm was intended for him, found the courage to live again and soon recovered. There is no doubt he would have died if the mistake had not been discovered.

There is a strange method of magical attack used on Savo Island and known in the Nggela Islands <note>original: "Florida"</note> called <term>vele</term>, a word which means "to pinch." The man who possesses the secret of this magic carries a bag on his back containing leaves and other items in which the <term>mana</term> <note>supernatural power</note> for this purpose resides. He seeks to find his victim alone. When he finds him, he seizes him, bites his neck, stuffs the magic leaves down his throat, and strikes him on the head with an axe, though not hard enough to kill him. He then leaves the man, who goes home, relates what has happened, and dies after two days. If the attack occurs at night, the man cannot identify his assailant; however, the <term>vele</term> is also used in broad daylight. In such cases, the assailant does not hide himself but tells the victim his name and commands him to make it known. Yet, as the victim goes home, the charm causes him to forget it. <header>XII.] *Metamorphosis. Dreams.*</header>

The practice of magic arts for the purpose of causing harm is called <term>gaqalera</term> in the Banks Islands and on Ambae, and it is always dreaded when someone falls sick. On Ambae, the wizards who practice it are believed to have the power of changing their shape. The friends of anyone suffering from illness are always afraid that the wizard who caused the disease might come in another form—such as a blowfly—and strike the patient. They sit with the sick person, using counter-charms to guard him and carefully driving away all flies, for fear that his enemy might arrive in that form. Some men, through <term>gaqalera</term>, can turn into a shark and eat an enemy, or more commonly, someone whom an enemy has hired the wizard to destroy. The story of Tarkeke shows that this belief also exists on <note>original: "Aurora"</note> Maewo, where, as on Ambae and Pentecost Island, magicians turn into eagles and owls as well as sharks. 

This power is not always used for malicious ends, as was shown by Molitavile on Ambae. A vessel "recruiting labor"—which the natives called a "thief-ship" <note>This refers to "blackbirding," the 19th-century practice of kidnapping or tricking Pacific Islanders into forced labor on plantations.</note>—had carried away some people from the island, and their friends were very anxious to know what had become of them. Molitavile, who had the power of changing his form, undertook to turn himself into an eagle and fly after the vessel. First, he told all the people of the village to stay away from the side of the open space between the houses from which he would take flight. Then he entered...

(4) ***Dreams.*** The native belief regarding the nature of dreams, and the role played by the human soul in dreams, is a subject of inquiry that belongs more to general questions about the people's conceptions of the soul and human life. However, the use of dreaming as a branch of magical practice is appropriate to discuss here. In Maewo (Aurora) in the <note>original: "New Hebrides"</note> New Hebrides, the "dreaming-man," or <term>tatua qoreqore</term>—who may also be a <term>gismana</term> (one who uses supernatural power) in other ways—is sought after in cases of sickness. 

In an ordinary case, when it is assumed that a ghost is the cause of the ailment, the friends of the sick man send for the professional dreamer. They now give him tobacco (where formerly they gave mats) to find out which ghost has been offended and to make amends with it. The dreamer sleeps and, in his dream, goes to the place where the sick man had been working. There, he is likely to meet someone resembling a small old man who is actually a ghost, and he learns the ghost's name. The ghost tells him that the sick man encroached upon his ground—the place he haunts as his own—while he was working. To punish him, the ghost has taken the man's soul and imprisoned it within a magic fence in the garden. The dreamer begs for the return of the soul and asks for pardon on behalf of the sick man, who meant no disrespect. The ghost pulls up the fence in which the soul is enclosed and lets it out; the man, of course, then recovers.

(6) *Divination.* There are many methods by which ghosts and spirits are believed to make known to men who use them the secret things which the unassisted human intelligence could not find out; and some of these hardly need the intervention of a wizard. The practitioner lifts his hands over his head and rubs them together while singing a magic song to call upon a ghost. The sign is given by the cracking of the joints; when the question concerns life or death, if the thumbs or shoulders crack, the man still lives; if the elbows crack, he is dead. Similarly, if a man sneezes, he will use *so ilo* to know who it is that is cursing him; he revolves his fists one over the other and then throws out his arms. The revolving motion represents the question, and the answer is given as he asks, "Is it So-and-So?" and his elbows crack. 

Another method of divination was occasionally used at Motlav in the same island group. Then a new bamboo pole, about ten feet long, was fitted to the bag and tied with one end in its opening. The bag was then laid upon the grave, while the men involved in the ritual held the bamboo in their hands. The names of the recently deceased were then called, and the men holding the bamboo felt the bag become heavy as the ghost entered it; the ghost then moved up from the bag into the hollow center of the bamboo. (7) *Ordeals*. To clear or convict an accused person, there are ordeals managed by men who possess the magic instruments and the knowledge of the charms used to activate them. There are several types of ordeals used at Saa <note>Saa: A prominent village and cultural area on the island of South Malaita in the Solomon Islands.</note> which serve as examples from the Solomon Islands. One is called the <term>dau he'u</term> <note>dau he'u: Solomon Islands term meaning "stone working."</note>, or stone working; knowledge of this practice is passed down from man to man along with the specific magic stone used. An accused person goes to the man who owns the stone and hires him to perform the ordeal. The people assemble and the accused denies the charge, submitting to the trial through his advocate <note>original: "compurgator" — historically, a person who swears to the innocence or character of an accused person to clear them of a charge.</note>. This advocate heats the stone and throws it from hand to hand; if his hands are not burned, the accused is declared innocent and pays a fee in porpoise teeth <note>Porpoise teeth were a primary form of traditional currency in parts of the Solomon Islands.</note>. Much preparation is involved, including the use of a very young coconut, the flower of a sugar-cane, and chanted charms to make the process <term>saka</term> <note>saka: A Melanesian term for spiritual "heat" or supernatural efficacy; the power that makes a ritual or object effective.</note>, or "hot" with supernatural power. It is likely that accusers sometimes make their own preparations using bribes. 

Another ordeal involves applying a lit bundle of coconut leaves to the legs of the accused, who either stands through it or is tied between two posts. This is performed with charms by the practitioner, who also receives a fee. In another type, the accused swallows a charmed stone heated by the hired specialist and is considered innocent if he suffers no harm. In a fourth type, the accused eats a piece of a coconut that has been made very *saka* for this purpose and broken into pieces; if he is guilty, he will later fall from a tree, meet with some other accident, or slowly waste away.

There is also a very sacred song that is considered very *saka*. Finally, there is the crocodile ordeal <note>original: "alligator" — Codrington likely refers to the saltwater crocodile, as alligators are not native to the Pacific islands.</note>, used in the channel between Mala Paina and Mala Masiki <note>Mala Paina and Mala Masiki: Now known as Big Malaita and Small Malaita.</note>, where these reptiles are very numerous. A man accused of a serious crime is taken there; the sorcerer who manages the ordeal calls the crocodiles with his charms, and the accused—who is confident in his innocence and in the sorcerer’s power—dares to swim across. No one will consider him guilty if he escapes. In this ordeal, it is also sometimes the man who knows the charm, rather than the accused, who submits himself to the test. On Lepers' Island <note>Lepers' Island: Now known as Ambae, in Vanuatu.</note>, a man will submit to being shot at with arrows to prove his innocence; if he is hit, he is naturally guilty; if he is innocent, Tagaro <note>Tagaro: A primary deity or culture hero in the mythology of northern Vanuatu, often associated with creation and protection.</note> will protect him, just as he protects any young man in battle whom he preserves so that he may become prosperous and great. In either case, Tagaro's favor is sought through the appropriate charm.

(8) *Poison*. It is more than probable that its certain and fatal effects were believed at the time to be due to powerful magical properties, rather than natural ones, with which it was endowed. The Savo <note>Savo: A volcanic island in the Solomon Islands near Guadalcanal, known for its distinct language and history.</note> people were known as great poisoners; Florida men who visited them were very careful about what they ate. The effect of the poison was that whoever had taken it fell sick, vomited, and afterwards died. The practice of this art was dangerous to the poisoner themselves; a known poisoner was put to death in Florida, and many innocent people were also killed because they were suspected or accused. In the Banks Islands, to poison someone was called *vangan pal*, which means "to feed by stealth." The people of Ureparapara in that group had a reputation for being poisoners, and others would obtain poison from there; in Mota, however, no one knew the art. On Lepers' Island <note>Lepers' Island: Now known as Ambae, in Vanuatu.</note> poison is called, by a similar expression, *aruwana*. All that I have learned about it is that its preparation is kept very secret, and that it is made with charms in the same way as the *garata* <term>garata: a form of destructive magic performed on a fragment of a person's food or possessions</term> described earlier.

In fact, the connection between native poison and the charm that works destruction through a fragment of food is complete: in one case, a portion of the food already eaten by the person to be harmed is mixed with certain magically powerful substances; in the other case, the magically powerful substances are mixed into the food yet to be eaten. ### (9) *Tapu* and Curses

The word "taboo" is one of the very few that the languages of the Pacific Ocean have contributed to the English language, and therefore its meaning is generally assumed to be understood. However, the *tapu* or *tambu* <note>original: "tapu" and "tambu" are regional variants of the same word</note> of Melanesia is not as prominent in native life as the *tapu* of Polynesia. It also differs, perhaps, in that it never signifies any inherent holiness or awfulness, but always a sacred and unapproachable character that is imposed upon something. 

This is not strictly accurate regarding the word in the Solomon Islands, where everything connected with a ghost of worship—such as a *tindalo*, *lio'a*, or *'adaro* <term>tindalo, lio'a, and 'adaro: various regional terms for the ghosts of deceased persons who are worshipped for their power</term>—is *tambu* in and of itself. However, it is accurate regarding the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides <note>New Hebrides: Now the nation of Vanuatu</note>, where that which is naturally sacred is called *rongo* or *sapuga* <term>rongo and sapuga: terms describing things that are inherently holy or set apart by spiritual power</term>. 

Still, in cases where the English word "taboo" can be used, there is always human authority and prohibition involved in Melanesia. Something, some action, or some place is made *tambu* or *tapu* by someone who has the power to do so—anyone whose standing among the people gives them the confidence to impose this status upon it. The power at the back of the *tapu* or *tambu* is that of the ghost or spirit in whose name, or in reliance upon whom, it is pronounced; for the *tapu* is a prohibition with a curse, either expressed or implied. 

Thus, in Florida <note>Florida: The Gela Islands in the Solomon Islands</note>, a chief will forbid something to be done or touched under a penalty. He might say, for example, *tambu hangalatu* <gloss>forbidden under penalty of one hundred strings of money</gloss>. Anyone who violates his prohibition must pay him a hundred strings of money. To a European, this seems like a proof of the chief’s personal power; but to the native, the power of the chief in this and in everything else rests on the conviction that the chief has his *tindalo* ghost at his back to enforce it. In particular cases, the awareness of this spiritual connection might feel remote, and the fear...

the fear of angering the chief is present and effective, but the ultimate authority behind a prohibition is the power of the *tindalo* <term>tindalo: a ghost of a deceased person who is worshipped as a powerful spirit</term>. If a common man were to take it upon himself to place a *tambu* <term>tambu: the Solomon Islands regional variant of "taboo," a sacred prohibition</term> on anything, people would assume he would not do so unless he knew he had the spiritual power to back it up. They would watch closely, and if anyone who violated his *tambu* were to fall sick, the man would be recognized at once as someone who possessed a powerful *tindalo*, and his social status would rise. 

Each *tindalo* has a specific leaf associated with it, and a man will mark his *tambu* using the leaf of his particular ghost as a sign. Other people do not always know which specific ghost the leaf belongs to, but they understand that by disregarding the mark, they are dealing with a powerful spirit and not just a man. The *tambu* is too useful a social tool to be abandoned even when its original religious meaning stops being observed. For example, a native Christian teacher—as a person of high social standing—does not hesitate to set a *tambu*; he explains that even if thieves do not fear a *tindalo*, they are still afraid of the man himself. 

In the Banks Islands <note>Banks Islands: An archipelago in northern Vanuatu</note>, there is a minor form of prohibition called *soloi*, as well as the more solemn *tapu*. In the *soloi*, there is probably no direct reference to a supernatural punishment. However, a man who possesses supernatural *mana* <term>mana: spiritual power or influence believed to reside in persons, spirits, or objects</term>—which he gains through his association with a spirit—will *va-tapu* (set apart from common use) a path, a group of trees, a section of the beach, a canoe, or a fishing net. No one would be surprised if illness immediately struck anyone who dared to break such a *tapu*. On the other hand, a person of no particular importance might set his *soloi* in front of his trees or garden when he wants to save the fruit and produce for a future feast; in this case, intruders would simply know that the owner is prepared to defend his property with his bow and arrows. 

Even stronger than the authority of an individual was the authority of the secret societies known as the *Tamate* <term>Tamate: literally "The Dead," these were influential secret societies in the Banks Islands</term>. Each society had its own specific leaf, and any member could use that leaf to mark a prohibition. To ignore this mark would provoke the anger of all the society's members. However, the anger of either an individual or a society whose prohibition had been ignored could usually be satisfied by the payment of a pig or a sum of money.

It is clear that a *tambu* functions much like a curse when the prohibition relies on calling upon an unseen power. For instance, at Saa <note>Saa: A village on the island of South Malaita in the Solomon Islands</note> a few years ago, the chief used a curse in the name of a spirit to forbid the young people of the village from attending the mission school.

It also describes how these traditional prohibitions transitioned into secular or social tools used by chiefs and teachers.</summary>

<page-num>217</page-num>
<header>XII.] Curses.</header>

...of a *lio'a* <term>lio'a: a ghost of significant power or high status</term>. In such a case, if only native ideas had prevailed, money, pigs, or valuable gifts would have been enough to *toto* <note>original: "toto," meaning to make amends or compensate</note> with the chief. He would have then been willing to *toto 'akalo* (page 137), meaning he would set the matter right by offering a sacrifice to the *lio'a*. However, in this instance, the Christian teachers—even though they were in real danger of losing their lives—refused to acknowledge the power of the *lio'a* and the curse. They would give nothing to the chief, who then claimed he was completely unable to remove the curse.

A curse used as a solemn oath or affirmation is very common in Florida Island, and no doubt in the other Solomon Islands. A man will deny an accusation by swearing by his forbidden food, *bulonggu*! <note>bulonggu: a personal taboo, often a specific food the individual is forbidden from eating</note> or by some *tindalo* <term>tindalo: the spirit of a deceased person who has become an object of worship</term>, such as Daula, the ghostly frigate-bird, or Bagea, the ghostly shark. The Florida people and their neighbors were likely sufficiently "advanced" to season their conversation with profane and vulgar swearing even before "contact with civilization" put those English words into their mouths which are too often the first they learn. I am not aware of this habit existing in the Banks Islands.

The more serious form of curse in the Banks Islands is to *ragona* <note>original: "ragona," meaning to make into a tangle</note>, which is to prohibit easy access or movement under the authority of a spirit's power. Therefore, to swear by the name of some ghost or spirit is to *rara ragonag*—that is, to speak in a way that causes a supernatural power to intervene. This intervention can only be removed by a sufficient offering to appease the person who placed the curse, who will then satisfy the being they invoked. 

To curse in the sense of expressing a wish for harm, with a mental or spoken reference to a supernatural power, is to *virnag*. This is the term for the formula used when pouring water into the native oven (page 147), and such a curse is also believed to be the cause of sneezing. Milder forms of curses are used to respond to a troublesome or rude request or remark, such as "*Iniko o suri tamate*" <note>original: "Iniko o suri tamate," meaning "You are a dead man's bone"</note>. Another form is what they call "sending off," *rarurog*, which involves mentioning certain trees that have a sacred character: *rawo mele!* (referring to a cycas tree), *rawo aru!* (a casuarina tree), or *rawo poga!* These expressions mean little more than "You be hanged!"

## CHAPTER XIII.

### POSSESSION. INTERCOURSE WITH GHOSTS.

It is difficult to distinguish the practice of magic arts from the display of a ghost's or spirit's power through possession. This is partly because a person may use magic to bring possession upon themselves, as is done for prophecy. It is also because the connection between the powerful unseen being and the person—no matter how that connection is formed or how it functions—is exactly what defines a wizard. 

Still, there is a clear difference between witchcraft and sorcery (where a wizard uses magic charms to force the unseen power into action) and the spontaneous display of such power by the spirit itself. This distinction remains even if only a few people are able to interpret these signs or experience them directly. In cases of madness, the local belief is that the person is possessed. However, the islanders also make a clear distinction between the words and actions of someone in a delirium caused by sickness (which they describe as "wandering") and those caused by actual possession. They feel sympathy for those with mental illnesses and treat them kindly, even though their traditional remedies are often harsh. 

On Florida Island, for example, a man named Kandagaru from Boli Village lost his mind; he chased people and stole items to hide them. No one blamed him for these actions because they knew he was possessed by a *tindalo* <term>tindalo: the spirit of a deceased person who has become an object of worship</term>. His friends hired a wizard who removed the *tindalo* spirit, and the man recovered. Similarly, not long ago on Lepers' Island <note>original: "Lepers' Island," now known as Ambae in Vanuatu</note>, there was a man who lost his sanity. The people suspected that he had accidentally stepped on a sacred place belonging to Tagaro <note>a high-ranking deity or culture hero in Melanesian mythology</note>, and that the ghost of the man who had recently performed a sacrifice there was angry with him.

Traditional healers were summoned; they identified the offending ghost by reciting the names of deceased men who might have been insulted. They then washed the patient with water that had been empowered with charms and burned the vessel used for the magic water under the patient's nose. In this case, the man recovered. In a similar situation, they would place pieces of the fringe from a mat that had belonged to the deceased into a coconut shell and burn it under the nose of the possessed person. 

There was another man who threw off his *malo* <term>malo: a traditional loincloth made of bark-cloth or woven fiber</term> and went naked during a feast—a certain sign of being out of his mind. He drew his bow at people and stole their belongings. The community felt pity for him and attempted to cure him. In that island, when a person in such a condition spoke, it was not with his own voice, but with the voice of the dead man possessing him. Such a person would also know where items were hidden; when he was seen approaching, men would hide a bow or a club to test him, and he would always know exactly where to find it. 

Thus, the type of possession that causes madness cannot be easily distinguished from the type used for prophecy, and a man might even pretend to be mad simply to gain a reputation as a prophet. At Sua, a man may speak with the voice of a powerful deceased man while his body undergoes the contortions that occur during possession. He calls himself by the name of the dead man speaking through him, and others address him by that name as well. While possessed, he will eat fire, lift enormous weights, and foretell future events. 

In the Banks' Islands, the people distinguish between possession by a ghost that enters a person for a specific purpose and possession by a ghost that has no apparent motive other than the fact that it is homeless. Because this spirit has no place in the land of the dead, it wanders mischievously about; they call this a *tamat lelera* <note>original: "tamat lelera," a wandering ghost</note>. Extraordinary feats of strength and agility were often performed under the influence of one of these "wandering ghosts." A man would move with supernatural speed from place to place; he might be heard shouting from the top of a tall tree on one side of a village, and a moment later, he would be in a tree on the opposite side. He would make sounds that no person in their right mind could produce, and his strength was so great that it took many men to restrain him. Such a man was...

Meanwhile, they would call out one name after another of deceased men whose ghosts were likely to be wandering about. When the correct name was called, the ghost would depart, though sometimes this treatment failed. 

It was a different matter when—as used to happen in the past—a ghost from *Panoi* <note>original: "Panoi"; the traditional underworld or abode of the dead in many Melanesian cultures</note> would enter a man for a specific purpose and speak with his voice. This did not happen to everyone, but only to certain people who were susceptible to this type of possession. Such a man would see a ghost somewhere, come home, and lie down sick. People would come to see him and, calling him by his name, ask what was wrong. He would answer, "It is not he, it is I"—meaning it was not the sick man speaking, but the ghost answering with his voice. 

Then the people would call out the names of those who had recently died to see whose ghost it was. When they hit upon the right name, the possessed man would answer, "It is I." He would then begin to weep and tell them that he had come back because he knew, while in *Panoi*, that his wife and family were not being properly cared for, or that his property was being wasted. He would scold his relatives for their misconduct and tell them about things they did not know, such as the location of lost property. 

Eventually, someone would bring in a bunch of strong-smelling leaves to drive the ghost away. The ghost would immediately sense their presence; even if the people hid the leaves and denied having them, it was in vain. They would catch hold of the struggling and howling man and put the leaves to his nose. He would appear to "die" as the ghost departed from him, just as the soul departs from a dying man. After a while, his senses would return, and he would declare that he knew nothing of what had been said or done since he first saw the ghost and became ill. Such a medium, though not a professional wizard, undoubtedly found it beneficial to receive these visits from the dead.

An **Omen** is a spontaneous manifestation or warning given by a supernatural power, rather than something sought out through the arts of **divination** <term>divination: the practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means</term>. # XIII. Omens and Vampires

...canoe <note>This sentence continues from the previous page's discussion of signs or rituals related to travel</note>, which might be considered an omen if the sign were not given in response to the wizard on board. Authentic omens are observed at Saa <note>A significant cultural area on the island of South Malaita</note>. There is a small bird named *visi* after its cry, which means "No." It also has other notes that resemble the voice of a man talking. If men starting on an expedition hear the cry *visi!*, it might not be enough to make them turn back, but if they later fail, they remember the warning. Conversely, if they hear its other notes, they are confident of success. A man working in his garden hears the bird and asks, "Is there fighting?" The bird answers *visi*, "No." He asks again, "Is it a stranger come from afar?" The bird either answers *visi* or chatters to give an affirmative reply. However, this is not taken very seriously. 

If a frog or some other creature that does not usually come indoors is seen in a house, it is considered an omen. The residents will go and ask a wizard what it means. If the creature comes and cries, they know that there will soon be mourning for a death. On that same island, there is a remarkable and rarely seen kind of snake called *mati e sato*; it is about ten inches long and glistens like gold. The natives say that when it is full-grown, it is so resplendent that nothing can be clearly seen except its eyes and snout. When held in the hand, it is exceedingly smooth and slippery. If one of these is seen in a house, it is a sign of death: if it is running, it signifies a violent death; if it is quiet, it signifies death by sickness. 

If the venomous snake *a'u* is seen in a house, it is a sign of death, fighting, or misfortune. If it is coiled up, it is a sign of a peaceful death; if it is running, there will be violence. When a person begins building a house or canoe, or starts clearing a garden, he will call out loudly; if something unusual appears afterward, it is a sign that the work will be interrupted by death or war. If nothing appears, all will be well. The sacred character of the *sigo* (kingfisher) in the Banks’ Islands has been mentioned previously, along with the fact that its cry is ominous. It is the same in Lepers’ Island <note>Now known as Ambae, Vanuatu</note>, where, if a party is going to battle and a kingfisher (*higo*) cries to the right, it foretells victory; if it cries to the left, it bodes failure.

# Possession and Interaction with Ghosts

Some people sought this power out of a morbid desire for communion with some ghost, and to gain it, they would steal and eat a piece of a corpse. The ghost of the dead man would then join in a close friendship with the person who had eaten the flesh, and would gratify him by afflicting anyone against whom his ghostly power might be directed. The man so afflicted would feel that something was influencing his life and would come to dread a particular person among his neighbors, who was therefore suspected of being a <term>talamaur</term> <note>A person, often associated with vampire-like qualities, who is believed to be possessed by or in league with a ghost</note>. When this suspect was seized and tested in the smoke of strong-smelling leaves—a form of trial by ordeal—he would shout out the name of the dead man whose ghost was his familiar, often the names of more than one, and finally the name of the man who was afflicted. 

The same name, *talamaur*, was given to someone whose soul was believed to leave their body to eat the soul or the lingering life-force of a freshly deceased corpse. There was a woman some years ago of whom the story is told that she made no secret of doing this. On the death of a neighbor, she reportedly gave notice that she would go in the night and eat the corpse. The friends of the deceased therefore kept watch in the house where the body lay. At the dead of night, they heard a scratching at the door, followed by a rustling noise close to the corpse. One of them threw a stone and seemed to hit the unseen thing. In the morning, the *talamaur* was found with a bruise on her arm, which she confessed was caused by a stone thrown at her while she was eating the corpse. Such a woman would feel a morbid delight in the dread she inspired and would also be secretly rewarded by those whose private spite she gratified.

A certain mysterious power was believed to belong to some men in the Banks' Islands <note>An archipelago in northern Vanuatu</note>, which the natives find difficult to explain. There is something belonging to a man called his <term>wuqa</term> or *uqa*. If a stranger sleeps in someone’s usual sleeping place in his absence and afterwards finds himself unwell, he knows that the *uqa* of the man in whose place he slept has struck him there. Or, if a person leaves a companion and goes elsewhere to sleep, the *uqa* of the man he leaves will follow him and strike him; he will wake up in the morning feeling weak and...

Although this is not done through witchcraft, a person is held responsible for what their *uqa* <term>uqa</term> <note>original: "uqa"; a spiritual influence or shadow-soul that can move independently of a person and cause harm or illness to others</note> does. They are required to pay money to the injured party and, through an act of will, must remove the malignant influence.

We should also mention certain tricks that ghosts or spirits play on people, or which people know how to provoke. At Mota in the Banks Islands, a little boy named Peitavunana (which means "Heavenly Water") was frightened and chased up a mountain by a ghost. People searched for him in vain, and a fight was even threatened between families. They performed divination for him, called *so ilo* <term>so ilo</term> <note>A method of divination practiced by cracking the finger joints to receive answers from the spirit world</note> (page 211), and a man from Vanua Lava announced that the boy would be found in a specific, very inaccessible place. He was indeed found there by a man named Somwaswas, at the root of a tree, crying and calling for his mother. His body was covered in excrement—believed to be the food of ghosts—and he was bleeding from the thorns through which he had been forced. In his hand, he held an unripe fruit of the mammy-apple <note>A tropical fruit, likely referring here to a species of Mammea or perhaps a papaya</note>. He said that his deceased mother had appeared to him and given him the food. Another little boy, Nungwia, while sleeping on the beach at night, was carried by a ghost into a very small cavity beneath a rock, a space so tight it would have been impossible for him to climb into it on his own.

On Lepers' Island <note>A historical name for the island of Ambae or Aoba in Vanuatu</note>, they have a specific way of playing with a ghost. They construct a small house in the forest near their village and decorate it with leaves and coconut fronds. The house has a partition dividing it in two, and a bamboo pole twelve or fifteen feet long is placed inside, with half of it on one side of the partition and half on the other. The men gather at night to test for the presence of a ghost, sitting in the house on only one side of the partition with their hands placed under one end of the bamboo. They close their eyes and call out the names of those who have recently died. When they feel the bamboo moving in their hands, they know the ghost of the last person named is present. They then ask, naming one of the men in the room, "Where is Tanga?" and the bamboo rises in their hands and strikes that person before sinking back down. Once they are certain of the ghost's presence, they tell it they are going outside, and they depart, singing,

In Mota a few years ago, they tried a practice of this kind that had long been out of use, with a success that caused alarm. A basket was fastened to the end of a bamboo pole and food was put in it; a man took the bamboo upon his shoulder and walked along with the basket at his back. Presently, he felt a heavy weight in the basket—as much as he could carry—a sign that a ghost had come into it. The bamboo then would drag people about, and if put up into a tree, it would lift them from the ground. This resembles a good deal a method of divination <note>The practice of seeking knowledge of the future or the unknown by supernatural means</note> used at Motlav and described above, but there is no divination in these particular tricks.

There was, and perhaps still is, in the Torres Islands something similar to this, when ghosts influenced and took possession of people through the use of sticks. This has been described by a native under the name of <term>Na tamet lingalinga</term> <note>Likely referring to "wandering" or "listening" ghosts; the term refers both to the ritual and the people subjected to it</note>, which is the name given to those who are subjected to the ghostly influence. It is performed, he writes, on the fifth day after a death. There was a certain man at Lo who took the lead, and without whom nothing could be done; he announced that he would descend into <term>Panoi</term> <note>The subterranean world of the dead</note>, the abode of the dead, and he had with him certain others as assistants. He and his party were called simply "ghosts" while engaged in the affair. The first thing was to assemble those who were willing to be treated in a <term>gamal</term> <note>A communal men’s house or public hall</note>—perhaps twenty young men or boys—to make them lie down on the two sides of the building, and to shake over them leaves and tips of the twigs of powerful and magical plants.

### xiii.] *Forms of Possession in the Torres Islands*

...with charms. Then the leader and his assistants visited all the sacred places haunted by ghosts, such as the spots where men wash off the black paint used for mourning. They gathered the ghosts as they went and became so heavily possessed themselves that they appeared to have lost their minds, although they followed a specific ritualized method. 

Meanwhile, the subjects lying in the <term>gamal</term> <note>A communal men's house or clubhouse found in Melanesian villages</note> began to be moved. Those who supposedly bring the ghosts to them walk quietly along both sides of the house from the outside, and then all at once, they strike the house along its entire length with the sticks they carry in their hands. This startles those inside, and they roll about on the ground in a state of distraction. Then the "ghosts" enter with their sticks; in this performance, each leader is believed to be a specific deceased person—one might be Tagilrow, another Qatawala. They leap from side to side, turning their sticks over to be beaten by the subjects on either side. 

The subjects are given sticks for this purpose, and as they strike the leader's stick, the ghost "strikes" or possesses them one after another. In this state, the sticks seem to draw them out into the open village square where they can be seen. They appear not to recognize or hear anyone except the "ghosts" who have brought this state upon them, and who alone can control them and prevent them from pulling down the houses. They are seized with a frantic urge to grab and strike with anything—bows, clubs, bamboo water-vessels, or even the rafters of the houses—and their strength is so great that a full-grown man cannot restrain a boy in this condition. 

After a time, the "ghosts" take them back into the <term>gamal</term>, where they lie exhausted. The "ghosts" then go to drink <term>kava</term> <note>A traditional beverage made from the roots of the *Piper methysticum* plant, used across the Pacific for its sedative and ritual properties</note>. As each drinks, he pours away the dregs while calling the name of one of the possessed individuals, and each person's senses return as his name is called. However, it is five days before they are well enough to move about again. This ritual was performed once after a Christian teacher had arrived at Lo; he allowed two of his students to attend to prove it was a fraud, but they were also possessed.

Similarly, a family group working in their garden might see smoke and sparks rising toward their village. They hear the hissing of flames and the popping of bamboo rafters; convinced their own house is burning, they run back to save what they can. When they reach the village, everything is quiet. The houses are all standing with doors fastened, just as they were during work hours. The trick has been played by a group who built a fire in line with the house. By exploding green reeds—which fill with steam when heated in the fire—and striking the ground with the tips of dry coconut fronds, they have imitated the sounds of a house fire with wonderful accuracy.

It is worth introducing here the Melanesian superstition regarding sneezing, which has been mentioned previously. In Florida <note>Now known as the Nggela Islands in the Solomon Islands</note>, when a man sneezes, people believe someone is speaking about him, is angry with him, or perhaps even cursing him by calling on his own *tindalo* <note>original: *tindalo*; a ghost or spirit of a deceased person who has become an object of worship</note> to "eat" (destroy) him. The man who sneezes then calls upon his own *tindalo* to harm the person who is cursing him. 

Similarly, at Saa <note>A region on the island of Malaita</note>, if a man sneezes when he wakes up, he cries out, "Who calls me? If it is for good, let it be; if for evil, may [Name] (naming a *lio’a* <note>original: *lio’a*; the ghost of a dead person</note>) defend me." In the Banks Islands as well, it is supposed that someone is calling a man’s name when he sneezes, whether for good or for evil. On Motlav <note>Motalava, an island in the Banks group</note>, if a child sneezes, the mother will cry, "Let him come back into the world! Let him remain." In Mota, they cry, "Live! Roll back to us!" The idea is that a ghost is drawing the child’s soul away. It is said that in Mota, when a man sneezes, he uses a form of divination to find out who is cursing him. He will also stamp his foot and shout, "Stamp down the mischief away from me! Let it be quiet! Let them speak their words in vain!"

...let them lay their plots in vain!"¹ <note>This phrase completes a prayer or protective spell against those who might be speaking ill of the sneezer</note>. There is a specific form of words used when one's stepfather sneezes (referencing page 40). ## CHAPTER XIV.

### BIRTH. CHILDHOOD. MARRIAGE.

**In** attempting to trace the course of a Melanesian life from birth to burial, we soon encounter practices connected with the <term>Couvade</term> <note>A custom where a father observes specific taboos or rituals—sometimes even staying in bed—to protect the health of a newborn</note>. A proper Couvade has perhaps been observed in San Cristoval <note>Now known as Makira in the Solomon Islands</note> alone, where the young father was found "lying in" <note>resting in bed as if recovering from childbirth</note> after the birth of his child; and it should be noted that this occurred in a place where the child follows the father’s kindred <note>a patrilineal system where the child belongs to the father's family line</note>. There is much, however, that approaches this practice.

At Saa <note>an area on the island of Malaita</note>, it is not only the expectant mother who is careful about what she eats; the father also refrains from certain kinds of food that would hurt the child, both before and after the birth. He will not eat pork, and he abstains from movements that are believed to cause harm, based on the principle that the father's movements affect those of the child. A man will not perform hard work, lift heavy weights, or go out to sea; he keeps quiet so that the child does not startle, overstrain itself, or throw itself about while he is paddling.

In the Banks Islands as well, both parents are careful about what they eat when a child is born; they consume only what would not make the infant ill if the baby were to eat it. Before the birth of her first child, the mother must not eat fish caught by a hook, net, or trap. After the birth of the first child, the father does no heavy work for a month; after the birth of any of his children, he takes care not to go into those sacred places <note>original: *tano rongo*</note> that the child could not enter without risk. It is the same in the New Hebrides <note>Now known as Vanuatu</note>; the expectant Araga <note>Araga is the language and people of North Pentecost Island</note> father keeps away from sacred places <note>original: *ute sapuga*</note> before the

<header>*Couvade. Infanticide.*</header>

child's birth, and does not enter his house; after the birth, he does work in looking after his wife and child, but he must not eat shellfish or other produce of the beach, for the infant would suffer from ulcers if he did. In Lepers' Island <note>Now known as Ambae</note>, the father is very careful for ten days; he does no work. He will not climb a tree or go far into the sea to bathe, for if he exerts himself, the child will suffer. If during this time he goes any distance, such as to the beach, he brings back with him a little stone representing the infant's soul, which may have followed him; having arrived at home, he cries, "Come hither," and puts down the stone in the house. He then waits until the child sneezes and cries, "Here it is," knowing then that the soul has not been lost.

Abortion and infanticide were very common. If a woman did not want the trouble of bringing up a child, desired to appear young, was afraid her husband might think the birth was premature, or wished to spite her husband, she would find someone to induce an abortion. This was done either by the juice of certain plants taken in a drink or by twisting and squeezing the fetus <note>original: "fœtus"</note>. Infanticide was more prevalent in some islands than others; since Christian teaching has been introduced, a great change is visible in Maewo <note>also called Aurora Island</note> and at Wango in San Cristoval <note>now Makira</note>, where in recent years the birth of an infant was indeed an unusual thing, and all the children in the villages had been bought from inland tribes. In those parts, the old women of the village generally determined whether a newborn child should live: if it was not promising in appearance, or likely to be troublesome, it was killed <note>original: "made away with"</note>. Its mouth might be stuffed with leaves and the body cast into a hole and covered with a stone. In the Banks Islands, if the infant was of the wrong sex or otherwise unwelcome, it was choked as soon as it was born. Male children were killed more often than females in that group; if there were female children already, another would not be desired. However, the females were more likely to be preserved—which is important to note—because the family line passes through the female side <note>a matrilineal descent system</note>, and because of the prospect of gain when the girl is eventually betrothed and married.

...killing one of a pair of twins, nor is there any widespread dislike for the birth of twins beyond the extra trouble they cause. In some places, such as Saa, twins are welcomed. At Motlav, the villagers are proud of their twins, and the parents and relatives treat them with great affection. No one would adopt just one of them, as it would spoil the pleasure of seeing them together and deprive them of their natural right to be with each other. The only unfortunate aspect is the extra work they require and the great sorrow the parents feel if they die. 

In Florida <note>Now known as the Nggela Islands</note> alone, there seems to be a suspicion that two fathers might be involved; however, they generally believe that the woman has trespassed on the sacred place, <term>vunuha</term> <note>a forbidden or sacred area</note>, of some ghost, <term>tindalo</term> <note>a deceased spirit with supernatural power</note>, whose power causes such births. On Lepers' Island <note>Now known as Ambae</note>, it is also thought that twins may be a gift from Tagaro <note>A prominent creator-deity in Melanesian mythology</note>. Women who desire a child will visit a sacred place in the hope that the spirit will grant them one, and sometimes he grants them two. There is currently a man on the island named Malavaiboe ("Pig-twin"), the surviving twin son of Arusese. The people believe he will become a great man—not simply because he is a twin, but because Tagaro gave the twins to his mother when she went to ask for a child.

At Saa, when a newborn infant is eight or ten days old, a sacrifice called <term>'unu qo</term> <note>original: "‘unu qo"; a pig sacrifice, see page 137</note> is made to the family <term>lio'a</term> <note>the ghost of a powerful ancestor</note> to protect against misfortune. On Lepers' Island, when the infant is ten days old and the mother has recovered, the father goes to the beach to wash the child's belongings. As he walks, he scatters little toy bows along the path if the child is a boy, symbolizing that he shall be a strong archer; if the child is a girl, he throws down pieces of pandanus fiber, the material used for making mats. This signifies that making mats, which serve as currency, will be her future work. If a child dies after eating a certain food for the first time, the parents will never eat that food again. 

At Araga <note>Pentecost Island</note>, a firstborn son remains for ten days in the house where he was born. During this time, the father's relatives bring food to the mother. On the tenth day, the relatives bring nothing, but the father gives them as much food and as many mats (which serve as money) as he can afford. They—
