<page-num>231</page-num>
<header>xiv. Ceremonies in Infancy. Dress.</header>

The relatives of the father (who are not considered kin to the infant) perform a certain ceremony on that day called <term>huhuni</term>. During this ritual, they lay mats and the strings used for tying pigs upon the infant's head. The father then tells them that he accepts this as a sign that they will feed and help his son in the future. This ceremony clearly indicates a movement toward a patriarchal system—a recognition of the blood tie through the father and the duties that result from it. 

Another sign of this advancing "father-right" can be seen in a very different custom practiced in the Banks Islands upon the birth of a first-born son. This event is marked by a noisy and playful fight called <term>vagalo</term>, after which the father "buys off" the attackers by paying money to the other <term>rere</term>—that is, to the kinsmen of the child and the mother. It is almost certainly a ceremonial, though playful, assertion of the mother's relatives' claim to the child as one of their own. The father's payment serves to settle their claim and secure his own position as the head of his family.

As children grow, they remain in the women's care within the house during their early years. They are commonly weaned once they can crawl. For boys, their first major step in life depends heavily on local customs regarding clothing. In the Banks Islands, where males of any age traditionally wore no clothes, boys were sent to sleep in the <term>gamal</term> <note>the public men's clubhouse</note> as they grew older. The parents would say, "He is a boy; it is time to separate him from the girls." They continued to take their meals at home until, eventually, their family purchased a place for them in the <term>Suqe</term> <note>The Suqe was a hierarchical social club or secret society central to Melanesian life, where members advanced through ranks by providing feasts and currency</note>. 

In the Torres Islands, a boy's nose is pierced on his third day of life for future ornamentation. In Florida <note>Now the Nggela Islands</note> and the surrounding area, boys of six or seven begin wearing the small cloth wrapper worn by males and are very particular about it. At Santa Cruz, boys initially go to the chief's <term>mandai</term> <note>a canoe-house and public hall</note> during the daytime and return home to sleep; after a while, they stop returning home at night. On that island, the indispensable nose-ring comes even before clothing: the hole for this is made in infancy and a small ring is inserted. When the ears are pierced, it is a great...

The occasion is marked by killing a pig, and this is done every time an additional hole is made; consequently, a Santa Cruz boy may be seen with more than thirty earrings. The Santa Cruz dress is extensive and is first worn during a feast accompanied by the killing of a pig. A boy's transition to wearing clothes depends, therefore, on the ability and willingness of his friends to provide the feast; as a result, some older boys continue to go naked if the family cannot afford it. 

The dress in the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>, specifically on Lepers’ Island <note>now Ambae</note> and Pentecost Island, differs little from that of Santa Cruz. The boy begins wearing his <term>malo</term> <note>a traditional loincloth made of woven fiber</note> when his parents decide he is large enough, and as soon as they can afford to host a feast. Before this, he has lived at home, but now he eats and sleeps in the <term>gamali</term> <note>the men's communal club-house</note>. 

At this stage, he begins a strange and strict period of social avoidance with his sisters and his mother. This is most intense regarding his sisters. He must not use any common noun that is also the name—or even part of the name—of any of his sisters, and they are just as careful to avoid his name. He may go to his father’s house to ask for food, but if his sister is inside, he must leave before he can eat. If no sister is present, he may sit down near the door and eat his meal. 

If a brother and sister happen to meet on a path, she will run away or hide. If a boy on the beach recognizes certain footprints as his sister’s, he will not follow them, and she will not follow his. This mutual avoidance begins as soon as the boy is clothed or the girl is tattooed. The partitions between boys and girls—which are necessary for running a modern school in this region—exist not to divide the sexes in general, but specifically to separate brothers and sisters. 

This avoidance continues throughout their lives. The distance between a son and his mother also increases as the boy grows up, though this shyness is usually more pronounced on her side than his. While he may go to the house to ask for food, his mother will bring it out but will not hand it to him directly; instead, she sets it down for him to pick up. If she calls for him to come, she addresses him using the formal plural—a more distant way of speaking. She says, "Come, you all," (<term>mim vanai</term>) <note>original: "Come ye"</note> rather than the singular "Come, you." If they speak together, she sits a short distance away and turns her face, for she feels shy in the presence of her grown-up son. The meaning of all this is clear: in Santa Cruz and the neighboring islands, the social separation of the sexes is a fundamental part of daily life.

### xiv. Social Avoidance and the Apprenticeship at Saa

...but it does not have this specific character. In Santa Cruz, men and women never work together in mixed groups or gather in a single crowd. Only men with their wives and children, or men with their mothers, work in the gardens. When a crowd assembles, the women stay at a distance. In Nufilole, one of the Swallow Islands, the separation is total; men and women are never outdoors at the same time. In the morning, the men go out first and return; after that, the women go to collect water. When the women return, the men go out again.

As mentioned in Chapters V and VI, there is no known ritual in these Melanesian islands for "making young men" (a formal initiation into manhood); there is only the process of joining various secret societies. The closest thing to such an initiation seems to be found at Saa. In that part of Malanta, a chief's son goes early to the <term>oha</term> <note>a canoe-house and public meeting hall</note>, while ordinary children still eat and sleep at home. He may go there when he is twelve years old. Before this, his family is very protective of him; he must not go under the women’s sleeping area, his mother must never use offensive language when scolding him, and he must not associate with older boys who might teach him bad habits. He is kept apart so that he does not <term>lo'u</term> <note>literally "to fall" or "be low"</note>, meaning to lose his status or become degraded¹. At first, he only goes to the *oha* during the daytime and returns to his mother to sleep. 

When the time comes, he is placed with boys of his own age to undergo a sort of <term>noviciate</term> <note>a period of training or apprenticeship</note>. This custom is now dying out; in the past, boys used to stay in the *oha* for years. First, there was a <term>lotu</term> <note>a sacrifice for purification; see page 137</note> to purify the boys. Afterward, they went out early every morning in a canoe to catch bonito fish, until each boy had caught one. Men paddled with the boys, with a boy sitting behind each man; when the man felt a bite, the boy behind him moved forward and helped to pull it in. The fish was then credited to the boy. He had caught a fish, an act for which one must be <term>saka</term> <note>to be possessed of a certain mysterious spiritual power</note> to...

¹ It is interesting that the word <term>lotu</term> <note>original: bowing down as in prayer</note>, which is commonly used to describe the adoption of Christianity in Polynesia and Fiji, appears with this meaning in the Solomon Islands. The original sense from which its use for the new religion came was that of bowing down, as in prayer. For a chief, going anywhere where women might be physically above his head is considered degrading; this explains the refusal of some chiefs to go below deck on a ship.

### Birth, Childhood, and Marriage

...catch <note>referring to catching a bonito fish, a key milestone</note>; and once he had reached a certain stage in life. A boy did not leave his seclusion as soon as he had caught his fish; instead, he remained for a duration fixed at his entrance. This timeframe was determined by his father’s rank, or the status to which his father aspired to elevate him, for the length of his stay depended largely on the amount of money the father was willing to spend on the associated feasts. Occasionally, a boy might leave before his time was up, as <term>Wateaado</term> did when his brother died and he was needed to take his place. At specific intervals during this seclusion, feasts were held, with a final grand celebration when the boy eventually emerged. There was no secret initiation, and nothing was formally taught to the boys; the only skill they learned was how to fish for <term>bonito</term> <note>a large predatory fish, related to tuna, which is highly valued in Solomon Islands culture</note>. When they finally came out, they were young men and effectively strangers to the village people, having grown up entirely out of their sight. This custom has now ended at Saa.

Circumcision is unknown in almost all the islands discussed here. It has spread from Ambrym to the lower end of Pentecost Island as a prevailing custom, though this development is relatively recent. It is performed at whatever age the boy's friends choose to host the accompanying feast. It is not considered a mark of initiation and carries no religious or superstitious weight; rather, it is a mark of social distinction. It is known but not yet practiced on <term>Lepers' Island</term> <note>modern-day Ambae</note>, but it is said to have already been introduced to the southern part of Aurora <note>modern-day Maewo</note>. A sharp piece of bamboo is used for the procedure. There is no doubt that this custom—for it is a social habit rather than a sacred rite—traveled from the east to the southern New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note> and has been in common use there for some time. In some of those islands, the local dress (if it can be called that) has even been adapted to accommodate it.

The childhood of a girl can hardly be distinguished by specific milestones, except for her progress toward marriage. In some places, being clothed and tattooed are necessary steps in this direction. In <term>Florida</term> <note>modern-day Nggela</note> and the neighboring regions, as well as in Santa Cruz, Pentecost Island, and most of the New Hebrides, a woman's dress consists of a petticoat made from strings of fiber or leaves. In the south-

<header>xiv.] Chastity. Prostitution.</header>

...the girls' behavior is closely observed before their betrothal and marriage are arranged. There was undoubtedly a significant degree of sexual freedom between boys and girls, and a lack of chastity was not viewed as a very serious offense. However, it is certain that across these islands in general, the people were not nearly as indifferent toward female virtue as they are commonly accused of being. There is often a very specific reason why local people might immediately present sexually available women to white visitors; these visitors then speak from experiences that reflect poorly on the white men who visited before them.

There is, however, a considerable difference to be observed between one island and another in this matter. An example of this can be seen in whether or not a language has a specific word for a "harlot" <note>original: "harlot"; a term for a woman who engages in prostitution</note>. On the island of Florida <note>modern-day Nggela</note>, such a woman is called a *rembi*, and until recently, she occupied a recognized place in tribal life. Usually, a woman was condemned to this lifestyle by the local chief as a punishment for misconduct, such as adultery or for "fornication" <note>sexual relations</note> within her own *kema* <term>kinship group</term> <note>the *kema* is a matrilineal clan; sexual relations within the same clan were considered a form of incest</note>. She effectively belonged to the chief, lived in one of his houses, and most of her earnings went to him. Once she had accumulated enough <term>porpoise teeth</term> <note>a traditional form of currency in the Solomon Islands</note> and shell money, she would be allowed to marry. Because her wealth made her a desirable bride, it was considered improper to mention her former career once she was married. While she was a *rembi*, she was not particularly looked down upon; people still respected social boundaries, such as not stepping over her legs, not going too near her, and not speaking to her without a specific reason.

At Wango on the island of San Cristoval <note>modern-day Makira</note> and in the surrounding areas, girls were very loose in their behavior before marriage, often earning money for themselves privately through prostitution. Additionally, there are professional prostitutes there called *repi*, including some unmarried girls and some widows.

The people at Saa on the island of Malanta <note>modern-day Malaita</note> considered themselves much stricter. If a girl from a high-ranking family was found to be pregnant before marriage, she would be killed, unless her lover could pay enough to save her life and take her as his wife. A girl from a common family—that is, one not related to a chief—would not be killed, but she might be permitted to become a harlot if her lover did not marry her. Sometimes a father allows his daughter to become a harlot to earn money; likewise, a chief at U’lawa will buy a girl from her father and keep her to earn money for him as well as for herself. However, such a *repi* on either island is not...

The high-ranking families in Ulawa are also strict, and mothers watch over their daughters carefully. At Santa Cruz, where the separation of the sexes is so strictly maintained, there are certainly public <term>courtesans</term> <note>original: "courtesans"; women who engage in prostitution, often associated with higher social circles or specific public roles</note>. In the <margin>[</margin> Banks' Islands, no such thing was known¹; in the old days, it was always the duty of parents to watch over their children, both boys and girls, and to reprimand and correct them if they saw them behaving improperly. Girls were never allowed to go about alone without their mother or an older friend. However common casual sexual encounters may have been, they were never permitted or considered respectable; public opinion was always on the side of virtue. There were respectable families where the girls were known or presumed to conduct themselves perfectly well—to *toga mantag* <note>a Mota phrase meaning "to live or stay well"</note>—and a girl from such a family would typically remain chaste until the time of her marriage. 

Children born out of wedlock were very rare in the Banks' Islands². A woman living without a husband would indeed sometimes be seen with children, but it was usually known in the community that she had been taken as a second wife by a man whose first wife was jealous and had driven <margin>[</margin> her from the house. In the Northern New Hebrides, such as Pentecost and Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae or Aoba</note>, prostitutes are unknown, though there are unmarried girls and married women who are known to secretly receive mats <note>woven mats were a primary form of currency and wealth in these islands</note> and ornaments in exchange for sex. There is a story from Lepers' Island about a man with two wives who, when he left home, hung a bag in his house which he expected to be filled with mats by the time he returned <note>implying he expected his wives to earn wealth through secret prostitution in his absence</note>. In these islands as well, a reputation for chastity is valued for its own sake, and in respectable families, care is taken of the girls. In every island, it can be said that there are households where it is understood that the family is generally

<header>XIV.] Betrothal. Tattooing.</header>

...well-behaved, and which are respectable accordingly; and everywhere there are families which are not respectable. <term>Bastards</term> <note>original: "bastards"; children born to unmarried parents</note> are generally very rare.

Betrothal <note>formal engagement to be married</note> comes very early in the life of many Melanesian girls; a man with a newborn son looks out for the birth of a suitable girl to be his son's wife. This is especially the case with people of consequence and wealth, and this begins the long series of payments and negotiations which only end at the marriage. The general character of these transactions may be understood by looking at how matrimonial affairs are managed in the various islands. Usually, it is the first marriage of the young man that is being planned; additional wives are added later with less ceremony, but not without a good deal of bargaining among the men involved and a great deal of business and discussion among the women. 

In Florida <note>now known as the Nggela Islands in the Solomon Islands</note>, a girl who has been engaged as an infant, and for whom some payment has already been made, is tattooed when she reaches the proper age. This practice, known as *uhunhu* <note>original: "*uhunhu*"</note>, is performed by a professional tattooist who receives a significant amount of money, pigs, and food for his art. A feast is held for him and for the assembled company of friends and relatives, who help share the expense. The pattern is first marked out in circles with a piece of bamboo, and the skin is then cut with a tool made from the bone of a bat's wing. The amount of tattooing varies, but the pain and swelling are always considerable. No girl would be considered ready for marriage unless she was tattooed; the performance of this operation is a sign that the time has come for the father of the young man to make a down payment toward the marriage. 

Further progress, however, may be delayed for months or even years before the future father-in-law finally arrives with his party to pay the full sum of money agreed upon. Then, after staying for at least two days while various traditional difficulties are intentionally put in the way, the girl is finally given up. An extra sum of money must then be paid, called *na rongo ni nagoli k-kesa* <note>original: "*na rongo ni nagoli k-kesa*"; literally, the money to break the doorpost</note>. This is the "money to break the post near the door" (the post one holds when going in and out of the house), symbolizing the end of her time living in her old home.

The betrothed children converse and play together at their ease, knowing what is planned; and this visit is repeated from time to time while the children are small. There is no real or feigned reluctance on her part, and her friends do not need to lift or carry her. However, it is sometimes a long time before the marriage is consummated because of the bridegroom's shyness, even though the parents encourage the young couple to be friendly and provide opportunities for them to talk and work together. 

A bride's virginity is a matter of great importance to her friends. This is not only because the boy’s family will refuse to pay the promised amount if her character is in doubt, but also because they value social propriety. This mostly applies to high-ranking families; among common people <note>original: "inferior people"</note>, early betrothals are unusual. In those cases, the young people have not always become friends beforehand, making the move to the bride's new home a more significant event. 

Similarly, in Santa Cruz, marriage engagements are often made during infancy. The father chooses a suitable girl sooner or later, but the boy is not informed. The parents on both sides exchange gifts and feather-money <term>a traditional currency made from the red feathers of the honey-eater bird</term>. In time, the boy is told that a girl has been engaged for him, but he is not told who she is. He is only warned not to go near a certain house, from which he guesses her identity. When the time comes, the young man is often very reluctant to marry; he cries and asks why they want him to leave. However, once married, he brings his wife to his father’s house until he builds one of his own².

In the Banks' Islands, friends make the arrangements and agree upon the payment. The young man, or his friends on his behalf, *secure the woman* <note>original: "la goro o tarine"</note> by giving money and pigs. Her friends then *reciprocate the marriage contract* <note>original: "tango goro o nago lagia," literally "lay hold on the face of the marriage"</note> by providing an answering gift.

When the matter is settled, the bridegroom’s friends prepare a feast, and the tail of the pig is given to the bride’s father. After the money is paid, the girl is taken as a wife without any ceremony. If a girl were engaged to an old man or someone she disliked, she might run away into the forest <note>original: "bush"</note> with the young man of her choice; in such cases, a pig given by his friends might resolve the matter. The payments for a wife are not very high in this island group, though they vary between the different islands. A girl betrothed as a child is often taken to her future home to be raised there, so she can get to know the people and, if she comes from another island, the local language. Engaged boys, girls, and young people in general are very shy about the arrangement and will hardly look at one another; however, as the time for marriage approaches, it is considered proper for the youth to give small presents and otherwise show her attention.

In the Northern New Hebrides, a girl betrothed in childhood is taken to her future father-in-law’s house and raised there. The boy often grows up thinking she is his sister and is very embarrassed <note>original: "ashamed," here referring to a sense of extreme modesty or social discomfort</note> when he learns the actual relationship between them. This, however, is not the common practice, as it is only the children of high-ranking people <note>original: "great people"</note> who are betrothed as infants. In Araga <note>now known as Pentecost Island in Vanuatu</note>, when a girl is old enough to be married, she is sometimes tattooed and always begins wearing her petticoat. A ceremony is held there when the wedding day arrives; people assemble in the center of the village, and the father of the bride or an influential friend makes a speech. The bridegroom sticks a branch of a <term>dracaena</term> <note>a genus of tropical shrubs often used in Melanesian rituals</note> into the ground and brings forward the pigs, food, and mats given for the bride. Then the speaker urges him to feed his wife properly and treat her kindly, and not to be moody with her. He then hands over the young woman, who is dressed in a new petticoat and wrapped in a new mat. A feast follows, and the bridegroom walks around his father-in-law or the speaker, stroking him to thank him. A sort of mock battle <note>original: "sham-fight"</note> takes place on the occasion, in which men are sometimes hurt; the two sides are the relatives of the bridegroom and those of the bride. # xiv. Betrothal

If her brothers <note>original: "brethren"</note> are offended, it is the groom’s responsibility to reconcile with them by giving a gift. Whether this can truly be called "capture" <note>referring to the anthropological concept of "bride-capture," where a woman is symbolically or literally taken from her family</note> is very doubtful; however, it certainly represents the feelings with which the bride’s relatives <note>original: "kinsmen"</note> view the loss of her labor. It cannot be the loss of any rights of social interaction, since she was socially off-limits <note>original: "unapproachable"</note> to all of them due to strict custom. The bride is taken by female friends to the house of the groom or his father—sometimes crying and being dragged along if she dislikes the match. An unwilling bride may refuse to sleep with her husband or run away to someone she likes better; in that case, if it seems her return is hopeless, a pig is given to her family as compensation and she stays with her new choice. 

Sometimes, the young couple is so shy with one another that they will not speak even after marriage, as it was considered improper to speak before the wedding. Friends and neighbors do not approve of this silence; for this reason, it is considered wise to ensure they are familiar with and like one another by bringing the engaged couple together as children. On Ambae <note>original: "Lepers’ Island"</note>, infant betrothals are the custom among high-ranking families <note>original: "people of consequence"</note>. When a girl is born to a chief, another chief will come to secure her for his son by giving a gift and holding a feast. 

If the boy is old enough at the time of the feast, he is made to take a young drinking coconut, place a dracaena leaf <note>a tropical plant often used in sacred or social rituals</note> in the opening <note>original: "eye"</note> of it, and give it to the infant’s mother for the child to drink. This ritual is called *huhu rahe goroe*, which means "to nurse her with a drinking coconut and secure her." <note>original: "huhu rahe goroe"</note> When the betrothed girl is about ten years old, the boy’s mother takes her to her own house to teach her household skills, and the children are raised together for a time. When she is growing older, her parents take her back to perform her tattooing, which consists of lines all over her body, though none on her face. Until this point, she has worn no clothing except on great occasions; now she is always clothed. In the house—

She wears only the *para* <note>a fringed band or skirt</note>, and when she is outdoors, she is wrapped in mats. During this period, the women from both families are very busy negotiating the bride price to be paid by the groom’s relatives, which varies significantly. If the young man is the son of a high-ranking leader <note>original: "great man"</note>, a tusked pig <note>Boars with circular tusks were, and in some areas still are, a primary form of currency and prestige in Vanuatu.</note> and a hundred mats are not considered too much; for common people, two or three ordinary pigs and fifty mats will suffice. These arrangements often take a long time because the women take great delight in the negotiations. While these talks continue, the young couple is encouraged to talk to one another and overcome their shyness. 

At last, the wedding day arrives. The young man’s friends take the pigs, mats, and uncooked food and place them in the center of the bride’s village. The bride’s friends have already prepared cooked food, and the two groups eat together; with this, the marriage is considered complete. The bride is carried on someone's back to her new home, wrapped in many mats and with palm-leaf fans held around her face, because she is expected to appear modest and shy. In the past, a house was always built in advance and food was prepared for the young couple, who ate together as a symbol of their union. Here, as in other places, a girl may run away to a man she loves. He may keep her if he can satisfy her family’s demands for compensation; however, sometimes he is afraid of the original groom’s friends, or he is too poor to pay off her family. In such cases, he is forced to refuse her, and she must return home—unless, indeed, she prefers to strangle or hang herself.

The social distance <note>original: "reserve"</note> maintained between those who have been brought together by marriage, and the practice of certain relatives avoiding one another, has already been mentioned. This custom is understood to begin as soon as the couple’s engagement is finalized. There is a unique example of this kind of social restriction on Florida Island <note>now known as the Nggela Islands in the Solomon Islands</note>, where there is otherwise no difficulty in meeting or using the names of people related by marriage. If a woman had a lover before her marriage, she will never mention his name after she is wed; instead, she calls him a *hanu* <note>original: "that person"</note>, and she will never meet him on a path. Her husband watches for this, and if he observes who the man is, he demands money from the former lover. Once that is paid, no further notice is taken of the matter; but

<header>xiv.] Adultery.</header>

If compensation <note>original: "satisfaction"</note> was refused, a quarrel would follow. A newlywed husband, without waiting for any evidence, would often beat his bride to force her to confess who her lover <note>original: "paramour"</note> had been.

The ancient customs of the people across all these islands were very strict regarding adultery. The punishment for the man was death, but this penalty was very generally reduced <note>original: "mitigated"</note> upon the payment of a fine. For instance, on Florida Island, a wronged husband would give money to the chief to have the adulterer killed; the accused man, if he was able, would pay compensation in money to both the chief and the husband to save his life. The woman, however, would likely be forced to become a <term>rembi</term> <note>a woman forced into prostitution for the community or a chief</note> for the profit of the chief. 

In Saa, an unfaithful wife is cast out, and the adulterer is punished with death, exile, or fines. In cases where adultery involves a chief’s family, the chief will have the adulterer killed, or, if he receives a large fine, will allow him to go live in Ulawa. A man’s friends will sometimes hide him for a while, hoping that the chief will eventually agree to accept a fine; if they find the chief to be unforgiving <note>original: "implacable"</note>, they will kill the man themselves or hand him over. 

When such a wrong occurs among common people, the friends of the husband and those of the adulterer will often fight over the amount of damages to be paid. Indeed, most of the warfare throughout all these island groups arises from this cause. A chief of Saa, Ulawa, Ugi, or San Cristoval who has ordered an adulterer's death constructs a <term>bea</term>—a stage or platform from which speeches are made—and rewards those who performed the killing. In Saa, the chief also performs a sacrifice called <term>tolo 'akalo</term> <note>see page 137; a ritual to clear away any spiritual danger or "ghostly" haunting that might affect the person responsible for a death</note> to protect himself from any danger that might follow him as the cause of the death. 

In the Banks Islands and northern New Hebrides, the treatment of adultery is very direct: the man is shot or clubbed by the husband or his friends in their first burst of anger, and the woman is beaten, scolded, and threatened with death. However, the matter is very generally settled by the payment of money and pigs. In former times, a wife who was jealous of her husband, or enraged by him in any way, would often commit suicide by throwing herself from a cliff or a tree, swimming out to sea, hanging or strangling herself, stabbing herself with an arrow, or thrusting one down her—

...throat; and a man who was jealous or quarreling with his wife would do the same. However, nowadays it is easy to run away with another person’s wife or husband on a labor vessel <term>labor vessel</term> <note>These ships were part of the "blackbirding" trade, transporting Pacific Islanders to work—often under coercive conditions—on plantations in Queensland, Australia, or Fiji.</note> to Queensland or Fiji.

Divorce is easy and common, and it can be said to occur at the will of either party, though it is naturally easier for a man to dismiss his wife than for a woman to leave her husband. The greatest obstacle is the property <note>original: "the property given for the wife," referring to the bride-price or marriage gift</note> given for the wife. A man does not wish to lose this investment, and he will try many times to bring back a runaway wife before he gives up on her, often giving presents to her relatives to encourage her return. If the separation is mutual and friendly <note>original: "amicable"</note>, the woman’s father will return what he received, with the intention of finding another son-in-law. After a woman has been married for some time, it is considered that she has "worked off" a good deal of the original payment made for her, and the exchange of a pig or two between the families settles all remaining claims. Generally speaking, husbands and wives get along well and are united by their great affection for their children.

The practice of the Levirate <term>Levirate</term> <note>The custom where a man is obligated or entitled to marry the widow of his deceased brother.</note> is followed as a matter of course. Because a wife is obtained for one member of a family through the contributions of the entire group, if that man dies, another family member is ready to take his place so that the family property is not lost. It is simply a matter of practical and economic arrangement whether a brother, cousin, or uncle of the deceased takes the widow. The brother is naturally the first choice; if a more distant relative takes the woman, he likely has to provide a pig to the family.

<margin><image-desc>Handwritten bracket and line marking the start of the following paragraph.</image-desc></margin>
On Lepers' Island <note>modern: Ambae, Vanuatu</note>, if a man who is a somewhat distant cousin of the deceased wishes to marry the widow, he adds a pig to the funeral feast held on the tenth or fiftieth day to indicate and support his claim. He also likely gives another pig to the widow’s sisters to gain their favor. If two men compete for the widow, she chooses one, and the successful suitor gives a pig to the man who was rejected. In essence, once the proper payment has been made for a woman, she belongs to the family that paid for her. Consequently, a man—as seen in the story of *Ganviviris*—might establish his nephew <note>original: "sister's son"</note> in life by handing over one of his own wives to him. This is not because the young man has a legal right to his uncle’s wives, but because the woman...

<header>xiv.] Polygamy. Polyandry.</header>

is already in the family. It is a rare thing for a woman to remain a widow for long, but there is a specific period and sign of mourning. In San Cristobal <note>original: "San Cristoval"; now known as Makira in the Solomon Islands.</note>, men and women wear large tassels of grey shells as earrings as a mark of widowhood. It is also very common to cut the hair short and daub the body with soot and ashes. In the Banks Islands, a widow or widower refrains from eating certain foods, such as yams, for a year or a shorter time, and wears a rope around the neck—a *ganaro* <term>ganaro</term> <note>A ritual mourning rope.</note>—as a sign of this restriction. To *val* or *naro* <term>val/naro</term> <note>Traditional terms for the act of ritual mourning or fasting.</note> in this way is a sign of mourning for any loss.

Polygamy is the rule, although a significant number of wives is found only among wealthy and older men. One wife is commonly enough for a man from Florida <note>Florida Island, also known as Nggela, in the Solomon Islands.</note>, who says that he can neither manage nor afford more than one. When a great leader like Takua had seven wives, it was considered a very high number. At Visale in Guadalcanal <note>original: "Guadalcanar"</note>, Tekaunga has, or had, sixty wives; in Florida, a wife costs a great deal, but in Guadalcanal, she costs very little. At Saa, ordinary men have two wives, while great men have eight or ten. In the Banks Islands, a well-to-do man ordinarily has two wives and may have three. A man from Vanua Lava was not long ago believed to have thirty. 

As a man advances in life and outlives his maternal uncles, his brothers, and his cousins, their widows tend to accumulate around him. These women are called his "wives"; they live in houses surrounding him and work for him, but he practically lives with only two or three younger women whom he has taken for himself. On Lepers' Island <note>Now known as Ambae or Aoba in Vanuatu.</note>, where men generally have two wives, a singular arrangement is approved of: a man who has a young wife takes an older woman—a widow—as a second wife to look after the first. Some men there have three or four wives; one great man recently had fifty wives, and his son and successor already has thirty. A chief further inland is credited with having a hundred. Polygamy in all these islands is a frequent cause of quarrels and bloodshed.

Anything properly called polyandry <term>polyandry</term> <note>A form of marriage in which a woman has two or more husbands at the same time.</note> is unknown, nor is it easy for the natives to conceive of it as a possible state of marriage. Still, cases are known in the Banks Islands where two...

## CHAPTER XV.

### DEATH. BURIAL. AFTER DEATH.

The belief that death is the separation of soul and body, and that the departed soul continues to exist with intelligence and some degree of activity, is a universal belief among Melanesians. However, they find it very difficult to explain exactly what it is that remains with the body during life and departs at death—what we call the "soul" in English. Like cultures far more academically advanced than themselves, they do not, in the first place, have a perfectly clear concept of what it is. Secondly, like all other people, they use words to represent these concepts that they admit are somewhat figurative and inexact when a precise meaning is sought. 

It is no surprise that, believing a "soul" exists in connection with the visible body, they imagine the soul as having a specific form and shape visible to the eyes once it is separated from the body. To Melanesians, thinking is essentially like seeing; anything they think about must have a specific form in order to be conceptualized. Therefore, a visible object that resembles the concept provides a convenient name for it. For example, if there are people who call the soul a "shadow," I do not believe for a moment that they think the shadow is literally the soul, or the soul a shadow. Instead, they use the word "shadow" figuratively to describe something belonging to a person that is like a shadow: definitely individual and inseparable from them, yet without physical substance. The word used in the Mota <note>Mota is one of the Banks Islands in Vanuatu; its language was used as a lingua franca by the Melanesian Mission.</note> language for "soul" means "shadow" in the Maori <note>The indigenous Polynesian people of New Zealand.</note> language, but

<summary>This chapter introduces Melanesian concepts of death and the soul, explaining how the people use figurative language, such as the concept of a "shadow," to describe the intangible nature of the spirit.</summary>

In fact, my belief is that in the original language this word did not definitely mean either soul or shadow, but had a meaning one can conceive but not express, which has come out in one language meaning shadow, and in the other meaning something like soul—that is, a 'second self'¹." So Mr. Fison <note>Lorimer Fison (1832–1907) was an Australian anthropologist and missionary who worked in Fiji.</note> writes: "The Fijian word for soul is *yalo*, and the word for shadow is *yaloyalo*. I have not been able to find any trace of the belief that shadow and soul are identical. I believe that Williams' <note>Thomas Williams, a missionary who wrote "Fiji and the Fijians" (1858).</note> remark about the 'two spirits' was the result of a confusion in his mind concerning *yalo* and *yaloyalo*." The Western observer is always ready to assume that the native takes a childish view and holds absurd beliefs. Yet, in reality, if the native were to put the observer through a close examination, the observer's own concepts would be found very indistinct and his expressions mainly figurative. Many a traveler, rather than a true observer, carries away as a sort of joke the story that the natives think their shadows are their souls, even though that traveler could not define exactly what he means by the word "soul" when he uses it himself. It may suffice to state that, whatever word the Melanesian people use for soul, they mean something essentially belonging to each person's nature which brings life to the body. It is the seat of thought and intelligence, exercising a power that is not of the physical body and is invisible in its action. A further understanding of their concepts will naturally follow from a study of the words they use.

It has been shown (on page 121) that among Melanesians there is a universal belief in the existence of personal, intelligent beings with power superior to that of men, who do not have bodies like those of mankind. These beings, whom we call **spirits** <term>spirit: in this context, a supernatural being that was never human</term>, are distinct from the disembodied spirits or souls of dead men, which we call **ghosts** <term>ghost: the soul of a deceased human being</term>. It is not surprising, therefore, that the same word used for "spirit" is also used to describe the soul of a man while it still inhabits and animates his body. The soul of a living—

<meta>This page continues the discussion of how Melanesian peoples conceptualize the soul, moving from the relationship between the soul and shadows to specific linguistic terms used in Florida (Solomon Islands) and the Banks' Islands (Vanuatu) to describe spirits, ghosts, and the animating force in living things.</meta>

<page-num>249</page-num>

# xv.] Souls.

A man in Florida <note>An island in the Solomon Islands, also known as Nggela.</note> is a *tarunga*, a spirit that is individual, not physical, and separable from the body, though in fact it is not often separated during his life. A spirit such as a *vigona* <note>A type of spirit often associated with natural phenomena or landmarks.</note> is also a *tarunga*, though the people are not very ready to acknowledge the existence of such a *tarunga*. During life, a man's *tarunga* leaves him in dreams and then returns; at death, the *tarunga* departs finally from the body. The corpse is simply a dead man, *tinoni mate*; the separated soul is no longer a *tarunga* (a spirit), but a *tindalo* (a ghost). However, *tarunga* is not exactly equivalent to "soul," any more than "spirit" is equivalent to "soul"; a soul is a *tarunga*, and no other name is given to it.

Pigs also have a *tarunga*. When a man sells a pig, he takes back its *tarunga* in a *dracaena* leaf <note>original: *dracæna*; a genus of tropical shrubs used in many Melanesian rituals.</note>, which he hangs up in his house. In this way, he does not lose more than the physical existence of the pig; the *tarunga* remains, waiting to animate some pig that will be born later. A pig is an animal of distinction and has a *tarunga*; yams and similar things have none, as they do not live with any kind of intelligence. Is it then to be said that a man and a pig are alike regarding the *tarunga*, and that each has a soul? A native person to whom this question is put clearly will laugh; such a thing cannot be. When a man dies, his *tarunga* becomes a *tindalo* (a ghost), and who has ever heard of a pig *tindalo*?¹

In the Banks' Islands, the spirit that never was a man, but was always superhuman in intelligence and power—and, as far as could be conceived of a personal being, was without a physical body—was called a *vui* (page 124). It would not be surprising, therefore, if the word *vui* were used to describe the soul; it is impossible to say that it would be used incorrectly, for the nature of a *vui* and of a soul is the same (page 124).² The words accepted in common use to represent the English word "soul" are *talegi* in Motlav and *atui* in Mota. A man's *talegi* leaves him in sleep—not in all dreams, but in those that leave a vivid impression of scenes and persons visited when the man awakes.

# Death. Burial. After Death. [CH.

When a man fainted, the *talegi* <note>A term in the Banks Islands for the animating spirit or soul-substance of a living person.</note> had gone out, but life remained. Life depends on the presence of the *talegi* in the body, and health depends upon its healthy condition. A ghost <note>original: "ghost"; here referring to the spirit of a deceased person.</note> can damage the *talegi*, either on its own or moved by magic charms, and then the man falls sick and his body is weak. Alternatively, the ghost takes the *talegi* away, and the man lies barely breathing; however, it would not be said that all disease is the result of the *talegi* being taken or damaged; it would not be said of ulcers, for example. The *talegi* has no physical form, but it is like a reflection or a shadow.

The Mota <note>An island in the Banks Islands of Vanuatu.</note> word *atai* is no doubt related to the Maori word *ata*, which means a shadow; however, *atai* never means "shadow" in Mota, nor is *niniai*—which means both shadow and reflection—ever used for the "soul." At the same time, it was thought that damage could be done to the body by means of the shadow or reflection. This occurred, for instance, when a shadow fell upon a certain stone (pages 182 and 184), or when a man's face was reflected in a certain spring of water (page 186). The power of the spirit, or *vui* <note>A non-human supernatural spirit.</note>, belonging to the stone or the spring could seize the man through his shadow or reflection, just as the power of a ghost could get a hold on a man through a fragment of his leftover food. In a way, the shadow was considered another version of the person. But it was never thought that the shadow *was* the soul.

Similarly, in Saa <note>A region on South Malaita in the Solomon Islands.</note>, they talk of a ghost snatching away the "shadow" of a child who startles in their sleep, and a doctor <note>In this context, a traditional healer or spirit-medium.</note> undertakes to bring it back. But, says Joseph Wate <note>A native of Saa and an important informant for the author.</note>, who tells the story, "They say shadow, but they mean something else, for the shadow of the child is seen the whole time."

The use of the word *atai* in Mota seems properly and originally to have signified something uniquely and intimately connected with a person and sacred to them—something that the person has taken a fancy to after seeing it in what seemed to be a wonderful manner, or something that someone else has shown to them as such. Whatever the thing might be, the man believed it to be the reflection of his own personality: he and his *atai* flourished, suffered, lived, and died together. But the word must not be supposed to have been borrowed from this use and applied secondarily to describe the soul; the word carries a sense with it which is applicable alike to that...

...second self, the visible object so mysteriously connected with the man, and to this invisible second self which we call the soul. There is another Mota <note>An island in the Banks Islands of Vanuatu.</note> word, *tamaniu*, which has almost, if not quite, the same meaning as *atai* <note>As discussed on the previous page, a term for a "second self" or soul-double.</note> when it describes something living or non-living that a man has come to believe has an existence intimately connected with his own. 

The word *tamaniu* may be understood to mean "likeness"; it is the noun form of the adverb *tama*, meaning "as" or "like." Not everyone in Mota had a *tamaniu*. Only some men imagined that they had this relationship with a lizard, a snake, or perhaps a stone. Sometimes the object was sought and found by drinking an infusion <note>original: "infusion"; a liquid made by steeping leaves, similar to a tea.</note> of certain leaves and piling up the dregs; whatever living thing was first seen in or on the heap was the *tamaniu*. It was watched but not fed or worshipped. The natives believed that it would come when called and that the life of the man was bound up with the life of his *tamaniu* (if it was a living thing) or with its safety. Should the *tamaniu* die—or, if it was not a living thing, should it be broken or lost—the man would die. Consequently, in cases of sickness, they would send someone to see if the *tamaniu* was safe and well. 

This word has apparently never been used for the "soul" in Mota, but on Aurora in the New Hebrides, it is the accepted equivalent. It is well worth observing that both the *atai* and the *tamaniu*—and it may be added the Motlav *talegi*—are things that have a substantial existence of their own, such as when a snake or stone is a man's *atai* or *tamaniu*. Therefore, when a soul is called by these names, it is conceived of as being substantial in some way. 

<note>An ink mark or artifact in the original text precedes the next sentence.</note> There is another word used in Mota that is never applied to the soul of a man, but it is very illustrative of native concepts. This word, *nunnuai*, is also common to Aurora, where it is used in a remarkable way. In Mota, a *nunnuai* is a lasting or recurring impression on the senses. For example, a man who has heard a startling scream during the day has it ringing in his ears; the scream is over and the sound is gone, but the *nunnuai* remains. A man fishing for flying-fish might paddle all day alone in his canoe with a long, light line fastened around his neck; he lies down tired at night and feels the line pulling as if a fish [is caught]...

To the native, it is not a mere trick of the imagination; it is real, though it has no physical form or substance. A pig, therefore, as well as ornaments or food, has a *nunuai*. However, a pig does not have an <term>atai</term> <note>A "shadow-soul" or spiritual double, as discussed on the previous page.</note>, or at least they might only hesitantly and carelessly say that it has one.

This word is undoubtedly the same as <term>niniai</term>, which means shadow or reflection. It does not mean "shade" in the general sense (which is <term>malumalu</term>), but refers specifically to the distinct figure cast by the blocking of light on the ground, or the image formed by reflection in water. There is no confusion in the native mind between a shadow and a reflection, but they use the same word to describe that specific, individual "something" which is itself insubstantial but so closely connected with the physical substance that gives it form.

<insert>Note: A pen mark bracket appears in the left margin next to the word "substance".</insert> This word, in the form <term>nunu</term>, is used on Aurora <note>The colonial name for the island of Maewo in Vanuatu.</note> to describe the imagined relationship of an infant to some thing or person from which its origin is somehow derived. Before her child is born, a woman might imagine that a coconut, a breadfruit, or some similar object has an original connection with her infant. When the child is born, it is considered the *nunu* of that coconut or whatever the object may be. As the child grows up, he must never eat that specific thing, or he will become ill. No one thinks there is a literal biological connection in terms of parentage; rather, the child is viewed as a kind of echo of that object.

There is another way in which a child is considered the *nunu* of a deceased person. For example, a man named Arudulewari is the *nunu* of a boy whom his mother raised and loved dearly. This boy died shortly before Arudulewari was born; the mother believed that her foster child wished to return to her, and that the new infant was his *nunu*. However, Arudulewari is not considered to be that same person, nor does he believe his soul is the soul of the dead boy. He himself is simply the *nunu*—the "echo" or "reflection"—of him. 

Similarly, a man named Vilemalas (a name which means "Bring the day after") was born after an adopted child of his mother’s had been killed and the body was not brought back until the following day; he is considered the *nunu* of the slain person, having come in his place. on the island of Mota, there is no such use of the word *nunuai*, but there is a notion that a man may have something—not exactly his *atai* or *tamaniu*—with which he is originally connected. It will become clear that there is significant agreement in both customs and beliefs, and universal consensus on certain details—such as the belief that the separated soul continues to exist, and the practice of honoring the dead with feasts where portions of food are offered to them. 

In the Solomon Islands, the ghost is the primary object of worship and therefore occupies a much higher place in the religious life of the people than it does on the islands to the east. For this reason, before discussing details, it is helpful to distinguish between the two classes of ghosts generally recognized in the Solomons. This distinction is between "ghosts of power" and "ghosts of no account"—between those whose help is sought and whose anger is feared <note>original: "deprecated"</note>, and those from whom nothing is expected and to whom no rituals are owed. When a distinguished man dies, his ghost retains the powers that belonged to him in life, but with even greater activity and stronger force. His ghost is therefore considered powerful and worthy of worship; as long as he is remembered, his aid is sought and worship is offered to him. He is called a <term>tindalo</term> in Florida or a <term>lio'a</term> in Saa. 

In every society, the majority of the population is composed of insignificant people—"a mere number, born only to consume the fruits of the earth" <note>original Latin: *numerus fruges consumere nati*</note>—who are of no particular account regarding bravery, skill, or prosperity. The ghosts of such people remain just as insignificant after death as they were before. They are considered ghosts because all people have souls, and the souls of the dead become ghosts. They are dreaded because all ghosts are awe-inspiring, but they receive no worship and are soon thought of only as the nameless crowd inhabiting the underworld.

In the Solomon Islands, specifically in Florida, when a person dies, their spirit (<term>tarunga</term>) becomes a ghost (<term>tindalo</term>), and the body is referred to as a "dead man" (<term>tinoni mate</term>). Some ghosts are worshipped and exert significant spiritual influence on the world as *tindalo* (as discussed in chapters 7 and 8); others are immediately forgotten by everyone except their immediate family. 

The corpse is usually buried. Commoners are buried in their own garden plots, while chiefs are sometimes buried within the village, and a chief's child may even be buried inside the house. The grave is not deep. It is treated as sacred in the sense that no one will step on any grave; however, the burial place of a man whose ghost has become an object of worship is a true sanctuary, called a <term>vunuha</term>. The skull is often exhumed <note>original: "dug up"</note> and hung inside the house. 

Men and women are buried in the same way, with their feet pointing inland. When returning from a funeral, the mourners take a different path than the one used to carry the corpse, to prevent the ghost from following them back. A man is buried with his money, porpoise teeth, and personal ornaments, with his bracelets placed on him upside down. These valuables are often secretly dug up again later. ### Florida. Burial Customs.
<sig>XV.]</sig>

They paddle out with the body, tie stones to his feet, and sink him. In Savo, nearby, common men are generally thrown into the sea, and only great men are buried in the ground. In Florida, the funeral of a chief, or of someone who is highly esteemed, is delayed for two days after death. After the funeral, the relatives and friends assemble to <term>kilo dato na tinoni mate</term>, which is to say, to partake in a funeral feast. They also hang the dead man’s cloth, his axes, spears, shield, and other possessions on his house, heaping yams and other food upon the ground. At the feast, a bit of the food is thrown into the fire for the deceased, with the call, "This is for you." As the mourners eat, they are anxious about swallowing the food properly; if a morsel sticks in anyone's throat, it is a <term>butuli</term>, an omen that the person will soon die. 

When they hang the dead man’s weapons on his house, they perform great lamentations. Everything remains untouched afterward, and the house is left to fall into ruin. As time goes on, it becomes covered with the vines of growing yams—a picturesque and perhaps even touching sight. These things are not set up so that they might spiritually accompany their former owner; rather, they are placed there as a memorial for him as a great and valued man, much like the <note>original: "hatchment" — a large, diamond-shaped board displaying the coat of arms of a deceased person, common in English funerals of the 17th-19th centuries.</note> hatchments of old times. 

With the same feeling of respect and affection, they cut down a dead man’s fruit trees. This is not done with any notion that these things will serve him in the world of ghosts; instead, they say that he ate of them when he was alive, he will never eat again, and therefore no one else should have them. 

There is a certain belief that burial is a benefit to the ghost. If a man is killed and his body is not buried, his ghost will haunt the place. When a man’s head has been taken and his skull added to a chief’s collection, the ghost haunts the area, at least for a time. This also happens when the arms and legs of men murdered or executed for crimes are sent to distant places to show what has been done. The ghosts of men whose heads have been taken are seen appearing without their heads. The abode of the departed is <term>Betindalo</term> <note>The spirit-world or "place of the tindalo."</note>; yet, ghosts do not only haunt their burial places and return for the sacrifices offered to them, but they are also heard playing at night, blowing on panpipes...

They are feared because all ghosts inspire awe, but they receive no worship and are soon remembered only as part of the nameless crowd in the underworld.

Men and women are buried in the same manner, with their feet turned inland. # XV. Florida Burial Customs

They paddle out with him, tie stones to his feet, and sink him. In Savo, nearby, common people are usually thrown into the sea, and only great men are buried in the ground. In Florida, the funeral of a chief, or of someone who is highly respected, is delayed for two days after death. After the funeral, the relatives and friends assemble to <term>*kilo duto na tinoni mate*</term> <note>literally: "to eat with the dead person"</note>; that is to say, to partake in a funeral feast and to hang the dead man’s clothing, axes, spears, shield, and other property on his house, while heaping yams and other food upon the ground. At the feast, a bit of the food is thrown into the fire for the deceased, with the call:

> "This is for you."

As the mourners eat, they are anxious about swallowing the food properly; if a morsel sticks in anyone’s throat, it is a <term>*butuli*</term> <note>a portent or bad omen</note>, signaling that the person will die. When they hang the dead man’s weapons on his house, they perform great lamentations. Everything is left untouched afterward, and the house is allowed to fall into ruin, becoming covered over time with the vines of growing yams. This is a picturesque and even touching sight. These items are not set up so that they might accompany their former owner as spirits; rather, they are placed there as a memorial to him as a great and valued man, similar to the <term>hatchment</term> <note>a display of a deceased person's coat of arms, common in historical European funerals</note> of former times.

With the same feeling of respect and affection, they cut down a dead man’s fruit trees. This is not done with any idea that these things will serve him in the world of ghosts; instead, they say that he ate from them when he was alive, and since he will never eat again, no one else should have them.

There is a belief that burial is a benefit to the ghost. If a man is killed anywhere and his body is not buried, his ghost will haunt the place. When a man’s head has been taken and his skull added to a chief’s collection, the ghost haunts the area, at least for a time. This is also the case when the arms and legs of men murdered or executed for crimes are sent to distant places to show what has been done. The ghosts of men whose heads have been taken are seen appearing without their heads. The home of the departed is <term>*Betindalo*</term> <note>the spirit world or underworld</note>; yet ghosts do not only haunt their burial places and attend the sacrifices offered to them, but they are also heard playing at night, blowing on panpipes.

Betindalo <note>Literally "the place of the spirits."</note> is apparently situated in the southeastern part of the great island of Guadalcanal <note>original: "Guadalcanar"</note>, to which the ghosts pass over through Gaeta, the district of Florida <note>Now known as the Nggela Islands.</note> nearest to it. Here, a "ship of the dead" appears—a concept that is almost unique in Melanesia. 

The people of Gaeta used to believe that all the ghosts of Florida traveled along a path through their gardens, leading to a point of land where they assembled. As they passed along, nothing was seen, but a twittering sound was heard; while they were waiting at the point, the sound of their dancing could be heard at night. From time to time, a canoe would come over from Guadalcanal and take the ghosts across to Galaga, which is opposite Gaeta. 

They landed first upon a rock near the shore, and there, for the first time, they became aware that they were dead. Once they arrived on the shore, they met a certain <term>tindalo</term> <note>A ghost or deceased spirit.</note> carrying a rod, which he would thrust into the cartilage of their noses to see if they were pierced. If the nose was pierced, there was a good path the ghosts could follow down toward Marau at the far end of Guadalcanal. However, ghosts who could not pass this test were not allowed to follow the path; instead, they had to find their way as best they could, with great pain and difficulty. 

Living men in canoes, when nearing the shore at Galaga, have claimed to see the forms of the dead and recognized specific people, but the figures disappeared as they approached. A man who was alive in Gaeta not long ago once appeared to die but revived to tell the story of how he had passed with others along the path of ghosts. He had gone to take his place in the canoe that came for them at night, but a tall, black <term>tindalo</term> whom he recognized forbade him from coming aboard and sent him back into the world of the living.

In Bugotu, on the island of Isabel <note>original: "Ysabel"</note>, the spirit—called the <term>tarunga</term>—leaves the dead man (<term>tinoni dhehe</term>) and becomes a ghost, or <term>tindadho</term>. The place of ghosts is the small island of Laulau, though they haunt their graves and are seen at night, disappearing when approached. As the ghosts fly through the air toward Laulau, they land first on certain rocks where they become aware of their sad condition. Living men visit the island, as told in the story of Samuku, and see these rocks; they also see forms that look like men...

Those who do not have the mark are thrown from the tree into the gulf beneath and perish even out of their ghostly life.

When a chief dies, they bury him so that his head is near the surface, and they keep a fire burning over it. This allows them to later take up the skull to preserve it in the house of the man who succeeds him in power. An expedition then sets out to procure heads in honor of the deceased, who has now become a *tindadho* to be worshipped. Anyone not belonging to the place will be killed for the sake of his head. The heads collected are arranged upon the beach and are believed to add <term>mana</term> <note>Spiritual power, influence, or efficacy.</note> to the new *tindadho*. Until these heads are obtained, the local people do not move about freely. The grave is built up with stones, and sacrifices are offered upon it¹.

Upon first arriving there, the ghost still feels like a man and does not realize his condition; he finds friends and gives them news of the place he has just left. They are inactive; they wander aimlessly and stay in caves. Men landing on the islands due to stormy weather see them on the beach; but they fear living men and disappear when approached closely. It must be understood that these *'ataro* <term>ataro</term> <note>original: "ataro"; a ghost or spirit.</note> who stay in Rondomana are merely the ghosts of common men who possessed no <term>mana</term> <note>original: "mana"; spiritual power, influence, or efficacy.</note> while they lived. However, there are also *'ataro* who are active and powerful—feared, invoked, and offered sacrifices—who remain fully active in the places where they lived as men. Here, as in other places, a man’s ghost possesses the power the man had during his lifetime in greater force, which he originally received through communication with the ghosts who preceded him. Those who have died recently have the most power, or at least are the most active sources of it.

The ghost of a great man who has recently died is the most respected; as the dead are forgotten, their ghosts are replaced by later successors to this unseen power. The bodies of common people are cast into the sea, but men of importance are buried, and some relic of them—such as a skull, tooth, or finger bone—is retrieved and preserved in a shrine in the village. 

Therefore, there are land ghosts and sea ghosts. The former are seen around the villages and heard speaking as they haunt their graves and relics; they look like men who have recently died, and their voices are hollow whispers. Their help can be obtained by those who know them, and they are believed to fight among themselves using ghostly weapons. 

The ghosts that haunt the sea hold a great place in the imagination of the natives of the southeastern Solomon Islands. Because these people love to illustrate their lives through sculpture and painting, they clearly show us how they imagine these ghosts to be. <meta>This page continues the exploration of death and the afterlife, specifically focusing on the different types of ghosts and their journey to the spirit world in Malaita and neighboring islands.</meta>

<page-num>260</page-num>
<header>Death. Burial. After Death. [CH.</header>

At Saa and in the neighboring parts of Malanta <note>modern-day Malaita in the Solomon Islands</note>, the same word is used for the soul of a living person and the ghost of an ordinary person: *'akalo*. This is another form of the word *'ataro* used in San Cristoval. The *'akalo*, which leaves the body in dreams and returns again, departs finally at death. After a natural death, the body is called *ra'e*; after a violent death, it is called *lalamoa*.

The ghosts of ordinary people are *'akalo* and nothing more. However, the ghosts of chiefs, brave warriors, men of remarkable success in life, or men who are *saka* <term>saka</term> <note>possessing spiritual or supernatural power</note> are expected to become *lio'a*. These are ghosts who also possess spiritual power and are worshipped accordingly. For example, when the ghost of a warrior is proven by evidence to be active, he becomes a *lio'a ni ma'e*, a ghost powerful for death. 

The origin of death is attributed—just as it is in the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>—to an old woman who, having changed her skin, later put her old discarded skin back on after it had become caught on a reed. 

Upon leaving the body, all ghosts first swim to a point of land at Saa, then to a point on Ulawa, then to the Three Sisters (*'Olu Malau*), then to a point on San Cristoval near Hada, and finally to Marapa, two islands located off Marau in Guadalcanal. While the body is rotting, the ghost is weak; when the smell of decay has ceased, the ghost becomes strong—it is no longer a man. 

The ghostly inhabitants of Marapa live a life somewhat like that of the physical world. However, the children chatter and annoy the older ghosts, so they are placed separately on the second island. Men and women ghosts live together; they have houses, gardens, and canoes, yet everything is unsubstantial. Living men who cross to Marapa see nothing, but there is water there in which laughter and cries are heard. There are places where the water is seen to have been disturbed, and the banks are wet as if bathers had just been there. A dead chief builds his canoe and his house there, modeled after those his living son is building, but they are built of the soft, edible hibiscus and come to nothing; it is like the play of children. 

This ghostly life is not eternal. The ordinary *'akalo* soon turn into white ants' nests, which then become the food of the ghosts who are still vigorous. Because of this, a living man might say to his idle son, "When I die, I shall have ants' nests to eat, but then what will you have?" The <meta>catchword: The</meta>

<page-num>261</page-num>
<header>xv.] Saa. Hades. Burial.</header>

*Li'o'a* <note>ghosts of high-ranking or powerful people</note> ghosts of power last longer because they are *saka* <term>saka</term> <note>possessing spiritual or supernatural power</note>, and the more *saka* they are, the longer they last. They are remembered and worshipped on earth, and as long as this continues, their strength remains. However, when men forget them and turn to worship those more recently deceased, and when no sacrificial food is offered to them, their power fades away. Eventually, they turn into white ants' nests <note>This represents the final stage of a ghost's existence when it is completely forgotten and loses all personality</note> like the others. 

There are two rulers of *Marapa* <note>the island of the dead</note> who are called *li'o*, though not strictly so, because they were never human and never pass away: the chief *Kari'eu*, and his subordinate, *Kikiriba'u*, "the cutter-off of heads." These two travel about in their canoes—one collecting ghosts, the other collecting heads. In times of sickness at Saa, if tree trunks are seen floating by at sea, they are said to be the canoes of *Kari'eu* and *Kikiriba'u*. 

The ghosts whose home is in *Marapa* can return to Saa to visit their village and their friends again. They are seen like shadows, having a certain fleeting and indistinct form; some are hideous, while others are not unpleasant. If a person who sees a ghost is not frightened, he can discern the features and know who it is; but if he is frightened, he sees only a "dreadful something." A man who wishes to see a ghost for some reason puts lime from his betel-box <note>a container for the ingredients used in chewing betel nut</note> upon his forehead, and then he sees them plainly.

The burial of common people at Saa is a simple affair; an ordinary man is buried the day after death, while a very low-ranking person is buried immediately. There is a common burial place which does not get filled up because the bones are periodically taken up after the flesh has decayed and are heaped to one side. 

Men of some rank and importance are not buried for two days. Women sit around the corpse and wail, *io pe'i rae* <note>literally: "wailing for the corpse"</note>, and people assemble to see the dead man for the last time and to eat the funeral feast. If a very great man dies, or a child who was much beloved by his father, the body is hung up in the father's house, either in a canoe or enclosed in the wooden figure of a sword-fish (*ili*). Very favorite children are treated in the same way. The figure of the sword-fish is sealed with resin like a canoe and painted; no smell at all comes from it. If the body is put into a canoe, they make fine shavings or chippings from a certain tree...

...to spread under and above the body, and they lay certain large leaves over that, with planks on top of everything. The canoe is not sealed with cement, yet there is very little smell. Sometimes the corpse is kept this way for years, either in the house or in the *oha*—the public canoe house—while waiting for a major funeral feast¹. When a year with a good harvest arrives, a man will say, "Now we will take Father out." At that time, if the deceased was an ordinary person, the corpse is taken to the common burial ground; if he was a chief, he is taken to the family burial place, where sacrifices are made as previously described (page 137). 

The skull and jawbone are removed, and these relics are called *mangite* <term>mangite</term> <note>relics, specifically the skull and jawbone of a deceased person</note>. These are *saka* <term>saka</term> <note>possessing spiritual or supernatural power</note>, meaning they are "hot" with spiritual power. Through these relics, the help of the *lio'a* <term>lio'a</term> <note>the powerful ghost of a high-ranking or influential man</note>—the ghost of the man to whom these remains belonged—can be obtained. The *mangite* is placed inside a hollow wooden carving of a bonito fish <note>a type of tuna that holds great symbolic and religious importance in Solomon Islands culture</note> and displayed in the house or the *oha*. It remains there until the *lio'a* is no longer remembered or loses its reputation for power. In the *oha* on the beach at Saa, the people recently made a boat-shaped container and placed all the old *mangite* of forgotten *lio'a* inside it. 

Sometimes a man will preserve his wife's body in this same manner. When she is finally taken to the burial place, her jawbone will be kept in a basket, or one of her teeth will be placed in a piece of bamboo and hung in the house as a memorial. This serves as nothing more than a keepsake, for a woman’s ghost can never be a *lio'a* (a ghost of power); she is merely an *akalo* <term>akalo</term> <note>a departed soul or ordinary ghost without spiritual influence</note>. Men will offer food as a sign of affection and remembrance to these *mangite*, as well as to the carvings and canoes containing the corpses.

Burial on land, however, is not the only practice at Saa. It often happens that the body of a chief or a person of lesser rank is cast into the sea—a practice called *kulu rae* <term>kulu rae</term> <note>burial at sea</note>—either at the request of the deceased or to save trouble. Friends tie a bag of sand to the feet of the corpse, paddle out, and sink the body in a specific area where there are underwater caves; the body never rises to the surface. When this is done, a *mangite* is still preserved in the form of hair or nails, which are tied in a bundle and hung up. Sometimes, though rarely,

<header>xv.] Saa. Burial. Santa Cruz.</header>

Sometimes a corpse is cremated <note>original: "burnt"</note> at the wish of the deceased ¹. When this is done, they preserve a *mangite* <term>mangite</term> <note>relics, specifically the skull and jawbone of a deceased person</note> by wrapping the head or enclosing it in a hollowed banana stem to protect it from the fire. The place where a corpse is cremated is considered sacred. Other corpses, again, are laid in a canoe or on a platform beside a place of sacrifice; holes are made in the bottom of the canoe, and bamboo pipes are set to carry away rain-water and the fluids <note>original: "liquor"</note> of the decomposing corpse into the ground. At one time at Saa, they did what they currently do in Bauro: they poured water on the corpse until the flesh was consumed, and then took the skull as a *mangite*. In these methods of disposing of the distinguished dead—whose ghosts are expected to be *lio'a* <term>lio'a</term> <note>the powerful ghost of a high-ranking or influential man</note> possessed of power—one can very probably see the effect of the belief mentioned previously: that the ghost remains weak as long as the corpse continues to smell. The *lio'a* of the dead man, whether sunk in the sea, cremated, enclosed in a case, or rapidly stripped of flesh, becomes active and available at once.

The ornaments of a dead man are buried with him or are kept in remembrance of him. A man’s coconut and breadfruit trees, and others, are cut down by his friends after his death out of respect to him, as they say; they deny that they think such things follow a man in any ghostly form, since it seems ridiculous to them to suppose that even pigs can have a soul, or *akalo* <term>akalo</term> <note>a soul or ghost</note>. To cut trees down in this way is to *ngoli* <term>ngoli</term> <note>the practice of cutting down a deceased person's trees out of respect</note>. For a dead chief, they *ngoli-ta'a* <term>ngoli-ta'a</term> <note>the practice of fencing a plot of ground as a memorial for a dead chief</note>: they fence around a certain plot of ground and place his canoe in it in his memory, along with his bowl and weapons. His friends add their own items in his honor and decorate the fence with leaves and flowers. For a man of no great social position, they content themselves with throwing yams and other food upon the roof of the dead man's house in his memory.

At Santa Cruz, the corpse is buried in a very deep grave inside the house, wrapped in many mats. For two days, they mourn <note>original: "cry over"</note> a man and then bury him; on the fifth day after the funeral...
