<meta>This page continues the discussion of burial customs and beliefs about the afterlife in the Solomon Islands and the Santa Cruz Islands, shifting from the preservation of relics to the destinations of the soul.</meta>

<page-num>264</page-num>
<header>Death. Burial. After Death. [CH. XV</header>

A funeral meal is eaten, and the ceremony is over. Inland, people dig up the bones again to make arrowheads and take the skull to keep in a chest in the house. They say that the skull is the man himself, and they set food before it. The departed souls are called *duka* <term>duka</term> <note>ghosts or spirits of the deceased in the Santa Cruz Islands</note>; they gather after death at a place called Natepapa, and from there they go on to the great volcano Tamami (called Tinakula). In this volcano, they are consumed by fire and renewed, and there they remain. Nevertheless, these spirits haunt the forests of Santa Cruz and are seen at night, especially when it is wet and dark. Men see them appearing like fire, with a glow under their armpits like fireflies, and they are very afraid of them.

In all these examples, the home of the dead has been shown to be on the surface of the earth, located on islands that are more or less distant from those where the living dwell, and which are all known and visited by living men. It is probable, however, that a certain belief in an underworld is also present, such as the *Turivatu* <term>Turivatu</term> mentioned in the Florida Islands sacrificial prayers (page 131). This is a region beneath the earth that corresponds to that country above the sky where the legendary figures Kamakajaku or Vulaninggela were said to have visited the sun. The belief in Santa Cruz that ghosts pass into the great volcano implies a descent below the surface, as does the similar belief on Savo Island that the volcanic crater there is the dwelling place of departed spirits. 

However, when we move eastward, the ghosts no longer have their homes upon the surface of the earth, but rather underground. From the Torres Islands to Pentecost in the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>, the name of the underworld is *Panoi* <term>Panoi</term> (with local variations of the name). All the openings into the earth—whether they are volcanic vents or mysterious pits—throughout all these neighboring islands lead down to it. In all these places, the ghosts assemble at certain locations and go down to what is their proper place, although they can return again to the earth. The exact location of Panoi is unknown, except that it is underground. Panoi is a single realm, not a separate place for the ghosts of each individual island. Interestingly, the people of the Torres Islands and those of Pentecost are unaware that they share this common belief and use the same word for it.

<page-num>265</page-num>
# XV. Origin of Death

...the Mota terms *atai* <term>atai</term> <note>a soul or essence of a person</note> and *nete* <term>nete</term> <note>another term for the soul or spirit</note>. The departed soul descends to Panoi <note>the underworld or land of the dead</note> near a rock called Vat Tugua, not far from the island of Lo. At this site, a very ancient casuarina tree <note>also known as an ironwood tree</note> growing at the high-water mark overhangs the sea, remaining unmoved even through the heaviest storms and highest tides. In these islands, the tradition was to place the bodies of the dead on wooden platforms near the houses to decay naturally; however, they have now begun to adopt the practice of burial.

The story of the Origin of Death, which was mentioned in the account of Saa (page 260), has similar versions in the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides. Originally, humans never died; instead, as they grew older, they would shed their skins like snakes or crabs and emerge with their youth restored. After some time, a woman who was growing old went to a stream to change her skin. According to some traditions, she was the mother of the legendary figure Qat; according to others, she was *Ul-ta-marama* <note>original: "Change-skin of the world"</note>. 

She cast off her old skin into the water and noticed that as it floated downstream, it became snagged on a stick. She then returned home, where she had left her child. However, the child refused to recognize her, crying that its mother was an old woman and not this young stranger. To comfort the child, the mother went back for her discarded skin and put it back on. From that moment on, humanity stopped shedding their skins and began to die. 

In another story from the Banks Islands, this woman is identified as *Iro Puget* <note>original: "Bird's-nest Fern"</note>, the wife of *Mate* <term>Mate</term> <note>the personification of Death</note>. There are many other such stories. In one version, the reason Death was introduced was the practical problem caused by the permanence of property; wealth remained in the same hands forever while men simply renewed their youth and lived eternally. Therefore, Qat sent for Death, who lived in Panoi (or near a volcanic vent in Santa Maria), and assured him that he could travel to Vanua Lava without being harmed. Death thus came forth. The people laid him on a board, killed a pig, and covered him over; then they proceeded to divide his property among themselves.

The meaning is that Ro Puget will be encountered at the entrance to Panoi, and she will treat anyone who has not followed the custom of ear-piercing in this manner. This belief is similar to those observed in Florida and Bugotu.

# XV. Death, Burial, and the Afterlife

...and eat the funeral feast. On the fifth day, when the conch shell was blown to drive away the ghost, Qat opened the covering over Mate <note>original: "Mate," the personification of Death</note> and found him gone; nothing but bones remained. 

In the meanwhile, Tangaro the Fool had been set to watch the way to Panoi <note>the underworld</note>, where the paths to the lower and upper worlds divided, to prevent Death from going below. However, the fool sat in front of the way to the world above and let Death go down to Panoi; all humans have since followed Death along that path. 

Another story makes the same fool—under his name of Tagilingelinge—the cause of death. When Iro Puget set him to guard the way to Panoi in anticipation of her own death, he pointed out that way to her descending ghost instead of the way back to the world. Because of this, she and all people after her died and never came back to life. 

In Lakona, part of Santa Maria, the story goes that Marawa stole a woman whom Qat had made (page 157). In the night, while Marawa and the woman were sleeping, Qat came quietly, pulled out their teeth, and shaved their heads. Then he took the hairy fibers <note>original: "plexus"</note> of the tree-fern and put it on their heads, giving them the names of baldness and of the "second hair," as gray hair has been called ever since. Then he spread spider’s webs over their eyes so that when they woke in the morning, their vision was dimmed. The woman refused to go back to Qat; so, in a song, he called for baldness, blindness, toothlessness, old age, and death, because she had disobeyed his word.

<margin>┌</margin> The soul—called *atai* <term>atai</term> <note>the "shadow" or soul-essence</note> or *talegi* <term>talegi</term>—leaves the body in some dreams. If for some reason it does not come back, the person is found dead in the morning. When a person faints, a state called *mate mule* <note>original: "mate mule," meaning "to die and return"</note>, the soul really starts on the way to Panoi but is sent back. The other ghosts hustle him away from the mouth of the descent, or his father or friend turns him back, telling him that his time has not yet come; this is what the person relates when he recovers. In true death, the separation of soul and body is complete. The *atai* or *talegi* becomes a *tamate* <term>tamate</term> or *natmat* <term>natmat</term>—a dead man or ghost—and the corpse is also referred to by the same word. The ghost, however, does not at first go far and may possibly be recalled; the neighbors, therefore, bite the finger of the deceased...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of death rituals in the Banks' Islands, moving from the myths of how death began to the practical customs performed at the moment of death and the various methods of disposing of the body.</meta>

<page-num>267</page-num>
### xv.] *Banks' Islands. Death. Burial.* 267

When someone is dying, people may try to rouse them by shouting their name into their ear, hoping the soul may hear it and return. Sometimes, it is even believed that the soul can be caught. A woman at Mota some years ago, knowing that a neighbor was at the point of death, heard something rustling in her house like the fluttering of a moth just as cries and wailing signaled that the soul had departed. She caught the fluttering thing between her hands and ran with it to the house of the deceased, crying out that she had caught the *<term>atai</term>* <note>The soul or "reflection" of a person</note>. She opened her hands over the corpse's mouth to restore the soul, but the person did not recover. 

The ghost does not leave the vicinity of the body immediately; it lingers around the house and the grave for five or ten days, making its presence known by noises in the house and lights upon the grave. In the Banks' Islands, it is generally not considered desirable for the ghost to stay longer than the fifth day, and there is a custom of driving it away with shouts and the blowing of conch shells; in some places, bull-roarers <note>An ancient ritual instrument made of a piece of wood tied to a cord, which makes a roaring sound when swung</note> are sounded. It is helpful to examine the proceedings that follow death in the various islands of the group before describing the journey of the departed ghost into the lower world and its condition there. These proceedings include mourning, the funeral, and the funeral feasts.

In the Banks' Islands, the dead are generally buried. It is the duty of the members of the other *<term>Vere</term>* <note>Matrilineal moieties or "sides of the house"; the society was divided into two groups that performed reciprocal duties</note>, the "other side of the house," to dig the grave. The burial takes place sooner or later depending on the respect and status accorded to the deceased. In an ordinary case, it happens on the second day; friends weep around the corpse, and women are hired to wail in the meantime. 

The place of burial is usually in the bush <note>original: "bush," meaning the forest or uncultivated land</note> not far from the village. However, a great man, or someone whose death was particularly remarkable, was buried in the village near the *<term>gamal</term>* <note>The men’s communal clubhouse</note>, and a favorite son or child might be buried within the house itself. In the latter case, the grave was opened after fifty or a hundred days, and the bones were taken up and hidden in the bush, or some of them were hung up in the house. Some bodies were not buried at all but were placed in the bush outside the village in a chest called a *<term>pugoro</term>*, similar to the ones used to store dried breadfruit, and left there to decay. ...to *salo* <note>original: salo; a method of exposing the body or placing it in a shallow grave</note>; as is also the practice of laying the corpse in a shallow cave under a projecting rock. There was, however, and still remains, a custom in some places of keeping the body unburied and decomposing in the house as a mark of affection. At Gaua, in Santa Maria, it was the women's responsibility to watch the corpse, which was laid on a mat over crossed sticks between two slow fires in the house for ten days or more, until nothing but skin and bones was left; during this time, they drank the fluids that dripped from the corpse. The same was done in former days at Mota. 

The description of the funeral of a man of rank at Motlav is generally representative of any of the Banks Islands. The corpse of a great man was brought out into the open space in the middle of the village, loosely wrapped in a mat, wearing his *malosaru* ceremonial dress and his *som ta Rowa* necklace. His forehead was smeared, or *il*, with red earth, *mea*. He wore his armlets and bracelets made of reversed pig's tusks, but no bow was placed in his hand. On his breast was a cycas leaf, *no mele*, which was the mark of his rank in the *Suqe* <note>A significant secret society and graded pathway to social status</note>, and the leaves of the crotons, *sasa*, belonging to his *Tamate* <note>Literally "The Ghosts"; a series of secret societies</note> societies. 

By his side were heaped bunches of coconuts tied together, along with plenty of old dry coconuts, yams of various kinds, caladium <note>A tropical plant with edible tubers</note>, and all kinds of food. A bunch of the leaves of a particular dracæna plant was stuck upon the heap—the *karia garame tamate*, or the "ghost's tongue dracæna"—all of which were afterwards piled upon the grave. Then, a man skilled in speech made an address to the ghost, telling him that when they asked him in Panoi <note>The underworld or land of the dead</note> whether he was a great man, he should describe what was heaped beside him. The orator would not overlook his faults¹; if he were a man of bad character, the orator would say to him, "Poor ghost! Will you be able to enter Panoi? I think not." 

Then the burial took place. Upon the grave was set a bamboo vessel of water with a coconut-shell cup, and a little dish with a roasted yam in it. As the food was eaten by rats, the living renewed it, for the rat might be the deceased himself—at least during the five days that the ghost remained around the place. At Gaua, they hang up pigs...

<page-num>269</page-num>
<header>xv.] Banks' Islands. Secret Burial.</header>

People believe that the animals they have killed, or parts of them, at the grave follow the deceased. When the man goes down to Bono or Panoi <note>original: Bono, Panoi; names for the land of the dead</note>, the ghosts there will see him arrive with these offerings and hold him in high regard. The Gaua people, however, deny that pigs have ghosts <note>See footnote 1</note>. It is interesting to observe how a judgment upon a dead man's merits was pronounced. Not long ago, when a corpse was being buried at Motlav, a man whom the deceased had mistreated followed the procession with a stone. He threw it on the body, crying out, "You have ill-used me and persecuted me to kill me—but you have died first!" 

At Gaua, when a great man died, his friends would not make it known immediately. They feared that those whom he had oppressed might come and spit at him after his death, or *gorgov* him—a way of cursing him by standing and bickering at him with crooked fingers and drawing in the lips. Relatives in Motlav watch the grave of a man whose life was bad, lest some man he wronged should come at night and beat upon the grave with a stone while cursing him. 

Sometimes friends will even perform a sham burial and hide the grave where the corpse is actually laid. This is because if a man possessed *mana* <note>spiritual power or efficacy</note> during his lifetime—to shoot and kill, to perform charms with the *talamatai* <note>a type of magical object or curse</note>, and in other ways—there will be *mana* for the same purposes remaining in his corpse. Other men will want to dig up his bones to make arrows and charms, or his skull to use as a spool to roll the string for tying their *talamatai*. For this reason, at Gaua, after a body has been dried over a fire, they bury the bones in the village under a large stone and cover it with another stone, so the bones cannot be taken for arrows. <note>Footnotes</note>
1. If the pigs that have been killed are seen in Panoi, it might be thought that they must have souls to be seen there, since their bodies remain at the grave. But this is not the native belief. They believe that for a pig or an ornament, there is a certain something—a shadow or echo of itself—that can be seen. However, they do not possess what a human has: the intelligent, personal, and spiritual part which separates from the body at death. When a ghost is seen, what is actually being seen? It is not the soul, the *atai*, but the dead man, the *tamate*. The *atai* can never be seen; only the *nunuai* (echo) or the *tagoayiu* (outline) of the body can be seen, and even then, only indistinctly. When an English ghost appears in the dead man's clothes as he lived, is it thought to be his soul that appears?

Friends bring a quantity of food of all kinds to hang up on white, peeled <term>palako</term> <note>white sticks used as ritual displays</note> sticks around the corpse when it is laid out in the middle of the village. Then, an orator makes a speech to the deceased, giving him messages to take to the dead. He bids the spirit to carry the news of the village—especially what has been done and what is planned within the various secret societies—and tells him which spirits in Panoi <note>original: Panoi; the underworld or land of the dead</note>, besides himself, the food hanging around him is intended for. 

When the speech is finished, two small yams or caladium <note>a tropical plant with edible roots, similar to taro</note> roots are roasted over a fire of coconut fronds lit for this purpose. This cooking is only symbolic, and the food is scraped with the left hand instead of the right <note>a ritual reversal, as the left hand is often associated with death or the spirit world</note>. A small joint of bamboo is filled with water and placed with the food into a new, clean basket for the ghost. At the same time, a pig is killed. When all this is completed, the body is wrapped in a mat and followed to the grave by all the men and women, while the children remain in the village. All the food is buried with the body; or, if there is too much, some is hung above the grave, where the bolder people secretly take it and eat it.

On the same island, the ghost is driven away five days after death with a peculiar ceremony. Bags of small stones and short pieces of bamboo are provided for the villagers, which are charmed by those who know the appropriate magic chant for the purpose. Two men, each holding two white stones in his hands, sit inside the dead man's house, one on either side. These men begin to clink the stones against each other, the women begin to wail, and the neighbors—who have all assembled at one end of the village—begin to march in a group to the other end. They throw stones into the houses and all around, beating the bamboo sticks together. They pass through the village until they reach the wilderness <note>original: "the bush"</note> beyond, where they throw down the bamboos and bags. 

By this act, they have driven out the ghost, who until this time has stayed around the house. During these five days, the widow has never left the dead man's bed except when absolutely necessary; even then, she leaves a coconut to represent her until she returns. At Motlav, the ghost is not...

<meta>This page continues the description of funerary customs in the Melanesian islands. It concludes a description of "ghost-driving" (a ritual to expel the spirits of those who died of infectious skin diseases) and begins a detailed account of the "eating the death" funeral feasts.</meta>

...driven away unless the man who has died was badly afflicted with ulcers and sores—either a <term>gov</term> <note>original: *gov*; a person covered in sores</note> or a <term>mamanigala</term> <note>original: *mamanigala*; a person suffering from a single large ulcer or more</note>. When such a person is dying, the people of his village send word in time to the next village to the west, as the ghost will travel outward following the setting sun, to warn the neighbors to be prepared. When the *gov* is dead, they bury him. Then, with shell trumpets blowing and the stalks of coconut fronds (stripped of some of their leaflets) beating on the ground, they chase the ghost to the next village. The people of that village take up the chase and hunt the ghost further westward, and so on until the sea is reached. Then the frond stalks are thrown away and the people return, certain that the ghost has left the island and will not strike another man with the disease.

The series of funeral feasts or death-meals—the "eating the death," as they call it—follows the funeral, or may even begin before it. This is the most important part of the commemoration of the dead; indeed, it may be said to be one of the principal institutions of the islands. The number of feasts and the length of time during which they are repeated vary greatly across the various islands and also depend on the respect in which the deceased was held. These meals are distinctly commemorative, but they are not entirely devoid of the purpose of benefiting the dead. It is thought that the ghost is gratified by the remembrance shown to him and honored by the impressive performance of this duty. The living also solace themselves in their grief and satisfy some of their sense of loss through this affectionate commemoration. 

It is not easy to determine how much people still feel that a friendly association between the living and the dead is continued by both partaking in the meal, as when a morsel of food is thrown aside while calling out to the deceased. At ordinary meals, when the oven is opened, a bit of food is put aside for the dead with the words: "This is for you; let our oven be well cooked." At a death-meal, the words are: "This is for you." # Death. Burial. After Death.

Others are thought to come and eat the food, which they say is given only as a friendly memorial, and as a way of bringing together those whom death has separated. However, it can hardly be doubted that the original intention, at least, was a shared participation in the meal. It is not entirely consistent, however, with the idea of an underground home for the dead that they should be imagined as present at the later feasts, though the very first feast is held while they are still believed to be nearby.

"Eating the death," <term>gana matea</term> <note>original: *gana matea*; a ritual feast commemorating the deceased</note>, begins with the burial. They eat first, as they say, his grave; after that, they "eat his days." The days observed are the fifth and the tenth, and after that every tenth day up to the hundredth; in the case of a father, wife, or mother, it may even continue as far as the thousandth day. At Nembek, a part of Gaua, where they lay the corpse between fires, they bury the remains and finish the death-meal on the fifth day.

At Tarasag nearby, when a great man dies, the people from all the surrounding villages bring mashed yams the next morning to the place where the dead man lies and eat them there. The local people begin the death-meals that day with a large ovenful of food and continue on the tenth day and every successive tenth day. Sometimes, for a very important man, they eat every day up to the fiftieth day, and then start the fifth and tenth-day feasts. To count the days so that guests from distant villages may arrive on the correct dates, they use <term>cycas fronds</term> <note>leaves from a palm-like cycad tree, often used for record-keeping or signaling</note>. Each party carries one, and the appointed days are marked by pinching off or turning down a leaflet as each day passes.

At Ureparapara, the first fire for the death-meal is lit on the day after the burial; after that, it is lit every fifth day up to the hundredth, and if they go beyond that, every tenth day up to the thousandth. At Lakona, on Santa Maria, immediately after a death, the pigs belonging to the deceased—which he has left as legacies—are distributed to his relatives, and one or two more are killed and the meat given to the local people. In the evening, the body is buried, or laid out in a chest or in a cave, and no food or water is placed with it. The next morning begins the counting of the

### xv.] Banks' Islands. Hades.

death-days. If the deceased was a prominent man, a *taruemele* <term>taruemele</term> <note>original: *taruemele*; a person of high rank or social importance</note>, a drum will be brought out and the people will dance. They say this is to "drive away their grief" so that they may eat the funeral meal with cheerfulness; visitors come to dance and are paid for their performance. The death-feast lasts only five days for a woman and six days for a man. The final ritual is unique to Lakona: on the sixth day after a death, each man kills a female pig, and the women come to buy the meat. This meat provides the food for the last funeral meal, called the *Vulqat* <note>original: *Vulqat*; the name for the final ceremonial meal in the mourning cycle at Lakona</note>. The following morning, the entire process is completed with a meal intended "to clear away the *Vulqat*."

When a ghost leaves its former home, it makes its way to *Panoi* <note>original: *Panoi*; the Melanesian underworld or land of the dead</note>. There are many entrances to this place, called *sura*, located throughout the various islands. Some are underground and hidden, while others are well-known landmarks, such as the Aliali rock on the mountain at Mota, the volcanic vents on the "burning hill" of Mount Garat overlooking the lake at Gaua, and the great mountain of Vanua Lava—the *Sur-lav*, or "great gateway" <note>original: *Sur-lav*; from *sura* (gateway) and *lav* (great)</note>. Ghosts gather on headlands before their departure, as well as at the mouths of these *sura*. On moonlight nights, they can be heard dancing, singing, shouting, and whistling using land-crab claws. 

It was believed that ghosts who had already descended into *Panoi* could return to these headlands and the *sura* entrances. Some thought these spirits would emerge to welcome the newly dead—sometimes with dancing—to show them their various gathering places and lead them into the underworld. There is also the idea that specific *sura* are reserved for different classes of ghosts. For example, there is the *sura tupa* <note>original: *sura tupa*; a portal for common or harmless spirits</note>, where simple, harmless people gather; and the *sura lumagar* <note>original: *sura lumagar*; a portal for the young</note>, where youths go who die in the flower of their age. This latter place is more pleasant than the rest, filled with all kinds of flowers and fragrant plants. This belief was held mostly by women, who thought deeply of those who died young, and especially of those who had been shot or killed on their account—those who "paid for them the price of their death" (*me matewolira ti*) <note>original: *me matewolira ti*; a phrase indicating a sacrificial or retaliatory death occurring because of a relationship with a woman</note>.

It is difficult indeed to obtain a precise and consistent account from the inhabitants of these islands regarding the condition of ghosts after they have arrived at *Panoi*, or a description of the place itself; nor—

Perhaps it is reasonable to expect it. However, the stories of descents to Panoi <note>original: Panoi; the underworld or land of the dead</note> reveal the common beliefs held by the native mind. Recognizing the truth that Panoi is not a single destination that is the same for everyone helps to reconcile these varying accounts; there is a corresponding distinction between one class of ghosts and another. This is clearly believed at Motlav <note>an island in the Banks group of Vanuatu</note>, where they say that when a ghost descends the *sura* <term>sura</term> <note>original: sura; an entrance or gateway to the underworld</note>, it is met by another ghost. Depending on the man's character during his life, he is either allowed to enter Panoi or sent back to another place; fearing that other place, the ghost instead wanders the earth. 

The true Panoi is a good place, but there is also a bad place, which is sometimes meant when the word Panoi is used. Thus, if a man has killed another through treachery or witchcraft, he finds himself blocked at the entrance to Panoi by the ghost of the man he wronged when he descends the *sura* after death. He sees another path leading to the bad place he dreads, and so he turns back to earth. If a person has killed a good man without cause, that good man’s ghost blocks his murderer; if a man has killed another in a fair fight, he will not be blocked by the man he slew. If a bad man killed another bad man, they would be together, but not in the true Panoi. 

This division is very important—that there are some ghosts who enter Panoi and some who are not allowed to enter, these last being of bad character. It is also very important, as it reveals native concepts of moral right and wrong so often denied to them, to observe what sort of men were admitted and who were refused. Who was the man of good character in life? It is answered that he was one who lived as he ought to do, *me toga mantag* <note>original: *me toga mantag*; lived properly or correctly</note>, an answer that may not necessarily have a moral meaning on its own. 

But who was the man of bad character? The answer is: one who killed another without due cause, or had caused a death by charms, or one who used to steal, to lie, or was given to adultery. Thus, those who enter the true Panoi still live as they ought, *we toga mantag* <note>original: *we toga mantag*; they live in a proper or harmonious way</note>; they live in harmony and in a good way of living. Those who remain in the bad place quarrel and live in misery—not in physical pain, indeed, but

<header>xv.] Banks' Islands. Judgment. Childless Ghosts.</header>

These ghosts are restless, wandering back to earth—homeless, malicious, and pitiable. These are the ones who eat excrement and open their mouths for wind; they are the ones who do harm to the living out of spite. They are dreaded as "eaters of men's souls" and haunt graves and woods. 

There is a unique belief in Lakona <note>an island in the Banks group of Vanuatu</note> concerning this kind of judgment after death. The ghost's path leads him to the volcanic vents of the burning hill, Garat, and as he runs along, the other ghosts assemble to receive him. They beat him—even though he is already a ghost—to death, then cut him into pieces, and each ghost takes a piece. They then reassemble him. If, during his lifetime, he had wrongfully shot the father, brother, or *sogoi* <term>sogoi</term> <note>original: *sogoi*; a specific category of kinsman or maternal relation</note> of any of the ghosts who have captured him, or if he has committed any other wrong, the ghost with the grievance will hide the piece of him that he took. The man will then remain incomplete, missing a part of himself. When he finally goes down to Panoi <note>the underworld or land of the dead</note> and the other ghosts ask what has become of that bit of him, he will tell them that someone has kept it from him because he had done them wrong.

The ghost of a *rasingona* <term>rasingona</term> <note>original: *rasingona*; a woman who dies in childbirth</note>—a woman who has died in childbed—cannot go to Panoi if her child lives, for she cannot leave her child behind. To prevent her from staying, people deceive her ghost by loosely wrapping a piece of a banana trunk in leaves and laying it on her chest when she is buried. As she departs, she believes she has the child with her. As she travels, the banana stalk slips around inside the leaves, making her think the child is moving; in her bewildered new condition as a spirit, this contents her until she reaches Panoi and discovers she has been deceived. In the meantime, the living child is taken to another house because they know the mother will come back to take its soul <note>In this context, taking the soul means causing the child's death so the mother can have the child with her in the afterlife</note>. She searches everywhere for the child in unending grief and rage; consequently, the ghost of a *rasingona* is particularly dreaded.

Panoi is nearby, located beneath the land of living men, just as death is near to life. If a man is nearly killed, he says, "I have been close to Panoi and have returned." Much there is similar to the world above, including villages, houses, and trees with red leaves.

In Panoi <note>the underworld or land of the dead</note> there is day and night; it is even a beautiful place. For instance, during a great festival when the village square is bright with flowers and colored leaves, and crowded with people dancing, drumming, and singing, the people say that it is "like a *sura* <term>sura</term> <note>original: *sura*; a term for a bright, festive scene or perhaps a celestial opening</note>, as if the mouth of Panoi were opened." 

When a ghost first descends, he waits outside the ghostly village; he is weak, and he stops there until he has recovered his strength. The other ghosts perform a dance in his honor. When he arrives, they ask him, "Have you come to stay?" If he has only fainted <note>and not actually died</note>, it is discovered then, and he returns to the living. The newly arrived ghost finds a life there that resembles earthly life, but it is hollow and unreal. There is nothing for them to do but talk, sing, and dance. There is no *gamal* <term>gamal</term> <note>the traditional men's communal club-house, essential to social life in the Banks Islands</note>, which is so indispensable to earthly life. Men and women live together without sexual intercourse. There is no fighting and no one in authority. There are no *vui* <term>vui</term> <note>spirits or supernatural beings that were never human</note> there, only the ghosts of men. 

A great man descends to the underworld as a great man, dressed in all his fine ornaments. However, the pigs killed for his funeral feast and the food heaped upon his grave do not go down with him as he does. He is a *tamate* <term>tamate</term> <note>a dead person or ghost</note>; as a dead man, he possesses the *atai* <term>atai</term> <note>soul or essence; in this context, something only humans possess</note> that he had under different conditions as a living man. His ornaments appear on his ghostly person, but they are only the *niniai* <term>niniai</term> <note>shadow, reflection, or ghostly double</note> of the objects, for such things—not even pigs—possess an *atai*. 

There is a further belief that there are compartments or enclosures fenced apart where those who have died violent deaths stay together. Those who have been shot with arrows are in one place; those who were killed by charms or sorcery are in a second; and those who have been clubbed to death are in a third. Those who were shot continually rattle the reeds of the arrows that killed them. Because of this, if a rat is heard in a house making that kind of noise, people say it is a "reed-rattling ghost," or *tamate ninginingi togo* <term>tamate ninginingi togo</term>. 

Unlike the *vui* <note>spirits</note>, the ghosts in Panoi do not have knowledge of things beyond their own sight and hearing. Nevertheless, people invoke them in times of need and distress as if they could hear and help. They return to earth whenever they please to see how their friends and property are doing, and they hear news of the world from newly arrived ghosts. These ghosts, as distinguished from...

<meta>This page continues the description of Panoi, the underworld of the Banks Islands, specifically discussing the interactions between the living and the dead and the belief in "descents" to the land of the dead.</meta>

<header>xv.] Banks' Islands. Descents to Hades.</header>

Those who have no home in Panoi are generally kind to living people; however, if their friends or property are damaged, they become angry and revengeful. It is true that people are afraid of these and all other ghosts, because a ghost is inherently a terrifying thing to a living person. They are seen, but not clearly—only their eyes, which look like phosphorescent fungi or something red. Life in Panoi is eternal, unless, as some say, there are actually two levels of Panoi, one below the other. According to this belief, the dead die and pass from the upper to the lower level, just as living men die and pass from the earth. From the lower level they never die, but instead turn into white ants' nests, *te nog qutete nia* <note>original: *te nog qutete nia*; meaning "they turn into termite mounds"</note>.

Descents to Panoi have been by no means uncommon. There was a woman, who died not many years ago, who once greatly desired to see her recently deceased brother. She perfumed herself with water in which a dead rat had been soaked to give herself a death-like smell; she then pulled up a bird's-nest fern, a *pugel* <term>pugel</term> <note>a large epiphytic fern, *Asplenium nidus*</note>, and descended through the hole she had opened. She had no difficulty in finding Panoi, and she saw friends there who were surprised to see her and never discovered that she was alive. She found her brother lying in a house because, as a recent ghost, he was not yet strong enough to move about. He warned her to eat nothing there, and she returned. This descent was made in the physical body, as was that of a man named Molborbor of Valuwa, who went down and saw his wife. 

However, a man in Motlav, who died more recently, used to go down in his sleep; his soul would descend while his body remained behind as if in a trance. He could do this at will and received payment for doing so, claiming to visit the recently dead about whom their friends were unhappy, and even claiming to be able to bring them back. He never actually brought any back; he said he had seen the persons and talked with them but was prevented from bringing them home. He, too, prepared for his soul's descent by washing his body with water in which a putrid rat, snake, or lizard had been soaked. 

In former days at Motlav, there was a man named Vanvanvegirgir who, when going down to Panoi in his *talegi* <term>talegi</term> <note>the soul or spirit of a living person, as opposed to a ghost</note>, once took another man with him in his physical body. This man had lately lost his wife and went to Vanvanvegirgir...

The ghosts detected the living man and cried out, "The smell of that world!" The two travelers claimed that they were truly dead. As the story explains, ghosts in Panoi have more physical substance than they do when they return to the living world; otherwise, the man could not have taken hold of his dead wife’s hand. When a ghost enters the living world, it is seen only as a <term>*taqangiu*</term> <note>original: *taqangiu*; an outline or shadow-like appearance</note>, something defined by an outline like a shadow. However, the ghost in Panoi—of which the earthly ghost is likely itself the "ghost"—has a <term>*tarapei*</term> <note>original: *tarapei*; a physical body or substance</note>, a body that has not only form and color but also a certain solidity.

There is a woman still living on Vanua Lava who turned her descent to Panoi to a useful purpose. Her husband, a man from Gaua, died, and she herself became so ill that she appeared to die. She recovered, however, and told the people that she had followed her husband to Mount Garat and had seen him there bound hand and foot. She declared that the ghosts told her this was done because he had not paid his debts. "Go back," they commanded her, "to the people of Gaua and say to them: pay your debts and do not kill one another; this is how we shall treat such men."

<header>xv.] New Hebrides. Journey of the Dead.</header>

In this place, he says, they believe that when the soul, <term>*tamani*</term> <note>original: *tamani*; the soul or spirit of a person</note>, leaves the body at death, it climbs into a tree containing a bird's-nest fern. Sitting among the fronds, it laughs and mocks the people who are crying and mourning loudly over him. There he sits, wondering at them and ridiculing them. "What are they crying for?" he asks; "Who is it they are sorry for? Here I am." For they believe that the real essence of a person is the soul, and that it has left the body just as a man throws off his clothes and leaves them behind; the clothes then lie by themselves with nothing in them. (The Maewo word <term>*garui*</term> <note>original: *garui*; an integument or outer covering</note> applies in such a case: the white of an egg is its *garui*, while the yolk is the "real thing"; the word for clothes is *garu*, meaning a covering). 

Then the soul travels through his gardens and along his usual paths, and finally leaves the area. He runs along the ridge of hills until he reaches the end of the island, where he comes to the "place of recollection." The Maewo name for this is <term>*rat dodoma*</term> <note>original: *rat dodoma*; the stone of thought</note>. If he remembers his child, his wife, or any of his possessions while there, he will run back and return to life. In this same place, there are also two rocks with a deep ravine between them; if the ghost successfully leaps across this gap, he is dead forever, but if he fails, he returns to life again. 

The ghost continues his course, running along the mountain range to the end opposite Raga (Pentecost Island) at the <term>*mate tasi*</term> <note>original: *mate tasi*; land's end or the brink of the sea</note>. When he arrives safely, all the ghosts of those who died before him assemble and receive him joyfully. They also believe that as he runs, the ghosts of those he wronged in this world—those he foully murdered with a club or arrow, or killed using magic charms—take their full revenge upon him. They beat him, tear him, and stab him with daggers called <term>*malaso*</term> <note>original: *malaso*; daggers similar to those used by men to slaughter pigs</note>. One of them will say to him, "While you were still in the world, you thought yourself a valiant man; but now we will take our revenge upon you."

For a girl, he builds a little house and plants a pandanus tree beside it to make mats with.

The latter are the recently dead who have just become aware of their condition. After this, the wives of the deceased, or his father and mother, do not go about as usual for a hundred days; they spend the day at home. Men may walk about, but the female mourners cannot go into the open, and their faces may not be seen; they stay indoors in the dark and cover themselves with a large mat reaching to the ground. In the early morning, the widow goes out of the house covered with a mat to weep at the graveside; she does this every day until the hundredth day, and also in the afternoon. And she is not alone, for many people from the village also weep. 

All the women put on a mat "as large as a single plank," which remains on their head as a sign that they are in mourning for the death, and they refrain from certain foods. The immediate relatives of the deceased may not eat yam, caladium <note>a type of taro or elephant-ear plant</note>, bananas, or other good food; they eat only the gigantic caladium, breadfruit, coconuts, and mallow <note>likely "island cabbage" or *Abelmoschus manihot*</note>, among other things. All of these they must seek in the wild <note>original: "bush"</note> where they grow naturally, as they are forbidden from eating those which have been planted in gardens. The markers made today can still be seen where the people of ancient times were buried. After the burial, if the deceased was a very important man with many gardens and pigs, they count fifty days and then slaughter pigs on the day called the *Ulogi* or *Sawana*. On the day of the *Ulogi*—the name refers to "the howling"—people wail at midday by the gravestones, which have been cleaned and decorated with leaves and flowers. Some people weep, while others begin a song sacred to the dead. 

When the earth ovens are opened, the assembled crowd departs. The people of the village then slaughter pigs and cut the tip off the liver of each one. The brother of the deceased goes near the woods <note>original: "the bush"</note> and calls out the dead man's name, crying, "This is for you to eat."

At this, everyone begins to weep again. They smear their entire bodies and faces with ashes and wear a cord around their necks for a hundred days to show <note>original: "shew"</note> that they are abstaining from good food. If they slaughter many pigs in this way, they believe it is a good thing; but if they do not, they believe that the dead man does not achieve a proper existence, but instead hangs from tangled vines <note>original: "creepers"</note>. They consider hanging on vines to be a miserable fate. This is the true and only reason why they slaughter pigs for a man who has died.

"Meanwhile," the author continues, "the ghosts already know the number of days since the latest person died. The relatives of the deceased have also counted the days until they should eat the death-meal in his honor—either the fifth or the tenth day—and a crowd has [assembled]..."

If even a small amount is given, they believe the spirits carry it away as if it were a massive quantity, and they return joyfully to Banoi <note>the underworld or land of the dead</note> with shouting and songs. They continue these rituals until the hundredth day, and after that, they no longer focus on it.

### The Origin of Death

On Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae Island in Vanuatu</note>, the origin of death was attributed both to the loss of the power to shed one's skin and to a natural defect that denied humans that power. Once upon a time, a woman and a crab argued about this; the woman claimed the crab was superior to humans because it could shed its shell, become young again, and live a long life. She wanted the crab to trade bodies with her, and she blamed Tagar <note>a creator deity or spirit in Melanesian mythology</note> because he did not make humans correctly. 

However, in accordance with the story told in various forms throughout the Solomon Islands, the Banks Islands, and the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>, humans did possess the power to shed their skin in ancient times. There was an old woman who had two grandsons. One day, while these two boys were playing by damming up the water of a small stream, the current carried down a Tahitian chestnut. One of the boys picked it up and gave it to his grandmother to roast. 

Afterward, the other boy—who had initially looked down on the chestnut—ran home unseen and ate it; so when the first boy went to retrieve it, the chestnut was gone. The boy scolded his grandmother for her neglect, and she, becoming angry in turn, said to the boys, "You two do not wish to live forever; instead, you would rather that we do not live at all." She had just returned from shedding her skin in the water further upstream, which the boys had been damming...

Since that time, humanity has lost the power of changing skins, and everyone has died.

At death, the soul (*tamtegi*), departs from the body. When it is certain that the soul is gone, the wailing for the dead begins. At first, the *tamtegi* does not go far away, and there are sounds that show its presence. The people never drive it away; it is only the soul of someone who has been eaten that is driven off with the blowing of conch shells. When the time comes, the soul departs, and that time is set at a hundred days. 

The corpse is buried wrapped in the mats that serve as currency <note>original: "money"</note>. When Mairuru <note>a notable figure or chief on the island</note> died, they wrapped him at once in mats and added more the next day, until the corpse with its wrappings was so large that it took two days to dig a grave for it; on the third day, they buried him. He was swathed in one hundred short mats and ten rolls of a hundred fathoms <note>a fathom is approximately six feet</note> each. However, Mairuru was a very great man; for common people, fifty mats would be enough for a man, and five for a boy. 

After the funeral, pigs and five chickens <note>original: "fowls"</note> are killed, and the chickens are roasted over the fire. When the meal is ready, the chief mourner takes a piece of chicken and yam and calls the name of someone from the village who has died, saying, "This is for you." He does this until he has called everyone whose death is remembered in the place, including the recently deceased, and has given each a bit of chicken and yam. What remains he eats himself, and then the assembled mourners eat; this is called "eating the grave." 

Counting five days from the death, they prepare the oven for "eating the death," and when it is opened, they give morsels to the spirits <note>original: "ghosts"</note>, just as they did on the day of burial. The same is done on the tenth day, which is a significant occasion with a large gathering, and the same again at a similar feast on the fiftieth day. Every fifth day there is also a death-meal, and the hundredth day is the last. On that day, for a very important man, there will be a hundred ovens. This final solemnity is remarkable. On that day <note>the hundredth day of mourning</note>, all the people gather in the center of the village. A man from the *vairung* <term>vairung: one of the two kinship divisions, or moieties, into which the society is divided</term> division—one who was related to the deceased through the male line but did not belong to the deceased's own division—climbs a tree. He calls out all the names of the deceased one after another, as a great man often possesses many names (page 114). There is a solemn silence as the names are called, and everyone listens for a sound. If any noise is heard, they take it as an answer from the dead, and everyone begins a wailing cry because it is the final time they will ever hear his voice. 

They have no intention of driving the ghost away; instead, they call to him to come and take all their food and everything they own, and to take it with him to Nggalevu <note>the spirit who rules the underworld</note>. If no sound answers the final call, they believe he has already departed. A man is buried with his bow and arrows and his finest ornaments, but his bracelets made of pig tusks are placed on him upside down. Nggalevu will recognize him as a great man by what he sees with him and upon him, for he will be seen just as a living man is seen, even though he is now a ghost, a *tamtegi* <term>tamtegi: the soul or ghost of a deceased person</term>. Exactly what form the ornaments and other objects take when they are "seen" in the afterlife is something the people have not deeply considered; however, they certainly do not think of the objects as having a *tamtegi* or a soul of their own. In fact, they find it amusing to be asked whether a bow has a "ghost" of its own. When a man dies, his coconut trees, fruit trees, and the crops in his garden are cut down and destroyed. They say this is done out of a feeling of tenderness and sorrow, so that no one but him shall ever enjoy them.

When the soul of the dead man leaves his home, it travels along the mountain path to Manaro, the lake that fills the island's volcanic crater. Sometimes, people notice fresh footprints on the path and go down to the villages to ask who has just died and traveled up the mountain. The home of the dead is called Lolomboetogitogi, and the descent into it is through a volcanic vent near the lake. There, the ghosts assemble. Nggalevu has always lived there; he is a *vui* <term>vui: a spirit that was never human, distinguished from the ghost of a dead person</term>, the master of the place who receives the newcomers. There is also a pig that the dead must pass. On the far side of the lake, which no living man has ever been known to reach, there is a volcanic vent that sends up clouds of steam. Men travel to the near side of the lake and climb a tree...

"You will be just as bad," says the rat. 

"But I shall live again," says the man. 

"No! You will be like me," says the rat. 

The other story is a variation of the common legend about changing one's skin. There was a man who had two boys living with him; he used to shed his skin every day and come out to work with them. One evening he put his old skin back on, and the boys killed him because they thought he had deceived them. If he had lived, all humans would have changed their skins and never died.

A ghost after death is called an <term>atmat</term> ("dead man"), but, as on Lepers' Island <note>Ambae</note>, the same word is used to designate a man's soul while he is alive. At death, the <term>atmat</term> leaves the body but lingers nearby for five days. It is not driven away, but departs on its own to the abode of the dead called <term>Banoi</term>. In cases of fainting, a person upon recovering says they were not permitted to enter. 

The corpse is watched until it is buried; in the case of a great man, this lasts for three or four days. The body is then rolled in the mats that are valued as currency and taken to the <term>gamal</term> <term>gamal: a men's communal house or clubhouse</term>. If it was a great man, many mats are used, and the wrapped corpse is propped up between two stakes. After a time, it is buried. A great man is buried in the village square in a <term>garu</term> <note>a stone-lined grave</note>, with stones erected and with dracænas <note>tropical shrubs with colorful foliage</note> and other brightly colored plants positioned around it. After the burial, a fire is lit for the funeral feast, and they continue "eating the death" <note>observing a period of ritual mourning meals</note> for a hundred days, which are counted on a cycas leaf <note>a palm-like leaf used here as a calendar</note>. As a sign of mourning, relatives smear themselves with soot and ashes. 

The ghosts, as they depart or are released, make their way down the coast along the beach to Vatang-gele, where they can be heard singing, shouting, and drumming. The gathering place before the descent into <term>Banoi</term> is a point of land facing the island of Ambrym. There, a stream exists that the ghosts cannot cross, and there is a tree from which they leap into the sea. A shark waits below to bite off the noses of those who have not sacrificed pigs in accordance with the customs of the island. There is a town in <term>Banoi</term> with houses, trees, sweet-smelling plants, and colorful shrubs, but there are no gardens because there is no work to be done. The ghosts of those who have died violent deaths stay together: those shot with an arrow still sticking in their body, or those killed with a club that remains fixed in their head. Those who died from a cough also stay together. When a ghost arrives carrying the weapon that killed them, they identify their murderer. When that murderer eventually arrives, the ghostly community will not receive them; the murderer must stay apart with others of their kind. To the question of how someone is received who has killed another in a fair fight, no certain answer can be given. 

Regarding the food of ghosts in Banoi <note>the underworld</note>, opinions differ. Some say they eat nothing, while others claim they eat waste and rotten <term>erythrina</term> <note>Erythrina: a genus of flowering trees, often called coral trees</term> wood. It is likely that only the ghosts rejected by the happier community consume this dismal food. 

Ghosts particularly haunt their burial sites and take revenge if offended. If a person trespasses on a dead chief's grave, the ghost will strike him, and he will fall sick. When seen, ghosts appear like fire. My informants tell me that no portion of food is offered to a ghost, though this is a doubtful statement; however, if they see bananas or other food rotting in a dead man’s garden, they say it is "the ghost's food." This does not necessarily mean they believe the ghost eats it, but rather that as the man has decayed, so has his food¹.

The body of a prominent man is not buried; it remains in the house inside a canoe or a drum. Women and children sleep around it to keep watch and remove maggots <note>original: "worms"</note>. After ten months, they take the skull, jawbone, and the long bones of the arms and legs and hang them in the house; the other bones are wrapped together and sunk in the sea.

...strangled accordingly. On Maewo <note>an island in the north of Vanuatu</note>, it has often happened that a woman has demanded to be buried with her husband or a beloved child. Not long ago, a woman insisted on this; they dug a grave, wrapped her in mats, and buried her alive with her child. On Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae</note> recently, when a man named Mairuru was buried, the people accused his wife of having poisoned him and wanted to bury her alive with him. She consented, but the presence of a Christian native prevented this from being carried out. The killing or burying alive of sick persons is a different matter.

# CHAPTER XVI.

## THE ARTS OF LIFE.

The previous chapters have mainly focused on subjects that require a deep understanding of the thoughts and ways of the Melanesian people—the kind of knowledge that can only be gained through personal acquaintance and fluency in their languages. This chapter will cover topics that are much more visible in everyday life and are easily observed by any visitor or traveler. These are the arts through which their culture expresses itself: how they build and decorate canoes and houses, plant and cultivate their gardens, create weapons and tools for war and work, catch fish, prepare food, make clothing and ornaments, and produce and use money as a medium of exchange.

Such a long list of skills and crafts shows that Melanesians do not rank very low among the world's developing societies <note>original: "backward peoples"</note>. Covering these matters fully and adequately would require a great deal of space. This is less necessary because much information has already been made public—for example, by Dr. Guppy regarding the Solomon Islands <note>Henry Brougham Guppy was a surgeon and naturalist who published "The Solomon Islands and Their Natives" in 1887</note>. However, there is certainly room for additional information, and even in these practical matters, there is great value in recording what the local people say about themselves.

(1) **Canoes**. People living on groups of islands are naturally seafaring, and canoes are usually among the first objects a visitor notices. In my own memory, hardly anything seems to have been more striking...

# CANOES

...than the difference between the canoes of the local people when we first traveled from the New Hebrides and the Banks Islands to the Solomon Islands. We exchanged the clumsy outriggered tree trunks of the eastern groups for the elegant shapes and brilliant decorations of the plank-built craft of the west. However, upon consideration, a sailing outrigger canoe should be ranked higher than one moved only by paddles. Certainly, the outrigger canoe is the defining characteristic of Melanesia. It is only in the Solomon Islands that plank-built canoes are seen; but even there, small canoes with outriggers are used. These are, in fact, the same as those found in Santa Cruz, the Banks Islands, and the New Hebrides; all are essentially hollowed-out tree trunks with outriggers attached. Double canoes <note>A vessel consisting of two hulls joined by a frame; though common in Polynesia, the author notes their absence here.</note> are not seen anywhere in these...

->MOTA CANOE.<-

To take the example of a Mota *aka* <note>aka: the Mota word for canoe</note>. The sail (*epa*) was formed of mats woven by women and sewn together by men with needles made of tree-fern wood or the bone of a stingray. The mast (*turgae*), which had a forked base, was set upon the middle of the three yoke-pieces (*iwatia*) that connected the outrigger (*sama*) with the hull. These yoke-pieces were fastened to the outrigger by being lashed to wooden pegs fixed into it. At the foot of the mast, the forked end of a boom (*panei*) was also placed; both were secured with ropes (*tali*), and the sail was spread in the triangular space between the mast and boom, lashed to both and dipping in a graceful curve between the two. In these canoes, which have a large sail rising into two curved horns, the people make long voyages to Vanikoro and other known islands, steering by the stars. The plank-built canoe of the Solomon Islands was likely not developed without knowledge of the outrigger <note>original: ¹; see footnote below</note>. In the straits between long islands like Malaita <note>original: Malanta</note> and Guadalcanal <note>original: Guadalcanar</note>, the islanders have long taken pride in the skill with which they build and paddle their canoes.

Ulawa was once a famous center for the manufacture and sale of these vessels <note>original: ²; see footnote below</note>. Canoes from Saa would undertake six-day voyages for trade and pleasure to Owa, Santa Ana, and Santa Catalina in one direction—steering by the stars at night—and to Alite <note>The area of Langa Langa Lagoon, Malaita</note> in the other. Large canoes also cross from Alite to Guadalcanal to exchange shell money and ornaments for food. On their return, when they are heavily laden, they throw out floats made of dry coconuts at night so they can rest and sleep. In Florida <note>The Nggela Islands</note>, the moon in her second quarter, when she appears to be lying on her back, is called a "canoe of Mala" <note>Mala: Malaita; this refers to the "wet moon" orientation</note>.

A very graceful little catamaran <term>catamaran: a multi-hulled or raft-like watercraft</term> is used within the reefs of San Cristobal <note>modern: Makira</note>. It is made of five or six stems from the fronds of the sago palm lashed together. The tips are pulled back toward the base with lines, and the end of the high, curved prow created by this tension is decorated with a crimson streamer. 

A first-rate war canoe takes a long time to build. For three successive years, I had the opportunity to observe one being constructed at Ha’ani, from the time the *bea* <note>a ceremonial platform or structure set up to collect funds</note> was erected to start the work, until the final ornamentation with shell carvings and streamers was completed. Such a canoe, forty-five feet long, could carry ninety men. The form of a Florida *peko* <note>a specific style of canoe from the Nggela Islands</note> is more graceful than those built in Ulawa. as many as thirty passengers <note>original: sitters</note>; when it was sealed with *tita* <term>tita: a natural resin or cement made from the crushed nut of the Atuna tree (Parinarium laurinum), used to waterproof canoes</term>, a hundred pigs were slaughtered for the feast. Such a canoe required a human life for its ceremonial launch <note>original: inauguration</note>¹.

In the Eastern Solomon Islands, if no victim was encountered during the first voyage of a new canoe, the chief to whom the canoe belonged would privately arrange with a neighboring chief to provide one of his men—likely someone without family connections or a stranger—who would then be killed, perhaps as he went out to look at the new vessel. It was considered a "kind" act to come up behind him and strike him without warning. Further west, captives were also kept specifically for the purpose of taking their heads when new canoes were launched.

It is remarkable that while the paddles used in the Eastern Solomon Islands as far as Florida <note>modern: Nggela</note> are pointed—some being very narrow and sharp indeed—those used in Ysabel <note>modern: Santa Isabel</note> have a bluntly pointed, short, and broad blade with a relatively long shaft. The Ysabel paddles have a crescent-shaped handle, while the former have a cross-bar <note>original: crutch</note> for the upper hand. The paddles of the Banks Islands and New Hebrides <note>modern: Vanuatu</note> are relatively shapeless and heavy.

A custom common to the Solomon Islands and the eastern island groups is the practice of taking a new canoe on a tour to show it off; a large party travels together and receives gifts at every place they visit. A great deal of trading is conducted between the various islands of each group; in two locations, the people live entirely by commerce and—

It was brought over secretly and placed in a *kiala* <term>kiala: a large canoe-house</term> built out of sight until a human head could be obtained. manufacturing. Rowa, one of the Banks Islands group <note>modern: Vanuatu</note>, has only a tiny population living on one of the islets of its reef. They still mainly obtain their food from Saddle Island <note>modern: Motalava</note> and Vanua Lava, trading fish and the shell money they manufacture at home in exchange. Not many years ago, it was believed that if food were grown at Rowa, it would cause a famine in Vanua Lava; it was also believed that if a sow were taken there, it would devour the people. However, the Christian teacher of the place, a Rowa man himself, has boldly faced both of these perceived dangers. The other major center of commerce is on the Alite islets, located close to the Malaita <note>original: Malanta</note> coast near Florida <note>modern: Nggela</note>. The inhabitants there are enemies with their neighbors on the mainland and have no gardens there; they purchase their primary food supplies from Guadalcanal <note>original: Guadalcanar</note> using the money and ornaments they manufacture.

(2) **Houses.** The typical Melanesian house requires very little description: a roof made of bamboos bent over a ridgepole, which is supported by two main posts, very low side walls, and ends filled in with bamboo screens. <margin>⎡</margin>The dwelling houses in the New Hebrides <note>modern: Vanuatu</note> and Banks Islands are poor and contain little that could be called furniture. One might see a cleverly crafted chest on legs used to store dried breadfruit; a fireplace sunk into the ground; and a hole with a pile of stones serving as an oven. There are wooden hooks, cut from branching trees, hanging from the roof with bags of food to protect them from rats. Large wooden platters with their pestles, bowls, bamboo tubes for water, and wicker dishes lean against the side walls. A few wooden knives and tools are tucked between the layers of thatch, and mats are spread upon the floor; these items are found everywhere. Often, there is also an inner chamber screened off with reeds. 

The door consists simply of several stalks of sago fronds with a stick threaded through their centers. This stick is thrust down between the double threshold of the doorway and tied from the outside through an opening left above the doorway for that purpose when the house is empty¹. XVI.] Houses.

The canoe house is the same in construction as a dwelling, but it is larger, stronger, and furnished with openings in the sides as well as doorways at the ends. The roofing is made from the thatch of the smaller sago-palm, which creates an excellent roof; the preparation and fixing of this thatch is the primary work of house-building. The palm frond—with its midrib removed, the leaflets doubled over a reed, and then pinned together with wooden skewers or spikes from the base of sago fronds (known as the Malay *atap* <note>original: atap; a type of roof shingle made from palm leaves</note>)—serves the same purpose in all these islands as a tile, slate, or shingle does elsewhere. <margin>A hand-drawn vertical bracket marks the text from "In the Solomon Islands" to "apparently unknown."</margin> In the Solomon Islands, the coconut frond is also used for roofing, as the smaller sago palm is apparently unknown there. The roofing in that region, however, is very fine; the *ataps* are laid very close together, and the thatch is extremely thick in large buildings such as the canoe-houses. 

These canoe-houses—called *oka* in Malaita <note>original: Malanta</note> and Makira <note>original: San Cristoval</note>, or *kiala* in Nggela <note>original: Florida</note> and Santa Isabel <note>original: Ysabel</note>, which correspond to the *madai* and *ofilau* of Santa Cruz—are fine and spacious buildings. For example, the *kiala* at Kolakamboa in Nggela was a hundred feet long, fifty feet wide, and fifty feet high. An *oka*, at least in Ugi and Makira, was decorated with all the skill of the noteworthy native artists¹. 

In these buildings, the large canoes are kept, men congregate, and young men sleep. Strangers are entertained there, and the huge wooden bowls used in feasts are stored within. The jawbones of pigs eaten or killed for such feasts are suspended from the structure, and the skulls of men killed in war—which were sometimes, no doubt, also eaten in that place—are hung up. In the *oka*, one also finds the *mangite* <term>relics or spiritual associations of the dead</term> of the deceased (page 262). The posts that support the ridge-pole and the purlins <note>horizontal beams supporting the rafters</note> of an *oka* are carved into figures of men, crocodiles, and sharks; a *kiala*, by comparison, is much less ornamented. 

A Solomon Island dwelling-house is certainly superior to those found in the Eastern groups. Its walls are higher, it is more generally divided into chambers by partitions, and it is furnished with more care.

> "...houses are built very long and have slight divisions in them, seldom more than two feet high." — Bishop Selwyn, Journal, 1881.

the walls, and sometimes a tiny house on piles is built in the middle. In former days, when a chief’s dwelling-house or canoe-house was finished, a human head was taken for it just as it was for a new canoe; a boy or woman was sometimes purchased to be killed. It is a matter of tradition that men were crushed under the base of the great pillar of such a house when it was set in its place. The tree-houses, known as *vako* <note>original: vako</note>, are not seen until Santa Isabel <note>original: Ysabel</note> is reached, where they are needed as a refuge from head-hunters. One of these, which Bishop Patteson climbed, was built at a height of ninety-four feet from the ground and was approached by a ladder from a fortified rock where the tree was rooted; the house, which had a platform <note>original: stage</note> outside it, was eighteen feet long, ten feet wide, and eight feet high. According to the account given of their first discovery, the houses at Santa Cruz were round; they are now square, though round houses are still said to be built. The only round house that has come to my attention was at Ha’ani in San Cristoval <note>now known as Makira</note>; it was built to contain and shelter the village drums and was an excellent building. Sometimes in the Banks Islands a *gamal* <note>a men's communal house</note> may be seen where the rafters are curved. It may be useful to note here how the two words for "house" spread through the islands; one, which in Malay is *ruma*, varies from that form in San Cristoval to '*ma*' in the Loyalty Islands and Santa Cruz; the other, which is *whare* in New Zealand <note>the Maori word for house</note>, is not nearly as common, but appears as *vale* and *hale* in the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>, and as *vale*, *rathe*, and *va’e* in the Solomon Islands¹. The absence of ancient house-mounds has been observed (page 48) and accounted for by the lack of permanence in village sites.

The floor has sunk below the outside ground level, and this area has been raised around the house by the accumulation of various rubbish. When a new house is to be built, the hollow inside is filled with the debris from outside, and the result is a slight elevation of the site. If an ancient site is seen to be four or five feet high, it must represent a very long period of occupation.

In two islands far apart—Santa Isabel <note>original: Ysabel</note> and Santa Maria—there are very remarkable structures to be seen. In Bugotu, Santa Isabel, Bishop Patteson slept in 1866 in a fortified place described as follows: "The site for the village has been chosen on a hill surrounded by steep, almost vertical coral rocks; the forest has been cleared for some distance all around to prevent any enemy from approaching without being seen. There is a stone wall of considerable height on the side where the rock is less steep, with one narrow entrance. This is reached only by a smooth, slippery tree trunk, laid at a somewhat steep angle over a hollow below." Similarly, at Tega, the people built a <term>toa</term> <note>original: toa; an impregnable fort or defensive position</note> on a rocky knoll in the middle of the village. These forts are built for protection against head-hunters. 

The stone buildings in a village in Gaua, Santa Maria, are very extraordinary; nothing like them has been seen elsewhere in these islands. There are three small <term>gamal</term> houses <note>communal men's houses</note> on platforms about ten feet high, built up with stones that have not been shaped by any tool, some of them being three feet long by two feet deep. The building is wonderfully square and regular; the style is quite <note>original: Cyclopean; referring to ancient masonry made of massive, irregular blocks fitted together without mortar</note> "Cyclopean," with the large stones ingeniously fitted and the gaps <note>original: interstices</note> filled with small stones. 

Besides these platforms, there are two or three obelisks about four feet high, and a small <note>original: dolmen</note> stone table <note>a structure of three stones, usually a flat stone supported by uprights</note>. There are also two <term>wona</term> platforms <note>stone platforms used for social status and ritual ceremonies</note>, such as are always seen near a *gamal* (page 101), but these are much larger and built of large stones put together very squarely. In one of these, there is a passage for pigs with a stone lintel. These remarkable works are shown in the frontispiece of this book. While it cannot be positively denied that such stone-work exists elsewhere in these islands, none has been reported, and in the neighboring islands there...

When he attained a rank in the *suge* <note>original: suge; a graded secret society or men's club central to social life</note> in which he had no equal, and was required to eat alone, he decided to build his *gamal* <note>original: gamal; a communal men's house</note> differently from those of other men. For this purpose, he hired men from Lakona on the same island, where they build their houses with small stones; they selected the stones that suited Vagalo's design and worked under his direction. This example of originality and individual enterprise, which produced a work unique in its kind, is very valuable. It may help explain the mysterious trilithon <note>original: trilithon; a monument consisting of two upright stones supporting a horizontal stone, like those at Stonehenge</note> found in Tonga.

### (3) Cultivations

The Melanesians are a horticultural people. The skill and care with which their gardens were planted and maintained could not fail to impress visitors from the beginning; this distinguished them clearly from the indigenous people of Australia. The Melanesian "laborer" taken to Queensland <note>Between 1863 and 1904, many Pacific Islanders were forcibly or deceptively recruited to work on sugar plantations in Australia, a practice known as "blackbirding."</note> was astonished to find men who, though they were black, had no gardens. These laborers did not bring back very flattering accounts of the white men’s farming methods, either. 

A garden of yams carefully trained to grow on reeds, kept entirely free of weeds, and beautiful with the lush leaves of the vines, is a magnificent sight indeed. For example, in San Cristoval <note>now Makira in the Solomon Islands</note>, gardens with various plots neatly marked and divided within a common fence show a precise respect for individual property rights. Gardens built and worked in terraces on the steep slopes of Meralava were created with great skill and effort. Likewise, the irrigated gardens of edible *caladium* or *arum* <note>original: caladium or arum; types of taro, a starchy root vegetable</note> in Aurora <note>now Maewo</note> and...

<header>Arts of Life. [CH.</header>

The irrigation works of Vanua Lava (if any survive the ruin caused by the labor trade <note>The "labor trade" or "blackbirding" involved the often forced removal of Pacific Islanders to work on plantations in Australia and Fiji, which devastated local populations.</note> on that island) are proof of considerable and very ancient skill in cultivation. The edible caladium <note>original: esculent caladium; commonly known today as taro</note> is grown for food in Egypt and Syria, and its use stretches in an unbroken chain from China throughout the islands of the Indian and Pacific Oceans. It is no accident that a dry garden, as opposed to an irrigated one, is called an *uma* in both Sumatra and the New Hebrides¹. The respective shares of men and women in garden work are settled by local custom. Cultivation has produced a wonderful variety in yams, bananas, breadfruit, and no doubt other common food-producing plants. I have a list of eighty names for different varieties of yams and sixty for breadfruit grown on the small island of Mota, most of which an experienced native recognizes and names at once. It may be said generally that the natives are fond of planting flowering shrubs and sweet herbs around their villages, but this is much more common in the Banks' Islands and the New Hebrides than in the Solomon Islands. The beauty and variety of hibiscus, croton, dracaena, acalypha, and amaranthus are surprising; no village is without its ornamental plants and flowers. In the Banks' Islands, they know how to graft the various kinds of croton. They take two young branches of equal size and break the end off each, removing an inch of the bark from the "stock" <note>the rooted part of the plant</note> and the same length of wood from the "scion" <note>the detached shoot being joined to the stock</note>, bringing the bark of each to meet exactly. This is only done during damp, hot weather.
