<page-num>305</page-num>
<header>XVI. Weapons and Fighting</header>

No one who has seen much of native life would deny that the bow is used in war, although in places like Florida <note>Florida Island, now known as Nggela Sule</note>, for example, its use is not actually that rare. In Florida, Guadalcanal, Isabel, San Cristobal, and to a lesser extent in Malaita, the standard practice is to fight with spears. This fashion may not be very old, at least if we consider the accounts of the first European explorers to be accurate. 

The use of the spear is accompanied by the shield; however, the spearmen of San Cristobal do not use such a defense. Instead, they deflect spears thrown at them with long, curved blades <term>glaives</term>, and the shields used in Florida are not actually manufactured on that island. Spears are generally made of palm wood, or ebony in Isabel. Most are barbed, but in Florida, the *kona* <note>a specific type of spear</note> are tipped with human leg bones that have been cut and broken into jagged points. 

Fighting with spears in the open, such as on a beach, does not usually result in many deaths and often resembles a series of individual duels. When a man was hit, his enemy would rush toward him with a club. There are occasions when a coordinated attack is made upon a village by enemies who have secured the help of numerous allies through payments and promises. Such an attack, if not immediately successful or defeated, becomes something like a siege. However, an open spear fight—the mutual spearing known in Florida as *vei tologoni*—is not common.¹ Ambushes set around a village at night, or waiting for a lone man on a path, are more frequent and lethal; in these encounters, the tomahawk <note>likely a metal axe acquired through trade</note> is now the most effective weapon. 

When a young warrior in Florida killed his first man, he would let the blood run from the weapon into his mouth. The bows of Malaita, which are powerful weapons, are commonly used in war on that island. Slings are also known in the Solomon Islands and are said to have been brought into use for attacking houses built in trees. Men never like to travel without carrying something in their hands to be used as a weapon...

---

¹ According to the account given by Takua <note>a prominent local leader</note> regarding the famous battle that established his authority in Florida, 200 canoes gathered from neighboring areas to attack Ta-na-ihu. Because their first attack was anticipated and therefore unsuccessful, they fought with spears on the slope of the hill for three days. The attackers then withdrew without significant losses on either side.

...in a sudden quarrel perhaps. In Florida <note>Florida Island, now known as Nggela Sule</note> and nearby areas, a paddle-shaped club is a favorite weapon to carry while walking; it is called *rau ni Aba*, or "the leaf of Aba," named after a place on Guadalcanal where they are manufactured. The spears, shields, clubs, bows, and arrows of the Solomon Islands are commonly found in museums. The spear <note>original: "isar"</note>¹ is practically unknown as a weapon in the Banks Islands; however, it is used alongside the bow in Ambrym. The Espiritu Santo spear, with its triple point and graduated barbs made of human bone, is perhaps the most terrifying of all these weapons. In places where they fought with bows, such as the Banks Islands, open battles were not common. Instead, there was much shouting of defiance, cursing, abuse, and boasting. Warriors would stamp their heels and grip the ground with their toes—a major sign of bravery—but this resulted in very little bloodshed². Slings, called *talvava* in the Banks Islands, were used chiefly in defense against a night attack. When an attack was expected, men would occasionally sling stones down the paths the enemy would likely use to approach; however, skilled slingers could also be very effective in a general fight. Clubs in the Banks Islands never seem to have been the carefully, and indeed beautifully, shaped weapons used in the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>; in the latter islands, these clubs are used to ward off arrows during combat.

The Melanesian weapons, however, which demand the most attention and require the most explanation, are the poisoned arrows, which are still poorly understood. The belief in the deadly toxicity of the poison used, and in the gruesome methods of preparing it, is too firmly established to be easily dismissed. Yet, a careful examination of poisoned arrows and their effects by English and French medical officers has twice resulted...

<page-num>307</page-num>
<header>XVI.] Poisoned Arrows.</header>

...belief carries over into the declaration that the supposed poison on the arrows is not actually poisonous, and that therefore the fatal effects of arrow wounds are not caused by the preparation believed to be toxic¹. From a scientific perspective, then, the view is clear; yet if we look at the matter from the local perspective, it is equally plain that the deadly quality they believe these weapons possess does not belong to what can strictly be called poison.

As mentioned previously (page 213), the Melanesian preparations used to make food deadly were not truly poisonous in a chemical sense. The effect was not thought to be produced by the natural properties of the substance used, but entirely by supernatural properties granted through magic arts—this was true even if the materials employed happened to have some harmful qualities. This is most certainly the local view of what they call "poison" on their arrows. What they seek, and firmly believe they achieve, is an arrow that possesses supernatural power, *mana* <note>a Melanesian term for spiritual or supernatural efficacy</note>, to cause harm. This power resides both in the material from which the arrow is made and in the qualities added through charms and magical rituals.

---

¹ "An Inquiry into the Supposed Poisonous Nature of the Arrows of the South Sea Islanders," by Staff-Surgeon A. B. Messer, M.D., Royal Navy (published by the Authority of the Lords of the Admiralty, 1876), reaches the following conclusions, among others: "That in the numerous cases in which men have been wounded by these arrows, no recorded instances are known of poisonous effects following." It also states, "That 'locked-jaw' <note>tetanus</note> is not the result of poison on the arrows; and as this disease is the only cause of death following these wounds, the arrows themselves are not in any way dangerous beyond the severity of the physical wounds and the conditions under which they are received." 

The Report of the Commission appointed by the Governor of New Caledonia in 1883 is quoted by Mr. Romilly in the chapter on Poisoned Arrows in *The Western Pacific and New Guinea* as completely dismissing "the popular notion of the fatal nature of these weapons." As Mr. Romilly refers to me personally, I may say that in the two cases he mentioned, the man who died had been little influenced by Mission teaching, while the one who survived had been greatly influenced by it. It is reasonable to attribute much of the survivor's lack of alarm and distress to that teaching. His constant exclamation was, "My mind is easy, I have heard the Bishop." In that year, 1870, I easily obtained information concerning these arrows in the Banks Islands, which is set forth here; everything I have learned since from other islands has shown this information to be correct. I do not remember hearing about the "renewal" of the poison, though that is likely enough.

preparations. The fact that a puncture wound in the tropics is often followed by tetanus (lockjaw), or that a fine point of bone breaking off in a wound is certainly dangerous and likely fatal, or that an acrid <note>original: "acrid" - sharp, stinging, or irritating</note> or burning substance introduced into the wound by the arrow will increase inflammation—these facts are completely outside the local perspective. The point is made from a dead man's bone and therefore possesses *mana* <term>spiritual or supernatural power</term>. It has been tied on with powerful *mana* charms and smeared with a substance that is "hot and burning"—just as the wound is intended to be—prepared and applied with magical spells. This is what they mean by what we, but not they, call "poisoned arrows." Once a wound is inflicted, its fatal effect is meant to be supported and sustained by the same magic that gave the weapon its supernatural power.

<margin>What we call "poisoned arrows" <note>See footnote 1</note> are used in the Solomon Islands, Santa Cruz, the Banks Islands, and the New Hebrides <note>now the nation of Vanuatu</note>.</margin> In the Torres Islands and Lepers’ Island <note>now Omba or Aoba in Vanuatu</note>, arrows used for fighting are not "poisoned," yet they belong to the exact same class as those that are; they are just as highly valued, trusted, and feared as the others—a very informative fact. On Lepers’ Island, both types are used. There is a significant difference in the size and weight of arrows from various islands, as well as in the proportions of their parts, but the structure is the same everywhere. There is a reed shaft, a foreshaft made of hard wood, tree-fern, or palm, and a point made of human bone. The point is inserted into the foreshaft, and the foreshaft into the main shaft; the joints are then firmly bound with fine string or fiber. <margin>^</margin> Santa Cruz arrows are consistently nearly four feet long and weigh about two ounces. Banks Islands arrows are about three feet nine inches long and weigh about an <margin>L</margin> ounce. Torres Islands arrows are only two feet ten inches long, weighing three-quarters of an ounce. One type of arrow has a head one foot long, an eight-inch foreshaft, and a twenty-inch reed shaft. The first is a heavy and powerful weapon requiring a large and powerful bow; the other is light and weak, hardly more than a human bone shaped for use with a bow. One is poisoned while the other is not, yet in the local estimation, both are equally deadly. Some arrows from the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note> and the Solomon Islands have a very small point made of bone. It is the human bone, above all else, that in the local opinion gives the arrow its effectiveness. The bone of any deceased person will suffice because any ghost possesses *mana* <term>supernatural or spiritual power</term> to affect the wounded person; however, the bone of a man who was powerful during his lifetime is more highly valued¹.

<margin>Handwritten vertical line and bracket mark in the right margin next to the start of the paragraph; a slash mark in the margin next to the word "magical".</margin>
Although it is the human bone that primarily gives the arrow its deadly quality, the bone must still be attached to the shaft using the magic charms that secure supernatural power for the weapon. The maker sings or mutters charms as he ties the bone to the foreshaft; consequently, as I have been told, the *mana* is concentrated where the bone joins the foreshaft. These charms are known only to a few specialists whose business it is to make the arrows. Nevertheless, if someone—as did a young man on Omba <note>formerly Lepers' Island</note> who made arrows from his brother’s bones—were to take the bones of someone he knew in life and call upon his ghost while binding on the head, his arrows would undoubtedly be considered perfectly prepared. The "poison," likewise, is an addition to the power of the bone; the magical effectiveness of this preparation is added to the supernatural power already residing in the dead man’s bone. Once the bone has inflicted a wound, the dead man’s power, which had been directed into the arrow through incantations <note>original: "incantations" — ritual chants or spells</note>, would ensure the wound is fatal. The preparation of burning juices mixed with charms, and smeared—

¹ The authentic Lepers' Island arrow, called a *lirae*, is made with a broad, white, jagged head of human bone about nine or ten inches long, without any poisonous preparation. They also use poisoned arrows manufactured in or purchased from Maewo. To create the *lirae*, the leg bones of ordinary men are exhumed from their graves. Not long ago, there was a man on that island who, out of affection for his deceased brother, dug him up and fashioned arrows from his bones. He went about with these, referring to himself as "I and my brother." Everyone was afraid of him, for they believed that his dead brother’s ghost was present to help him.

The charms placed upon the bone carry something like inflammation itself to the wound, and the ghost will cause it to inflame.

The treatment of the wounded man follows the same principle of sympathetic magic. If the arrow, or a part of it, has been left in the wound or extracted using leaf poultices, the fragments are kept in a damp place or wrapped in cool leaves; it is believed that this will keep the inflammation low and cause it to subside quickly. Shells, which have been empowered by charms, are kept rattling above the house where the wounded man lies to ward off the hostile ghost. In the same way, the man who inflicted the wound does not stop after firing the shot. He and his friends will drink hot and stinging juices and chew irritating leaves; pungent and bitter herbs will be burned to create an irritating smoke. A bundle of leaves known to the shooter or bought from a wizard—a <term>qesis</term> <note>a magical charm bundle</note>—will be tied to the bow that fired the arrow to ensure a fatal outcome. The arrowhead, if recovered, will be placed in the fire. The bow itself will be kept near the fire to make the wound it inflicted "hot," or, as is the custom on Lepers' Island <note>now Ambae</note>, it will be placed in a cave haunted by a ghost. The bowstring will be kept pulled tight and plucked occasionally to cause nerve tension and the spasms of tetanus <note>lockjaw, a common fatal complication of wounds described here</note> in the wounded man.

The preparation of the poisoned arrows in Aurora <note>now Maewo</note>, New Hebrides, is described as follows by a native writer:

> "When they have dug up a deceased person's bone, they break it into splinters, shape it correctly, and sit down to rub it against a piece of brain-coral with water. After that, it is fixed into a piece of tree-fern wood; not everyone can do this, only someone who knows the necessary charms. When that is done, the thick juice of the <term>no-to</term> <note>original: *excævaria agallocha*; the milky mangrove or 'blind-your-eye' tree, known for its irritating sap</note> is applied to it. Then it is placed in a cool spot on the side wall of a public hall where no fire is lit, so that the cold may settle on it and it may become moldy. Then they dig up the root of a vine they call <term>loki</term>, and after stripping off the bark, they scrape the inner fibers into a leaf. That leaf is wrapped in another and placed on the fire. When it is cooked, it is wrapped in the fibrous web from the leaf-sheath of a coconut tree and squeezed into a leaf of the nettle tree. Then, using a stick, they..."

They are then kept indoors, wrapped up, for five days, after which the substance turns white. Another mixture, thought to cause more inflammation and to act more quickly, is made with the juice of *toi*, a species of <term>euphorbia</term> <note>a genus of plants commonly known as spurge, often containing a milky, irritating sap</note>. The common result of a wound from any of these arrows—whether "poisoned" or made of bare bone—is certainly <term>tetanus</term> <note>a serious bacterial infection that causes painful muscle spasms and lockjaw</note>, which is expected by the natives. Even if, however, the *loki* <note>a climbing plant used in the poison mixture</note> is, as has been supposed, some kind of strychnine, it is well established that this is not the actual cause of the disease. If it is asked how the very common belief arose that these arrows are poisoned with putrefying human flesh, when the preparation is actually wholly vegetable as described above, I can only conjecture that the natives answered "dead man" to the inquiries of early traders. The native meant that the deadly qualities of the weapon came from the "dead man" whose bone was used to make the arrow head;

Europeans, conceptualizing this as poison rather than magic, assumed that the "poison" was derived from a human corpse. If it is asked why—if the arrows are not actually toxic—the islanders are so afraid of them and careful not to touch them, it is enough to say that they firmly believe they are deadly. This conviction will likely outlast their belief in the specific power of the supernatural charms used to create them.

(5) ***Tools and Implements.*** 

Before the introduction of metal, the adzes <term>adze</term> <note>a tool similar to an axe, but with the blade set at a right angle to the handle, used for smoothing or carving wood</note> with which most native work was performed were made of stone in some islands and shell in others. The division is very distinct: the Solomon Islanders (except for those on Rennell and Bellona) use stone, as do the people of the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>. Conversely, the people of Santa Cruz, the Torres Islands, <margin>Materials used for tools</margin> and the Banks Islands used shell—specifically the shell of the giant clam. 

The form of the stone adzes from Florida Island and the shell adzes from Santa Cruz is the same: roughly cylindrical, with the cutting edge being a segment of the tool's circumference. The stone adzes of the Eastern Solomon Islands and the New Hebrides, as well as the shell <margin>Regional variations in tool shape</margin> adzes of the Banks Islands, share a different general form: a long oval cross-section where the flattish sides meet to form the edge. The shell adzes of Santa Cruz are beautifully finished, while those of the Banks Islands are often very rough.

In the Banks Islands, the cream squeezed out from grated coconut was often cooked over the embers in the shells. The bowls of the south-eastern Solomon Islands—some of them remarkable for their enormous size, some for their fantastic shape, and all for their truly beautiful ornamentation—represent the practice of stone-boiling <term>stone-boiling</term> <note>a method of cooking by placing heated stones into a vessel filled with water or food</note> in their purpose, if not always in their daily use. The oval wooden bowls, called *wumeto*, of the Banks Islands sometimes stand on legs. The pestles in very active use there for making a mash called *lot* in broad wooden dishes are made of wood. These are sometimes decorated with the figure of a bird at the upper end—an almost unique instance of carved figure ornamentation on the tools of these people. It goes without saying that all Melanesian people are mat-makers; the remarkable thing is that in Santa Cruz alone is found a loom with which beautiful mats are woven using the fiber of a banana tree cultivated specifically for that purpose. These looms are identical to those used in the Caroline and Philippine Islands and in Borneo.

### (6) Fishing

A large part of the livelihood of Melanesians is generally and naturally derived from the sea, though the character of the shoreline affects the extent of the fishing industry. Something to eat alongside vegetable food is always sought after, and shellfish, octopus, and similar items from the reefs are in daily demand. Fish are caught by angling from the shore or from canoes, by nets, by shooting with arrows or spearing, in woven pots <note>fish traps made of wicker or basketry</note>, by using poison, and by the use of torches at night.

Hooks, which are now generally replaced by modern versions, were most commonly made of tortoise-shell. In the Solomon Islands, the hook common in the Pacific was beautifully crafted: a piece of mother-of-pearl, with or without a wooden back, had a tortoise-shell hook bound to it with a few beads on a short string, requiring no bait <note>this functioned as a lure, mimicking the appearance of a small fish or insect</note>. The very small fish-hooks made of mother-of-pearl and tortoise-shell—either material alone, or a type of shell that might imitate a beetle—found at Savo, San Cristoval <note>now known as Makira</note>, and Ulawa, were among the prettiest and most skillful products of native handiwork. The flying-fish is caught not with a hook, but with a double prickle <term>double prickle</term> <note>a type of gorge hook where a straight, sharp piece is swallowed by the fish and then pivots to become stuck</note> made of tortoise-shell or spines from palm trees.

When a fish is seen above the net, the line is hauled up; the ends of the rods come together, and the net forms a bag that traps the fish. Fishing with a kite is practiced in the Solomon Islands and Santa Cruz. The kite is flown from a canoe, trailing a line with a cluster of spider webs or fiber. As the kite drags this along the surface of the water, fish with projecting lower jaws get their teeth entangled in the material. On Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae Island in Vanuatu</note>, small fish are caught in nets made of spider webs; in the Banks Islands, they are driven by children into barricades of dead coral. 

A unique method of catching sharks is practiced at San Cristoval <note>now Makira</note>, which is said to have been adopted from Santa Cruz. An outrigger canoe <term>outrigger canoe</term> <note>a boat with a lateral support float fastened to one or both sides of the hull</note> is used with a bamboo platform built over the outrigger. One man paddles the canoe while another on the platform shakes coconut shells strung on a loop of bamboo to attract a shark with the sound. When a shark approaches, the man lures it with a fish and prepares a noose. Once the shark swims into the noose, it is caught, hauled onto the platform, and killed with a club. This takes place some distance from the shore to avoid dangerous man-eating sharks, as the ones caught in this manner are intended for food. 

The dugong <term>dugong</term> <note>a large marine mammal similar to a manatee</note> is caught, though rarely, at the Bugotu end of Ysabel Island. The reef and lagoon between Ra and Motlav islands is occasionally the scene of an exciting fish hunt, where a school of fish is driven into the shallow reef by a long line of people shouting and slapping the water with their hands. I have seen at Lakona on Santa Maria, and no doubt the same thing is seen elsewhere, a large fish trap in which reed fences guide the fish into circular enclosures as the tide recedes, from which they cannot escape. Stone walls designed to trap fish as the tide ebbs are common in the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>. 

Freshwater fish are abundant wherever there are streams and lakes. Some are recognized by the locals as living only in freshwater; others, they say, live in both the river and the sea, *sale rua tasi* <note>original: "sale rua tasi"; literally "belonging to two waters"</note>. In the mud of the irrigated gardens of Aurora <note>now Maewo</note>, an edible fish is found. Eels are abundant but are not eaten in some places. In the *tas* <note>original: "tas"; the local word for lake or sea</note>, the lake of Santa Maria <note>Gaua Island</note>, the eels grow very large. When the water level is low, the people dig pits along the edge of the lake, and the eels make their way into these when the water

### (7) Food and Cooking. 

The yam is undoubtedly the primary staple food of the Melanesians, although in some areas *taro*—the edible caladium plant—is grown much more extensively. Observers have noted that a single island can have a vast number of yam varieties. There is also a significant difference in the general shape of the tubers between the eastern and western island groups. For instance, Solomon Island yams are round, compact, and not very large. In contrast, in the New Hebrides <note>now Vanuatu</note>, at least one yam has been measured against the height of a man and found to be over six feet long. 

A species of yam with a prickly vine is very commonly grown; it is known as *tomago* in the Banks Islands, *mitopu* in Santa Cruz, *pana* in Florida Island <note>Nggela Sule</note>, and *hana* in San Cristoval <note>Makira</note>. Another prickly variety, the *qauro*, grows wild in the Banks Islands. It is sometimes cultivated there and eaten during times of food scarcity after being grated and washed in seawater. 

The caladium is only called *taro* by the locals when they believe they are speaking English. There are many varieties of this plant grown in the dry soil of the hills, as well as in the expertly irrigated gardens of Aurora <note>Maewo Island</note>. The giant caladium—called *via* in both the Banks Islands and Madagascar—is eaten in the New Hebrides and the Solomon Islands. 

Bananas also provide a great deal of food in numerous varieties. On Lepers' Island <note>Ambae Island</note>, the fruit seems to be a larger part of the diet than in other places. Breadfruit is rare in the Solomon Islands but is perhaps most abundant at Mota and the other Banks Islands. In those locations, it forms an important part of the food supply; it is dried over a fire, wrapped in strips of leaves (a technique also used in the Solomon Islands), and preserved in chests. The practice of making *madrai* <note>a Fijian food made from fermented breadfruit or starchy roots</note> is not found here. In the Banks Islands, the pith of the sago palm is processed by washing it into...

sago starch in a trough made from the tree's stem and cooked into cakes, but it is rarely used as a staple food. In Santa Cruz, however, it occupies an important place in the diet; sago pith cooked whole was the main provision for canoes from Tikopia that visited the Banks Islands one year during my stay. 

Melanesian natives are very fond of mashing yams, taro, and breadfruit, eating the resulting puddings with a sauce made from the creamy juice squeezed from grated coconuts. This sauce is cooked either by stone-boiling <note>a method of boiling liquids by dropping fire-heated stones into a vessel</note> or in coconut shells over a slow fire. The leaves of a hibiscus (similar to the <term>manihot</term> <note>cassava or manioc</note>) and those of many other trees are cooked in the ovens. Tapioca has also been introduced to the islands. 

The nuts of the <term>canarium</term> <note>original: "canarium"; the Pacific almond or Galip nut</note> have a very important place in native cooking. While a fair amount of cooking is done by roasting items like fish, mashed food, or eggs—wrapped in leaves and laid upon the embers—and thin yams that are continually scraped and turned, all substantial meals are prepared in the native oven. Although there are differences in local details, the general method is the same and the result is excellent, as the food is steamed in its own juices. 

The hole in the ground that forms the oven is usually a permanent fixture, with its pile of fire-resistant stones lying nearby. A fire is lit in the hole, which is lined with stones; this heats both the lining stones and others heaped on top of the flames. When the fire has burnt down, these upper stones are removed with wooden tongs. The food, wrapped in leaves, is arranged inside, and the hot stones are placed between the larger parcels and over the top. The entire oven is then sealed with leaves or sometimes covered with earth. Water, either salt or fresh, is poured in to create steam, and the cooks carefully watch for and seal any gaps where steam might escape. 

This process is time-consuming and occupies much of the day for the native men, who cook for themselves. It is perhaps a pity that the introduction of iron pots and saucepans is changing native cooking for the worse, likely because they are faster to use. Great care is taken to wash one's hands before cooking; to eat <term>panlepa</term> <note>a Banks Islands term meaning to eat with dirty hands</note> is considered a disgrace in the Banks Islands. Fire is produced using the stick-and-groove method <note>rubbing a hard stick along a groove in a softer piece of wood until the friction creates an ember</note>.

<header>Dress.</header>

Bark cloth is made from the paper mulberry, though somewhat crudely, in Ysabel and worn in Florida; until recently, it was also made in Ulawa and San Cristoval. A rougher kind, perhaps always made from the bark of banyan figs, is used in the New Hebrides. When such cloth was in use, the local name for it—such as *tivi* in Ysabel and Florida, or *sala* in Ulawa—was readily adopted for European cloth. In Aurora, the word *garu* is used for cloth, and in the Banks Islands nearest to Aurora, *gagaru* is used; these are undoubtedly identical to the Maori words *kahu* and *kakahu*. 

In Mota, the word *siopa* was immediately applied to European clothes. This was surprising, as the natives there knew nothing of *tapa* <note>original: "tapa"; bark cloth made in many parts of the Pacific</note>. The native explanation is that the Tongans, who visited the Banks Islands for two years and established a short-lived settlement on Qakea, wore *siopa*. The inhabitants have, in fact, shifted the vowels in *siapo* or *hiapo* (related to the Maori *hiako*, meaning "bark"), which is the name for bark cloth in Tonga and Samoa. In Motlav, the word *malsam* was applied to cloth; its first syllable is likely the common word *malo* used in Fiji and elsewhere. 

It is strange that among the people of the Banks Islands, where the men were content to go without any covering at all, the art of making a very handsome and elaborate dress was known. This was the *malo saru* <term>malo saru</term> <note>a ceremonial garment put over the head, made of variegated matting</note>, which consisted of four pieces of variegated matting joined at the neck. It was worn during dances by those of high enough rank to do so. This art died out some years ago with the last two men who practiced it. Two *malo saru*—probably the only existing examples—are kept in the British Museum, one of which is shown on page 108. From all appearances, the work, which closely resembles that of the Santa Cruz mats, must have been produced on a type of loom, just as those mats were.

The dress of women varies remarkably and does not always correspond with the changes in men's attire. In Florida and the neighboring Solomon Islands, where male dress is minimal but perhaps sufficient, the women wear short petticoats made of fiber. In the south-eastern Solomon Islands, male attire is very sparse, and the women are satisfied with a fringe. Conversely, the men at Santa Cruz are extensively dressed in what might be called the clothing of the...

On Lepers' Island <note>original: "Lepers' Island"; now known as Ambae in Vanuatu</note>, a crimson dye is applied to mats through a stencil made of banana leaf.

(9) **Money.** In all the islands currently being discussed, there is some recognized medium of exchange, but the shell currency of the Banks Islands and of the Solomon Islands is perhaps the only one truly worthy of the name "money." It is likely that the most popular personal ornaments everywhere have a certain relative value and are exchanged for food, other necessities, and the general equipment of native life. In addition to these, there are industrial products made for the sole purpose of exchange, which may be called mat-money, feather-money, and shell-money. 

Mat-money is used in the northern New Hebrides, specifically on Aurora <note>now Maewo</note>, Pentecost, and Lepers' Island. These mats are long and narrow, created for no other purpose than to represent value; on Aurora and Lepers' Island, they are valued more the older and blacker they become. Women weave <note>original: "plait"</note> them—either family members or women hired for the task. On Aurora, the name for these is *malo* <note>original: "malo"</note>, which is also the name of the dress worn by some men there, as it is by all men on Lepers' Island. 

The mats are stored in small houses specially built for them, in which a fire is kept constantly burning to blacken them; when they are thick with soot, they are considered particularly valuable. Their value, however, is determined by the number of folds, which are counted in tens; a mat of twenty folds is called "double," and one of thirty folds is called "treble." Although these mats can be used to buy anything of equal value, they are mostly used for purchasing advancements <note>original: "steps"</note> in the *Suqe* <term>Suqe</term> <note>a graded secret society or social club prevalent in northern Vanuatu</note>. If a man wants to raise funds for this, he sends a pig into a village where he knows mats are available, and he receives mats of less value than his pig; when he can return the mats, he recovers his pig <note>this functions as a form of collateral or pawnbroking</note>. 

On Lepers' Island and on Pentecost, these mats are called *maraka* <note>original: "maraka"</note>. On Pentecost, red mats called *bwana* <note>original: "bwana"; a word which means "pandanus" on San Cristobal</note> are of the highest value. On Lepers' Island, the ancient and decaying ones that have hung in the house for a long time are very highly prized, though the value is still determined by the number

A middle-sized mat can buy a tusked pig. A wealthy man will keep fifty mats or more in his house, hung up and left to decay as a visible proof of his ancient wealth. Mat-money is also lent at interest, and thus becomes a source of further wealth. There is no fixed rate of interest; the lender receives whatever amount he is able to demand, up to a double return. In these three islands <note>Aurora (Maewo), Pentecost, and Lepers' Island (Ambae)</note>, the shell discs known as *som* and *hom* are beautifully prepared and crafted into armlets and necklaces. These are highly valued, but they are not used as a form of money.

**Feather-money** is unique to Santa Cruz. It is made from the small red feathers found under the wings of a parrot, the *Trichoglossus Massena* <note>the Coconut Lorikeet</note>. These birds are caught in the deep forest, where they are very tame, using bird-lime <note>a sticky substance</note> smeared on a rod. A man carries this rod in his hand, and the birds perch upon it. To ensure success, the hunter must take care not to eat anything hot or fatty, or the birds will not approach him. 

The small red feathers are first glued onto pigeon feathers, and these are then bound onto a prepared foundation in rows, so that only the red color is visible. A length of this feather-money, called *tauau*, is about fifteen feet long; it is coiled up and stored with specific ornaments. Short pieces are also made for convenience when negotiating prices. On festive occasions, the dancing ground, known as the *nava*—which is fenced in with huge discs of coral—is decorated with the uncoiled feather-money belonging to those hosting the feast.

<header>XVI.] Money.</header>

...the ears of the flying-fox are used in the same way as feathers <note>referring to the feather-money described on the previous page</note>. Shell-money in the Solomon Islands and the Banks Islands differs widely in one respect. In the Solomon Islands, it is carefully and evenly made in some places and consists of two types of lesser and greater relative value <gloss>1</gloss>. In contrast, in the Banks Islands, the shell-money is universally rough and unfinished, with only the quantity being of concern. However, in the Banks Islands, the actual character of money is more clearly defined, and the practice of money-dealing is surprisingly developed. 

In the Solomon Islands, porpoise teeth in San Cristoval and Malaita, and dogs' teeth in Florida and Ysabel, are used as currency with a fairly fixed value. Regarding dogs' teeth, only the teeth immediately behind the canines are considered valuable; for these to be worth much, they must be very white and sound <gloss>2</gloss>. 

The shell-money used in Florida and at Saa is manufactured at Alite and is mostly exchanged for pigs. The discs are carefully and accurately made from certain shells that are broken and then rubbed into shape. The holes for stringing are drilled with a pump-drill—called <term>puputa</term> in Florida and <term>nono</term> in San Cristoval—which is fitted with a point of flint or obsidian. These discs serve as ornaments as well as currency. The money is either white, <term>turombuto</term>, or red, <term>rongo</term>. Generally, all of it is referred to as <term>rongo</term>, and there does not appear to be a fixed exchange rate between the two types. Six coils, totaling about ten fathoms <note>a fathom is approximately six feet, measured by the span of a man's outstretched arms</note>, is called a <term>rongo</term>, and ten <term>rongo</term> of either red or white is an <term>isa</term>. 

Anything can be purchased with shell-money. While the money is lent, it is done without interest in the Solomon Islands. In this final detail, the Banks Islanders are so advanced that it is difficult to believe they are so uncivilized in other respects. While their material currency is crude, their systems and terms for money-lending are extremely elaborate. To create the money, the body of a shell, <term>som</term>, is broken, and the tip is rubbed on a stone using a pointed stick inserted into the broken end until the inner portion is reached...

<gloss>2</gloss> In Florida, one dog's tooth is equal in value to five porpoise teeth. In San Cristoval, one dog's tooth is worth one or two porpoise teeth, depending on the quality.

<meta>This page continues the description of the production and valuation of shell-money in the Banks Islands, specifically detailing the manufacturing process, the counting system, and the social practices of debt and interest.</meta>

<page-num>326</page-num>
<header>Arts of Life. [CH. XVI.]</header>

Once the hollow of the shell is reached, a stick is inserted into the hole appearing at the tip. Then, the broken base of the shell is ground smooth against a stone. In this way, one shell is used for each individual disc; no drill is needed, and in fact, none is known in this region. 

The shell discs are strung onto a slender strip of hibiscus bark. This shell-money, called <term>som</term>, is acceptable for any kind of purchase, but its primary use is for buying advancement through the ranks of the <term>Suqe</term> Club <note>the Suqe was a prominent graded secret society that determined social status</note>. 

The <term>som</term> is organized and counted in coils. Two sticks are driven into the ground, and the money is wound (<term>siga</term>) around them. A single turn from one stick to the other and back again is called a <term>tal</term>. Ten rounds (<term>tal sangavul</term>) constitute a hank or coil, known as a <term>qatagiu</term>. When the quantity is less than a full <term>qatagiu</term>, it is counted by the number of <term>tal</term>. The length of a full turn is one fathom—the measurement of a man’s outstretched arms, called <term>rova togtogoa</term>. If a smaller measurement is used, the <term>qatagiu</term> is named accordingly. 

Wealthy men accumulate large quantities of this money, though possessing one hundred <term>qatagiu</term> is enough to make a man considered rich. This accumulation results from the systems of the <term>Suqe</term> and <term>Tamate</term> Clubs <note>secret societies described in chapters 5 and 6</note>, as well as from the practice of money-lending. However, according to local beliefs, the unseen spiritual influence called <term>mana</term> is the true cause of wealth. 

The rate of interest is 100 percent <note>original: "cent. per cent."</note> regardless of how much time has passed. When a man borrows (<term>aru</term>) and an owner lends (<term>tawe</term>), a debt (<term>pug</term>) is established. A debt is not only created by borrowing; sometimes a rich man will impose a loan on a friend. For the sake of his own reputation, the friend is obligated to accept the loan and eventually repay it with a double return. 

The pressure put on a debtor who fails to pay when payment is demanded is remarkably effective. All the men from the creditor’s village, bringing their wives with them, come and sit on the debtor’s property. The debtor must light his fire and cook food for all of them. If the payment is not produced, they stay overnight, go home the next morning, and repeat the visit after a while. Eventually, the debtor’s neighbors and friends pity him and help him with food and money until he scrapes enough together to pay the debt. A man borrowing money from a friend to pay off a debt asks him—

to shield him, *ti goro*, or to stand between him and his creditor. If a man borrows money and then lends that same money to another person, he is said to *tul* the lender—meaning to treat him unfairly. If a man uses money he has borrowed from one person to pay off a different creditor, he is said to divert the payment, *viro goro*, into a different channel. 

When a man borrows, for example, ten strings of money from another, he will often make the creditor his own debtor as well by lending that person about four strings of his own money. This smaller counter-loan is called a *tano rarav*, or a "drawing-place." To make such a loan is described as "putting down rollers in the path," *lango goro*, as if one were preparing to haul up a canoe. This practice is thought to make the transaction easier for the original borrower; because he has now also become a creditor, he cannot be so easily pressured for repayment <note>original: "dunned"</note> by the person he borrowed from.

To pay a debt is to "close it up," *wono*. Money transactions play a major role in indigenous life: social advancement is secured by possessing shell-money, because a person cannot take the necessary steps to rise in the <term>Suqe Club</term> <note>a graded secret society central to Melanesian social life</note> without it. Social status is maintained through wealth because a moneyed man holds his debtors under his thumb; by his power to force a loan upon others, he can turn rising men into his debtors and effectively hold them back. 

Through the institution of the Suqe, money was kept in constant circulation in both large and small quantities. The tiny reef island of Rowa supplies common money, as well as a finer variety used only as decoration. This ornamental money is sometimes extremely small and delicately made. Before the introduction of glass beads, it was occasionally strung with a unique stone or a growth <note>original: "concretion"</note> from a shell¹. In the Torres Islands, where the natural materials for shell-money are not found, the people now trade with beads. These beads have, to some extent, replaced shell-money for small purchases in the Banks Islands as well. Formerly, their very attractive arrows were used as a form of—

1. Starting in the west, any distinctive features can be found in the ornamentation appearing on the lime-boxes of Ysabel <note>Santa Isabel</note>. However, there is and has been so much interaction with islands further west that the style of New Britain ornament is represented in certain items, such as the paddles of Bugotu. The beautifully made and decorated shields and clubs that have been common on Florida Island <note>the Nggela Islands</note> were actually manufactured on Guadalcanal; the clam-shell discs covered with a plate of tortoise-shell, carved into an open-work pattern, belong to all these western islands. Patterns of lines and circles used in tattooing or carved into coconut bottles are also characteristic of this region.

# CHAPTER XVII.

## DANCES. MUSIC. GAMES.

(1) **_Dances_**. It can be confidently stated that in the Melanesian islands discussed here, dances have absolutely no religious or superstitious character, even though visitors frequently identify them as "devil dances" and "devil grounds." <note>The author is correcting common European misconceptions that local customs were inherently satanic or religious.</note> Men and women always dance separately. The songs that accompany these dances are undoubtedly indecent in some cases, and while I have never heard of any indecent dances myself, I would by no means deny that they exist. 

One might think there is a superstitious element in dances where the performers are supposed to be "ghosts," but this is only because ghosts are believed to enjoy dancing just as much as living men. Similarly, it might be assumed that when members of the <term>*tamate*</term> <note>original: "ghost clubs"; these were secret societies or spirit associations</note> dance in masks representing birds or fish, they are dancing to honor what might be called their "totems." However, there is not the slightest reason to believe that these club emblems possess any such character. 

On the island of Ambrym <note>now part of Vanuatu</note>, a drum is set up when a death-feast is celebrated. This drum is carved into the likeness of a face and is undoubtedly meant to represent the deceased person. Consequently, one could say that dances are performed before images of ancestors, and the deceased might be referred to as either a "god" or a "devil" depending on the terms used. <note>The author notes that these terms are often translations of local words for spirits that do not carry the same moral weight as in English.</note> Nevertheless, it is ultimately just a festival held in memory of a recently deceased member of the community, and the dancing and drumming are simply parts of the festivity. 

Women’s dances are everywhere ungraceful and uninteresting; in the <term>*rorohi*</term> <note>a traditional dance of the Nggela Islands</note> of Florida <note>the Nggela Islands, Solomon Islands</note>, they sway their bodies...

<summary>This page argues that Melanesian dances are social and commemorative rather than religious or "totemic," clarifying that even "ghost" masks and ancestor drums are part of community festivals rather than worship.</summary>

The most graceful men's dance <margin>)</margin> I have seen is one performed in San Cristoval <note>now Makira</note> and Saa, where the performers wave dancing-clubs as they represent scenes of fighting, accompanied by a very soft and melodic song. 

The general term for men's dancing in Florida <note>the Nggela Islands</note> is *gavai*. In the *nilaru* dance, they sit as if they are paddling a canoe; in the *kaukamumu*, there is a concert of many bamboo pipes played in specific tunes without any singing. This is a performance that men supposedly learned from ghosts and was brought over from Laudari in Guadalcanal. Groups of men practice these dances until they are perfect and then set out on a voyage to neighboring islands. This practice of "going dancing," or *gavai tona*, involves exhibiting their performance everywhere; they receive hospitality and handsome presents wherever they go. After such a party returns, they will divide a large sum of money—between two hundred and five hundred *rongo* <note>traditional shell money</note>—among themselves. 

In Santa Cruz, every prominent man has a dancing ground, or *nara*, near his house, which is fenced with huge discs of coral. The great aim in dancing there is to stamp the feet in perfect unison with the loudest possible impact. <margin>]</margin> Many of the Banks' Island dances, which involve elaborate figures carried out with the greatest precision, are truly beautiful and interesting. The performers—their heads wonderfully adorned and their limbs decorated with shining fringes of unopened palm fronds—advance and retire in two lines, weave in curves, and cross and recross in ranks. They wave their arms and stamp their feet, upon which rattling anklets made of empty nut shells are hung, all to the beat of a bamboo drum carried by a leader or beaten by a seated performer. To keep themselves on the correct steps, they repeat the words of the song belonging to the dance to themselves. The favorite time for dancing is a moonlight night, if the dance is the main event; the dancing and drumming of the common feast goes on during the daytime.

(2) ***Songs***. Words fitted to music are the songs and poetry of the people; the character of the tunes differs more across the various groups and islands than the general character of the words. There is no concept of poetry without a tune, though tunes without words are not unknown. In *songs*, certain words or forms of expression which are not used in everyday speech are everywhere thought poetical and appropriate, and words are lengthened or shortened to fit the meter. In the Banks Islands, the use of a distinct song-dialect is very remarkable. In this dialect, not only are words used that are never heard in speech—some probably ancient <note>original: archaic</note> and some borrowed from a neighboring island—but words are also shortened or lengthened to suit the tune. Furthermore, in each island, the song-language is so different from ordinary speech that the two appear to be two separate dialects, as completely as the dialogue and chorus of an ancient Greek play <note>In classical Greek drama, the spoken dialogue used a different dialect (Attic) than the sung chorus (Doric)</note>. The difference is least obvious in Gaua, Santa Maria, and probably most obvious in Mota. On one side of Mota, songs are composed in something like the language of Gaua; on the other, in something like that of Motlav. Yet the language of no Mota song is the actual spoken language of Gaua or Motlav, nor is a Mota song quite in the song-dialect of Gaua or Motlav. Every one of the Banks Islands has at least one form of speech for songs and another for common use, while some, like Mota, are not content with only two. In Santa Maria, however, while the spoken language of Lakona is very different from that of Gaua, the songs are almost, if not entirely, the same. A poet or poetess of more or less distinction is probably found in every sizable village throughout the islands; when some remarkable event occurs, such as the launching of a canoe, a visit from strangers, or a feast, song-

### XVII. Songs

Song-makers are hired to celebrate an event and are rewarded for their work; otherwise, a specific occasion might inspire a song for which—in the Banks Islands, at least—a gift is given to the composer in appreciation. In Florida <note>In the Solomon Islands</note>, a song is called a *linge*. A song written about someone or in their honor is known as that person's song, *na lingena*. In the Banks Islands, a song is called an *as*, and the song of the person being celebrated is *na asina*. To compose a song in Florida is described as "fitting it" (*kanggea na linge*); in Mota, it is called "measuring it" (*toro as*).

New words are often fitted to old tunes, but new tunes are also invented and old ones modified. In the Banks Islands, a song follows a regular structure of successive parts with distinctive names. Each part is introduced by a vocal prelude that marks the *qau-as*—literally the "knee," or the turn of the song. Some songs are led off by a single voice (*we put*), while others begin with many voices together (*we saru*). Sometimes the group of singers is divided: one group starts the song (*we tiu*), and the rest follow with an answering part (*we sarav goro*). While some songs are undoubtedly coarse or explicit, many others are entirely decent. Some have beautiful melodies and lyrics, and some exhibit genuine poetic quality, even if much of the style is traditional.

The following song certainly possesses poetic merit and, when translated, reflects well on the creative abilities of the people. It was composed at Lakona, on the island of Santa Maria, in honor of a man named Maros during his absence at sea. It is considered "his" song, and he is the speaker in the opening section <note>original: exordium; the introductory part of a composition</note>.

> "*Leale! ale!* <note>A rhythmic vocal chant or prelude</note> I am an eagle; I have soared to the farthest, dim horizon. I am an eagle; I have flown and landed at Mota. I have sailed with a whirring sound around the mountain. I have passed island after island in the West, traveling to the very edge of heaven <note>The horizon</note>. I have sailed; I have seen the lands. I have sailed in circles; I have been driven by strong currents. A bad wind has blown me off course, pulling me away from the two of you. How shall I find my way back to you both? The roaring sea stretches out empty, keeping me away from you. You, Mother, you are crying for me; how shall I see your face? You, Father, are crying for me; how shall I see your face? I only long for you and weep; it is a heavy burden to me. I wander like an orphan, all alone—and who is there to be my companion?"

### (3) Musical Instruments

The drum, in many forms, may be said to be the characteristic instrument of Melanesia. Yet, there seems to be no use for such a thing in Florida <note>the Nggela Islands</note>, and perhaps no knowledge of a native drum in Santa Cruz. The common form of drum is represented by a joint of bamboo with an open longitudinal <note>lengthwise</note> slit; this may be seen in various sizes from the largest to small bamboos. This same design is followed in the construction of drums made from tree logs. In these, the trunk of a tree of a suitable kind and size is hollowed out through a long and narrow opening at the side. The lip of this opening, which is cut thin, receives the beat of the drumsticks. These drums are very resonant and well-toned, and they can be heard at a great distance. 

The skill of the drummers and the pieces they perform are quite impressive, such as when two or even three performers sit down at one drum and play a piece of native drum-music in the Banks Islands, or when three drums of different size and tone—as I have heard at Saa—are played together with surprising precision and variety. At Saa and on San Cristoval <note>modern: Makira</note>, there are large houses built specifically for the drums; the story of the settlement at Saa (page 49) shows how highly good drums are valued. In the Banks Islands, a drum is called a *kore*; on Lepers' Island, it is a *singsing*. A large *singsing*—and some are very large indeed—has a handle left in the wood when the end is squared off.

In all these islands, the drums lie horizontally on the ground, but in Ambrym and the southern New Hebrides <note>modern: Vanuatu</note>, they stand upright. The base <note>original: "butt"</note> is buried in the earth, and the tapering top is carved into the shape of a face. If the bamboo drums are large, an assistant holds them while the performer beats them; small ones can be carried in a dancer’s hand. Strictly speaking, instruments like these are likely incorrectly called drums <note>technically, these are "slit-gongs" or idiophones, which produce sound through the vibration of the instrument's body rather than a stretched membrane</note>. I have seen the hollow trunk of a tree fern set up in the ground with a mat tied over the top to form a drumhead, which is then beaten with the fists. I have also seen a thin, broad slab of wood—likely cut from the buttress <note>the wide, stabilizing root structure at the base of a tropical tree</note> of a tree—laid over a hole dug in the ground and struck with a heavy stick <note>original: "rammer"</note>. These, however simple <note>original: "rude"</note>, may be called true drums.

# XVII. Musical Instruments

Bamboo pipes from the Banks Islands, known as *nggore*, produce a plaintive, delicate music. The corresponding *nggore* of Lepers' Island <note>modern: Ambae Island, Vanuatu</note> is longer—about three feet—and has four holes, allowing native songs to be played. 

The *waru*, or double flute, from the same island consists of two lengths of slender bamboo with a natural knot between them. A hole is carved on either side of the knot on the upper side, with two additional holes at both ends, one above and one below. When playing the instrument, the performer places the knot and its two holes into his mouth. His outstretched hands support the bamboo, and he modulates the sound using his fingers and thumbs on the holes at the ends. The bamboo used is no more than two-thirds of an inch in diameter because the people do not like a loud or harsh sound; in the ears of the locals, the music of the *waru* is "excellent to hear."

In the Solomon Islands, the bamboo jew's-harp—called the *nene* in Florida <note>modern: Nggela Islands</note>—is common, though it is unknown in the Eastern Islands. A stringed instrument is also found in the Solomon Islands, known as the *kalore* in Florida. It is made from a piece of bent reed or bamboo about a foot long and half an inch in diameter. Two strings are stretched from end to end, passing over small bridges that are pushed toward the ends to tighten them; both strings are tuned to the same note. The performer holds the curved back of the instrument in his mouth <note>using the mouth as a resonator to amplify the sound</note> and strikes the strings with a small plectrum <term>plectrum: a small flat tool, like a pick, used to pluck or strum strings</term> of reed held in his right hand. With the fingers of his left hand, he holds the *kalore* so that he keeps one of the strings permanently stopped; he can then stop the free string as the tune requires to produce higher notes. The music produced is not very audible to anyone except the performer, who finds great delight in it.

Among musical instruments, one must also include castanets made of nut shells and seeds. These are worn on the ankles or wrists during dances, or, as in Santa Cruz, hung upon dancing-clubs. These are important accessories, especially in a stamping dance such as the Banks Island *gal*. # XVII. Dances, Music, and Games

In the Banks Islands, to add to the noise <note>original: "din"</note> of the many drums, large and small, at a feast, I have seen a man shaking dry seashells in a woven mat bag. On Aurora <note>modern: Maewo Island, Vanuatu</note>, they fasten bamboo rods pierced with holes to the tops of trees to create an **Aeolian** flute <note>a flute played by the wind, named after Aeolus, the Greek god of the wind</note>, similar to those mentioned by Dr. Tylor in his *Early History of Mankind*.

### 4. Games

A game belonging to the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides <note>modern: Vanuatu</note> is *tika* (called *tiqa* in Fiji). It is played with reeds thrown against the ground in such a way that they bounce into the air and fly a considerable distance. In some islands, such as Santa Maria <note>modern: Gaua</note>, a string is used to provide momentum <note>original: "impetus"</note>, and on some islands, the reed is also thrown from the foot. 

The game is played by two teams, who count "pigs" for the longest throws; the number of pigs recorded as gained depends on the number of knots in the winning *tika*. There is a specific season for the game: the time when the yams are harvested. The reeds that had been used to support the yam vines apparently served as the original rods for *tika*. When two villages engage in a match, they sometimes come to blows. There are marks on the *tiqa* to show to whom they belong. 

It is remarkable that in Mota, a decimal system <term>decimal: a base-10 counting system</term> of numerals is used in this game, which is distinct from the quinary system <term>quinary: a base-5 counting system</term> used on every other occasion of counting. On Florida <note>modern: Nggela Islands</note>, there are also specific numerals used in a game, but these are only the common numerals in an altered form. 

In the Banks Islands, boys play hide-and-seek, called *rurgonaqona*. There are two sides, and if the seekers do not find the boy who is hiding, he suddenly jumps up and counts a "pig" against them. There is also a kind of prisoners' base called *taptapau*. Each party has a base <note>original: "cooking-place"</note> or *um*, in which they are safe, and outside of which they may be caught. On Lepers' Island <note>modern: Ambae Island</note>, they have football, played by men and boys on two teams between two fences. They use a native orange, a breadfruit, or a coconut as a ball. The goal is scored when the ball is driven past...

...is equipped with a shell scraper. In the Museum at Batavia <note>modern: Jakarta, Indonesia; original: "Batavia" was the colonial name</note> is a similar seat with the tail of a horse and an iron scraper.

### 4. Games (continued)

...either end from between the fences; a "pig" <note>a unit of scoring</note> is counted for each goal. In the same island, in a game called *kaliweli tambagau*, two parties sit opposite one another in the moonlight. A man or boy from one side comes forward holding the door-shutter of a house—a *tambagau*—before him, and the other side tries to guess who he is and calls out his name. If they fail, a "pig" is counted against them; if they succeed, one of their party takes the door. Women play the same game among themselves. They also have a game similar to "hunt-the-slipper," and play at hiding canarium almonds <note>a large, oily nut common in the Pacific</note>, counting "pigs" for each successful find.

Cat's-cradle—known in Lepers' Island <note>modern: Ambae Island, Vanuatu</note> as *lelegaro* and in Florida <note>modern: Nggela Islands, Solomon Islands</note> as *honggo*—is common throughout the islands and involves many complex figures. I have seen a game in Florida in which two groups of boys tossed a rough ball back and forth on the points of sticks, the object being to keep it from hitting the ground for as long as possible.

In the Solomon Islands, the primary game involves throwing and dodging spears, or using sticks instead of spears. This is represented in the Banks Islands <note>a group of islands in northern Vanuatu</note> by two parties throwing native oranges at each other. At Lakona <note>a district on the island of Gaua</note>, they used to gather in a friendly way at the *sarevnate*, or shooting-ground, to practice archery at one another with their bows and arrows. In the Banks Islands and Torres Islands, and undoubtedly in other groups, they use the surf-board, called a *tapa*.

In Mota <note>an island in the Banks group</note>, *taplapui* is a race to be the first to reach a certain object; *tititiro* is the practice of throwing at a tree or some other target. Archery is practiced using banana trunks set up as targets. Even counting is made into a kind of game; in the Banks Islands, lines are arranged on the sand or on a board in a specific pattern representing numbers, and these are counted with the finger to the rhythm of a whistled tune. Something similar is done in Florida, where players stick their fingers into the sand in numbers according to a counting song brought from Alite <note>modern: Langalanga Lagoon, Malaita</note>.

Boys sitting together in a tight circle will toss another boy, who stands among them, from side to side. The boy in the center holds himself as stiffly as he can so that he is thrown like a log of wood. Children in the Banks Islands, when a rainbow is seen, play at "cutting off its end" (*tolo gasiosio*); they believe that if they can cut it short, the rain will stop. In the Banks Islands, there is even a certain approach to...

...acting; a man will imitate the voice and gestures of another, the limping gait of a disabled person, the fury of a man in a rage, or will pretend to be a woman, all for the amusement of a crowd.

### (5) Toys

Kites, which are used for fishing in the Solomon Islands and Santa Cruz, are used as toys in the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides <note>modern: Vanuatu</note>, though they have not been common in recent years. They have their own season, being made and flown when the gardens are being cleared for planting. The kite is steadied by a long tail made of reeds, and a well-made one will fly and hover very well. In the Banks Islands, the name for a kite is *rea*; on Ambae Island <note>original: Lepers’ Island</note> it is *mala*, meaning "an eagle."

The use of the bull-roarer <note>a flat piece of wood swung on a cord to produce a deep, vibrating roar</note>, known as a *buro*, in the "Mysteries" <note>secret religious or initiatory societies</note> at Florida <note>modern: Nggela Islands</note> has been mentioned previously. It is only in that location that the object carries any superstitious character. There is no mystery about it when it is used in the Banks Islands to drive away a ghost—as in Mota, where it is called *nanamatea* ("death-maker")—or to make a mourning sound, as in Merlav, where it is called *vorung-tamb* ("a wailer") and used the night after a death. Otherwise, it is a common plaything; in Vanua Lava they call it *mala* ("a pig"), named after the noise it makes; in Maewo it is a *tal-viv* ("a whirring string"); and in Araga it is merely a *tavire bua* ("a bit of bamboo").

Rattles are simply toys; in the Banks Islands, the dry seed-pods of a cassia tree are tied in a row between two strips of bamboo. In the same island group, the name of a toy, *taplagolago*, has been adopted as the word for the English "wheel," and subsequently for any wheeled vehicle or machine. Children used to make a broad hoop from a sago palm frond and set it running down a hill, shouting, "*taplagolago!*" ("It runs by itself!").

Tops in the Solomon Islands are made from a palm nut and a wooden pin; the entire visible length of the pin (between two and three inches long) sits below the head of the nut. To spin the top, a doubled string is wound around the shaft, and the two ends are pulled sharply apart. A similar top was used on Pitcairn Island by the children of the *Bounty* mutineers and their Tahitian wives.

Whistling was rarely used by the islanders as a way to produce a tune, though a song might be whistled without the words. In the Banks Islands, there is a specific way of whistling a man’s name to call him, known as *woswos-loglog*.

# CHAPTER XVIII.

## MISCELLANEOUS.

(1) **Cannibalism**. It can be safely stated that in the Banks Islands and Santa Cruz, cannibalism did not exist, although the inhabitants were aware that others practiced it. About fifty years ago <note>around 1840</note>, a group of people from Tonga settled briefly on the small island of Qakea. When they eventually departed following a period of fighting, they left behind evidence that they had eaten those they had killed. This caused such horror and rage among the local people that when another party from Tonga returned to the same place a year later, they were immediately attacked. 

In the Solomon Islands, it is surprising that the practice has actually expanded in recent times. The elders of Florida <note>modern: Nggela Islands</note> assert that human flesh was never eaten except during religious sacrifices, and they claim that the practice of human sacrifice itself was recently introduced from further west. The coastal people of Bugotu <note>on Santa Isabel Island</note> say the same about themselves; however, they frequently accuse the inland tribes of the same island of being cannibals who kill people specifically for food. This is despite the fact that the coastal and inland groups interact freely and speak very similar languages. 

A few years ago, an inland chief named Nunu was rumored to say that pig's meat tasted bad to him, but human flesh was sweet. It was said that if a man climbed up to Nunu's village and arrived sweaty from the effort, sitting down to cool off before presenting himself, Nunu would view the sweat as a sign of "fatness" and would want to eat him. Similarly, in Ulawa, there—

is no eating of men. It is believed that the *lio'a* <term>spirits of deceased powerful men</term> do not like it. At Saa <note>on the island of South Malaita</note>, it was not the ancient custom of the area, and even today the elders will have nothing to do with it. Younger men, however, have adopted the practice and eat the bodies of those killed in battle. They have followed the customs of men from the eastern coast who have lived among them, as well as the Bauro people of San Cristoval <note>modern-day Makira</note> whom they have visited. 

The inhabitants of San Cristoval not only eat the bodies of those slain in battle but even sell the flesh. While not unheard of, killing specifically for the purpose of eating human flesh is rare, and it marks the reputation of the man who does it. This is a subject on which stories from traders are often unreliable. 

In the Northern New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>, cannibalism certainly exists. I have no information regarding the practice on Aurora <note>Maewo</note>, but an eyewitness told me about what is done on Pentecost Island. After a particularly violent fight, they would take a fallen enemy and eat him as a sign of rage and indignation. They would cook the body in an oven, and everyone—including women and children—would eat a small portion. When there was less animosity, the victors would take the flesh of a dead enemy away to be cooked and shared with their friends. According to my informant, on the neighboring islands and on the far side of his own island, people kill specifically for the sake of eating. 

On Lepers' Island <note>now known as Ambae</note>, they still eat human flesh. However, it was not the common fashion to eat enemies killed in fair fighting. Instead, it was a murderer or a particularly hated enemy who was eaten out of anger and as a way to humiliate him. Such a person was cooked like a pig, and the men, older women, and boys ate him. The boys were afraid, but they were forced to do it. The local sentiment is that eating human flesh is a terrifying thing, and therefore a "man-eater" is seen as someone who fears nothing. On this basis, men will sometimes buy flesh when someone has been killed so that they may earn a reputation as valiant men by eating it. One man on Lepers' Island mourned for many days after the death of his son and refused to eat until he bought a piece of human flesh for himself and his surviving son. It was a gruesome act, intended to match the darkness of his grief.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of social customs in the Melanesian islands, moving from cannibalism to the practice of head-hunting and the treatment of strangers.</meta>

<page-num>345</page-num>
<header>XVIII.] Heads. Castaways.</header>

(2) **Heads.** Head-hunting is not practiced by any of the people living east of Santa Isabel <note>original: "Ysabel"</note>; that is to say, they do not organize expeditions for the sole purpose of obtaining heads. In Bugotu, at the southeastern tip of Santa Isabel, the people have suffered—and still suffer—most seriously from the attacks of head-hunters from further away. These expeditions follow the coasts for great distances, sometimes traveling for months. They have reached Malaita <note>original: "Malanta"</note> and Guadalcanal. In one most disgraceful instance, head-hunters were even brought to the Florida Islands <note>now known as the Nggela Islands</note> on a European ship. 

The practice, however, of taking heads and preserving them as signs of power and success is common throughout the Solomon Islands generally. The heads of enemies killed in a fight are preserved as trophies and displayed on platforms, as seen in the Florida Islands, or hung up under the eaves of the canoe-house, as in San Cristobal <note>now known as Makira</note>. When a chief, in the exercise of his authority, had a man killed for a crime, or had him murdered out of revenge or hatred, or for a sacrifice, he added the head to his collection; it was a sign of his power and greatness. Consequently, because the more heads he could show, the more his power was visible, he was ready at every opportunity and on any pretext to take a life and a head. 

When a chief had a man killed, he would keep the head but send the legs and arms to his neighbors to show what he had done. If, for example, an accused man escaped from Mboli in the Florida Islands to Savo, the Mboli chief would send a request—accompanied by a gift of traditional money—to the Savo chief to have him killed. The Savo chief would keep the head and send a leg or arm back to Florida, where the chief would hang it up to display his power. These heads, taken and preserved in this way, are distinct from the heads of deceased relatives, which are kept as memorials of affection. Skulls may be seen suspended at the entrance of a Solomon Island <term>oha</term> <note>a canoe-house</note> and a New Hebrides <term>gamal</term> <note>a men's clubhouse</note> alike, but the meaning in each case is probably quite different.

(3) **Castaways.** Throughout the islands, a stranger was generally viewed as an enemy to be killed. For instance, in the Florida Islands, a stranger who had escaped from a shipwreck onto a small island was killed as soon as he was seen; he was spoken of as a "floating coconut" <note>meaning he was considered ownerless property or a mere resource to be taken</note>.

<summary>This page describes head-hunting in the Solomon Islands as a demonstration of a chief's political power and prestige, while also noting the general hostility toward shipwrecked strangers.</summary>

<header>Miscellaneous [Chapter XVIII]</header>

ashore. There was a common belief that a stranger would bring disease or some other misfortune with him. However, it was often a question of whether a castaway was truly a "stranger." If he were recognized as belonging to a hostile district, there was no doubt about his fate; but if he fell into the hands of those who belonged to the same social division, such as a <term>kema</term> <note>original: "kema"—a matrilineal clan or moiety in the Solomon Islands</note> or <term>veve</term> <note>original: "veve"—a matrilineal descent group in the New Hebrides/Vanuatu</note>, he would probably be saved. 

It was not uncommon for canoes to be blown by the wind from Santa Cruz and the Reef Islands to Malaita <note>original: "Malanta"</note> and Ulawa. The men on board these vessels were not seen as total strangers, even if they were not personally known. They were men from known lands, not strange beings like white men who seemed to come from outside the known world. They were therefore received as guests, sometimes eventually establishing themselves by marriage, or sometimes waiting for an opportunity to return home. Over time, many single canoes have been blown away from Polynesian islands and have drifted to the Banks Islands; in many cases, these castaways were treated kindly and have added their lineage to the native population. Within the last forty years, men from Tikopia have twice been received with great kindness at Mota.

(4) **Slaves.** There is no such thing as slavery in the way it is typically defined. In head-hunting expeditions, prisoners are taken for the sake of their heads—to be used whenever a ritual occasion requires them. These people live with their captors in a condition very different from freedom, but they are not captured or kept for the purpose of forced labor. 

In these same islands, when a successful attack and massacre provides the victors with many heads, they often spare and carry off children, whom they raise among their own people. Such a <term>seka</term> <note>original: "seka"—a captive or person taken in war</note> will certainly be the first to be killed for a ritual head or a sacrifice before any native member of the community is chosen, but otherwise, he lives as an adopted member. He shares the work, pleasures, and dangers of those he lives with, and he often becomes a leading figure among them. A refugee or a castaway is not a slave but a guest; while his life is naturally valued much less than that of a local man and useful services are expected from him, he mixes freely and on equal terms with the common people.

<summary>This page describes the treatment of castaways and captives in Melanesia, explaining that while strangers were often feared as sources of disease, those with recognizable clan ties were often spared. It also distinguishes Melanesian "seka" (captives) from Western concepts of slavery, noting that while captives could be used for sacrifices, they otherwise lived as integrated members of the community.</summary>

<page-num>347</page-num>

->**XVIII. Burying and Burning Alive**<-

(5) **Burying alive.** Nothing seems more cruel than the practice of burying sick and elderly people alive, yet it is certain that when this was done, it was generally intended as an act of kindness. It is true that sometimes the relatives of the sick became tired of waiting on them and buried them when they thought they should be ready for it; but even in such cases, the sick and elderly accepted it. It was common for them to beg their friends to put them out of their misery. Some years ago, a man on Mota <note>An island in the Banks Islands of Vanuatu.</note> buried his brother, who was extremely weak from influenza; however, he heaped the earth loosely over his head and went back from time to time to ask him whether he were still alive. In recent years, though old people still ask for it, their friends will not consent. Not long ago on Pentecost Island, a woman was buried after a lingering sickness during a time of famine, and she was heard crying in her grave for three days. On Lepers' Island <note>original: "Lepers' Island"—now known as Ambae Island, Vanuatu.</note>, the patient was sometimes strangled with their own consent¹.

(6) **Burning alive.** This has only been heard of at Araga <note>A district and language group on the northern part of Pentecost Island.</note> on Pentecost Island. During times of war there, if a great man were very angry with a hostile party, he would burn a wounded enemy. When peace had been made and the chiefs had ordered everyone to behave well so the country might settle down in quiet, if anyone committed a crime that would break the peace—such as adultery—they would tie him to a tree, heap firewood around him, and burn him alive. This was done as a proof to the opposing party of their hatred of his wickedness. This was not done calmly as a standard legal execution, but as a horrific act, performed specifically for the sake of the horror it caused—a horror that was still visible in the voice and face of the native who told me about the roaring flames and shrieks of agony.

***

¹ On the same island, in the interior <note>original: "bush country"</note>, there was a great man who had a poor brother. During a time of famine, the poor man stole food, rather than asking for it from his brother or taking it from him. The chief buried his brother alive, despite the entreaties of his own wife and the poor man's pleas for mercy. He bound him, dug a grave, lined it with mats, threw him in, and buried him. This act was shocking to the public opinion of the islanders, but it served to mark him as a "great man" who would do exactly as he pleased.
