(7) **Heavenly Bodies.** There is no evidence of a belief that any heavenly bodies are living beings; in the Banks Islands, the Sun and Moon are thought to be rocks or islands. On Lepers' Island <note>original: "Lepers' Island"—now known as Ambae Island, Vanuatu.</note>, a story is told that the Sun and the Moon quarreled while the Sun was making a mash of wild yam. In a rage, the Sun threw the mess at the Moon's face, creating the splashes that can still be seen there today; however, this is told without any serious conviction. It is commonly believed that there is a human being, male or female, in the Moon. The stories of Vulaninggela and Kamakajaku show the belief in Florida <note>original: "Florida"—now known as the Nggela Islands in the Solomon Islands.</note> and Ysabel <note>original: "Ysabel"—Santa Isabel Island in the Solomon Islands.</note> that there is a person who accompanies the Sun, and whose name is Sun, rather than the Sun itself being a person. In Florida, the name of the "Man in the Moon" is *Ngava*; when the Moon rises full, the people cry out, "There is Ngava sitting." Every new moon is thought to be literally new. 

No natural cause is supposed for eclipses, unless they are attributed to the magic of some weather-doctor. An eclipse is a wonder and a portent, bringing an appalling sense of danger. This fear finds expression in shouting, blowing conch shells, and beating house roofs, though with no very distinct purpose of driving the fearful thing away. Eclipses of the sun are not recognized as occurring at Mota. When a remarkable comet—called in the Banks Islands a "smoking star"—appeared in the year 1882, the people of Lepers' Island blew conch shells to drive it away, or at least to divert the impending mischief. A falling star is seen as the same sort of omen; it suggests that some great man will die or that there will be an attack by enemies. 

The appearance of two stars close together, called *warue* on Lepers' Island, signifies war. The people of the Solomon Islands are more concerned with the stars than their Eastern neighbors, perhaps because of their longer sea voyages; the people of Santa Cruz and the Reef Islands excel all others in their practical astronomy. The inhabitants of the Banks Islands and the Northern New Hebrides content themselves with distinguishing the Pleiades <note>A prominent star cluster often used by ancient and indigenous cultures to track seasons.</note>, by which the approach of the yam harvest is marked. They also call the planets <term>masoi</term> <note>original: "masoi"—derived from the word for "roundness."</note> to distinguish them from the stars, which they call <term>vitu</term>. In Florida, the early morning star is called <term>gama ni votu</term>, meaning "the quartz pebble for setting off to sea"; when it rises later, it is called <term>gama ni ndani</term>...

the shining stone of light; the Pleiades are *togo ni samw*, the company of maidens; Orion's belt is the *peko*, the war canoe; the evening star is *taovarongo diva*, "listen for the oven," because the daily meal is prepared as evening draws on; stars are called "dead men's eyes." At Saa <note>original: "Saa"—a linguistic and cultural area on South Malaita in the Solomon Islands.</note>, the Southern Cross is *ape*, the net, depicted with four men letting it down to catch the palolo <note>original: "palolo"—a marine worm that rises to the surface in massive numbers during specific lunar phases; its appearance is a major seasonal marker.</note>, and the "Pointers" <note>the stars Alpha and Beta Centauri</note> are two men cooking what has been caught, because the palolo appears when one of the Pointers rises above the horizon. The Pleiades are *apurunge*, the tangle; the Southern Triangle is "three men in a canoe"; Mars is the "Red Pig."

(8) **Months and Seasons.** The moon is naturally the measure of time. There is no native notion of a "year" as a fixed period of time; the word *tau* or *niulu*, which corresponds most nearly to the word "year," actually signifies a "season," and is only now used to mean the space of time between recurring seasons. Thus, the yam has its *tau*, its season of five moons from planting—when the erythrina <note>original: "erythrina"—the coral tree, which produces bright red flowers used as a seasonal indicator.</note> is in flower—until the harvest after the palolo has come and gone. The breadfruit has its *tau* during the winter months. The banana and the coconut have no *tau*, as they bear fruit at all times. 

The concept of a year as the time from one yam harvest to the next, or from one palolo season to another, has been readily adopted; however, it is very doubtful if such a concept was originally native. It is impossible to fit the native sequence of moons into a solar year. Months are named based on what is done and what happens when the moon appears and while it lasts; consequently, the same moon may have different names. If all the names of moons used in a single language were arranged in order, the periods of time would overlap, and the "native year" would be artificially made up of twenty or thirty months. 

The moons and seasons of Mota in the Banks Islands may serve as an example. The garden work of the year is the principal guide to the arrangement, following the succession of: 
1. clearing garden ground (*uma*); 
2. cutting down the trees (*tara*); 
3. turning over and piling up the debris (*rakasag*); 
4. burning it (*sing*); 
5. digging the holes for yams (*wur*) and planting (*riv*). 

Then follows the care of the yam plants until...

the harvest, after which preparation for the next crop begins again. At the same time, the regular winds and calms are observed, along with the growth of grass, the noticeable flowering of certain trees, and the budding of the few deciduous trees <note>trees that shed their leaves annually</note>.

When a certain grass, *magoto*, sprouts, the winter (as it must be called) is over. When the coral tree <note>original: *erythrina* or *rara*</note> is in flower, it is the cool season. Therefore, *magoto* and *rara* are names of seasons used by the locals and correspond roughly to summer and winter. The strange and exciting appearance of the well-known marine worm, the palolo <note>original: *un*, an annelid or segmented worm</note>, serves as a major marker of the seasons. 

The April moon coincides roughly with the time of the *magoto qaro*, or fresh grass. During this time, the clearing <note>original: *uma*</note> of gardens takes place while the trade wind blows steadily. This is followed by the *magoto rango*, or withered grass. Both are months for cutting down trees in the gardens <note>original: *vule taratara*</note>, and during the latter month, the debris is burned. 

In July, the coral tree begins to flower; this is the *nago rara*, or the "face of winter." Gardens are fenced, and it is a month for planting yams <note>original: *vule vutvut*</note>. Planting continues into August, when the coral tree is in full flower <note>original: *tur rara*</note>, and the Malay apple <note>original: *gaviga*</note> flowers at the same time. The southeast wind, known as *gauna*, blows; the yams begin to sprout and are supported with reeds. 

In the following month, the coral tree puts out its leaves, marking the end of the season <note>original: *kere rara*</note>. The yam vines grow up the reeds and are trained <note>original: *taur*</note> upon them. The reeds are broken and bent over <note>original: *ruga*</note> to allow the vines to grow freely. The ground is kept clear of weeds, the tendrils curl, and the tubers form well. 

Then come the months of calm, when three lunar months are named after the *un* (palolo worm). First is the *un rig*, the "little palolo," also called *un gogona* or "bitter palolo," when a few of the worms appear during the full moon. It is now the *tau matua*, the season of maturity. Yams can be eaten, and if the weather is favorable, a second crop is planted. The *un lava*, or "great palolo," follows. During the full moon of this month, the worms appear on the reefs in swarms for a single night. The entire population goes to the beach to collect the *un* using every available vessel and tool. This is the month of the yam harvest, when the vines are cut <note>original: *goro*</note>...

<header>XVIII.] Mota Months. Narcotics. </header>

In the old days, this was done with a shell, and the tubers <note>yams</note> were very carefully taken up with digging sticks to be stored. A few *un* <note>original: palolo, a type of edible sea worm</note> appear during the next moon, the *werei*, which can be translated as the "rump" or tail end of the *un* season. In this moon, they begin again to *uma* [clear the gardens]. The wind blows again from the west—the *ganoi* wind—over Vanua Lava. It is now November or December, and the *togalau* wind blows from the northwest. It is exceedingly hot; fish die in the shallow pools, and the reeds shoot up into flower. It is the moon of "shooting up," known as *vule wolgoro*. 

The next month is the *rusiaru*, when the wind beats upon the casuarina trees on the cliffs. The month after that is called *telemavuru*; the wind blows hard and drives off flying fragments from the seeded reeds. These are the hurricane months. The last in the cycle is the month that "beats and rattles," *lamasag noronoro*, referring to the sound of the dry reeds. The wind blows strong and steady, and work begins again; they *vukasag* [dry the debris of their clearings] and prepare the fences for new gardens. By this time, the intense heat has passed, the grass begins to grow again, and the winter months return.

(9) **Narcotics.** The use of the areca nut (*mbua*), chewed with the betel leaf and the addition of coral lime, is universal in the Solomon Islands and Santa Cruz, and extends as far as Tikopia. To the eastward, however, it is unknown. Solomon Islanders on their way to Norfolk Island look wistfully at a species of areca palm in the Torres Islands; the natives of that group sometimes chew these nuts to quiet hunger, but they are not a satisfactory substitute for those who know the *mbua*. Travelers can replenish their stock of betel leaves in the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>, where that pepper plant grows naturally, but they feel they have passed into a foreign region. 

In the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides, they drink an infusion made from the root of the *Piper methysticum* <note>original: a species of pepper plant</note> well known as *kava*. It is called *gea* on Mota and *maloro* on Aurora <note>the island of Maewo</note>. In the Banks Islands, this is such a recent introduction that its use had not yet spread to Santa Maria <note>the island of Gaua</note> as of a few years ago. The difference in the way it is prepared seems to point to two distinct sources or times of introduction. In the Banks Islands, drinking *gea* is called *woana*...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of narcotics in Melanesia, moving from the use of betel nut to the preparation of kava and the historical introduction of tobacco via European contact.</meta>

<page-num>352</page-num>
<header>Miscellaneous. [Chapter XVIII.]</header>

The root is chewed by the drinker; when the fibers are separated, a little water is taken into the mouth to assist in squeezing out the saliva. Water is added again in the coconut-shell cup, and once the fibers are removed and squeezed thoroughly over the cup, the potion is ready. In Aurora <note>Maewo</note>, the *malowo* <note>kava</note> is pounded with a rough coral pestle and mortar. The moderate use of this narcotic has no bad effect; however, excess—which is perhaps more common in the New Hebrides <note>modern-day Vanuatu</note>—makes a man listless and stupid. The plant used is not indigenous; there is indeed a pepper of the same species that is very common, but it will not work for the *woana* <note>kava drink</note>. As has been shown, there is a certain sacred character about the plant, and its use is confined to men. 

The introduction of tobacco into common use in the Northern New Hebrides and the Banks Islands is quite recent, but the people are now devoted to its use. Smoking was universal in the Solomon Islands—at Florida <note>Nggela</note>, Ysabel, and San Cristobal—thirty years ago, among men, women, and even infant children; at that time, the tobacco was grown and prepared by the natives themselves. Yet, it was not known at Saa <note>on Malaita</note> at that time, though it has since been introduced from Arosi in San Cristobal. The older men at Florida remember when it was a new thing in their childhood. 

For many years, there has been a great deal of interaction with whalers at San Cristobal; the people there have no native name for tobacco and, I believe, never grew it, so its introduction there is easily explained. In Florida, the native-grown tobacco—now discarded for the much stronger *tambaika* <note>trade tobacco, likely a corruption of "tobacco"</note>—was called *vavuru*, and the dried leaves were made into twists. The pipe, formerly made of a shell and a reed in obvious imitation of the European pipe, is still called *pipiala*; the old people say that the seed originally came from a ship¹.

This was probably the *Southern Cross* <note>the mission ship of the Melanesian Mission</note>. The name given to ships at first was *ungaungau*, not *taka* as it is now. Ships were thought to belong to *tindalo* <note>ghosts or ancestral spirits</note> and to portend a famine; those who saw them ran away and hid themselves in their houses. <page-num>353</page-num>
<header>XVIII.] Counting. Measurements.</header>

(10) *Counting and Measurements.* The systems of counting used among Melanesians could well be displayed and explained here, but I have treated that subject elsewhere. It is, however, reasonable to say something regarding their methods of counting. The fingers are the natural tools for counting; however, there is a curious variation in how they are used. In the Banks Islands, the right thumb is turned down first, followed by the fingers of the right hand and then the left; both hands, with closed fists, are then held up together to show the completed ten. It is the number of fingers turned down that is noted, not those that remain standing. In Florida <note>Nggela</note>, they begin with the little finger. In Lepers' Island <note>Ambae</note>, they begin with the thumb, but after reaching five with the little finger, they do not move to the other hand; instead, they extend <note>original: "throw up"</note> the fingers they had turned down, beginning with the forefinger and using the thumb to represent ten. The use of the cycas leaf <note>a palm-like plant used as a tally</note> for counting (page 272) is common in the Banks Islands and the New Hebrides <note>Vanuatu</note>. A string with knots to mark the days is used in the Solomon Islands. In Florida, stones and *Canarium* <note>tropical nut</note> shells are used to help with counting; at a feast, a man will walk around with a basket, and everyone present will put some small object into it so that the number of guests entertained may be known. At Saa <note>on the island of Malaita</note>, when yams are counted, two men count out five each to make ten; as each ten is completed, they call out "one," "two," and so on. A man sits nearby, and when "ten" is called (representing a hundred), he sets down a small yam as a tally.

The natural measure of length may be said to be the fathom <note>the distance between the fingertips of outstretched arms</note>, called *goto* in Florida and *rora* in Mota. Examples of more specific measurements can be taken from Mota: the taut fathom, <term>rora taglagau</term>, is the line stretched as far as possible with the arms thrown back; <term>rora ale lue</term>, the "fathom of looking out," is measured by a line stretched away as far as possible by the left hand but held by the right hand upon the shoulder, where the face turns round to

to <note>This text continues the discussion of tobacco from the previous page</note> Florida and Bugotu by Europeans who were not whalers; their pipe in form, and perhaps in name, does not suggest a connection with the tobacco-smoking of New Guinea.

reaching that point; another is *avawo sus*, measured from the outstretched left hand to the right nipple; *alo masale pei*, "at the watercourse," measured from the left hand to the breastbone <note>The "watercourse" refers to the sternum or the center of the chest</note>. Lesser measurements include *alo virngai*, measured from the armpit; *alo maluk*, from the hollow of the elbow to the tips of the fingers; and *sogo siwo*, from the wrist to the finger ends.

(11) **Salutations.** People living in small communities who are always in sight of one another have little need for formal greetings, and there is little to be said on the subject regarding Melanesia. If someone passes through a village, he will be asked where he is coming from and told to continue on his way as a form of greeting; upon leaving, he will say, "You stay." 

There is, however, a friendly action in the Banks Islands called *varpis*. Two men each insert the middle finger of their right hand between two of their friend's fingers, grip them tightly together, and then quickly pull them apart with a loud crack. This is a greeting and a sign of fellowship and approval. Kissing is not native to the islands; *punpun* <note>original: "punpun"</note> is a similar action, involving sniffing with the nose rather than rubbing noses. This is not considered proper or becoming to do except with children. Rubbing noses is practiced only in the Polynesian settlements. 

It is not the custom to say anything by way of thanks. In fact, it is considered somewhat improper to show outward emotion when a gift is received or when friends reunite. Silence with downcast eyes is the sign of the "inward trembling" or shyness that they feel—or believe they ought to feel—in such situations. There is no lack of a word that can be accurately translated as "thank," and certainly no one who has earned it would say that Melanesians lack gratitude, though outsiders are often quick to claim they do.

(12) **Wild Men.** In Florida <note>Nggela Islands</note>, the people believe that on the mountains of Laudari—the part of Guadalcanal visible from their own island—there live wild men whom they call **Mumulou**. They are described as humans who possess a language. The hair on their heads is straight and reaches down to their legs; their bodies are covered in long hair, and they have long nails. They are large and tall, but no larger than the size of a normal man. The coastal people of Laudari say that one was killed not long ago, and so they claim to know exactly what they look like. They live in...

<meta>This page continues the description of local folklore, specifically focusing on the widespread belief in "wild men" throughout the Melanesian islands and the author's interpretation of these legends.</meta>

<page-num>355</page-num>

### XVIII. Wild Men

They live in caves in the mountains; they plant nothing and eat snakes and lizards. They eat any coastal man they can catch. They carry bags on their backs filled with pieces of obsidian <term>a naturally occurring volcanic glass used to make sharp tools or weapons</term>, which they use to pelt any men they see. They also set nets around trees to catch men who have climbed them, and they use spears as well. 

In Saa, it is said there are *Mumu* <note>A legendary forest-dwelling creature in Solomon Islands folklore</note> in the forest. These are human and very small in stature, but very strong and swift. They have very long hair and long nails, which they use to tear coastal men apart to devour them. They travel in groups of three: a male, a female, and a child. Finally, men from Saa who have served on the "thief-ships" <note>original: "thief-ships"; a reference to "blackbirding" vessels used to kidnap or coerce islanders into forced labor</note> have claimed that Australian Aboriginal people resemble the *Mumu*. 

In the New Hebrides <note>Modern-day Vanuatu</note>, similar creatures are seen basking on the rocks on the slopes of the great volcano of Ambrym. Even on the small island of Mae, they used to be seen—though they are now extinct—on the Three Hills. On Lepers' Island <note>Modern-day Ambae</note>, these wild men are called *Mae*. They have long hair and long teeth, dwell in caves, steal pigs, and will seize and eat any man they meet alone. In the night, they can be heard crying in the valleys; it is said then that the *Mae* is washing her child. The name suggests some connection with the superstition described previously (page 188), but they do not call any snake a *mae*, and these beings are considered men. 

However much these stories vary, the belief can be said to be general from Ysabel to Mae, just as stories of wild men have been common in New Zealand. Descriptions very similar to these are even found in serious scholarly treatises on humanity. It is certain that the Melanesian belief has no foundation in modern fact regarding the existence of either ape-like men or man-like apes. It is a question of whether the belief is based on the memory of large apes <note>Simians</note> in the former homelands of the Melanesian people. To me, so far as it has any foundation in fact at all, it appears to be a fanciful exaggeration of the differences between the coastal people and the people of the *uta* <note>The interior or "inland" regions of an island</note>. The coastal people are very inclined to exaggerate these differences, as the inlanders have no canoes and cannot swim. They are the true "man of the woods" <note>original: "orang utan"; from Malay *orang* (man) and *hutan* (forest)</note>—the "bush-man" of Pidgin English.

# CHAPTER XIX.

## STORIES.

**The** native stories or folk-tales that follow were all translated from manuscripts written for me by the inhabitants of the various islands where these stories are told—with the exception of the first one. That first example was recorded by the Reverend Alfred Penny on Florida <note>The Nggela Islands in the Solomon Islands</note> in the native language as he heard it told. I have made the translations as accurate and literal as possible. The detailed wordiness <note>original: "prolixity"</note> of a native narrative is a very characteristic feature; it is also possible that, due to the varying storytelling skills of individual writers, differences in the narrative styles of the eastern and western island groups of Melanesia may be visible. 

The value of authentic native stories is beyond question. They illustrate native life through the specific details that arise during the narrative; they are full of the concepts that the native people hold about the world around them; they show the native mind active in fancy and imagination; and they provide a rich collection of subjects for comparison with the folk-tales of other parts of the world. 

To the question of how far those who tell and those who hear these stories believe them to be true, it is difficult to give a definitive answer. To some extent they are believed, and to a great extent they are treated as flights of fancy. A storyteller, warming to his subject and visualizing everything he relates in his mind, very likely believes it all as he tells the tale. Indeed, a story will often be quoted to explain or support a statement...

<summary>This page introduces a collection of Melanesian folk-tales, explaining that they were mostly written by native islanders and highlighting their value for understanding local culture and imagination.</summary>
<keywords>folk-tales, Melanesia, Florida Island, Alfred Penny, oral tradition, cultural anthropology, storytelling style</keywords>

--- Page 390 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of Melanesian storytelling, specifically addressing whether these stories are believed to be fact or fiction, before beginning a collection of animal fables.</meta>

<header>The Heron and the Turtle.</header>

...and would have little impact if they were not presented as true. Because a story has been told and heard for generations, it is not usually subject to much doubt or criticism. However, it is safe to say that for the native people, a story is not considered a piece of history. The miraculous events are not taken very seriously, no matter how much they are enjoyed. Of course, anything seems possible when magic is involved and spirits are the actors. For example, no one doubts the existence of spirits like *Qat*, and the stories say he performed certain feats. I do not think, however, that the natives seriously believe that birds and fish can talk; I have never found evidence that they fail to distinguish between living and non-living things, or between birds, beasts, and humans. When an owl in a story speaks and cooks food, both actions are treated as fantasies rather than facts. The native mind is full of keen intelligence and should not be judged incapable of inventing wonders or enjoying flights of fancy, though even in their most imaginative stories, they stay within the bounds of generally accepted beliefs. In Florida <note>The Nggela Islands in the Solomon Islands</note> and in Mota, there are specific terms for these kinds of stories—*tugu ni pitu* and *kakae lea*—which signal the fictional nature of the narrative.

<margin>1. These stories are divided into three categories here: I. Animal Stories, which mostly involve birds and fish (as is natural on islands with very few mammals); II. Myths and tales about the origin of things; and III. Wonder Tales.</margin>

"Come and save my life," said the heron; and the *Boila* said to him, "Wait a bit." Then there came...

After this, the people of Hagelonga <note>A village or district in the Nggela Islands</note> went to fish. In the end, all the fish in the sea come along, and they do not pull up the net.

<header>### XIX. The Heron and the Turtle</header>

While the village adults were far away, the Heron (*Soo*) <note>original: "Soo"</note> came along, and the boys said to him, "Where have you come from?" 

The Heron said to them, "I am just wandering about." Then he asked them, "Would you like me to dance for you?" 

The boys replied, "Yes, we would like you to dance for us." 

The Heron said, "Bring me the porpoise-tooth and dog-tooth ornaments belonging to your fathers and mothers, so that I may dress myself in the finest clothes." 

They brought him the best ornaments, and he dressed himself up in them and danced for them. He danced along toward the enclosure <note>original: "fence"</note> where the Turtle was kept. When the Turtle saw him coming, he cried out, "Now I am going to die, my brother!" 

The Heron said to him, "And now I shall save your life, because you saved mine before." 

The Heron went into the house where the boys were, and there he danced for them. He sang:

"**Kerembaembae! Kerembaembae!**" <note>This is a magical chant or refrain used in the story</note>
"Your leg that they tied is now loosened!" — and his leg was loosened.
"**Kerembaembae!** Your head has slipped out!" — and his head slipped out.
"**Kerembaembae!** Your front is free!" — and his front part was free.
"**Kerembaembae!** Your back is free!" — and his back part was free.
"**Kerembaembae!** All the rest of you is free!" — and the rest of him was free.
"**Kerembaembae!** Follow the path!" 
"**Kerembaembae!** Reach the sand!" 
"**Kerembaembae!** Down into the sea with you!" 
"**Kerembaembae!** Dive out of sight!" 
"**Kerembaembae!** Go a fathom's length!" 
"**Kerembaembae!** Go two fathoms!" 

In this way, the Turtle escaped with his life. 

When the people returned from the inland gardens and came out into the clearing, they looked at the enclosure. But the Heron was gone, and they said, "Someone has stolen our turtle!" 

They asked the boys, "Who has been here just now?" 

The boys said, "Only a Heron came here and danced for us. We gave him all your things, and he tricked us so that we did not go and look after the turtle." 

The people of the village felt very bitter about this. They went and looked at the path, and there they saw the tracks of the turtle. They said, "Yes, he has certainly saved himself; nobody has stolen him."

### 2. THE THREE FISH. UREPARAPARA. <note>Ureparapara is one of the Banks Islands in northern Vanuatu.</note>

This is the story of the Boxfish <note>original: "Watwata," an *Ostracion*</note> and the Sole. The two were scratching one another, and the Sole said to the Boxfish, "Scratch me." But the Boxfish said, "No, you must scratch me first." So the Sole scratched the Boxfish and scratched him thoroughly. But the Boxfish said, "Brother, you have scratched me poorly!" The Sole replied, "No, it is all right." Then the Boxfish said, "Well! Now I shall scratch you in my turn." After that, he scratched the Sole until he made him extremely thin <note>This explains why the Sole is a flatfish.</note>. The Sole said, "Well! You have scratched me poorly, but the two of us will play hide-and-seek." The Sole said, "You shall hide first." 

After that, the Boxfish hid and got out of sight under a stone. The Sole searched for him and found him. Then it was the Sole's turn to hide, and he buried himself in the sand; the Boxfish searched for him in vain. But the *Song*—a fish that shows its teeth—stood by and laughed at the Boxfish; and that fish has worn a grin ever since. The story is finished.

### 3. THE RAT AND THE RAIL. UREPARAPARA.

A Rat and a Rail <note>original: "Porphyrio," a species of swamphen or waterbird</note> were taking a walk together, and they found a Malay apple tree <note>original: "gaviga-tree," a species of *Eugenia*</note> with ripe fruit. They stood under it and argued over which of them should climb up. The Rat said, "Rail, you climb up!" The Rail said, "You!" They argued until the Rat finally climbed up. 

Then the Rail begged the Rat, "Brother, give me that dark, ripe one." But the Rat ate it and threw down only the seed <note>original: "stone"</note>. Then the Rail said again, "Brother, give me that one; it is very ripe indeed." But the Rat ate it all and again threw down only the seed. In this way, the Rail begged for fruit again and again, and the Rat treated him the same way every time. 

At last, the Rail made one more request to the Rat: "Brother, give me that one that is ripe and red." The Rat took it and threw it down onto the Rail's forehead, and there it stuck fast <note>This explains the red "frontal shield" or fleshy plate on the forehead of the Rail bird.</note>. "Oh, brother!" said the Rail, "You have made fun of me, my brother; but make..."

"Hurry up and come down, be quick about it!" Then the Rail took the unfolded leaf of a *dracaena* <note>original: "dracæna," a genus of tropical shrubs often used in Melanesian rituals</note>; and as the Rat was coming down the trunk of the tree, the Rail stood ready and thrust the leaf hard into the Rat's rump, where it stuck fast. ### 4. THE BIRDS' VOYAGE. MOTA. <note>Mota is an island in the Banks group of Vanuatu; its language was used as the primary mission language in the region.</note>

There is a story to tell. They lived in their village. The *tawan* <note>The *Pometia pinnata*, or Pacific lychee, a tree with edible fruit</note> was in fruit at Qakea <note>A small island near Mota</note>; the wind began to blow. Then they said, "Well, now at last we will paddle over and eat *tawan*." So they made a start and went, gathering from here and there. 

And the *renga*, or Green Parrot, said, "I am going with you." 

But they said, "Oh, no! You just go back, otherwise your father will be angry with us because of you." 

And he sang: "I will go and tell my daddy! The wind has blown hard against you; it beats against you, beat, beat!" <note>The bird's song functions as a threat or a curse that would cause bad weather for their voyage.</note> 

"Oh, well! Come along!" they said, and he climbed on board. 

Then the *Wasia* <note>A species of bird, likely a parrot or honeyeater</note> said, "You fellows, where are you going?" 

And they said, "To Qakea, to eat *tawan*." 

So he said, "I will go with you." 

And they said, "Stay where you are, otherwise your father and mother will scold us on your account." 

Then he sang: "I will go and tell my daddy! The wind has blown hard against you; it beats against you, beat, beat!" 

"Oh, well! Come along!" they said, and he climbed on board. 

Then the Pigeon said, "You fellows, where are you going?" 

And they said, "On a voyage." 

And he said, "I will go with you." 

But they said, "Not you; otherwise your father will scold us about you." 

And he sang: "I will go and tell my daddy! The wind has blown hard against you; it beats against you, beat, beat!" 

"Oh, well! Come along!" they said, and he climbed on board. 

And when everyone was on board, there was a Hermit Crab sitting there, and he said, "Friends, just let me come too." 

But they said, "You just stay there to look after our island." 

And he said, "No, my brothers, do not make me miserable." 

And they said, "No! Only those of us who can climb are going, not you—"

### 5. THE SHARK AND THE SNAKE. LEPERS' ISLAND <note>Now known as Ambae</note>.

This story is about the Shark and the Snake. They had a quarrel, and the Shark told the Snake to come down into the sea so that the Shark might eat him. The Snake said to him, "They will kill you, and then I shall eat a bit of you." Later, when people killed the Shark, the Snake went down into the sea and ate the Shark.

### 6. THE HEN AND HER CHICKENS. LEPERS' ISLAND.

This is about a Hen that had ten Chickens. As they went about seeking their food, they came across the tuber of a wild yam, a <term>gigimbo</term>. After a while, the tuber got up and ate one of the chickens. They called out to a <term>Kite</term> <note>A type of bird of prey</note>, which said to the Hen, "Put them under my wings." So they went there and stayed. 

Presently the Tuber came and asked the Kite, "Where are they?" 

"<note>original: *He-i*</note> No," said he, "I don't know." 

So the Tuber scolded the Kite; and the Kite flew down, snatched it up from the ground, and hovered with it high in the sky, and then let it drop to the ground. Then another Kite took it up, hovered in turn in the sky, and dropped it; it fell down and broke in two. So the two Kites divided the Tuber between them. Because of this, some tubers are good and some are bad. We call the good tuber by the name <term>nggeremanggegnneni</term>.

## II. MYTHS AND TALES OF ORIGINS.

### 1. THE STORY OF KAMAKAJAKU. BUGOTU, YSABEL ISLAND <note>Bugotu is a region on the southern end of Santa Isabel Island in the Solomon Islands.</note>.

He lived upon the hill at Gaji. While he was mending his nets, he looked down at the ocean and saw that it was extremely dark. His grandchildren went down to the sea to fish upon the reef, and Kamakajaku said to them, "Go and collect some salt water for me from that spot where the sea looks so dark." 

His grandchildren went down and fished on the beach with nets; afterward, they collected the salt water, returned to the village, and gave it to him. He said to them, "Give the dish here, and I will pour it out to see if its blackness is like what I saw from above." He poured it out and looked, but he did not find it to be like what he had seen from his place upon the hill.

The next morning, he took the salt-water container and went down himself. He placed a piece of obsidian <note>A sharp, volcanic glass often used as a cutting tool</note> in his ear and went down to the sea. He left his bag, club, and shield on the beach. Taking the container in his hand, he waded out and swam away from the shore. He kept looking back toward the hill where he lived, but he could not see it yet. He continued to swim out from the shore until he could finally see the hill at Gaji, and then he dipped the vessel into the water. 

Immediately, the surface of the sea began to roar and bubble. He heard a *Kombili* <note>original: *Kombili*, a King-fish (Scomberomorus)</note> approaching—a very great fish. It came and swallowed him, then swam off with him toward the east, toward the rising sun. It traveled with him until it arrived at a shallow place. The fish thrashed about so much that Kamakajaku realized there was probably a beach nearby. 

"Here I am," he said. He thought of the obsidian in his ear, felt for it, and found it. He cut open the belly of the *Kombili* and leaped out, where he saw a great brightness. He sat down and wondered, "I wonder where I am?" 

Suddenly, the Sun rose with a loud bang, rolling from side to side. The Sun said, "Don’t stand in my way,"

<summary>This page recounts the beginning of the legend of Kamakajaku, a hero who seeks the source of the sea's deep color, is swallowed by a giant fish, and is carried to the edge of the world where the sun rises.</summary>
<keywords>Kamakajaku, Bugotu, Ysabel Island, Gaji, solar myth, king-fish, obsidian, origin stories</keywords>

"If you do not, you will die immediately; stay on my right," the Sun said. He stepped aside until the Sun rose and moved away, and then he followed him. The two of them ascended toward heaven, traveling until they arrived at the village of the Sun's children. The Sun said, "You stay here." So Kamakajaku remained there with the Sun's children and grandchildren while the Sun went off. 

While Kamakajaku stayed there, they asked him, "Where did you come from?" 

He replied, "From the earth. I lived in my own home, and while I was gathering salt water, a great fish swallowed me, which is how I reached your fine village." 

So they lived together. The people above ate only raw food, but he showed them how to use fire so they could eat cooked food. 

Eventually, they said to him, "Do not go to that place; it is forbidden <note>original: taboo</note>." Then they went about their business. 

He stayed at the house and thought about what they had said. "They told me not to go there," he said to himself. He went over anyway and lifted a stone that served as the covering for a hole in the sky. He looked down upon his home at Gaji and wept. 

When they brought him food, he would not take it. So they asked him, "Did you go over to the far end of the house there? We forbade you from going there." 

"Yes," he admitted. 

"And do you want to go back down?" they asked. 

He replied, "Yes." 

So they built a small house for him. They gave him a banana and some seeds from the *pau* tree <note>A tree used for making dye</note>. They took a length of cane, tied it to the ridgepole <note>original: saddle-piece</note> of the house, and Kamakajaku sat inside. Then they lowered it down. 

They instructed him, "When you hear the birds and such things calling, do not look out. But when you hear the cicadas <note>original: cicalas</note> and the creatures that live on the earth crying out, then you may look out." 

And so they lowered him down and down. Whenever one length of cane proved too short, they tied another to it, until the house reached the hill and came to rest. 

His friends had been searching for him, believing he was already dead. On the day he returned from heaven, they rejoiced to see him again, and their hearts were glad. He lived for a long time afterward until he died on his hill at Gaji. And so it is finished; yes, it is just this: the Story of Kamakajaku.

<header>XIX.] Samuku. The Mim . .</header>

### 2. **THE STORY OF SAMUKU. BUGOTU, YSABEL ISLAND.**

Samuku lived in his village and built his house. He worked hard, and his affairs were many and successful. He took a wife and married, and the two of them lived well together, in perfect agreement. They worked, and they had plenty of food. 

One day, Samuku came home and asked for food because he was hungry, but his wife had not prepared any. Samuku was angry with his wife and scolded her severely. 

His wife said to him, "I am tired of making food for you. Your father and mother are dead—who else is supposed to make you food? Go and see them in Tuhilagi <note>In Solomon Islands mythology, Tuhilagi is a place associated with the spirits of the dead</note>," she said. 

Samuku was angry, and as he sat and thought, he said, "Fine, I will go and see them." 

So he hauled down a canoe and put out to sea toward Tuhilagi. He landed at *Lelegia tarunga*, the Ghosts' Mangroves, stepped onto the beach, and went inland, where he found a company of ghosts. 

They asked him, "Why have you come here? You are not dead yet," they said to him. 

Samuku answered, "My wife scolded me and sent me here." 

At night he stayed in a house, but when morning came, the house disappeared. He played a trick on the ghosts by making a fishing net, and they went to fish with it. He could see the forms of the ghosts, but the net got caught in the coral. When it grew light, the entire company of ghosts departed from him, so he went down and slept on the sand. The people of a certain place found him and took charge of him; he stayed with them until he died. 

This is the end of the story of Samuku; it is not a very long one.

### 3. **THE MIM. TORRES ISLANDS.**

They say that the Mim people <note>The Mim are legendary small, supernatural beings in the folklore of the Torres Islands</note> dragged yams from place to place. They brought them ashore at Hiw and then dragged them to Tugua; for this reason, the yams at Hiw and Tugua are very large and long. 

However, when they dragged them along here to Lo, all the people were down on the reefs fishing and heard nothing of it; nor

The people didn't know anything until they found the skins <note>original: "rind"</note> of the yams sticking to the roots of the trees along the path. They picked these up and planted them; for that reason, the yams on the island of Lo are not very large, but they are plentiful enough. Because the Mim people <note>Mythological beings or ancestors in Torres Island folklore</note> sliced their yams in half for the men of Hiw and Tugua, and then passed on to Toga and sliced them again for the people there, the yams in those places are very large and long. 

Afterward, they crossed to Ureparapara, where the people sliced the yams in half and planted them. They did the same in all the islands in that direction; it was only at Lo that the people did not see or hear what was happening. The crowns <note>The top part of the yam used for planting</note> of the yams remained and were planted somewhere. The Mim people went dragging the yams through all the islands, shouting and calling to the men of every place to come and slice the yams and take the burden from them.

### 4. THE ORIGIN OF POISONED ARROWS. AURORA ISLAND <note>Now known as Maewo</note>.

I have often heard them telling the story about it in this way. They say that in the old days, there was no fighting. But there was an old man named Muesarava who was blind and used to stay in the house doing nothing. He heard a pigeon calling, took a bow and a broad-headed arrow, and went under the tree. The pigeon dropped a bit of the fruit it was eating, and that blind man fired a shot at random <note>original: "at a venture"</note> into the tree, hitting the pigeon without seeing it. 

He took it up, went and put it into the oven together with the yams, and sat down and sang a song. However, two young fellows came along and quietly opened old Muesarava’s oven, and they ate up his pigeon along with some of his yams. Then they went to another place and sang a song back to him. He heard it and went back to eat his pigeon, but he found when he uncovered the oven that it had been eaten, and that something foul <note>original: "something not good"</note> had been put in its place. Then he was extremely angry and plotted a fight against the people of the place where the two young men had come from, who had—

<page-num>369</page-num>
<header>XIX.] Origin of Poisoned Arrows.</header>

...stolen and eaten Muesarava's food. In response, Muesarava began to make fighting arrows out of human bones. Muesarava went and dug up <note>original: "grubbed up"</note> with his hands a boy who had died; he took his bones, beat them into splinters, and rubbed them until they were sharp. His enemies, for their part, knew nothing of this; they only carved wood into shape, or used the bones of fish or birds to fix into their arrows, while Muesarava prepared human bones. 

When they fought, they shot at him and hit him, but he did not die; however, when he shot them, they could not survive, but all died instantly. They fought again and shot at him, hitting him once more, but he did not die. But whenever Muesarava shot at them and hit his mark, they all died. Because this happened so often, and they saw that they were dying in huge numbers, they asked Muesarava why it was that they could shoot him without him dying, while everyone he shot died. Therefore, he told them, "Go and dig up one of the dead men I have shot, scrape his bones, and tip your arrows with that." They followed his advice and did as he had told them; and when they fought again, they shot him, and he died immediately.

That object—the human bone that Muesarava ground to a point for himself with his own hand—still remains and has not yet decayed <note>original: "spoilt"</note>. The reed-shaft has rotted and been replaced over and over again, but that human bone still remains; I have seen it myself in my brother’s possession; it still exists. The people think a great deal of it, believing that there is supernatural power, *mana* <note>The Melanesian concept of spiritual efficacy or power</note>, in that *toto* arrow <note>A specific type of ceremonial or powerful arrow</note>. If there is a rumor of fighting, and that arrow is pointed in the direction from which the threat comes, the fighting comes to nothing.

The man wished to steal Tagaro's pig, a *rawe* <note>A highly valued pig with tusks that have grown into a circle</note>, so he caught the pig and...

->6. **HOW TAGARO MADE THE SEA. AURORA ISLAND.**<-

They say that he made the sea, and that in ancient times the sea was quite small, like a common pool upon the beach. This pool was at the back of his house, and there were fish in the pool, and he had built a stone wall around it. 

Tagaro had gone out to look at the various things he had made, and his wife was in the village. His two children were at home, and he had forbidden them from going to the back of the house. So when he was gone, the thought entered the minds of those two: "Why has our father forbidden us to go there?" 

They were shooting at lizards and rats, and after a while, one said to the other, "Let us go and see what it is he has told us to keep away from." So they went and saw the pool of saltwater with many fish crowding together in it. One of the boys stood on the stones Tagaro had built up; he saw the fish, shot at one, and hit it. As he ran to catch hold of it, he knocked down a stone, and then the water ran out. 

Tagaro heard the roaring of the water and ran to stop it. An old woman <note>Likely a reference to Tagaro's mother or wife in the myth</note> laid herself down in the path of the water, but nothing could be done. Those two boys who had thrown down the stone took clubs shaped like knives and prepared a passage for the sea, one on one side and the other on the other side of the place, and the sea followed as it flowed. They believe that the old woman turned into stone and lies now on the part of Maewo <note>Maewo is the indigenous name for Aurora Island</note> near Raga <note>Raga is the indigenous name for Pentecost Island</note>.

# 7. HOW TAGARO THE LITTLE FOUND FISH.
### AMBAE <note>original: "Lepers' Island"; this was a colonial name for the island now known as Ambae.</note>

They say that he pulled down his canoe and paddled out in search of fish. He saw a great rock standing in the sea and floated there gently without paddling to see whether he would find fish or not. He saw many fish rising up to the surface from under his canoe, and he fed them with the food he had in his hand. He noticed that these fish knew how to eat the food of the land. Then he said, "I am going to leave you, but the day after to-morrow I shall grate some *loko* <note>original: "loko"; a type of pudding made from grated starchy vegetables like yams or taro.</note> for you to eat, and I shall pour coconut sauce over it and bring it here to you." 

So he left them and stayed at home for one day, as the story goes. When the second day came for him to go, he took that *loko* which he had seasoned with coconut juice, launched his canoe, and paddled out to the place where those fish were. He called them with a song, which he sang like this:

"My fish, whatever you are! Nice little fish, here is your food with sauce, your food prepared with coconut sauce." <note>original: "Bulenggu sara ige ! ige ruwen, mo gaigei rororoa, mo gaigei rororoa sobe"</note>

However, there was another person named Merambuto who stood on the beach and heard Tagarombiti <note>Tagarombiti translates to "Tagaro the Little."</note> calling his fish with that song. The next day, Merambuto made haste to prepare food during the night. In the early morning, he pulled down Tagarombiti's canoe and paddled out until he came to the place where Tagarombiti had floated before. He sang that song again: "My fish, whatever you are!" 

When those fish heard his voice, they noticed it was loud and did not rise to the surface, because they knew it was a different person by his loud voice. Merambuto realized that they were not rising, so he changed his voice to be small like Tagarombiti's. He called them with a small voice, singing that song: "My fish, whatever you are!" 

When the fish heard that the voice was small, they all rose to the surface, and he caught every one of them with a hook. He then hurried to paddle ashore and went back into his village, and...

### 8. STORY OF THE OLD WOMAN: HOW SHE MADE THE SEA.
### AMBAE <note>original: "Lepers’ Island"; the colonial name for the island now known as Ambae.</note>.

Nobody knows what her name was, but she was an old woman. There were two children who lived with her in her house, but nobody knows what their father’s and mother’s names were; the story says that the mother of these two was the daughter of this old woman. 

Her house was a good one, fenced about with reeds. There was a fence all around the house, and there was also a fence built against the back of the house. Those two children were forbidden to go into that back area because she wanted to be there by herself. Inside that little fence at the back of the house, she carefully placed a leaf of the *via* <note>original: "gigantic caladium"; a large-leafed tropical plant.</note>. They say that she always urinated <note>original: "made water"</note> into that leaf, and she was always very strict in forbidding those two from going there, lest they should see it. These two children were both boys, and they were always shooting...

lizards. So one day, when the old woman went into the garden to work and to bring back food for the three of them, she said to those two, "Do not go there!" and they answered, "Very well, we shall not go." She went out of the house and into the gardens, and the two brothers played with their bows, shooting lizards. After a while, one said to the other, "It would be a good thing to go and see what it is that the old woman has forbidden us to see." "Very well," said the other, "let us go." 

So they went, and they saw a *via* <note>The *via* is a type of giant taro (*Alocasia macrorrhiza*) known for its massive leaves that can hold significant amounts of water.</note> leaf with water in it. Then they saw a lizard sitting on a part of that leaf, and one of them shot at it; however, he missed the lizard and hit the leaf, and the water that was in it quickly burst forth. The old woman heard it and realized that those two had probably shot the leaf. She stood up and cried with a loud voice, "Pour round about and meet! Pour round about and meet!" <note>original: *Horodali bulu, korodali bulu!*</note> and twice again, "Round about the world! Round about the world!" <note>original: *Dali ure, dali ure!*</note> And thus, for the first time, the sea stood full around the whole world, for before that, they say there was no sea. So, you might say the old woman made the sea herself.

### III. WONDER TALES.

#### 1. THE STORY OF DILINGAVUV. TORRES ISLANDS.

They were living in their village, and Dilingavuv's companions made a garden and planted bananas in it. When the bananas bore fruit and ripened, Dilingavuv went every day and ate bananas in their garden—not eating them on the ground, but climbing into the trees to eat. After a while, he was discovered. One of the party went into the garden and saw him up in a banana tree eating, so he ran and told the others. He said, "You fellows, I have seen the one who steals and eats our bananas!" 

Then Maraw-hihi <note>A character whose name likely links him to the "Marawa" or "spider" spirit common in Melanesian folklore.</note> said, "Carve out bows for us so we can go and shoot and kill him." 

But they said, "Maraw-hihi, no one will be able to shoot and kill him." 

"I will shoot him and kill him," said Maraw-hihi. 

"It is completely impossible," they replied. However—

They carved bows for themselves and tipped their arrows; and when that was finished, Marawhihi said, "Let us go after him one by one."

But Marawhihi insisted that someone must go again, so another went, and the same thing happened. Thus, they all went in turn and returned to argue with Marawhihi, saying, "It is impossible to do." 

Then Marawhihi said, "I shall do it myself; I shall shoot him and kill him." Now, they say this Marawhihi was more clever than all the others. He went last and saw Dilingavuv sitting in the banana tree. He stepped along on tiptoe under the banana tree, and when Dilingavuv stretched out his arms, Marawhihi was not frightened by him. Instead, he shot him with a bird arrow made of <term>casuarina</term> <note>Casuarina is a genus of trees often called "ironwood" due to the extreme hardness of their timber.</note> wood. Marawhihi ran to tell his friends, but Dilingavuv got up from under the banana tree and went home to his mother. When he reached his mother's house, he called to her from outside. She answered him, "What is it, my son?" 

He said, "Give me an axe." 

His mother asked, "What are you going to do with it?" 

But he deceived her and did not tell her that Marawhihi had shot his ear off. Instead, he went and carved a new ear for himself out of the root of a tree. The name of that tree is the *Raw*. As he was chopping the *Raw* root, he chanted, "Chop in pieces! Chop asunder!" 

However, Marawhihi had sent one of his men to spy. The man listened and heard him saying, "Chop in pieces! Chop asunder!" He ran back and told Marawhihi that Dilingavuv was carving himself a replacement ear. 

After this, Marawhihi and his men prepared a feast and danced every day. When Dilingavuv heard of it, he said, "I will go and have my revenge." Dilingavuv did not go directly to them in the open clearing but stayed at the edge of the village. There, he built a fire and roasted his chestnuts. He heated stones in the fire, dug a very deep hole, and covered the opening with a dancing dress made of leaves. He sat there and watched them dancing. Before long, as they were dancing, one of the men stepped out to catch his breath. When he saw Dilingavuv sitting and eating chestnuts, he called out to him, asking for one. 

"Run over here," said Dilingavuv. 

So the man ran over to him and sat down on the dancing dress; as he threw himself down to sit, he fell straight into the hole. Dilingavuv played the same trick on the entire company at that dance, letting them all fall into that one pit, with Marawhihi falling in last of all. 

Then Dilingavuv took the stones he had heated over the fire and threw them down into the hole to kill the men with the heat. But as he threw them down, Marawhihi said to his companions, "Move over to this side of the pit," and they did so; because of this, not one of them was killed. Dilingavuv, however, went home thinking he had killed them all. 

Then Marawhihi said to his men, "Do you know how we shall save our lives?" 

They answered, "We are all as good as dead already." 

"Not at all," Marawhihi said, "I know very well that we shall not die." 

Then Marawhihi looked up out of the mouth of the pit and saw a banyan branch bending over the opening. He said, "Let us <term>ker galagalaput</term> <note>original: *ker galagalaput*; a technique of shooting one arrow after another, making each one strike and fix itself into the back of the one before it to form a chain.</note> at that banyan branch." 

They did so, and the reed shafts of the arrows they had shot reached all the way down to them in the pit. Then Marawhihi said, "Climb up along the shafts." 

They said to him, "You go first, and we will follow you." 

So he climbed up the line of arrows and got out of the pit, and in this way, they all saved their lives.

### 4. THE GHOST-WIFE: A STORY FROM MOTA.

This is a story to tell. They were living in their village when a famine prevailed. There was a woman and her son, and they both were very hungry. After a time, the mother went to dig *qauro* <term>wild yams</term> for them to eat. When she had finished digging the *qauro*, she would return to her son in the village. 

As she went, she found a *gaviga* <note>original: *gariga*; the Malay apple tree</note> tree in fruit in a deserted garden. She put down her basket, took a stick with a crook, and pulled down the branches of the *gaviga* with it; then she gathered the fruit with her hands and ate. When she had finished eating, she put some seeds into her basket, and as she walked along, she broke the tips of the branches to mark the path. 

When she arrived at the village, she said to her son, "Take the things out of our basket." He took them out one by one, and as he did so, he found the *gaviga* seeds which his mother had put there. 

Then her son said to her, "What is this you have been eating, that you have put the seeds in the basket for me to see?" 

His mother said, "Where?" 

Her son took out the *gaviga* seeds. Then his mother said to him, "Oh! <note>original: *Eai!*; an exclamation of surprise or denial</note> I don't know; I suppose someone else put them there." 

But he said, "No! You have been eating them today."

If she tries to pluck hibiscus leaves, they are in her hand already. If she tries to take a coconut, there is a coconut already in her hand.

As evening approaches, the two of them go home. Her husband returns and sees them, and he asks, "What did you two eat?"

She says, "The two of us have been working in our garden; we dug a yam for our food, plucked hibiscus leaves, and gathered coconuts."

But her husband says to her, "That is not true. I have been to our garden and saw one thing, but I did not see at all that a yam had been dug—not in the least—and no coconuts have been taken."

The woman says to him, "No, that isn't right; we certainly got the food from our garden."

But the man says, "No; there is probably someone else who has given it to you."

She says, "Who is there that would bother themselves with us? It would have to be a ghost <note>original: "ghost" — in Melanesian culture, this often refers to a spirit or supernatural being (*vui*) rather than just the soul of a deceased person</note>, I suppose!"

He says, "Tell me who gives these things to you."

"Who would there be to give me anything?" she asks.

The man says, "No! Tell me the truth."

Then the woman says to him, "Well then, come along; the three of us will go to our garden."

So the three of them set out and arrived at the garden. The woman says to him, "Well, look here. You are angry with us, but you may see for yourself." Then she touches a taro plant, and it was just as before, and she touches the yams, and it was the same.

Then the man says, "No; someone else has been giving you these things." As he says this, he grabs a stick and beats her, saying, "You do not belong down here on earth; you belong above the sky. What have you been doing here? Go back to your own country!"

She says, "Very well, I will soon go back to my own country." One day later, he beat her again and then went off.

XIX.] Ganviviris.

When she sees that he is gone, she gathers banyan leaves into a heap and sets fire to them. They begin to burn. Then she says to her child, "Sit here, and I will go to the other side of the fire." She goes to the other side of the fire, and the smoke rises straight up into the clouds; the mother ascends within it. Her child cries beside the fire, but she continues up into the clouds ¹.

### 5. GANVIVIRIS. MOTA.

The story about what Ro Som <note>Ro Som is likely a spirit or a supernatural figure acting as a patron</note> did for *Ganviviris* is not an ancient one; he was a man whom my father’s grandfather and his friends had actually seen. He was an orphan; both his father and mother were dead, and he lived with his mother's brother. His uncle did nothing to help him advance in the <term>suqe</term> <note>suqe: a graded social hierarchy or secret society central to Melanesian life, where members gain status through feasts and payments</note> club; he remained an <term>avlara</term> <note>avlara: a person of no rank who has not yet entered the graded society</note> because he was a lazy fellow. Whenever they called him to go to work, he would refuse; and when the others had all gone inland to the gardens, he would go down to the beach to shoot fish, doing nothing else day after day. 

But one day, when they had called him to work and everyone had departed, he took his bow and went down to Ngerenow. There he saw a <term>samwa</term> <note>samwa: likely a type of large fish or sea creature</note> slowly swimming along and rolling from side to side quite close to him. He took an arrow tipped with casuarina wood <note>casuarina: a very hard wood often called "ironwood," commonly used for spear and arrow tips</note> and drew his bow to shoot. Just as he was releasing the string, he heard a voice urging him on, saying, "Let it fly! Shoot!" He lowered his arrow from the bowstring, thinking it was a—

---

¹ Here the manuscript ends. The story continues by relating that the man found his child crying for its mother beside the fire and refusing to be comforted. He sought help from all the birds and living creatures, but none would listen to him until he came to the Spider, <term>marawa</term>, who readily undertook to bring the child to its mother. He spun a line from earth to heaven, took the man and the child on his back, and carried them safely up. A feast was going on in heaven, and the two sat down in the circle of spectators. The men were dancing around the drum, and the women were tramping around in pairs. Each time the mother passed the child, it cried out, "Mother!" She stopped at last and asked, "Who is it that cries 'Mother!' to me?" Recognizing her child and husband, she agreed to return, and the Spider carried all three of them safely back to the earth.

So Ganviviris dived out of the cave and went back into the village and said to his uncle, "*Tata* <term>Tata</term> <note>A term of respect used for a father or, as in this case, a maternal uncle who acts as a guardian</note>, tell those three wives to weave me ten bags." 

And his uncle said to him, "What do you have belonging to you to store in them? You are a penniless fellow, and one who never plants or harvests." 

But he said, "Oh! Just let them be woven." 

So his uncle said to his wives, "You are to weave bags for Ganviviris." 

And the three of them cried out, "Oh! Who is going to listen to him, an *avlava* <term>avlava</term> <note>original: "avlava"; a person of no rank or social standing; a variation of "avlara" from the previous page</note>, a fellow who does nothing at all?" 

But his uncle said, "Weave them just to see what his nonsense means; then we shall see what sort of property he has to store in them." 

So the three women wove the bags. And in the night, Ro Som came to Ganviviris and said, "Make haste to hang up your bags." And the next day he hung up the bags; and in the night as he was lying down to sleep, he heard the rafters creak again because of the money which was filling the bags. He got up and felt those ten bags one after another, and every one was quite full. 

And Ro Som said to him, "Tell your uncle to give you his third wife." So he spoke to him about it, and his uncle let him have her. And he said again, "*Tata*, let us break up firewood for the day after tomorrow."

### XIX. Ganviviris

But his uncle said to him, "What property do you have to offer so we can buy your rank? You are a penniless fellow with no income." 

Ganviviris replied, "Lend me some money and a pig to make the first payments." He only said this, however, to test his uncle.

His uncle answered, "I will not consent to let you have any of my property. Why should I? You are a lazy man." 

But Ganviviris said, "*Tata* <term>Tata</term> <note>maternal uncle or father-figure</note>, let us chop firewood the day after tomorrow; tomorrow we will go into your gardens, and I will look for some taro there." 

So they went to the gardens, and he said to his uncle, "Put up a <term>*palako*</term> <note>original: "palako"; a sign or mark placed on a garden to prohibit anyone from taking the crops</note> as a warning against taking anything from these gardens." 

His uncle said to him, "You are marking a huge amount of food; what do you have of your own to pay such a high price?" 

He replied, "You will pay the high price." 

But the uncle said, "I will not listen to you regarding my money and my food." 

So they went back into the village, and everyone there heard what had been done. They laughed at Ganviviris, saying that he would never be able to afford the "eating" ceremonies for his <term>*suge*</term> <note>original: "suge"; the graded secret society or club where members rise in rank by providing feasts and shell-money</note> rank. 

But the next day they chopped firewood, and he bought the taro at a high price, paying ten coils of shell-money for each garden. His uncle said to him, "You have bought food at a high price and succeeded in that; but now you must distribute money to everyone for your *suge* initiation. Where will you get anything for that?" 

Ganviviris said, "That will be your doing, of course." 

But his uncle had no wish to give him any money, so he said, "Let us bring the taro tomorrow and crack almonds for the feast." 

Then Ganviviris said again to his uncle, "*Tata*, have your children twist some cords." So his two children and his wives twisted the rope. 

The neighbors asked his uncle, "They are twisting cords, but where is the pig tied up by the house to be bound by them?" 

He replied, "Bah! <note>original: "Exi!"; an exclamation of disdain or surprise</note> We have never seen him own a single thing; he is a pauper." 

But in the evening, Ganviviris went and got four pigs and tied them up near the village. In a single day, he completed the ceremonies for the <term>*aririk*</term> and the <term>*qalagiar*</term> <note>specific degrees or levels of rank within the *suge* society</note> ranks. 

And during the night, Ro Som <note>the spirit or personification of shell-money</note> said to him, "You are to take all your ranks in the *suge* here at Qakea; you are not to take any at Mota. If you disobey my instructions in this, you will die."

### 6. THE LITTLE ORPHAN. MOTA.

This is a story to tell. There were people living in their village and the boys were growing up. Their father and mother said to them, "Go down to the beach and catch fish with hooks and lines for us, and we two will go inland to the gardens to get vegetables for us all to eat with the fish." 

The boys said, "Very well." The parents went up to the garden, and the boys went down to the beach. 

As they were going along the path, the Little Orphan said, "Let me go with you." 

But they said, "*E-o-o!* <note>original: "E-o-o!"; a strong exclamation of refusal or disagreement</note> Not you, a little orphan! We will go by ourselves, for we are children who have fathers. If you were to go with us, what would you eat? You have no father and no mother—who will give you vegetable food <term>vegetable food</term> <note>In Melanesian culture, a meal consists of a "relish" (fish or meat) and a "food" (the starchy staple like yam or taro). The boys are taunting the orphan because he has no parents to provide the essential staple to accompany a catch of fish.</note> to eat with your fish?" 

So they went on ahead, and the Little Orphan followed behind. Those who were the children of fathers went down to the main beach, but the Little Orphan went down a steep path eastward to the landing-place at Sanwawa. There, he fished for himself with a line and hook. 

When he saw the others climbing back up into the island, he also strung his fish together and climbed back up himself. When he came near them, they said, "Do not walk with us; you have no father and no mother to give you vegetable food to eat with your fish." 

So they climbed up, the boys in front and the orphan behind. But while they continued on the way home, he stopped short, went into his cave, and roasted his fish. When he had roasted them, he took—

**Note.**—Two more stories from Mota, found in native manuscripts, are too long to include here in full. 

One is the story of *Wowut-ta-Taragaviga*, whose parents kept him inside the house until he was grown, then helped him advance to the highest *suqe* <term>a graded secret society or social hierarchy</term> rank. Another man from the same island, while taking the same step in rank, sent a portion of his feast to *Wowut-ta-Taragaviga* by way of an orphan, as everyone else was too afraid to approach the *gamal* <term>a men's clubhouse or meeting house</term> of such a high-ranking man. Wowut took a liking to the orphan and paid him with money. The boy returned again and again with food until he had "thousands of pieces of money, thousands of boars, and thousands of pigs with curled tusks," and with these, he promoted himself to a high *suqe* rank. When Wowut died, he directed that when his friend came to mourn him, he should be given Wowut's wife in memory of him. 

The other is the story of *Qat-wuruga*, who was born to a mother who had been killed by a fall from a tree; he grew up in the forest like the children in the Story of Taso. His maternal uncle finds him and takes him home, where the uncle’s wives neglect and mistreat him, giving him the name "Scurfy-head." The boy begs his uncle to take him back to the forest, and the uncle carries him out of the sight of the sea into the heart of the island of Vanua Lava. 

There he settles himself, and after a while, he begins snaring birds. One day, the fat of a bird roasting over the fire dripped through the earth onto the head of Wetopunpun, who lived beneath the ground. This was the boy’s father—either the ghost of his dead father or a *Vui* <term>a spirit or supernatural being, often with creative powers</term>. Using the magic charm "*Soso-punpun, Soso-punpun*" (similar to the *Kerembaembae* chant in Story No. 1), he creates food, gardens, a village, a *gamal*, pigs, fowls, and a drum—all forms of traditional wealth. 

*Qat-wuruga’s* uncle comes to visit him and assists his advancement to the highest ranks of the *suqe*, receiving the required payment of pigs. His wives, skeptical at first, go to a *kolekole* <term>a secular festival or dance involving the display of wealth</term> and see the youth they once despised in all his splendor. They desire to stay as his wives and even make him cut open his chest to give them some of his liver to eat <note>The liver was often considered the seat of the emotions or life force in Pacific cultures</note>. 

A canoe from Maewo arrives, and the visitors find the fresh emblems of his rank. They challenge him to compare his wealth with theirs and are left open-mouthed with astonishment at the number of jawbones <note>Pig jawbones were displayed as trophies to prove how many animals a man had slaughtered for ritual feasts</note> of the pigs he has killed for his feasts. They trick him into falling asleep and carry him off to their own island to kill and eat him. While they are—

### 7. THE WOMAN AND THE EEL. AURORA <note>original: "Aurora"; the colonial name for the island of Maewo in Vanuatu</note>.

A woman went to soak pandanus leaves in the water to prepare them for weaving mats; she placed them there in the evening and went home. In the morning, she went to collect the leaves from the water, but when she went to take them out, she saw they had turned into an eel. She ran back and told some men who were occupied with the <term>suqe</term> <note>original: "suqe"; a graded social hierarchy or secret society</note>, and they ran down, tied a cord to the eel, and dragged it up to the village. 

However, there was a disabled man who could not go with them, and he lay in the <term>gamal</term> <note>original: "gamal"; a men's clubhouse or communal meeting house</note>. Next to the <term>gamal</term> grew a croton tree; as they dragged the eel up, it curled its tail around the croton, nearly breaking it, and the disabled man saw this. They pulled hard on the eel until it released its tail from the tree, and they brought it into the village and laid it at the entrance of the <term>gamal</term>. 

When the men ran off to get firewood and banana leaves to cook it, the eel spoke to the disabled man, saying, "When they are eating, do not join them; let them eat by themselves." Consequently, the man did not eat. They placed the eel in the <term>suqe</term> oven to be cooked and covered the oven. When they opened it, everyone took a piece of the eel—every single one of them took a piece. When their leader <note>original: "great man"</note> said to them, "Now, get your portions ready," they all prepared them. Then he said again, "Now let us eat," and they all took a bite at once. 

But as they took that first bite, their legs turned into eels. They bit a second time, and their entire bodies turned into eels. They bit again, and they were completely transformed into eels. The leader glided away first, and they all followed him into the water.

***

...making preparations for their dance and feast, one of their party takes pity on him, unties him, and delivers him; the two of them paddle back to Vanua Lava. But when they reach Qat-wuruga's place, everything has disappeared. 

When he was first captured, his father Wetopunpun had gone to the beach and sat there grieving. The people of Qakea, seeing him there day after day, paddled over and took him to their village, where there was a famine. There, using his charm "Soso-punpun," he caused gardens full of food to appear. The people grew envious of him, so he left them and sought a solitary place, where he sat down by the side of Ro Som <note>likely a spirit or a significant landmark</note> with all his possessions around him. A stone located there representing him remains a place of sacrifice to this day.

<header>xix.] *The Little Owl. The Winged Wife.*</header>

### 8. THE LITTLE OWL. AURORA <note>original: "Aurora"; the island of Maewo in Vanuatu</note>.

This is a story about two women who were gathering firewood and found a young owl—a bird with white feathers and very large eyes. It was a young bird of this kind that they found. One day, the two women went to check on their little bird and found that he had turned into a man; so they took him into the village, and he became their husband. 

The three lived together in perfect harmony; they built their house, worked in their garden, and remained this way for many years. But after a time, he began to beat them when they quarreled. They scolded him for it, saying, "You there, you are a bird and our property because we found you; why do you beat us like this?" 

He replied that he would leave them. In the evening, he drank <term>kava</term> <note>original: "kava"; a traditional sedative drink made from the roots of the *Piper methysticum* plant</note> and forbade them from blowing on the fire <note>likely to keep the house dark so they wouldn't see his transformation</note>. But when he lay down to sleep, the two women blew the fire into a bright blaze and looked at him. He turned back into a bird and flew away. The two women cried out after him, and he threw down money <note>likely shell money, used traditionally in Melanesian cultures</note> to them as he left.

---

### 9. THE WINGED WIFE. AURORA.

This is a story about the women who were said to belong to heaven and had wings like birds. They came down to earth to bathe in the sea, and when they bathed, they took off their wings. 

As Qatu <note>also known as Qat; a central hero and trickster figure in Melanesian mythology</note> was walking about, he happened to see them. He took one pair of wings, went back to the village, and buried them at the base of the main pillar of his house. Then he went back again and watched them. When they had finished bathing, they went and picked up their wings and flew up to heaven; but one could not fly because Qat had stolen her wings, and she was crying. 

Qat went up to her and spoke to her deceptively, asking, "What are you crying for?" 

She replied, "They have taken away my wings." 

Then he took her to his house and married her. Qat’s mother took her with her when they went to work; and when...

As she wept, her tears flowed down onto the ground and wore a deep hole in the earth. When he saw that the first arrow did not fall back, he shot again and hit the end of the first arrow. He shot many times, always hitting his mark, until a chain of arrows reached all the way down to the earth. 

Then, a banyan root grew upward, following the path of the arrows. Qat took a basket of pork in his hand and climbed up to heaven to search for his wife. He found a person there hoeing the ground; he also found his wife and prepared to take her back. He said to the person who was hoeing, "When you see this banyan root, do not disturb it." 

However, as the two were climbing down the banyan root and had not yet reached the ground, that person chopped the root off. Qat fell to the earth and was killed, and the woman flew back to heaven. That is the end of the story.
