So they lay there, rolling along on the smooth ground, and by and by they grew strong. Then they found dry leaves in which rainwater had collected, and they sipped and drank. They also came upon a root of *gena* <term>original: "gena"; a ginger-like plant (Zingiberaceae)</term> and sucked it; this *gena* has a bulbous lump at its root where water accumulates in a small hollow.

They stayed by the *gena* root until they were strong enough to move about. Then they began to wander and made their way out of the thicket. As they wandered along, they came to a place where there was a sow with her young, and they sat and watched her. Now, this sow was the property of their maternal uncle, Qatu. They sat there, waiting for the coconuts with which the sow was fed. 

After a while, their uncle Qatu arrived, sat down, and called his sow. The sow came with her litter of piglets, and Qatu chopped up their food for them. When he had finished cutting it, he did not stay until it was all eaten; instead, he turned his back and left. Then the two children came out and drove the sow away. They took the chopped coconuts for themselves and sat down to eat. Meanwhile, the sow went up into the village and cried out to her owner, Qatu. 

The next morning, when he came down to feed the sow, they did the same thing. The sow went off to her owner, and they gathered up the chopped coconuts in their arms and took them away to eat. Qatu noticed that his sow was always coming back to him and was thin, with no fat on her at all. He asked himself, "I wonder why my sow keeps coming back to me as if I hadn't fed her? Why is she not fat? I will sit and observe what it is that makes her return to the village." 

So, after feeding her, he pretended to leave but circled back so that he might see what was happening to his sow. He stood and watched as the children came out. Qatu said to them, "So, is it you who are always driving away my sow? I have seen her coming back to me hungry." These two twins let the food slip from their arms and stood there ashamed, biting their fingers. <term>Qatu</term> <note>original: "Qatu"; a central figure and culture hero in the mythology of the Banks Islands</note> asked them, "Where do you come from?" 

They told him how they had lain and rolled on the ground until they found their way out of the thicket, how they saw the water and drank it, and how they came to the root of the <term>gena</term> <note>original: "gena"; a ginger-like plant with water-holding roots</note> and sucked it. They explained how doing so made them grow strong, and how they saw the sow and filled their bellies with the food she was eating. <term>Qatu</term> understood without a doubt that these were the children of his sister, whom <term>Taso</term> <note>original: "Taso"; a legendary cannibal giant</note> had killed long ago.

<term>Qatu</term> called to them and went up to the village, hiding them at the far end of his house. He commanded <term>Ro Motari</term>, his wife, to go into the garden to dig some yams and bring back tender hibiscus leaves—the kind that locusts eat—to make a yam-mash for the two twins. <term>Ro Motari</term> did as she was told; she gathered the leaves, dug the yams, and returned to make the <term>loko</term> <note>original: "loko"; a traditional dish of mashed yams</note>. 

When the earth oven was closed, <term>Qatu</term> told <term>Ro Motari</term> to go and cut down coconut fronds for mats, to weave and spread them out, and to prepare a pillow. Then <term>Qatu</term> told <term>Ro Motari</term> to go to the far end of the house. When she went, she saw the two little twins sitting at the back of the house inside the pig fence. She ran back and cried out to <term>Qatu</term>, "Lili! Lili! <note>An exclamation of surprise or excitement</note> What are these little ones to me? Are they my children, my brothers, or my grandchildren?"¹ <term>Qatu</term> said to her, "O-o-o! They are your grandchildren." So she and <term>Qatu</term> gladly took them into the main part of the house and gave them food, and the boys stayed with them. 

After a while, they grew big, and <term>Qatu</term> carved bows for them made from the <term>rachis</term> <note>original: "rachis"; the central midrib or stem of a leaf or frond</note> of sago fronds. When they were able to shoot lizards, he broke those bows, took them away, and made them better ones. When they could shoot geckos, he again took the bows away, broke them, and shaped new ones for them.

¹ In another version of the story: "When <term>Motari</term> saw the two handsome boys with their white hair, she liked them and asked <term>Qatu</term>, 'Are these my children or my husbands?' And <term>Qatu</term> said, 'Yes indeed, your husbands, for they are my sister’s children.'" <note>This variation likely reflects different regional kinship systems or marriage customs where a mother's brother's children (cousins) might be referred to in such terms.</note>

<summary>Qatu discovers that the children stealing his pig's food are his lost nephews, the sons of his sister killed by Taso. He brings them home to his wife, Ro Motari, and begins training them in archery.</summary>

Qatu made different bows for them and attached points to their arrows. When they were able to shoot the small birds called *talagoras* <note>original: "talagoras"; a species of small bird</note>, he took their bows away and broke them. He then made much larger bows than before and added points to their arrows; soon, they were able to shoot doves. In this way, they became skilled at shooting all kinds of birds. Next, he carved clubs for them, which they used to kill rats. He eventually took those away and broke them as well. Finally, when they had grown into young men, he made clubs for them once more. For one, he carved a club shaped like an *oi utu* <note>original: "oi utu"; the fruit of the *Barringtonia* tree, which is large, fibrous, and has four distinct corners</note>, and for the other, a simple *tarara* <note>original: "tarara"; a type of club featuring a ring and a spike</note>.

Qatu raised the twins until they were quite large. One day, he told them about <term>Taso</term> <note>original: "Taso"; the legendary cannibal giant</note>, warning them not to wander carelessly or go near Taso's territory without a good reason, because Taso had killed their mother and was a man-eater. After considering this, the twins placed a <term>taboo</term> <note>original: "taboo"; here used as a supernatural omen or 'life-token'</note> upon a bunch of bananas belonging to them. They said to their uncle Qatu, "If you go into the garden and see our bunch of bananas beginning to ripen at the top and ripening downwards toward the end, then Taso has killed us. But if you see that it has begun to ripen at the bottom and is ripening upwards, then we have killed him." Their uncle then turned away and went his own way, while the twins set off to take Taso by surprise.

They arrived at Taso's home but did not find him there, for he had gone down to the beach to sharpen his teeth. <note>A tooth of Taso is still to be seen at Maewo.</note> The twins asked Taso’s mother, "Where has Taso gone? We have come here to see him." Taso’s mother invited them to come up and sit by the *gamal* <note>original: "gamal"; a Melanesian men's clubhouse</note> to wait for him. They went up to the *gamal* and sat there. At that time, short, round yams had been harvested and a fire was burning in the *gamal*. The twins heated the yams and pulled out the stones that lined the ovens, placing them on the fire so they could pelt Taso with them. There were two fireplaces in the *gamal*, one at each end. 

Taso's mother came down from the house, lay on the ground, and sang a song, calling down to Taso on the beach. This is the song: "Taso! Come up and eat the dead man, eat one!" <note>original: "Taso! surovaro ganga tamate, a ganga i tuara"</note>

<summary>Qatu trains the twins as hunters before they set out to find the giant Taso, leaving behind a ripening banana bunch as a supernatural omen of their success or failure.</summary>

"*Gaku i tuara*, Taso!" <note>original: "gaku i tuara"; a ritual chant or call associated with the giant</note> (Taso! Look out for your dead man to eat, one for you, one for me. Taso!) Taso was sitting on the beach and heard his mother calling to him, so he got up and came back along the path. As he came, he turned his head from side to side and struck the trees, and they came down with a crash <note>This demonstrates the giant's immense size and destructive strength</note>. 

But the twins had prepared for their attack on Taso with red-hot stones and cooked yams. They stood with their feet firmly planted and waited for him inside the <term>gamal</term> <note>original: "gamal"; a large communal clubhouse used by men for social and ritual purposes</note>, one at one end and the other at the far end. Then they heard Taso arrive and ask his mother, "What is it, mother?" 

And she said, "What is it but dead men for us to eat, sitting right there in the <term>gamal</term>?" 

So Taso went up to the <term>gamal</term>, and as he stepped over the rail at the door, one of the twins took up a red-hot stone and threw it at him, hitting him. When he ran down to the other end of the building, the other twin threw at him and hit him as well. Taso cried out, "It is in vain that you throw at me! I will eat you both today." 

As he ran to one end of the <term>gamal</term>, one of the twins threw at him; as he ran to the other end, the other twin threw. They continued to attack him until his bones shook within him, and he lay down, only groaning. Then the twins leaped upon him and beat him to death with their clubs. Next, they went down to the house and dragged out the old woman, Taso's mother, and clubbed her; they clubbed them both to death. They set fire to the houses over the bodies and began their journey home. 

Meanwhile, Qatu and Motari <note>Qatu is a legendary hero and creator figure in Melanesian mythology; Motari is often his companion or younger brother</note> were standing in the garden listening to the popping of the bamboo rafters as they burned, wondering what was happening over there: "Those two have probably come across Taso and he is killing them." 

Qatu started off and met the twins on his way, and they told him that they had killed Taso. He said to them, "I forbade you to go there; you have disobeyed me, and he very nearly ate you." So the matter was finished; they killed Taso and avenged their mother, whom Taso had murdered.

<summary>The twins successfully ambush and kill the cannibal giant Taso and his mother using red-hot stones and clubs, finally avenging their mother's death despite Qatu's warnings.</summary>

### 11. ABOUT BETAWERAI A SNAKE. AURORA.

The story began in this way: a woman and her child went to harvest pandanus leaves to weave mats. The boy saw a young snake on the stalk of a leaf and begged his mother to let him have it because he wanted it, but his mother forbade him from taking it. However, he insisted that he wanted it, so he took hold of the little red snake and put it in the hollow trunk of a tree called an <term>ugara</term> <note>A local species of tree</note>. He put it into the hollow and fed it rats, birds, black lizards, or pork, and that snake grew extremely large. One day, after he killed a pig, he went to give the snake some meat, but the snake snatched the pig from him and ate the boy as well. Then it crawled out of the hollow tree, entered the village, and ate all the people in the place.

But there was one pregnant woman who survived. She dug a pit, took a thin flat stone and laid it over the opening, and stayed inside it. There she gave birth to her children, who were twins, and the three of them remained in that pit in the ground. Meanwhile, the snake finished eating all the people and then went to make its home in a banyan tree. It gave birth to a great many young ones, with two being the leaders among them. The name of one of these was Betawerai; this one was not able to move about but stayed always on a branch of the banyan. We call the branch of a large tree like a banyan a <term>tawerai</term> <note>original: "tawerai"; literally 'the flat of the hand,' describing the shape of the large, flat branches</note>, and the snake was named after that: Betawerai, meaning "At the branch." 

The other leader used to travel very far away, searching diligently for men or pigs to eat, and his name was Walolo. One day, the two children of the woman who lived in the ground asked their mother to make them bows and arrows. Afterward, they said they would go into the village to find that snake, shoot it, and kill it. But when they had gone and seen the banyan tree from a distance where Betawerai and Walolo lived, they saw that the branches, the little twigs, and the leaves were covered with nothing but snakes...

"Turn and come to Betawerai, the wind is North-west, it blows against my face. Walolo! Walolo! come here! Walolo! Walolo! come here!" <note>original: *Risurisu vano, Betawerai, a lang togalau, ti uvi goro nanagoku. Walolo! Walolo! go vano mai! Walolo! Walolo! go vano mai!*</note>

They say that Walolo heard him singing and thought that something had happened. He came spinning end over end like a thrown stick, and as he drew near, he heard plainly that it was Betawerai's voice, and he thought that there was surely a man there to eat. Therefore, he came in great haste, spinning toward those two. One of the boys shot him with an arrow, and then the other shot, and both hit him. He tried to rush upon them, but one shot and the other shot, and both hit him again. They continued shooting like this until they shot him to death. Then they went after Betawerai, pulled him down to the ground, and killed him as well. 

When they had killed the snakes in this way, they heaped them up at the roots of the banyan tree and brought plenty of wood to burn them. The great heap of snakes was burned up as a sign that the devouring snake was destroyed. Then the three of them—the two boys and their mother—returned to their village and lived there.

### 12. THE STORY OF BASI AND DOVAOWARI. AURORA.

There was a girl named Basi from the village of Dama, and her mother, who was a snake, lived in a cave there. There was also a young man living at Tanoriki named Dovaowari. One day, Basi and another girl (who I suppose was her sister) went down to the beach to collect salt water <note>To "dip" or collect salt water was a common way to obtain salt for seasoning food</note>. Dovaowari also went down to bathe in the sea, but on a different part of the beach. You know our customs, that...

...we always like to style our hair to make it white and curly—in ringlets, like the style you see among the Opa people <note>original: Opa; today known as Ambae, an island in Vanuatu where people historically used lime to bleach and style their hair</note>. 

Two girls stood looking across toward another part of the beach and saw a man bathing. He was washing his hair until it was extremely white. They said, "Let us go and see who that is bathing." They went and saw that it was Dovaowari. He asked them what they were looking for, and they replied that they had seen him from a distance and had come to get a closer look at him. 

Basi said to the other girl, "Go home to our mother and tell her that I am following Dovaowari." Dovaowari tried in vain to forbid her from following him, saying that he was poor and had no money, no property, and no garden. But she argued with him, insisting that she would certainly go with him. So he said, "Well, we will go together." 

Then the other girl went back to their mother—the Snake—and Basi followed Dovaowari to be his wife, and so they were married. However, Basi kept visiting her mother at Dama <note>Dama: A village or district on the island of Maewo</note>, which was a long way off. Dovao <note>Dovao: A shortened version of the name Dovaowari</note> was annoyed by this, and he told Basi to go and ask her mother to move to their village so they could all live together. 

Basi replied, "Mother cannot come here to this place." Yet she went and pleaded with her, and the mother eventually agreed that the move would be possible. But the main thing the mother thought about was how she would manage, because she was a very long and large snake; if a small house were built for her, it would not be enough. She considered this and said to Basi, "Go and tell my son-in-law to build me a house, and let there be ten chambers <note>chambers: rooms or partitioned sections within a longhouse</note> in it." 

Dovao did not yet know the truth <note>Dovao was unaware that his mother-in-law was actually a giant snake</note>. When he heard about the house with ten chambers, he was astonished and thought to himself, "What is this for?" When the house was finished, Basi brought the news, saying, "Your house is finished." But she had warned them beforehand, "I shall arrive in the night; if my son-in-law hears anything, do not let him take any notice of it." 

So, in the middle of the night, they heard an earthquake, thunder, and a massive rumbling, as if the entire world were coming to an end;

When she reached that place, her tail entered first and coiled itself in the first chamber, and then in the second, until all those rooms were filled with the giant snake. Her head, which was that of a woman, lay opposite the door, even though the entire house was full of the snake's body. In the morning, the people came to see this person and saw that it was a snake with a human head. Whenever Dovao and Basi went anywhere and returned, Basi would go to her mother, that snake, and rub noses with her <note>original: "rub her nose upon her"; a traditional Melanesian greeting</note> and lie close to her; but her husband did not like that sort of thing. 

For that reason (and because the snake devoured the pigs and chickens that came near the door), when there was a festival at another village some distance away, Dovao told some of the people that he and his wife were going to the dance, and while they were away, they were to set fire to the house and burn it down so as to incinerate the snake with it. 

But the snake knew this. She called Basi and told her that they were going to set her on fire and burn her that night. "When you are standing at the festival," she said, "if you see sparks, run quickly back to me." And so it happened; while Basi was dancing, she saw sparks flying and ran back quickly. She leaped into the fire, and both mother and daughter were burned to death. 

A long time later, the charred liver was found and still remains—the liver of Basi and of her mother. I have seen a bone from them in the possession of some wealthy people; they say there is *mana* <term>spiritual or magical power</term> in it for attracting pigs and for illicit encounters with women when men blacken the area under their eyes with it.¹

The bamboo was placed by the fireplace, and there it stayed. After many days, when Tari was going out to work, he told his wife to cook some food for him, and she went to prepare it. When he heard this, he told her to sit and watch who was doing it. 

She sat by the side wall of the house and saw Deitari (Tari’s blood) <note>Deitari means "Tari's blood"; the boy was miraculously born from his father's blood</note> creep out of the bamboo vessel which Tari had set aside. She saw that he was exceptionally handsome, and she hid him. When Tari came in from work, he asked his wife, "Haven’t you seen him?" 

She replied, "What was that you put by the fireplace?" 

"I didn't put anything there," he said. 

But his wife said, "That is not true; you put something small there in a bamboo." 

Then he remembered his blood and said to his wife, "My blood was in that bamboo." 

His wife said, "I saw him come out of that bamboo you put there." 

So she brought the boy out, and Tari rejoiced greatly to see him. One day, as they were living together, the boys of the village—and Deitari with them—went to bathe in the stream and sing songs. There was a man called Taepupuliti, and they say he changed himself into a fish, devoured the boy who had come out of the bamboo, and went off with him to a different country. 

Tari sent every kind of fish and bird to search for Deitari. He found a little fish that was extremely thin, and this fish and Deitari’s father eventually found the boy hidden in the back of Taepupuliti’s house. The two men, Tari and Taepupuliti, sat down to drink *kara* <note>original: "kara"; likely *kava*, a traditional sedative beverage made from the roots of the *Piper methysticum* plant</note>. The father of the one who had been devoured let the liquor fall from his mouth as he drank so that the *kara* did not affect him; but as for the man who had eaten the child, the drink affected him very much <note>meaning he became heavily intoxicated or sedated</note>, and the father was able to carry his son away again.

...into it and turned into a fish. Whenever he wanted to eat a human, he would enter that fish and travel to Opa or Raga <note>modern: Aoba (Ambae) and Pentecost Islands in Vanuatu</note>.

One day, while the father was away in his garden, his son remained in the village. The father had strictly forbidden the boy from entering the inner part of the house. However, while his father was gone and he was left alone with his mother in the village, the boy began playing by himself. He decided to go and see exactly what it was that his father had forbidden him from seeing. 

He went to the far end of the house and discovered the hollow figure of the fish lying there. He climbed inside it. In this magic, a kingfisher <note>A bird often associated with omens in Melanesian folklore</note> flies down as a signal whenever someone enters the fish figure. There was an old woman lying in the house, and when she heard the kingfisher, she followed the ritual of breaking a stick; this act caused the image to go into the sea. 

When the boy climbed into the fish figure and the kingfisher landed on the roof, the old woman heard it and broke a piece of firewood. Immediately, the fish figure—with the boy still inside—went down into the sea and crossed over to Opa. 

The father, still in his garden, heard a noise and ran back as fast as he could, but he found that the fish had already departed. To follow him, the father wove together the fiber from a coconut <note>original: "the stuff that is on a cocoa-nut"</note> into a rough shape. He placed it on his chest and entered the sea to search for his son. 

He eventually found the boy at Opa. He discovered that the people of Opa had very nearly shot the boy. The father rescued him and brought him home. As they were returning, they saw a man sitting in a breadfruit tree. The father said to his son, "Go and eat him." 

The son replied, "How can I go, father? He is on dry land." 

His father hit him hard and said, "Go! You are the one who wants to eat a man." 

Then the boy went, and as he moved toward the shore, the sea rose up with him onto the land. He was carried right up into the breadfruit tree, where he reached the man and swallowed him. They returned to the back part of the house and placed the man there, for he was not yet dead. 

When they left him at the far end of the house, the man moved around and saw the sea, the sharks, and the fishes with their mouths open, waiting to devour him. He remained there until he died.

### 15. THE WOMAN AND THE GHOST. AURORA <note>modern: Maewo Island, Vanuatu</note>.

This is a story about a woman who lost her husband and went in search of him, carrying her child with her. A ghost met the woman while she was carrying the child on her hip, and the woman mistakenly thought the ghost was her husband. 

The three of them went down to the beach to fish with torches <note>original: "burn for fish"</note>. The ghost said to the woman, "You go and fish with the torch, and I will look after our child." 

When the woman went off with the torch, the ghost ate one of the child's fingers. Its mother asked him what was hurting the child, and the ghost replied, "Nothing; a mosquito bit it." After he had spoken, the child stopped crying; the woman soon discovered that it was a ghost because he had eaten the child entirely. 

She then knew for certain that it was a ghost. She had set up coconut branches along the shore as decoys. When the ghost had finished eating the child, he went to eat the mother; as he ran along to catch her, he ate the branches she had set up, thinking the branches were the woman. 

The woman ran away quickly and climbed into a pandanus tree <note>A palm-like tree with prop roots and edible fruit common in the Pacific</note>. When the ghost tried to climb up to eat her, the woman pelted him with the fruits to knock him down. She continued to do this until dawn; when it was light, she saw that the ghost turned into a hermit crab.

---

### 16. A STORY ABOUT TAGARO THE LITTLE. LEPERS' ISLAND <note>modern: Ambae Island, Vanuatu</note>.

They say that Tagaro went to a part of the island called Vagimbangga to pay for a pig, and on his return, the sun set while he was still in the forest. He was hungry, for he had nothing at all to eat. 

Beside the path, they say there was a single *gaviga* tree <note>The Malay apple or mountain apple (*Syzygium malaccense*), which produces a red, pear-shaped fruit</note> with many branches and ripe fruit on it. He climbed up to eat and to sleep for a while in that tree. In his hand, he carried his conch-shell trumpet to blow as he went along the path. 

In the middle of the night, when he had finished eating, he climbed further up to the top of that *gaviga* tree to sleep and rest there. Just as he began to fall asleep, he heard the voices...

<summary>This page contains two Melanesian folk tales: one from Aurora about a woman who outwits a child-eating ghost, and the beginning of a story from Ambae about the hero Tagaro the Little.</summary>
<keywords>folklore, Tagaro, Aurora Island, Maewo, Lepers' Island, Ambae, ghosts, Melanesian mythology, gaviga tree, pandanus</keywords>

--- Page 443 ---
<meta>This page continues the legend of Tagaro the Little from Leper's Island (Ambae), who had gone to pay a visit and fallen asleep in a tree.</meta>

<page-num>410</page-num>
<header>Stories. [CH. XIX.</header>

...of a number of people coming along underneath the *gaviga*-tree <note>The Malay apple tree (*Syzygium malaccense*), which produces edible red fruit</note>. And he woke up thinking that it was probably his brothers looking for him, but it was not so; these were different persons. These were Mera-mbuto and his brothers coming along, and they climbed up the *gaviga*-tree themselves. 

Tagaro-mbiti sat perfectly still so they would not see him, and he heard one of them say, "This is my branch" <note>original: *Ineu ranganggu ngaha*</note>, and another cried, "This is my branch," and they all said the same. Then Mera-mbuto said, "This is my branch at the top" <note>original: *Ineu ranganggu ngaha lo vuhungegi*</note>; and he said this with a loud voice. 

Mera-mbuto climbed straight up to the top of that *gaviga*-tree, and there he found Tagaro-mbiti. Then Mera-mbuto said, "Who are you?" 

And he replied, "I am Tagaro-mbiti." 

Now, they say that this Mera-mbuto and his brothers lived in a cave. Mera-mbuto asked Tagaro again, "What is that in your hand?" 

And he said, "The voice of you and me, to be sure" <note>He is referring to a conch shell trumpet</note>. 

Mera-mbuto begged him to speak into that conch so that he might hear it; but Tagaro said, "Wait a bit until I go back to my dwelling place. When I get there, you will hear me whistle; then you shall speak with the voice of us two so that I may hear it for myself." 

Mera-mbuto made haste down from the tree, and his brothers asked, "Are we to come too?" 

"No," he said, "I am only going to relieve myself <note>original: "get rid of a mess"</note> and then I shall come back." 

In this way he deceived them. When he reached his dwelling, the cave, he whistled for Tagaro to hear, so that Tagaro would blow the conch. Tagaro heard Mera-mbuto whistle, and he put forth all his strength to blow the conch hard. As he blew, Mera-mbuto’s brothers every one fell from the tree; Mera-mbuto himself was delighted and jumped high again and again in his cave. His head struck against the rock, and the rock stuck fast into his head, and there he died. 

His brothers who had fallen down also died, every one of them; for that reason, people say that bushes grew up in the place where Mera-mbuto’s brothers fell. When it was light, Tagaro-mbiti returned to his home.

<summary>Tagaro the Little tricks the foolish Mera-mbuto and his brothers by using a conch shell, leading to their accidental deaths and the growth of wild bushes where they fell.</summary>
<keywords>Tagaro-mbiti, Mera-mbuto, Ambae Island, Melanesian mythology, folktale, conch shell, Malay apple tree, origin story</keywords>

--- Page 444 ---
<meta>This page continues the folk tales from Lepers’ Island (Ambae), specifically following the interaction between the clever Tagaro and the foolish Mera-mbuto.</meta>

<page-num>411</page-num>
<header>xix.] Mera-mbuto and Tagaro.</header>

### 17. About Mera-mbuto and Tagaro. Lepers' Island <note>Now known as Ambae Island in Vanuatu; the name "Lepers' Island" was given by Captain Cook due to a misunderstanding of a skin condition common among the inhabitants.</note>.

Mera-mbuto prepared food for himself and then invited Tagaro to come so that they might eat together. So Tagaro came to him in his house, but Mera-mbuto's food was exceedingly bad. As they ate, Tagaro did not actually eat any of it; instead, he wrapped the food up to trick Mera-mbuto and went and threw it away, then returned to his own house. 

Afterward, Tagaro sent for him, saying, "Mera-mbuto, come here to my house." Mera-mbuto came, and the two of them ate. The food was excellent, and Mera-mbuto liked Tagaro's food very much, realizing that he had made his own very poorly. So Mera-mbuto wondered silently, "What kind of thing is this that we two are eating?" He asked Tagaro, and Tagaro told him, "I have grated up my barrow pig <term>barrow pig</term> <note>A barrow pig is a male pig that was castrated before reaching sexual maturity.</note>." So Mera-mbuto went and grated up his own barrow pig, and in due course, the two of them ate it. 

After this, Tagaro invited Mera-mbuto to eat with him in return at his house. Again, Mera-mbuto asked him, "What food is this we are eating?" Tagaro was tired of being asked and decided to deceive Mera-mbuto, saying to him, "It is my mother; I cooked her in the oven." So Mera-mbuto went home and actually cooked his own mother in the oven. 

After this, Tagaro said to him, "Light a fire over me." So Mera-mbuto came, tied up the door of Tagaro's house, bound it very tight, and set fire to the house. Then Tagaro cried out; Mera-mbuto said to him, "Don’t cry! You tricked me before, and now you are about to die for it." He thought that Tagaro was dead, but he was not; Tagaro had dug a hole and stayed safely inside it. 

In the morning, thinking Tagaro was dead, Mera-mbuto came by, but Tagaro had been sitting there waiting for him for a long time. So Mera-mbuto asked him, "Are you still sitting here like this?" Tagaro said, "Yes." 

Then Mera-mbuto said to him, "It is my turn now; tonight, you set fire to my house." So Tagaro set fire to his house, and the fire consumed him.

<summary>This page recounts a traditional folk tale from Ambae (Lepers' Island) where the clever Tagaro repeatedly tricks the foolish Mera-mbuto into harming himself, eventually leading to Mera-mbuto's death in a fire.</summary>
<keywords>Mera-mbuto, Tagaro, Lepers' Island, Ambae, Vanuatu, barrow pig, trickster, folk tales, mythology</keywords>
